Every dossier, in reading order, as one continuous document — built for printing, saving, or reading straight through.

Download the PDF — 2363 pages, 3 MB   Download the EPUB — 1013 parts, 1514 KB

A5, set for reading rather than for screen: no images, no navigation, one part per page-opening, every source list kept. The EPUB is the same 1013 parts as reflowable text for a reader; both are generated from this page.

Each part keeps its own source list. Claims are quoted and attributed; where a claim has been tested, the test is linked alongside it. Inclusion is not endorsement. Use your browser’s Print command for a paper copy — the layout switches to black on white automatically.

The Larger Globe

Live debate — marginal

People who say the Earth is larger than we are told usually mean one of three things. They may mean the planet is physically growing — the expanding Earth. They may mean the map is deliberately truncated, with whole continents hidden past the ice. Or they may mean we are on the inside of a sphere, looking at a concave shell — the “cell Earth”.

All three appear below, in the order they were proposed, with the people who proposed them named.

1. The Expanding Earth (the real scientific heresy)

This is the only one of the three that was ever a serious scientific hypothesis, argued in journals by professional geologists for most of the twentieth century. Its founding observation is the one everybody now accepts: Africa and South America fit together like torn paper.

  • 1888

    Nikolai Yarkovsky publishes a book linking expansion to gravity and chemistry — one of the earliest mechanical attempts.

  • 1912

    Alfred Wegener proposes continental drift. The fit of the continents is now on the table, and nobody has a mechanism.

  • 1927–1940

    A German-language wave: Lindemann (1927), Bogolepow (1930), Hilgenberg (1933), Keindl (1940). Hilgenberg is generally credited with the first globe-assembly of the continents on a sphere roughly two-thirds the modern diameter.

  • 1956–1969

    The English-language second wave: Egyed, Carey, Heezen, Barnett, Brösske, Neyman, Creer, Dearnley, Jordan, Steiner, Meservey. Australian geologist S. Warren Carey becomes its most prominent voice.

  • 2007–present

    James Maxlow’s quantitative expansion model, and Giancarlo Scalera’s work at the Italian national institute of geophysics, keep a slow-expansion version alive.

What they actually argue

The core claim is simple: new ocean crust is created at the mid-ocean ridges (nobody disputes this), but it is not destroyed at the trenches in equal measure, so the planet’s volume must increase. In Carey’s version, subduction is largely a myth. In the softer “slow expansion” version, some subduction is allowed but not enough to balance the ridges.

Their strongest point is a real one: the ocean floor is geologically young everywhere. None of it predates the Mesozoic. In a constant-size Earth you must destroy all of it; in an expanding Earth you can simply have made it.

“A profound consequence of seafloor spreading is that new crust was, and is now, being continually created along the oceanic ridges. This idea found great favor with some scientists who claimed that the shifting of the continents can be simply explained by a large increase in size of the Earth since its formation. However, this so-called ‘expanding Earth’ hypothesis was unsatisfactory because its supporters could offer no convincing geologic mechanism to produce such a huge, sudden expansion.” USGS, This Dynamic Earth

The two versions, and the numbers

A 2016 comment in the journal History of Geo- and Space Sciences splits the school in two: slow expansion at roughly 0.5 mm per year of radius increase since formation, and fast expansion at roughly 5 mm per year since the Triassic. The same paper argues that space geodesy, gravimetry and seismology leave room for 0.1–0.4 mm/yr today — and calls the theory’s obituary premature.

That is the strongest surviving version of the case, and it is worth stating plainly: it is a fraction of a millimetre per year, and it is contested.

What the evidence says

Plate tectonics won because it supplied a mechanism that works: Harry Hess and Robert Dietz’s seafloor spreading, with ocean crust descending at trenches. The key question USGS poses — how can crust be added at ridges without the planet growing? — is answered by subduction, and subduction is now imaged directly by mantle tomography.

On the measurement side, a NASA-led team publishing in Geophysical Research Letters in 2011 used space-geodetic data and found an average radius change of 0.004 inches (0.1 mm) per year — “statistically insignificant”. The Pacific Northwest Seismic Network summarised it as a change of less than a millimetre every five years, consistent with no change at all.

And the historiography has turned: a 2014 paper in the same journal as the 2016 defence is titled, flatly, “The Earth expansion theory and its transition from scientific hypothesis to pseudoscientific belief”, arguing that expansionists survived plate tectonics by rejecting contrary evidence and waiting for a physics revolution that never came.

2. The Earth is far bigger than admitted

This is the version with no paper trail. It typically arrives as a video: the known continents are said to occupy only a fraction of a much larger plane, with the rest hidden behind an Antarctic ice boundary or edited out of satellite composites.

It has no named originator, no published model and no measurement, which is exactly why it cannot be tested — the missing land is defined as unreachable. Its function is structural: it exists to explain why nobody has seen the rest of the world. See Beyond the Ice Wall.

3. The Concave Earth — we are inside the sphere

The most philosophically aggressive version. The planet is a hollow shell and we live on its inner surface, with the universe compressed into a small bright core at the centre, which we mistake for a distant sun and stars.

Its American prophet was Cyrus Reed Teed, a Utica physician who took the name Koresh. After an 1869 electrical experiment — he claimed to have been knocked unconscious and woke with the cellular cosmogony revealed — he founded the Koreshan Unity, which in 1894 established a colony at Estero, Florida. His 1898 book with Ulysses Grant Morrow, The Cellular Cosmogony, laid out the geometry.

Morrow then did something unusual for this literature: he built an instrument. The “rectilineator” was a graduated straight-edge used along the beach to measure whether the water surface curved up or down over distance. The Koreshans reported a concave result. The National Center for Science Education’s history of the episode walks through where the experiment went wrong — the same class of error that sank the Bedford Level flat-Earth measurement: a short baseline, unaccounted refraction, and a target that could not be levelled precisely enough.

The colony survived until 1961; its grounds are now a Florida state park. The concave model survives online, largely because it elegantly explains why rockets “come back” and why nobody has photographed an edge.

Why the concave model fails

It has to invert every line of sight and every gravitational measurement at once, and it predicts a horizon that curves upward and objects that vanish from the bottom first — both of which are directly checkable with a telescope, a boat and a lake. It also makes the Moon and planets interior objects whose phases and parallax would not match observation. The 19th-century test was a good instinct; the instrument was simply not precise enough to detect a curvature of a few centimetres over a few kilometres.

How this connects to the rest of the archive

  • Hollow Earth shares the shell geometry but keeps us on the outside — see Hollow Earth.
  • Inner sun is the standard light source for both the hollow and concave models.
  • Giant fauna — the claim that expansion explains giant insects and dinosaurs — is a recurring argument in the expansionist literature and reappears in Dragons & Dinosaurs.
  • The ice wall is where the “bigger Earth” version hides its extra land.

Flat Earth & the Firmament

Debunked

Flat Earth is the oldest cosmology in the archive and the only one with a continuously operating institution. It also has the most clearly defined internal structure, which makes it the best place to learn how these systems work: every anomaly has a patch, and the patches are invented on demand.

What the modern model actually claims

There is no single flat-Earth model. Britannica’s survey identifies the common form — a circular disc, North Pole at the centre, a wall of ice at the edges — and then two competing mechanical variants:

  • The “US model” — the Sun and Moon are small objects, roughly 50 km across, circling about 5,500 km above the disc, with the stars fixed to a rotating dome above them. Day and night come from the Sun acting like a spotlight.
  • The “UK model” — no gravity at all; the disc accelerates upward at 9.8 m/s², and what we call falling is the floor rising to meet us.

Physics World’s 2020 survey of the movement notes that many adherents also place the whole disc and its atmosphere inside a hemispherical “snow globe” from which nothing can fall off the edge — which resolves the obvious objection that we would see the rim.

Their evidence, in their own words

The Flat Earth Society’s own FAQ lists the standard four:

“The horizon always rises to meet eye level — which is impossible on a ball earth. The surfaces of bodies of water has been shown to be level. If the Earth was a Globe, this would not be the case. There is no visible curvature to the horizon even from airplanes. We don’t even have a full shot of the Earth rotating from space!” The Flat Earth Society, FAQ

Each is answerable in a sentence, and the answers have been published for two centuries. The horizon rises to eye level because the eye is only a few metres above a sphere 12,742 km across; at 10 km altitude the true horizon drop is about 3.2°, small but measurable. Water is level locally — a plumb line is perpendicular to the surface at every point, which on a sphere means every point has its own “level”. And full-disc rotating imagery exists from geostationary weather satellites; the 2015 DSCOVR “EPIC” camera returns a full sunlit disc from a million miles out.

Where the movement came from

The modern revival is usually dated to Samuel Birley Rowbotham, writing as “Parallax”, and his 1849 pamphlet expanded into Zetetic Astronomy. His signature demonstration was the Bedford Level experiment: place markers at equal height at either end of a six-mile straight canal, view them through a telescope, and if both appear level, the water is flat.

It worked — and it was quoted as proof for over thirty years. The flaw was the atmosphere: light bends over a long, warm, still water surface, lifting the distant marker back into view. Alfred Russel Wallace eventually repeated the experiment with a calibrated sight and won a libel case over the resulting dispute. The Conversation’s history of the episode is the clearest short account.

The firmament

The dome is the theological layer. In the King James Bible, Genesis 1:6–8 has God make a rāqîa‘ to divide the waters, and the Authorised Version translates it “firmament” — a word that in English implies something solid. Hebrew scholarship is close to unanimous that rāqîa‘ means an expanse or spreading-out, not a crystal vault, and the same root is used for the expanse of the sky.

This produces an unusual split. Young-Earth creationist organisations — hardly friendly witnesses to mainstream science — have published detailed refutations of flat Earth, arguing that the Hebrew does not support a solid dome and that verses about the “circle of the earth” (khûg, meaning roundness) cannot be reduced to a two-dimensional disc. The Adventist Biblical Research Institute reaches the same conclusion independently.

What the evidence says

Gravity is the fatal problem. A disc has a centre of mass at its middle, so gravity would pull everything toward that point, not straight down. James Davis of Columbia’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory puts it simply: on a disc, water would flow to the centre and trees would grow at an angle. There is no way to derive the observed 9.8 m/s² everywhere from a thin disc.

The geometry is checkable with a phone. Eratosthenes’ shadow measurement, the differing altitude of Polaris with latitude, the southern sky’s rotation about a different pole, the 24-hour sun of the Antarctic summer, and the existence of time zones all follow from a sphere and contradict a spotlight sun over a disc.

Antarctica is a continent, not a rim. Reuters and USA Today have both fact-checked the ice-wall claim with satellite imagery, circumnavigation records and the simple fact that people live and work there year-round. The most-shared “flat Earth map” with concentric ice rings has been traced to an art-forum illustration.

Why it persists anyway

Physics World’s report frames it as a trust problem rather than a geometry problem: the model’s appeal is that it makes the reader the final authority and the institution the liar. Every failed prediction can be reassigned to “the conspiracy” — which makes the belief unfalsifiable, and therefore not a scientific claim at all.

That structure is worth carrying into the rest of the archive. It is the same move that keeps the inner sun lit and the extra continents hidden.

Hollow Earth & the Inner Sun

Fringe claim

Hollow Earth is the most generative theory in this archive. It has a genuine scientific origin, a documented political near-miss, a real utopian colony, and a fictional literature that has been mistaken for testimony for eighty years. Almost every other hidden-world claim borrows a piece of it.

The scientific origin: Edmond Halley, 1692

The theory begins with a problem in navigation. Compasses did not point consistently north; the deviation varied by location and over time. Halley — the comet Halley — collected magnetic readings across the Atlantic and concluded that the poles themselves were drifting.

His explanation, read to the Royal Society in a series of papers from 1681 and published in 1692, was that the Earth is a hollow shell containing inner spheres, each rotating at a different rate, with a luminous atmosphere between them. The multiple rotating layers would produce the observed drift. He did not propose openings at the poles; that was added a century later.

The Library of Congress’s research guide on hollow-Earth literature and Discover magazine’s three-century history both trace the line from Halley forward. What is notable is that Halley’s motive was data: a wobbling compass needed an explanation, and a nested rotating Earth was, at the time, a candidate.

Symmes and the holes

On 10 April 1818, a War of 1812 veteran and trader named John Cleves Symmes Jr. circulated a broadsheet now known as Circular No. 1:

“I declare that the earth is hollow and habitable within; containing a number of solid concentric spheres, one within the other, and that it is open at the poles twelve or sixteen degrees. I pledge my life in support of this truth, and am ready to explore the hollow, if the world will support and aid me in my undertaking.” John Cleves Symmes Jr., 1818 — quoted by HISTORY

His elaboration is where the imagery comes from. The openings are thousands of miles across and curve so gently that a ship could sail in without noticing. Inside is “a warm and rich land, stocked with thrifty vegetables and animals if not men.” The auroras are reflections of the inner light. Arctic animals that vanish in winter have gone inside to escape the cold.

Symmes spent a decade lobbying for an expedition. He never got one, but his chief publicist, Jeremiah Reynolds, did — Congress funded the United States Exploring Expedition of 1838–1842, the first American scientific voyage to the Antarctic, though by then the hollow-Earth rationale had been dropped. Academic histories treat Symmes as an accidental founder of American polar exploration.

He also founded a genre. Symzonia: A Voyage of Discovery (1820) was the first hollow-Earth novel; Poe’s Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym and Verne’s Journey to the Centre of the Earth followed.

Koreshanity and the inside-out Earth

See The Larger Globe for Cyrus Teed’s concave version — the same shell, with humanity on the inside. Teed’s Koreshan Unity colony at Estero, Florida, built a real instrument to test it, which is more than most of this literature manages.

The modern canon: 800 miles of rock, 1,400 miles of hole

Twentieth-century hollow-Earth belief is largely downstream of Raymond Bernard’s The Hollow Earth (1979). The University of Alaska Fairbanks’ Geophysical Institute summarised its contents:

  • The shell is about 800 miles thick.
  • Polar openings are about 1,400 miles across, with edges curving smoothly from the outer surface to the inner.
  • A traveller could walk or sail over the lip “like an ant crawling over the lip of a coffee mug” without noticing.
  • Pilots never see the holes because compasses mislead them into believing they crossed the pole; they actually follow the hole’s “magnetic rim”.
  • The proof text is a remark attributed to Admiral Richard E. Byrd: “I’d like to see that land beyond the Pole. That area beyond the Pole is the Great Unknown.”

The Byrd problem

Byrd is the load-bearing witness, and the archive holding his papers is unambiguous. The Byrd Polar and Climate Research Center at Ohio State University states that the Papers of Admiral Byrd contain no evidence supporting the claim that he flew into a polar opening.

What does exist is The Missing Diary of Admiral Richard E. Byrd, a short text that surfaced decades after his death and describes an inner civilization with advanced technology. Researchers tracing its provenance place it alongside Bernard’s book as modern occult fiction rather than an expedition record. Byrd’s real flights, including Operation Highjump, are documented in contemporaneous newsreels and the documentary The Secret Land.

The inner sun

The interior needs light, so the model supplies a small central sun — sometimes a glowing core, sometimes a “soft, diffused” illumination. In Symmes it is a inner luminary reflected as the auroras; in Bernard it is a central sphere.

This is the weakest joint in the whole structure, and the reason is thermodynamic. A body radiating enough light to support a forested interior for millions of years needs a power source, and no candidate survives inspection: a small star would have to be absurdly dense to sustain fusion, and a chemical or radioactive source would exhaust itself. The heat would also have to escape somewhere, and the shell above it would conduct it to the surface — producing a measurable geothermal signature that does not exist.

What the seismic data says

Earthquake waves map the interior. When a quake happens, P and S waves travel through the planet and are recorded worldwide. S waves cannot pass through liquid, and both P and S are refracted by density changes — producing the famous “shadow zone” where no direct waves arrive. The pattern of arrivals matches a solid inner core, a liquid outer core, a mantle and a thin crust. A hollow shell would produce a completely different pattern: waves would ring around the shell and the shadow zone would not exist.

Density is measured independently. The planet’s mass is known from satellite orbits and its volume from geodesy. The resulting mean density, about 5.5 g/cm³, is far too high for a hollow body of crustal rock. A hollow Earth would have to be made of something denser than anything in the crust, in a shell 800 miles thick — and that material would have to be invisible to seismology.

The poles have been visited. There are permanently staffed research stations at the South Pole, aircraft cross the Arctic routinely, and satellite radar altimetry maps the polar ice to the metre. A 1,400-mile hole would be the most photographed feature on the planet.

What it feeds

  • The ice wall / world beyond — the polar opening is the doorway past the rim. See Beyond the Ice Wall.
  • Tartarus and the underworld — the shell’s interior is the modern home of the classical pit. See Tartarus.
  • Hidden fauna — mammoths, dinosaurs, “advanced civilizations” and the Greys all get relocated inside. See Cryptids and Dragons.
  • Underwater worlds — a hollow shell implies interior oceans. See Underwater Worlds.

Beyond the Ice Wall

Debunked

“The world beyond the ice wall” is what happens when two older theories are joined. From flat Earth it takes the rim: Antarctica as a circular wall enclosing the known continents. From hollow Earth it takes the doorway: the wall is not an edge but a gate, with more land behind it.

Neither half is new. The novelty is the composite, which spread through short-form video after roughly 2020 and now functions as a complete alternative geography.

What the claim says

  • Antarctica is not a continent at the south pole but a wall encircling the known world.
  • Beyond it lie additional continents, sometimes inhabited, sometimes ruins.
  • Ordinary people are not permitted to go and verify this.
  • The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 exists to enforce the prohibition.
  • Admiral Byrd’s 1947 expedition encountered what is back there, and a suppressed diary records it.

The Byrd story, checked

Richard E. Byrd is the central witness, and the claims about him have a documented paper trail — just not the one the videos cite.

Operation Highjump (1946–47) was real: the largest Antarctic expedition ever mounted, with thirteen ships, aircraft and roughly 4,700 men. Its stated purpose was to establish a research base and conduct aerial surveys — Little America IV. USA Today’s fact-check states plainly that historical records show no evidence it was sent to investigate an ice wall. Contemporary coverage exists, including the documentary The Secret Land.

What Byrd actually discovered that feeds the legend is the Bunger Hills — an ice-free oasis of dark rock and meltwater lakes surrounded by the ice sheet, which he described as “an island suitable for life … in a universe of death.” A real, strange, genuinely beautiful place. Add a mythical wall, and an oasis becomes a tropical hidden world.

The diary is a separate problem. The Missing Diary of Admiral Richard E. Byrd describes flying into the interior and meeting an ancient civilization with advanced technology. Researchers tracing its publication history place it with Raymond Bernard’s The Hollow Earth as twentieth-century occult fiction; the Byrd Polar and Climate Research Center at Ohio State holds his actual papers and reports no evidence for the flight. Byrd’s real quoted line — “I’d like to see that land beyond the Pole” — is a remark about unexplored territory, which is how exploration works.

The treaty, checked

The Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959 by twelve nations and now has over fifty parties. Its provisions: the continent is used for peaceful purposes and scientific research; military activity is prohibited; territorial claims are frozen; nuclear testing is banned; and inspections are allowed.

It contains no restriction on visitors. Tourism is a substantial industry — tens of thousands of people land in Antarctica each year, mostly via the Antarctic Peninsula, under IAATO guidelines. National programmes run annually, and the US Antarctic Program alone staffs three year-round stations.

The Long Now Foundation’s essay on the subject makes the sociological point well: Antarctica is genuinely hard to reach, access really does run through government logistics, and that bottleneck is readable as secrecy even though it is a function of distance, weather and cost.

What the evidence says

Antarctica is a continent. It has bedrock, mountains, subglacial lakes and a geological history continuous with Gondwana; it is not a ring. Satellite imagery shows its actual shape — a roughly circular landmass offset toward the Atlantic, with the Antarctic Peninsula reaching toward South America. Reuters and USA Today have both fact-checked the rim claim against this imagery and against circumnavigation records.

It has been crossed and circumnavigated. The continent was first reached in 1821, the pole in 1911, crossed overland in 1957–58, and circumnavigated by ship and by ski. A wall has no interior to cross.

The famous map is an illustration. The most-shared image of concentric ice walls ringing the continents was traced by Reuters to a post on an online art forum, not to any survey.

Why the composite is so durable

It solves three problems at once. It explains why nobody has photographed the extra land (it is forbidden). It gives the flat disc an edge without requiring anyone to fall off it. And it provides a physical location for everything else — the inner sun’s light leaking through, the giants, the surviving dinosaurs — without needing them to be nearby.

That is the signature move of a mature conspiracy cosmology: one unreachable place absorbs all the unruly evidence. The same structure appears in the hollow Earth’s interior and in the “classified” files of real proven conspiracies, which is part of why the real ones matter — they demonstrate what actual suppression looks like, with documents, and it does not look like this.

Underwater Worlds

Live debate — Real gap, speculative filling

The statistic, done properly

For years the number quoted everywhere was “more than 80 per cent of the ocean is unexplored and unmapped.” NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information has used that framing, tied to the Nippon Foundation–GEBCO Seabed 2030 project, which aims to complete a bathymetric map of the entire ocean floor by 2030.

The figure moves as the mapping proceeds. As of April 2026, NOAA Ocean Exploration put the share of the global seafloor covered by modern high-resolution multibeam sonar at 28.7 per cent — up from roughly 23 per cent a few years earlier. Which means just over seventy per cent still has no high-resolution map.

Two distinctions matter, and almost every viral post collapses them:

  • Mapped is not explored. A sonar swath gives you depth, not biology, chemistry or video.
  • Low-resolution mapped is not unmapped. Satellite gravimetry gives us a coarse global seafloor — enough to see mountain ranges and trenches, not enough to see a city block.

So: the deep sea is genuinely the least-known surface on Earth, and it is also genuinely being mapped at speed. Both statements are true.

What is actually down there

The real ocean floor outperforms most of the fiction. The Mariana Trench’s Challenger Deep is roughly 10,900 m down, where pressure is over a thousand atmospheres. Hydrothermal vents support chemosynthetic ecosystems with no sunlight at all — tube worms, vent crabs, microbes that metabolise sulphur. NOAA’s Okeanos Explorer and similar programmes regularly return with species new to science; a single seamount survey can produce dozens.

The point for this archive: the ocean makes a specific kind of claim possible. An unexplored space is not evidence of anything in it, but it is a licence to imagine — and imagination is what these theories trade in.

Real drowned cities

These are not conspiracies; they are archaeology, and they are extraordinary.

  • Thonis-Heracleion, Egypt — a major port at the mouth of the Nile, submerged by subsidence and earthquake, rediscovered in 2000 with intact statues, ships and temple remains.
  • Pavlopetri, Greece — a Bronze Age town off the Peloponnese, one of the oldest known submerged urban sites, with streets and building foundations still legible.
  • Port Royal, Jamaica — the pirate city that sank in the 1692 earthquake, now a UNESCO-listed underwater site.
  • Atlantis — the one that is not on this list. See below.

These discoveries matter because they show how the legend grows honestly: every real submerged city is a plausible seed for a “lost civilization” story, and each one that gets found makes the next claim feel more reasonable.

Atlantis in Plato’s own words

Atlantis is not a folk memory. It appears in two Platonic dialogues, Timaeus and Critias, as a thought experiment about a powerful island empire that attacked Athens and was destroyed by the gods in a single day and night. Plato says the story came from Egypt via Solon, and — crucially — he places it beyond the Pillars of Hercules, in the Atlantic, roughly 9,000 years before his own time.

No Bronze Age Atlantic island continent of that size exists; the seafloor there has been mapped in detail and has no sunken landmass. The academic consensus treats Atlantis as Plato’s political allegory. The claim survives because it is unfalsifiable in the right way: whenever a candidate site fails, the date or the location can be moved. Dozens of proposed locations now exist on five continents.

The inner-earth connection

Hollow-Earth literature needs water, and it gets it by postulating interior oceans — Symmes’s inner world had seas, and Bernard’s had rivers. In the composite cosmology of the ice wall, the “underwater world” is often not beneath the sea at all but beneath the shell. The two ideas blur because both are about a place you cannot reach.

The difference is testability. Deep-sea claims can be and are checked: sonar, ROV dives, eDNA, sediment cores. Every year the searchable ocean gets smaller. Interior-ocean claims cannot be checked at all, because the model defines the interior as inaccessible.

What this page is not saying

It is not saying the ocean is fully understood. It is the opposite. The correct statement is: the seafloor is less mapped than Mars, and there is a real, funded, international effort to fix that. The existence of a gap in knowledge is not evidence for a specific thing inside the gap — it is a reason to keep looking, and to be suspicious of anyone who fills the gap with a city and charges admission.

The Bloop: the loudest thing in the ocean

In 1997, hydrophones operated by NOAA's Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory — listening for submarine activity and earthquakes — recorded an ultra-low-frequency sound in the southern Pacific. It was loud enough that it became the most famous unidentified noise in oceanography, and it acquired a nickname: the Bloop.

The popular version added three things the data did not have. It placed the sound in the Mariana Trench — the recording was actually from the far south Pacific, thousands of kilometres away. It described a creature larger than a blue whale — the sound was consistent with many sources. And it asserted that the noise was “louder than any animal”, which was true of the recording, not of the claim.

NOAA eventually attributed the Bloop and several similar sounds to icequakes: fracturing and movement of Antarctic ice sheets, which generate exactly this kind of very-low-frequency, long-duration signal. The other famous recordings in the same family — “Train”, “Whistle”, “Slow Down” — got similar explanations, with the last of them traced to a drag event from a large iceberg.

What makes this entry worth keeping is how the myth survives the answer. The explanation is published by the agency that made the recording, and the leviathan version is still the one in the videos — because an icequake is not a story.

Lost Continents

Live debate — Invented, then drowned for real

This is the cleanest case in the archive of a scientific placeholder escaping into myth. You can watch it happen in the documents, decade by decade, with names and dates.

Lemuria: a zoologist's land bridge

In April 1864, the British zoologist Philip Lutley Sclater published a paper in The Quarterly Journal of Science proposing a submerged land connection between Madagascar and India. His reason was entirely practical: lemurs live in both places and nowhere in between, and in an age before plate tectonics the usual explanation for that was a land bridge.

He named it Lemuria, after the lemurs. Ernst Haeckel then proposed the same bridge as a possible cradle of humanity. Both men were reasoning from the evidence available; both were also wrong in the way that pre-plate-tectonics biogeography was wrong.

Plate tectonics dissolved the need for the bridge. India and Madagascar separated, and the lemurs were on the right side of the split. Sclater's hypothesis was abandoned by zoology.

What happened next

In 1888 Helena Petrovna Blavatsky published The Secret Doctrine, and Lemuria became something else entirely: the home of the “third root race”, a civilisation of giant, telepathic beings destroyed in a cataclysm, with Atlantis following as the fourth.

This is the moment the concept changes genre. Blavatsky's system was explicitly racialised — a hierarchy of “root races” with superior and inferior branches — and historians of the period note that it fed directly into the racial pseudoscience of the early twentieth century. It is worth saying plainly: the Theosophical Lemuria is not a charming folktale, and its afterlife includes some genuinely ugly material.

Mu is the Pacific cousin, popularised by James Churchward from the 1920s, and it has the same structure: a lost mother civilisation, a sunken continent, and a claim that its wisdom survives in fragments.

Atlantis and Hyperborea, briefly

Atlantis comes from Plato — a moral allegory, not a travel report; see Underwater Worlds. Hyperborea was a Greek legendary northern land of eternal spring, mentioned by Herodotus and Pindar, and it has been relocated to the Arctic, to Britain, and to the interior of the Earth by different writers. Neither has an archaeological site, and both have been searched for continuously for two centuries.

What geology actually confirms

There are real lost lands, and they are better than the myths in one specific way: they have maps and dates.

  • Zealandia — a 4.9 million km² region of continental crust in the southwest Pacific, formerly part of Gondwana, now 94% submerged. A 2017 paper in GSA Today argues it should be recognised as a continent, not a collection of fragments. It is real; it is just mostly underwater.
  • Sundaland — the exposed Sunda Shelf, which joined Sumatra, Java, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula during low sea levels of the last glacial period, and was drowned as the ice melted.
  • Doggerland — the North Sea bed that connected Britain to continental Europe until the Holocene sea-level rise. Fishing trawlers have brought up mammoth bones and worked flint from it for a century.
  • Kerguelen Plateau, Maui Nui, Ferdinandea — a partly submerged microcontinent, a drowned Hawaiian island, and a volcanic island that has surfaced and sunk at least four times.

None of these hosted a lost civilisation with psychic powers. All of them were real places where people or animals lived, and their shorelines are now under water — which is exactly the seed that the Lemuria story grew from, and the reason it feels plausible.

The Tamil Kumari Kandam

There is a separate and older tradition: Tamil literature describes a lost southern land, Kumari Kandam, swallowed by the sea. Colonial-era writers, encountering this, merged it with Lemuria — a fusion that Frontline (The Hindu) traced in 2011 as an example of how a Western invented continent got absorbed into a local myth and then returned as “evidence”.

That fusion matters for how this archive reads: the same story can be independently true as literature and false as geography, and the two get welded together by people with an interest in the welding.

The pattern

A hypothesis with a gap in it → a name → an occult system that fills the gap with civilisations → a century of paperbacks → a documentary. Plate tectonics closes the original gap, and nothing happens to the myth, because the myth stopped needing the gap long ago.

Compare the expanding Earth, which lost its gap and faded, with Lemuria, which lost its gap and became a franchise. The difference is not evidence. It is narrative.

Dual Suns, Dual Stars

Live debate — Tested hypothesis

The half that is right

Most Sun-like stars are not alone. A 2021 analysis using Gaia mission data identified about 1.3 million binary pairs — 2.6 million stars — within roughly 3,200 light-years, and concluded that roughly half of all Sun-like stars are gravitationally bound to a companion. For the most massive stars, the fraction approaches 100 per cent.

The nearest system, Alpha Centauri, is a triple: two Sun-like stars orbiting each other and a red dwarf, Proxima, loosely bound to both.

There is a stronger version still. A 2017 analysis of the Perseus molecular cloud by Sarah Sadavoy (Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory) and Steven Stahler (UC Berkeley) found that the only model reproducing the observed mix of young single stars and binaries was one in which all Sun-like stars form initially as wide binaries, which then either tighten or break apart within about a million years.

On that model, our Sun very likely had a sibling — and lost it. “We are saying, yes, there probably was a Nemesis, a long time ago,” Stahler said.

The half that is wrong

The Nemesis hypothesis is a specific, testable proposal: that the Sun has a faint companion on a long, eccentric orbit which periodically perturbs the Oort Cloud, sending comets inward and producing a ~26-million-year cycle of mass extinctions. It was proposed in 1984, and it fits neatly with the popularity of “Planet X” in the same period.

Nemesis has never been found. Infrared surveys, proper-motion catalogues and wide-field imaging have repeatedly failed to detect a companion of the required mass and distance. As BBC Future summarises it, the idea has fallen out of favour since 1984 after multiple surveys and studies found nothing.

And that is the correct scientific outcome for a failed prediction: not a conspiracy, just a hypothesis that lost.

“Fortunately for us, our Sun does not have a companion today. If it did, the gravitational pull of a solar sibling could have disrupted the orbit of the Earth and the other planets.” BBC Future, “The search for the Sun’s missing twin” (2024)

“Second sun” photographs

Every few months a photo circulates showing two suns in the sky. These are almost always optical phenomena with well-understood physics, and the two main culprits are:

  • Sun dogs (parhelia) — bright patches either side of the Sun, produced by sunlight refracting through hexagonal ice crystals in cirrus cloud. They sit at a fixed 22° from the Sun and are common in cold climates.
  • Lens flare — internal reflections inside a camera lens, which mirror the Sun across the frame’s centre and move with the camera.

The distinguishing test is trivial: a sun dog stays put relative to the real Sun as the camera moves; a flare moves with the lens.

Two suns in myth

Dual-sun imagery is genuinely old. The Chinese myth of the ten suns — archer Hou Yi shoots nine of them down — is a classical example of a sky with too many suns, and it is a story about drought, not astronomy. Norse and Vedic material contains comparable doubling motifs. It is worth separating three claims that get merged online:

ClaimStatus
The Sun once had a binary companionPlausible, likely — most Sun-like stars form in pairs
A companion star exists now and is being hiddenNo evidence — would be infrared-bright and gravitationally obvious
Photographs show a second sun in the skyOptics — parhelia or lens flare

The inner-sun variant

Hollow and concave Earth models need a light source inside the planet, and this is often described as a “second sun” — a small, central luminary. It is a different claim from Nemesis and should not be conflated with it. Its problems are thermodynamic rather than astronomical: an interior light source bright enough to sustain an ecosystem for geological time has no viable power source, and its waste heat would be detectable at the surface. See Hollow Earth.

The bottom line

Binary stars are the norm, not the exception — that part of the fringe intuition is correct and genuinely interesting. But “most stars are binary” does not imply “our Sun has a hidden twin”. The Sun’s mass, the orbits of the planets and the infrared sky have all been measured to a precision that rules out a companion of any plausible size within light-years.

Tartarus, the Pit

Documented — Primary text

Of all the places in this archive, Tartarus has the best documentation — because it survives in complete poems that have been continuously read for twenty-seven centuries. That makes it useful: you can read exactly what the source says, and then watch what later claims do to it.

The primary sources

Tartarus appears in two roles, sometimes in the same poem. It is a place — the deepest region of the cosmos — and it is also a being, one of the primordial entities that come into existence alongside Chaos and Gaia.

Hesiod’s Theogony (c. 700 BC) is the key text. In the opening cosmogony, Tartarus is the third thing to exist, “dim Tartarus in the depth of the wide-pathed Earth.” Later, after the Titanomachy, Zeus hurls the defeated Titans into it, and Hesiod gives the geography:

“A brazen anvil falling from heaven nine nights and days would reach the earth upon the tenth: and again, a brazen anvil falling from earth nine nights and days would reach Tartarus upon the tenth.” Hesiod, Theogony 720–725

It is enclosed by a bronze fence with “night spread in triple line all about it like a neck-circlet,” sealed by bronze gates that Poseidon fitted, and guarded by the Hundred-Handers. Inside, direction itself breaks down.

Homer’s Iliad (8.13–16) uses the same geometry as a threat: Zeus says he could hang a god from a chain and drop them so far that they would land in Tartarus, “as far beneath Hades as heaven is above earth.”

The Theogony also makes Tartarus a parent: with Gaia he fathers Typhoeus (Typhon), the hundred-headed storm-monster who nearly takes Zeus’s throne and is finally buried under it — the origin, in Hesiod’s account, of the destructive winds.

Two different underworlds

It is worth being precise, because the popular retelling usually isn’t:

NameWhat it is
HadesThe realm of the dead, ruled by the god of the same name; the destination of ordinary mortals.
TartarusThe deepest pit, far below Hades; a prison for gods and monsters, not a general afterlife.
ElysiumThe blessed region; later sources make it Tartarus’s opposite.

Over time the words blurred. Britannica notes that Tartarus gradually came to mean the entire underworld. In Virgil and later Roman writers it is a place of punishment for human sinners as well as Titans — a development Hesiod would not recognise.

Why it matters to this archive

Because Tartarus supplies the vocabulary that hidden-world theories still use. When a modern interior is described as a pit with a gate, guarded, containing giants, reached by descending impossibly far — the imagery is Hesiod’s. The transfer happens in three moves:

  1. Poem → place. A cosmological image is read as a literal geography.
  2. Place → interior. The pit is relocated into the Earth’s shell, which the hollow-Earth literature supplies.
  3. Interior → prison. The “fallen angels” and giant narratives of Genesis 6 and the Book of Enoch get bolted on, producing the modern “Tartarus is where they put the Nephilim” claim.

The New Testament does use the word: 2 Peter 2:4 says the angels who sinned were cast into Tartarus — the only occurrence in the Greek New Testament — which is why the term survives in theological English. That is a deliberate allusion to the Greek image, not a geological report.

How to read it

Tartarus is the strongest case in this archive for a claim that is true as literature and false as geography. There is nothing to debunk in Hesiod, because Hesiod was not making a measurement. The error only appears when a poem is converted into a map — and that conversion is always the interesting moment, because it tells you what the converter wanted the world to look like.

The same pit under other names

  • Sheol (Hebrew Bible) — the shadowy place of the dead, sometimes deep, sometimes simply “the grave”.
  • Helheim (Norse) — the cold realm of the dead, reached by crossing a river and passing through a gate.
  • Duat (Egyptian) — the underworld the sun passes through each night, with gates and guarded hours.
  • Diyu (Chinese) — the subterranean courts of judgment, layered into levels.

Every one of these has been used in modern fringe writing as evidence of a global memory of a real hollow interior. The alternative, and the one folklorists prefer, is that human beings bury their dead, imagine them below, and build architecture around the same few requirements: an entrance, a guard, a depth, and a reason to stay out.

Giants

Debunked — Hoaxes & misreadings

The textual tradition

Giants are not a fringe import. They are in the canon.

  • Genesis 6:1–4 — “The Nephilim were on the earth in those days,” after the “sons of God” took human wives. The word nephilim is of uncertain meaning; the most common proposal links it to nāpal, “to fall”. The same passage calls them gibborim, “mighty men”.
  • Numbers 13:28–33 — the spies report the Anakim in Canaan and say “we seemed like grasshoppers”.
  • Deuteronomy 2–3 — the Rephaim, Emim and Zamzummim; Og of Bashan, whose iron bed is described as nine cubits long.
  • 1 Samuel 17 — Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span in the Masoretic text.
  • Greek myth — the Titans, the Gigantes who war on Olympus, and Typhoeus.
  • Norse myth — the jotnar, whose size is often more about scale than stature.

Note how few of these words actually mean “giant”. Biblical scholarship is fairly clear that several are ethnic or status terms — Rephaim, Anakim, gibborim — which the King James translators rendered as “giants”. That translation choice is where a lot of the modern certainty comes from.

Josephus and the bones

The first-century historian Flavius Josephus is the most-quoted ancient witness, and he is worth reading exactly:

“There remained still a race of giants, who, by reason of their huge frames and figures in no way like the rest of mankind, were an amazing spectacle and a tale of terror to the ear. Their bones are shown to this day, bearing no resemblance to any that have come within men’s ken.” Josephus, Antiquities 5.125

Josephus says he has seen giant bones displayed at Hebron. The Torah.com’s study of “premodern encounters with giant bones” argues the obvious: the ancient world was full of enormous fossil bones — mammoth, mastodon, elephant, giraffe, whale — and had no concept of extinct species. A fossil femur from a proboscidean is a giant’s thigh.

This is the single most useful explanation in the dossier, because it scales. It accounts for giant bones in Greece, in China (where “dragon bones” were ground into medicine), in Native American traditions, and in the biblical accounts, without requiring a conspiracy or a lost race.

The Cardiff Giant, 1869

The modern giant-skeleton genre begins with a business dispute. In 1866, Binghamton cigar-maker George Hull argued with a Methodist revivalist about whether the Bible’s giants were literal. Hull decided to find out what people would believe.

He bought an eleven-foot block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa, shipped it to Chicago, had it carved into a ten-foot-five man, aged it, shipped it to his cousin William “Stub” Newell’s farm in Cardiff, New York, and buried it. In October 1869, hired well-diggers hit stone three feet down.

Newell charged 25 cents a head, then 50. Hull sold the figure for $23,000. P.T. Barnum offered $50,000, was refused, and had an exact copy made — which he exhibited as the real one, prompting the line attributed to showman David Hannum that a sucker is born every minute. Cornell’s first president, Andrew Dickson White, visited and immediately saw it was a statue. Hull eventually confessed.

The photographs

Modern “giant skeleton” images are almost all digitally composited. A 2016 paper in a George Fox University collection describes the genre precisely: “badly photoshopped YouTube videos, often set to ominous, mystical music, featuring 50-foot skeletons next to hapless shovel-wielding desert workers and heavy machinery.”

The giveaway is always the same — inconsistent lighting and shadows, a skeleton with no excavation matrix, no museum accession, no publication, and a site that cannot be revisited.

What archaeology shows

The Levant is one of the most intensively excavated regions on Earth. No outsized human skeletons have been recovered there. The National Center for Science Education puts it bluntly: “There is no more reason to think the natives were gigantic than there is to claim that the San Francisco Giants baseball team consists of gargantuans.”

What does exist: individual humans at the extreme end of normal variation. Robert Wadlow reached 2.72 m (8 ft 11 in) and is the tallest verified person in recorded history; acromegaly and gigantism are documented endocrine conditions. A 2.7 m man is remarkable, not a species.

What also exists: real Megafauna. Gigantopithecus was a genuinely enormous ape — up to 3 m and 300 kg — that went extinct perhaps 300,000 years ago, and is one of the few fossils ever offered as a serious basis for giant-human legends. It was an orangutan relative, not a person.

Why the legend keeps its grip

Because it is doing several jobs at once. It explains large ancient architecture without granting the builders credit. It supplies a lost golden age. It gives “fallen angels” a physical archaeology. And it is uniquely easy to fake — a photograph of a big skeleton requires no theory, which is why the fakes spread faster than any rebuttal.

The same three functions appear in Dragons & Dinosaurs and in the “advanced civilization” strand of the world beyond the ice.

Dragons & Dinosaurs

Live debate — Contested origin

The puzzle

Dragons appear in China, in Mesopotamia, in Greece, in Wales, in Mesoamerica, in Aboriginal Australian rock art and in San rock painting in southern Africa. The specific creature varies — serpent, four-legged firedrake, rain-bringing spirit, hoard-guarding worm — but the family resemblance is strong enough that the question “where did dragons come from?” is a real academic question, not a fan question.

The phylogenetic answer

In 2013, Julien d’Huy and colleagues applied the methods of evolutionary biology to mythology. They coded dragon motifs from 23 regions, built phylogenetic trees the way you would for species, and looked for the tree most consistent with the data.

The result, as the University of Bristol’s palaeontology blog describes it, was a very high likelihood that the dragon myth has a single origin, and that the patterns fit human migration unusually well — “stronger than those produced by most biological data.” On their reconstruction, the first dragon story was being told perhaps 75,000 years ago in southern Africa, and it travelled with people as they dispersed.

That is a striking result, and it is also contested — phylogenetic analysis of folklore depends heavily on how you code a motif, and a single origin is not the only reading of the data. But it moves the question from “dragons must be memories of dinosaurs” to “dragons are a story that spread.”

Fossils in the ground

The other major strand is Adrienne Mayor’s work on fossil knowledge in the ancient world. The argument: ancient people found enormous bones eroding out of the ground, had no concept of extinct species, and reconstructed the animals from the skeleton up. Her best-documented case is the griffin: the gold-guarding griffin of Scythian legend closely matches Protoceratops, whose fossils — complete with nests and eggs — are abundant in the Gobi Desert where the Scythians mined gold.

The same logic runs through Chinese “dragon bones”, which were collected, sold as medicine and eventually recognised as fossils; Peking Man was found at a well-known dragon-bone site outside Beijing.

Ronald Hutton’s 2024 Gresham lecture proposes a three-stage model that fits all of this together: a basic human fear of apex predators, then the visual evidence of fossils and rare sea creatures like giant squid, then regional literary traditions (the benevolent Chinese dragon, the Christian firedrake).

The creationist reading

A completely different explanation is argued by young-Earth creationist organisations, and it should be stated in their own words rather than paraphrased:

Claim — Answers in Genesis / Creation Ministries

If dinosaurs were created on Day Six and survived the Flood on the Ark, then people groups after the Flood would have lived alongside them until they died out. Those people would not have used the word “dinosaur” — coined in 1841 — but “dragon” or “monster”. Therefore ubiquitous dragon legends are exactly what the creation model predicts, and the dating methods that place dinosaurs 65 million years ago are the thing that is wrong.

The argument is internally consistent, and its appeal is obvious: it turns a global folklore pattern into evidence. Apologetics Press makes the same case at length, and Creation Ministries’ article on “dinosaurs and dragons” is the most complete version.

What the evidence says

The stratigraphy is not ambiguous. Non-avian dinosaurs disappear from the fossil record at the Cretaceous–Palaeogene boundary, about 66 million years ago. The earliest hominins appear in the last several million years; Homo sapiens in the last 300,000. USGS states it directly: “After the dinosaurs died out, nearly 65 million years passed before people appeared on Earth.”

The specific “dinosaur” identifications fail on inspection. A 2013 paper in Palaeontologia Electronica went through the Greco-Roman material case by case: the dragons of Pliny and Aelian are snakes — the epithets are ophis, serpens, anguis; the “theropod” in the Nile Mosaic of Palestrina is a mammal, possibly an otter; the “dinosaur” in a Pompeii fresco is a crocodile; the “pterosaurs” on an Alexandrian coin are winged snakes.

Birds are dinosaurs. The one way in which humans do live alongside dinosaurs is the one creationists do not need: avian dinosaurs are everywhere, and the lineage is well documented in the fossil record.

The living-dinosaur claim

The same logic produces Mokele-mbembe, the sauropod said to inhabit the Congo Basin, and the Lake Champlain and Loch Ness “survivors”. These are covered in Cryptids. The pattern is consistent: a large unexplored region, a local tradition, a Western expedition, no specimen.

What dragons are actually good at

They are the most successful monster design in human history, and the reasons are practical: a serpent body reads as dangerous from any angle, wings add threat, fire explains destruction, and a hoard gives it a reason to be somewhere. You do not need a dinosaur to invent that. You need a story.

Cryptids

Fringe claim — Unverified

What cryptozoology claims to be

The term was coined by Bernard Heuvelmans, a Belgian zoologist, for the study of “hidden animals” — species reported but not yet described. In principle this is a real activity: the okapi, the coelacanth and the giant squid were all once “cryptids”. In practice the field’s famous cases have not produced a specimen in a century of looking, and the reason is not that nobody has tried.

Bigfoot / Sasquatch

The name is modern and has a documented etymology. “Sasquatch” is an anglicisation of a Coast Salish word, popularised in the 1920s by a British Columbia teacher and bureaucrat — and the original stories, as McGill University’s Office for Science and Society points out, described tall, long-haired people who wore clothes, lived in villages and could be spoken to. That is not a furry ape. The translation drifted, and “long hair” became “covered in fur”.

The iconography comes from 1958 (Bluff Creek footprints and the term’s spread) and 1967 (the Patterson–Gimlin film). The film has never been conclusively debunked and has never been validated either. The problem is not the film; it is everything that should accompany a breeding population of 2.5-metre primates across North America:

  • No body, no skeleton, no roadkill, no zoo specimen.
  • No DNA — despite environmental DNA sampling becoming routine and cheap.
  • No clear photographic sequence in the age of the smartphone.
  • A population needs hundreds of breeding individuals to avoid inbreeding; hundreds of large primates leave physical traces.

There is also a statistical finding that reframes the sightings. A 2024 preprint by Floe Foxon found that Bigfoot reports rise and fall with local black bear populations across the US and Canada. That does not prove any individual sighting was a bear — but it is what you would expect if most were. Foxon’s conclusion is the modest one: if you think you saw a sasquatch, it was probably a bear.

The Loch Ness Monster

This is the best-documented case, which makes it the most instructive. The modern phenomenon starts in 1933 with a road being built along the loch and a surge of local reporting; the following year came the “surgeon’s photograph” — a head and neck above the water, taken by a respected London doctor, which anchored the plesiosaur image for decades.

In the early 1990s, Christian Spurling came forward and said the photograph was a hoax: a clockwork toy submarine with a plastic-wood neck, photographed in a quiet bay with the far shore in frame to establish scale, published under the name of a reputable doctor who played along as a joke.

In 2019, a University of Otago team led by Neil Gemmell took hundreds of water samples around the loch and sequenced the eDNA. Result: no plesiosaur, no large marine reptile, no unexpected large vertebrate. They did find a great deal of eel DNA — enough that Gemmell said a giant eel could not be ruled out, a caveat widely reported as “Nessie is an eel”. Follow-up work has since argued that eels of the required size are implausible.

The pattern is the point: the strongest evidence was a photograph, the photograph was a confession, and the environmental survey found the ordinary loch.

Yeti, Mokele-mbembe, and the rest

  • Yeti — the Himalayas; the 1951 Shipton footprint photograph is the iconic artefact and has been argued to be a human-made impression (the “odd depressions” suggest deliberate shaping).
  • Mokele-mbembe — a sauropod-like animal reported from the Congo Basin, the cryptozoological link to living dinosaurs. Repeated expeditions, no specimen, no photograph, no scat, no carcass.
  • Chupacabra — Latin American livestock deaths, traced in many cases to coyotes and dogs with severe mange; the “alien” silhouette is a hairless canid.
  • Mothman — Point Pleasant, West Virginia, 1966–67; a case study in how a local panic plus a newspaper creates a durable legend.
  • Lake monsters generally — Loch Morar, Lake Champlain, Okanagan; the same structure of eyewitness reports, tourism incentive and no specimen.
The honest assessment

Individual reports are often sincere and sometimes unexplained. That is different from a species. The scientific bar is a type specimen — a body, or at minimum diagnostic DNA — and cryptozoology has had a century to produce one for its flagship animals while the cost of genetic sequencing has collapsed.

That is why the field matters to this archive. It is the cleanest available demonstration of the difference between evidence (a photograph, a footprint, a story) and proof (a specimen). Every other claim in these pages is asking you to accept the first as the second.

The Giant Trees

Debunked

The claim

The “Silicon Forest” or “petrified giant trees” theory holds that certain rock formations — above all Devils Tower in Wyoming — are the remains of enormous trees, hundreds of metres tall, from a lost age when the planet supported a giant biosphere. The story usually adds that an “incredibly large petrified root system” has been found beneath the Tower, and that this has been “covered up”.

The images that spread are genuinely striking, and the resemblance is real: Devils Tower is a tall, fluted, flat-topped column standing alone above the plains. Human pattern-recognition does the rest.

What the Tower is

Devils Tower is an igneous intrusion — magma that pushed up into existing sedimentary layers and cooled underground without erupting, then was exposed when the softer rock around it eroded away. It is about 386 m tall, and it is the world’s largest example of polygonal columnar jointing.

The rock is phonolite porphyry, a rare volcanic rock. The relevant point is mineralogical: it is composed of feldspar and hornblende. There is no lignin, no cellulose, no wood anatomy of any kind — and a fossilised tree preserves cell structure even when replaced by silica.

The columns themselves are a cooling artefact. Molten rock contracts as it solidifies; the contraction has to go somewhere, so it cracks. Because the stress is most efficiently relieved by three fractures meeting at 120°, the cracks form hexagons. Columns grow perpendicular to the cooling surface. Fast cooling makes narrow columns; slow, insulated cooling makes large ones — which is why the Tower’s are so spectacular. The same process produces the Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland and Devils Postpile in California, neither of which has ever been claimed as a tree stump.

The Tower is also not the only formation in the American West with this geometry; the “forest” claims tend to be applied to whichever basalt column field is currently going viral.

Claim — social media, c. 2019 onward

“Scientists discovered that the Devil’s Tower butte in Wyoming is originally a giant tree after finding an incredibly large petrified root system underneath.”

The fact-check

Reuters checked this claim in 2020. A National Park Service geologist responded that “there is no evidence to support such a theory as a tree stump or petrified tree roots,” pointing to the NPS’s own account of the Tower’s formation. There is no published discovery of a root system. The claim is a caption attached to someone else’s photograph.

The scientific literature on the Tower is not settled on every detail — geologists still argue between laccolith, stock, volcanic plug and maar-diatreme models for the intrusion’s shape — but none of them involve biology. The disagreement is about magma plumbing, not about whether the rock was ever alive.

The trees that really are giant

The anti-climax is better than the myth. There are genuinely enormous trees, and they are documented individually:

  • Coast redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) — the tallest living trees; “Hyperion” in California is 115.9 m, verified by climbing and tape.
  • Giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) — the most massive; “General Sherman” has a trunk volume around 1,500 m³.
  • Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona — real petrified wood from the Late Triassic Chinle Formation, where silica replaced the organic tissue of fallen conifers over 200 million years. You can see the growth rings and cell structure.
  • Ancient clonal trees — Pando, a quaking aspen colony in Utah, is a single connected organism covering tens of hectares.

Real petrified wood is the perfect control. It is wood turned to stone, and it still looks like wood — rings, bark texture, cell walls under a microscope. Devils Tower looks like a stump from a distance and like a crystal from a centimetre away.

Where it fits

The giant-tree theory is a scale argument: if the world once held trees a kilometre high, it could hold giants, and the geological timetable would have to be wrong. It attaches easily to the young-Earth literature and to the “suppressed history” frame of the proven-conspiracy pages — where the absence of evidence is read as evidence of suppression, rather than as an absence of evidence.

Tartaria & the Mud Flood

Debunked

This is the newest theory in the archive and the fastest-growing. It has no founding text, no named authority and no agreed model — which is exactly why it has spread: anyone can add a building to the list.

Its nickname is exact. Architectural Digest-style coverage and the design press have both called it “the QAnon of architecture”, and the phrase fits: a loose set of visual hunches, endlessly recombined, with an unnamable enemy at the centre.

What is claimed

  • A technologically advanced worldwide empire — Tartaria — existed before the modern era, with free or wireless energy.
  • It built the grand classical and beaux-arts buildings now attributed to the 18th and 19th centuries.
  • A global catastrophe, the “mud flood”, buried the lower floors of these buildings in metres of mud.
  • A reset followed: the survivors rebuilt over the ruins, rewrote history, and demolished the remaining buildings to hide the evidence.
  • Famous demolitions are therefore cover-ups — the Singer Building, the original Penn Station, the temporary exhibition halls of the world’s fairs.
  • Some versions add giants, as in other dossiers; the “orphan trains” of the 19th century become children stolen from Tartarian families.

Where it actually comes from

The name is real and so is the confusion behind it. “Tartary” or “Great Tartary” was a European label for the vast interior of Asia — Siberia, Central Asia, Mongolia, stretching toward Afghanistan — used on maps by people who had no interest in distinguishing the many cultures living there. It was a geographical shorthand, not an empire.

The conspiracy version has a traceable lineage in Russia. Anatoly Fomenko’s “New Chronology” from the 1970s and 1980s argued that conventional ancient history was largely fabricated; Nikolai Levashov’s occult-nationalist writing popularised a lost Tartaria as the “real” name of Russia. The Russian Geographical Society has publicly rejected the theory, and has responded by publishing maps of Tartary from its own collection — showing the word as a regional label.

Since about 2016 the idea has been detached from that Russian nationalist frame and rebuilt in English-language video, where it merged with the older “mud flood” motif.

The three pieces of “evidence”, examined

1. Buried ground floors and half-windows

The single most persuasive image in the theory: an old building whose basement windows sit half below the modern pavement, as though the street had risen around it. The Tartarian reading is a flood of mud.

The documentary answer is that streets really did rise — deliberately, in cities all over the world, in exactly the period the theory points at. As horse-drawn traffic gave way to streetcars and then automobiles, steep grades were cut down and low ground was filled up; Seattle’s regrade projects buried many first floors so thoroughly that the old street level is now a tourist attraction. Skeptoid’s episode on the subject identifies at least one photograph used in the videos as Seattle’s street-raising, repurposed as global evidence.

The second half is simpler: basements have windows because cellars need light and ventilation, and a window that is half-sunk is what you get when a pavement is raised by a few courses of stone. No flood is required.

2. World’s fair buildings

This is the theory’s strongest-looking case, and it collapses on a single fact: world’s fairs were temporary by design. The 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago — the “White City” — was built in plaster, staff and timber over a few years, intended from the start to be demolished, and it was. The 1915 Panama–Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco was likewise a temporary installation, and the Palace of Horticulture in it is one of the buildings most often posted as Tartarian.

Expositions were the era’s biggest architectural commissions. They were photographed relentlessly, planned in published drawings, reported in the trade press, and their demolition was news. The claim requires all of that to be forged, which is a far larger conspiracy than the one being proposed.

3. Star forts

Star-shaped fortifications — Palmanova, Bourtange, the trace italienne across Europe and the colonial world — are offered as an energy grid. They are actually the solution to a specific military problem: bastions angled so that no wall can be approached without being swept by flanking fire, which became necessary once cannon could knock down a straight curtain wall. The geometry is a firing solution, not a circuit diagram.

What the record shows

Buildings have architects, contracts, payrolls, photographs, newspaper accounts and municipal records. In Australia, AAP FactCheck checked the Tartarian claim against two of Sydney and Melbourne’s best-known buildings and found their construction fully documented — the Queen Victoria Building’s statues, for instance, were carved in the 1890s by a named sculptor, William Macintosh.

There is no geological, sedimentary or archaeological evidence anywhere on Earth for a global mud flood of the kind described. A worldwide event that buried cities on every continent would leave a distinctive layer; it does not exist.

And the chronology fails in the opposite direction too: the theory needs the 19th century to be a fiction, while the 19th century is the best-documented century in human history — censuses, birth registers, tax rolls, photographs, ships’ manifests, telegraph records.

Why it works so well

Because it asks you to look out of the window. Most conspiracy theories require you to accept a claim about a place you will never visit; this one points at your own high street. High ceilings, deep basements, ornate stonework, a building older than its neighbours — all of it becomes evidence, and the evidence is free.

That is also its weakness. The same observations have unglamorous explanations that anyone can check: ceiling heights follow heating technology and status display; basements follow storage needs and street grades; ornament follows the availability of cheap skilled labour and the Beaux-Arts fashion. The theory is a machine for converting ordinary urban fabric into proof, and it runs on not knowing how buildings work.

How it connects

  • Giants — the Tartarian population is often said to have been enormous. See Giants.
  • Free energy — the same claim as the “suppressed technology” strand in Proven Conspiracies, where you can compare it with what documented suppression looks like.
  • Reset history — a softer version of the “much bigger Earth, hidden continents” argument in The Larger Globe: the past is not unknown, it is withheld.

Ancient Astronauts

Fringe claim — Unsupported

Ancient astronaut theory — paleocontact — holds that extraterrestrials visited Earth in prehistory, were mistaken for gods, and either taught humanity or engineered it. It is the best-selling fringe theory of the last sixty years, and it has a genuine intellectual lineage that is worth setting out before the rebuttals.

The lineage

  • 1919

    Charles Fort’s The Book of the Damned collects reports that science had ignored and suggests the Earth might be “property”, observed and occasionally visited. Fort was half satirist, but he supplied the frame: the anomaly as a rebuke to authority.

  • 1947

    The flying-saucer era begins and retro-fits history: if objects are in the sky now, they may have been then.

  • 1966

    Shklovskii and Sagan’s Intelligent Life in the Universe treats paleocontact as a serious possibility to be examined — and Sagan later becomes one of its sharpest critics. Both positions are consistent: the question is legitimate, the evidence is not there.

  • 1968

    Erich von Däniken’s Chariots of the Gods? sells in the tens of millions and turns the idea into a mass phenomenon.

  • 1976

    Zecharia Sitchin’s The Twelfth Planet builds an entirely different version from Mesopotamian texts: the Anunnaki, a planet called Nibiru, and human beings as a manufactured workforce.

  • 1978

    Robert Temple’s The Sirius Mystery argues the Dogon of Mali preserved knowledge of a companion star to Sirius.

  • 2009 – present

    Ancient Aliens turns the material into a television format, recycling and extending every exhibit below.

Sitchin’s specific claim

It is only fair to state it as he did, because it is a real argument with real texts behind it. Sitchin read the Sumerian and Akkadian corpus as follows: the Anunnaki were not gods but visitors from a twelfth planet, Nibiru, on a 3,600-year orbit; they came to Earth to mine gold; when their labourers rebelled they engineered a hybrid — Homo sapiens — from their own genetic material and that of existing hominids. The Sumerian “fashioning of man from clay” becomes a mythologised memory of genetic engineering; the long lifespans of the Genesis patriarchs become inherited Anunnaki longevity.

This is superficially scholarly: it cites tablets, gives transliterations, and builds a system. That is precisely why Assyriologists have answered it in detail rather than dismissing it.

The Assyriological answer

The word Nibiru exists in astronomical texts, and in those texts it refers to a celestial body associated with the god Marduk — commonly understood as Jupiter, or as a crossing-point in the sky. It is not described as a planet on a 3,600-year orbit, and that orbital period is not in the tablets. Michael Heiser’s paper “The Myth of a 12th Planet” works through the occurrences one by one and shows Sitchin supplying meanings the scribes did not write.

The same critique applies to his etymologies: DIN-GIR, the Sumerian sign for “god”, is translated by Sitchin as “pure ones of the blazing rockets” — a reading that requires splitting a single noun into two and choosing a dramatic sense for a syllable that means “sharp-edged”.

And the Anunnaki themselves are, in the mainstream reading, a group of Mesopotamian deities — with a role in the underworld and in the assembly of the gods — not a species from another planet.

The exhibits, one at a time

The Palenque sarcophagus lid

The most reproduced “astronaut” image in the world: the Maya king Pakal on his tomb lid, apparently reclining in a cockpit with his hands on controls. The University of Pennsylvania Museum’s Expedition article walks through the actual iconography — Pakal is shown at the moment of death, falling into the open jaws of the underworld, with the World Tree of Maya cosmology growing from his body and a celestial bird at its crown. It is a statement about kingship and cosmic order. The “rocket” is the tree, and the “flames” are the jaws.

The Nazca Lines

Von Däniken’s argument was that the lines only make sense as runways for aircraft. The archaeology says otherwise: the geoglyphs are shallow scraped lines on desert pavement, too soft for any landing gear, many of them figures rather than straight runs, and the straight lines are consistent with processional paths and water ritual. See Mysteries for the current scholarship.

Puma Punku

The precision-cut andesite blocks at Tiwanaku in Bolivia are genuinely impressive, and the claim is that their geometry is too exact for stone tools. Experimental archaeology has repeatedly demonstrated that hard-stone working with hammerstones, abrasives and patient labour produces exactly these forms; the “impossible” joins are also explained by the blocks being recut and reused over centuries. The site has a long, well-studied construction sequence.

The Dogon and Sirius

Temple’s claim was that the Dogon knew of Sirius B — a white dwarf invisible without a telescope — before astronomers did. The anthropological record is more complicated: the ethnographies on which the claim rests were collected in a period of intense contact and include material that appears to have come from European sources, and later fieldwork by Walter van Beek found the Dogon did not maintain the system as reported. It is not a clean case of preserved ancient astronomy.

Crystal skulls

The British Museum’s skull, long presented as Aztec, has been examined with scanning electron microscopy. The tool marks show rotary wheels and abrasives that were not available in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica; the quartz matches Brazilian or Madagascan sources; and the carving lacks Aztec or Mixtec iconography. It is a nineteenth-century European fabrication made for the curiosity market. The Oxford TORCH project’s write-up gathers the studies.

The Great Pyramid

Not a mystery of construction so much as a mystery of logistics, and the logistics have been filling in fast: the Wadi al-Jarf papyri include a logbook from a work gang transporting limestone, and the workers’ village, bakeries and ramp systems at Giza have been excavated for decades. None of this requires anything but organisation, stone, copper tools and a great deal of food.

Why the theory keeps winning anyway

Because it is a moral argument disguised as a historical one. It says: these achievements are too great for the people we have been told built them. The rebuttal is not “they were simple” — it is the opposite, and it is the most interesting thing in this dossier. Ancient people were extraordinary engineers, astronomers and administrators, and the archaeological record shows them solving problems in detail. The insult in the theory is that it takes the credit away from them.

The Conversation’s 2026 assessment makes the same point from the other direction: the theory endures because it answers a modern anxiety about human potential, not because the evidence improved.

Where it overlaps with the rest of the archive

  • Giants and fallen angels — Sitchin’s Anunnaki occupy the same narrative slot as the Nephilim: superior beings breeding with humans.
  • Hidden technology — the “suppressed free energy” claim in Tartaria is the same shape, moved forward two centuries.
  • Inner worlds — the hollow-Earth literature absorbed UFO lore wholesale; see Hollow Earth.
  • Dragons and dinosaurs — both are attempts to fill the deep past with something the textbooks deny; see Dragons.
