Proven Conspiracies

Documented

“Conspiracy theory” has become an insult, but a conspiracy is simply an agreement to do something harmful in secret — a crime with more than one participant. Some of those were committed by governments, and were later proven with documents.

Six cases follow. Each is here for the same reason: to show what evidence of a real cover-up actually looks like — a paper trail, a whistleblower, an inquiry, a named official, and a date.

1. MKUltra — the CIA’s mind-control programme (1953–1973)

Approved by CIA Director Allen Dulles in 1953 and run largely by chemist Sidney Gottlieb, MKUltra funded research into behavioural control: LSD, hypnosis, sensory deprivation, electroshock. It operated through universities, hospitals and prisons, and in many documented cases the subjects did not consent.

Its most notorious strand was Operation Midnight Climax: CIA-linked safe houses where men were dosed without their knowledge and observed through two-way mirrors.

The human cost has a name. Frank Olson, an Army scientist at Fort Detrick, was secretly given LSD at a November 1953 meeting and died days later in a fall from a New York hotel window. His family had the body exhumed in 1994; a forensic report found a head injury that may have preceded the fall. Prosecutors investigated for five years and could not prove murder — so the manner of death remains disputed even though the dosing does not.

How it was proven: a 1974 New York Times investigation, followed by the 1977 Senate Church Committee hearings. Roughly 149 subprojects are documented — and the record is incomplete because Richard Helms ordered the files destroyed in 1973.

2. COINTELPRO — the FBI against its own citizens (1956–1971)

The FBI’s counter-intelligence programme surveilled, infiltrated and disrupted political groups: the Communist Party USA, the Socialist Workers Party, the Black Panther Party, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference — and Martin Luther King Jr. personally. On 21 November 1964 an anonymous “suicide package” was mailed to King, assembled by the Bureau.

How it was proven: in March 1971 a group calling itself the Citizens’ Commission to Investigate the FBI burgled the Bureau’s Media, Pennsylvania office and mailed the files to journalists. The programme was exposed, and formally terminated. The Church Committee then documented its scope.

3. Tuskegee — 40 years of untreated syphilis (1932–1972)

The US Public Health Service studied the progression of syphilis in 399 Black men in Macon County, Alabama, without telling them their diagnosis. Even after penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s, treatment was withheld so the study could continue. It ran for forty years.

How it was proven: a 1972 Associated Press story by Jean Heller, then a federal panel, congressional hearings, and a $10 million settlement. President Clinton formally apologised in 1997.

One correction matters, because the popular version exaggerates it: the men were not deliberately infected. A separate programme in Guatemala (1946–48), documented by a presidential commission in 2011, did intentionally expose people to sexually transmitted infections without consent. Both were abuses; they were not the same abuse.

4. The Gulf of Tonkin — the second attack that did not happen (1964)

On 4 August 1964, the Johnson administration reported that North Vietnamese vessels had attacked two US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin. Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution three days later, authorising military action in Southeast Asia — the legal basis for the escalation of the Vietnam War.

The second attack did not occur. Communications were misread under pressure, and the intelligence was presented with more confidence than it deserved.

How it was proven: the Pentagon Papers (1971) and, decisively, declassified NSA signals-intelligence material. The NSA has published its own internal history, “Skunks, Bogies, Silent Hounds, and the Flying Fish: The Gulf of Tonkin Mystery, 2–4 August 1964”, along with the original intercepted traffic.

5. Iran–Contra (1985–1987)

Senior National Security Council staff — principally Lt. Col. Oliver North, with National Security Adviser John Poindexter — arranged secret arms sales to Iran while the US publicly refused to negotiate with hostage-takers, then diverted the proceeds to the Contras in Nicaragua after Congress had explicitly banned military aid to them (the Boland Amendment).

How it was proven: exposure in a Lebanese magazine in November 1986, then the Tower Commission, congressional hearings and Independent Counsel Lawrence Walsh’s investigation. Several convictions followed; some were later overturned on immunity grounds.

6. The tobacco industry (1950s–1998)

Internal industry documents show that companies understood the cancer risk and the addictiveness of nicotine while publicly funding doubt, attacking the science, and marketing “safer” cigarettes. The strategy was explicit: manufacture uncertainty and sell it.

How it was proven: litigation discovery, most famously the 1994 release of millions of pages from Brown & Williamson and others, and the 1998 Master Settlement Agreement. The documents are now a public archive used by historians and epidemiologists.

The pattern — and why it matters for the rest of this archive

Every case above has the same four features: a specific claim, a named institution, a paper trail that survived, and a mechanism of exposure — a burglary, a leak, a lawsuit, a congressional subpoena.

Now compare that with the claims in the other dossiers. “The Earth is hollow” has no memo. “A second sun is hidden” has no budget line. “The ice wall is guarded” has no unit, no payroll and no defector. Six decades of real conspiracies have produced tens of thousands of pages of documentation; the cosmology claims have produced photographs of a rock.

This is not a rhetorical trick. It is the strongest argument in the archive: we know what a cover-up looks like, because we have the files.

Two more worth knowing

  • Operation Northwoods (1962) — a Joint Chiefs proposal to stage attacks on US targets to justify invading Cuba. It was proposed and rejected, declassified in 1997. Real document; never executed. A useful reminder that “they discussed it” is not “they did it”.
  • Mass surveillance — the NSA’s bulk collection programmes, disclosed by Edward Snowden in 2013, were subsequently reviewed by courts and Congress and partly curtailed. A genuine secret, revealed by a named source with documents.

7. Operation Mockingbird — the CIA and the press

The claim, made for decades and dismissed as paranoia: the CIA had penetrated American news organisations and used journalists to place propaganda.

It was substantially confirmed. The 1975–76 Church Committee investigations into intelligence activities opened the archive, and in 1977 the journalist Carl Bernstein published “The CIA and the Media” in Rolling Stone, based on interviews and internal documents, describing a programme to recruit and cultivate journalists, editors and publishers — with figures in the hundreds, including people at major newspapers, magazines, and broadcasters.

The nuance matters as much as the confirmation. Much of the relationship was “friendly” cultivation rather than formal employment: a journalist who would take a call, plant a story, or hold a line. Some were on the payroll. The point is not that every story was dictated; it is that a secret channel existed, was used, and was concealed from readers — which is exactly what critics had alleged.

8. The Nayirah testimony — a war sold with a story

In October 1990, a 15-year-old girl identified only as “Nayirah” testified before a Congressional human rights caucus that Iraqi soldiers had entered a Kuwaiti hospital, removed babies from incubators and left them to die on the floor. The testimony was credited with helping shift American public opinion toward war.

It was arranged. Nayirah was the daughter of the Kuwaiti ambassador to the United States, and the hearings had been organised with the help of Hill & Knowlton, a public relations firm working for a Kuwaiti-funded group. The incubator story was promoted as research; later investigations found no evidence for it, and reporters established that the witness's identity had been concealed deliberately.

The episode is now a standard case study in how a democracy can be moved to war by a manufactured story told in an official setting — and, notably, it was exposed by journalists rather than by any internal check.

9. The Business Plot — a coup offered to a general

In 1933 the retired Marine Corps Major General Smedley Butler — the most decorated Marine of his era, and by then a fierce critic of war profiteering — told a congressional committee that a group of wealthy men had approached him to lead a fascist veterans' organisation and march on Washington, in effect a coup against President Roosevelt.

The House committee chaired by John McCormack investigated, took testimony, and reported that it had found evidence of an attempt to establish a fascist organisation and that the plotters had approached Butler. The alleged go-between was Gerald MacGuire, a bond salesman for a Wall Street firm. No one was prosecuted.

Historians differ on the scale — how far the money went, how serious the operational planning was, whether some witnesses exaggerated. What is documented is that the approach happened, that Butler reported it, and that a congressional committee took it seriously enough to write it up. That is the useful middle case: not a fantasy, not a fully executed plot, but a real attempt that failed and was then investigated openly.

10. Watergate — the conspiracy that ended a presidency

In June 1972 five men were arrested burgling the Democratic National Committee offices in the Watergate building. Two Washington Post reporters, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, followed the money and the connections toward the White House while the administration dismissed the story as partisan invention.

The cover-up collapsed through documented evidence: the Senate hearings in 1973, the revelation of the White House taping system, and the tapes themselves. The Supreme Court ordered them released in July 1974; Nixon resigned in August.

Watergate is the benchmark for this whole dossier. It shows what a real conspiracy looks like from the outside — an actual crime, actual concealment, and a trail of documents, money and recordings that eventually outran the people hiding them. Every claim in these pages that is filed as Documented had to meet that standard. Every claim filed as Debunked failed it.

11. Operation Paperclip — the scientists who were hired

After the Second World War, the United States recruited German scientists and engineers — including Wernher von Braun, who had led the V-2 rocket programme — to work on American rockets and weapons. The programme was called Operation Paperclip.

The part that was rumoured and then confirmed is the paperwork: officials removed or softened Nazi Party membership and war-crime connections from the personnel files of recruits so they could be cleared to enter the country. More than 1,600 people were brought over, and their work fed directly into the US space programme and the missile arsenal.

The moral accounting is genuinely contested, and the archive does not pretend otherwise. Von Braun's V-2 was built with forced labour, and more people died making it than were killed by it. The programme's defenders argue that the alternative was Soviet recruitment; its critics argue that justice was traded for technical advantage. What is not contested is that the recruitment happened and the records were sanitised — which is the definition of a cover-up, documented in the government's own files.

Appendix: not a plot, a vindication — Semmelweis and the invisible particles

Some of the best evidence that the establishment can be catastrophically wrong comes from medicine, and the standard case is Ignaz Semmelweis.

In 1847, working at the Vienna General Hospital, Semmelweis noticed that the maternity ward staffed by doctors had a far higher death rate from puerperal fever than the ward staffed by midwives. The doctors came to the ward straight from autopsies. He ordered handwashing in chlorinated lime solution, and mortality in his ward fell sharply — in his reported figures, from around 10% to around 1–2%.

He was not believed. His explanation — “cadaveric particles” carried on hands — had no mechanism anyone accepted, his manner was combative, and he published nothing for years. He lost his post, and in 1865 he was committed to an asylum, where he died at 47 of an infection from a wound.

Germ theory arrived afterwards: Pasteur's work in the 1860s, Koch's identification of specific pathogens in the 1870s–80s. Semmelweis was vindicated, decades too late, and the phrase “Semmelweis reflex” now names the rejection of evidence because it conflicts with consensus.

Why this belongs in this dossier and not in a conspiracy one

Nobody was conspiring. The doctors who rejected Semmelweis were not hiding data; they were reasoning inside a framework that had no place for invisible contagion. That is the more common failure, and the more instructive one: institutional resistance is usually not a plot — it is a paradigm with inertia.

The archive keeps both cases because they are often confused. MKUltra above was a conspiracy: a secret programme, hidden from the public, exposed by documents. Semmelweis was a failure of consensus, exposed by replication. Telling them apart is the difference between history and the stories people tell about history.

Dyatlov Pass

Documented — Largely solved

The facts, without the fog

In late January 1959 a group of nine from the Ural Polytechnic Institute set off to ski across the northern Urals. Their leader was Igor Dyatlov, 23. They were experienced — this was a Grade III route, the hardest Soviet classification.

They camped on the slope of Kholat Syakhl, "Dead Mountain". Searchers later found the tent still standing, cut open from the inside, with most of the group's clothing and boots left behind. Nine sets of footprints led downhill toward the tree line, some in socks, some barefoot.

Two were found under a cedar tree beside a small fire; three more between the tree and the tent, apparently trying to return; four in a ravine, in a makeshift snow shelter. Causes of death: hypothermia for most, and severe chest and skull trauma for the ravine group — injuries, the autopsy said, comparable to a car crash, with no corresponding external wounds.

Small oddities fed the legend: a camera with unexplained frames, slightly elevated radiation on one sweater, and a missing tongue and eyes in one body (consistent with scavenging and decomposition in water). The Soviet investigation closed with "a compelling natural force" and a classified file.

The theories, ranked honestly

  • Infrasound / paradoxical disrobing. Katabatic winds around the mountain could produce infrasound, inducing panic; severe hypothermia famously causes paradoxical undressing. Plausible for the flight and the discarded clothes, but weak on the fractures.
  • Secret weapons test. No test site nearby, no document, no radiation pattern consistent with a blast or fallout.
  • Yeti / UFO / "the unknown". No physical evidence of any kind, and the story only needs them if the avalanche fails — which it no longer does.
  • Slab avalanche. The strongest explanation, and the one that has been modelled.
The 2021 paper

Johan Gaume and Alexander Puzrin published a study in Communications Earth & Environment modelling the specific snow and slope conditions. Their conclusion: a small slab avalanche, delayed by two and a half to nine and a half hours after the slope was cut, was consistent with the injuries — including the chest and skull fractures caused by a low-density snow slab hitting people lying in a ravine — and with the hikers' decision to cut into the tent and flee downhill.

The delayed release is the key insight: it explains why experienced mountaineers camped on a slope that looked safe, and why they left in panic rather than digging out gear.

What remains open

Not everything is nailed down: the exact timing, why the group split, and the minor anomalies in the file. A scientific explanation does not need to account for every detail to be the best available one, and the honest position is "avalanche, with residual uncertainty" rather than "solved beyond question" or "unexplainable".

That is the useful lesson here, and it is the same one as the wider anomalies page: "unexplained" is a statement about the state of the evidence, not a permanent property of an event. Cases get solved, and the legend outlives the solution.

Unresolved Disappearances

Live debate — Still open

Why this page exists

Disappearance is the purest kind of mystery: there is no artifact to argue about, only an absence. That makes these cases unusually vulnerable to storytelling, and unusually good practice for reading evidence carefully. Each entry below separates what is documented, what is the leading explanation, and what nobody knows — and two neighbouring pages, Roanoke and Dyatlov Pass, show what it looks like when a disappearance stops being one.

1 · Flight MH370 Open

On 8 March 2014 a Malaysia Airlines Boeing 777 left Kuala Lumpur for Beijing with 239 people aboard and stopped talking to air traffic control about forty minutes later. Military radar tracked it turning back across the Malay Peninsula and out over the Indian Ocean. Automated satellite "handshakes" continued for hours, and analysis of their timing placed the final position on one of two long arcs; the northern arc was ruled out, leaving a stretch of the southern Indian Ocean west of Australia.

In July 2015 a flaperon from a 777 washed up on Réunion, and further pieces were confirmed as belonging to the aircraft. The underwater search covered 120,000 square kilometres and found nothing; the official search ended in 2017, a private effort in 2018. The aircraft's location is broadly known and its wreck has never been found.

Documented: the diversion, the satellite data, the confirmed debris. Leading explanation: an intentional diversion and a controlled flight into the southern ocean. Unknown: who was flying, why, and where the wreck lies.

2 · The Mary Celeste Open

Found on 5 December 1872 between the Azores and Portugal, the brigantine was under sail with no one aboard, her cargo of industrial alcohol partly emptied, her single lifeboat missing, and the last log entry eleven days old. There was no sign of violence, no bodies, and the ship was still seaworthy enough to be sailed to Gibraltar.

The explanations on offer are all partial: an alcohol-vapour explosion that panicked the crew into the lifeboat, a waterspout, a rogue wave, piracy, insurance fraud. The vapour theory fits the evidence best — nine barrels were empty and the hold showed no fire damage — but it does not explain why the lifeboat was never found and why a competent crew did not simply return to a ship still afloat.

3 · Amelia Earhart Open

Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared on 2 July 1937 while trying to find Howland Island, a two-kilometre speck in the Pacific, at the end of a 4,000-kilometre leg. Radio transmissions were heard, increasingly strained, and then nothing. The US Navy searched 250,000 square miles and found no trace.

The best-supported hypothesis is that they landed on the reef at Nikumaroro, where the international group TIGHAR has recovered artefacts including a fragment of aircraft aluminium and a piece of a shoe, and where human bones were found in 1940 and judged male at the time — a judgement later disputed. It is suggestive, not proven. Claims that they were captured by the Japanese rest on hearsay and a photograph that has been shown to predate the flight.

4 · The Sodder children Open

On Christmas Eve 1945 a house in Fayetteville, West Virginia, burned to the ground. Nine children were inside; four got out, and five — aged five to fourteen — were never found. The fire was intense enough that the family assumed the worst, but no remains were ever recovered from the site, and the house burned quickly enough that an arson inquiry was opened.

The family spent decades investigating: a billboard alongside a highway, a suspicious phone call, a report of children glimpsed in a passing car. The official position is that the children died in the fire. The absence of remains is real and genuinely odd; it is also possible in a hot, collapsing, heavily excavated fire scene. This is the archive's clearest example of a case where a family's refusal to accept a probable answer is entirely understandable and still not evidence.

5 · The MV Joyita Open

In 1955 the Joyita left Samoa for the Tokelau Islands with 25 people and was found five weeks later, half-submerged and abandoned, hundreds of kilometres off course. Her radio was broken and set to a dead channel, her clocks had stopped, and a doctor's bag and the captain's briefcase were missing. Nobody was ever found.

Fiji's inquiry concluded that the vessel had taken on water through a corroded pipe, that the passengers had taken to a raft or been swept off, and that the captain had died trying to raise help. It is a competent explanation with holes in it — the missing briefcase, the state of the radio — and no better one has replaced it.

6 · Percy Fawcett Open

The British explorer walked into the Mato Grosso in 1925 with his son and a companion, looking for a lost city he called "Z", and never came out. Over the following decades, dozens of people died or vanished looking for him. His final letter said he would proceed without guides and expected to be delayed.

The most plausible account is that the party perished in the forest or was killed by an indigenous group defending its territory — a scenario supported by oral accounts collected much later. The romantic version, that Fawcett found his city and chose to stay, has no evidence at all. Archaeology since the 2000s has found large pre-Columbian settlements in the Amazon, which vindicates part of his intuition without rescuing his expedition.

7 · The Moptera and the small cases

Most disappearances are quiet. Fishing boats, solo hikers, people who walked out of hospitals. Official statistics on missing persons are large — the FBI's missing-persons file runs to tens of thousands of open cases at any time — and the overwhelming majority resolve, usually within days, without a mystery.

The famous cases above are famous because they are photogenic, not because they are representative. Reading them well means holding two things at once: something genuinely unexplained happened, and the most likely explanation is still something ordinary that left no trace.

The pattern in all seven

Every case has the same shape. A real event; a document trail that stops; an explanation that fits most of the evidence; and a residue nobody can close. The honest label is "open", and an open case is not evidence for anything specific — not for aliens, not for conspiracy, and not for the supernatural.

Where a case does close, it closes on evidence: the Dyatlov Pass avalanche model, the Croatoan carving and hidden fort, the Romanov graves. That is the standard worth applying everywhere.

The Voynich Manuscript

Live debate — Genuinely unsolved

What it is

A codex of about 240 vellum pages, now Beinecke MS 408 at Yale, named after Wilfrid Voynich, the book dealer who bought it in 1912. It contains an unknown script — written left to right, in a fluent, practised hand — alongside illustrations: plants that match no known species, astronomical/astrological diagrams with zodiac symbols, and pages of small figures bathing in interconnected pools.

Radiocarbon dating of the vellum in 2009 gave a range of roughly 1404–1438. The inks are consistent with that period. This is the one hard fact that constrains everything else: it is not a modern forgery made on old blank parchment, unless the forger was extraordinarily well equipped.

Its provenance is documented from the sixteenth century: it appears in the collection of Rudolf II in Prague, was owned by the alchemist Georg Baresch, then Athanasius Kircher, and passed through the Jesuit college at Frascati before Voynich.

Why it resists

The text behaves oddly in ways that are measurably real. Word-length distribution, Zipf's-law behaviour and the repetition of common tokens all look language-like rather than random. But the vocabulary is small and repetitive, there are almost no corrections, and the same words recur in similar positions across sections — properties consistent with a constructed language, a cipher with a small plaintext vocabulary, or a very careful hoax.

That combination is what defeats attempts. A cipher needs a key or a crib — a known plaintext to anchor the mapping — and no crib has ever been identified. A natural language needs identifiable roots, and none have been convincingly matched.

The decipherment claims

Every few years a new solution is announced: a Turkish scholar's claim, a "proto-Romance" reading, an elaborate acrostic, a Hebrew cipher, an Aztec connection. The pattern is consistent — the method is applied, a few words appear to make sense, and then the reading fails to generalise, or requires a different substitution for each section, or produces text nobody else can reproduce.

Properly evaluating these is not snobbery. A real decipherment (Egyptian hieroglyphs, Linear B, Mayan) had three features: it explained the whole corpus, it predicted readings of new passages, and independent specialists could apply it. No Voynich claim has managed the third.

What the honest answer is

We do not know what it says, whether it says anything, or who made it. The leading candidates are a cipher of a natural language, a constructed language or personal code, and a hoax designed to look meaningful — and the evidence does not currently distinguish them.

"Unsolved" is the correct scientific answer here, and it is worth contrasting with the claims that manufacture a solution. The archive keeps this page in Live debate because the argument is real and ongoing, not because the mystery is being protected.

One useful consequence: the Voynich is the best available test of intellectual honesty about unreadable evidence. Anyone who tells you they have cracked it should be asked the same three questions — does it explain everything, does it predict, and can others reproduce it?

Oak Island

Debunked — Two centuries, no treasure

The story

In 1795 a young man named Daniel McGinnis reported a circular depression on Oak Island, Nova Scotia, with a block-and-tackle hanging above it and a sapling at its centre. Digging revealed layers of logs at regular intervals, then a stone slab inscribed with symbols, then — depending on the teller — a platform, a cipher stone, and flood tunnels that fill any shaft with seawater as soon as it is opened.

From there the legend assembled its cast: Captain Kidd's hoard, Spanish gold, the lost treasure of the Templars, Francis Bacon's manuscripts proving he wrote Shakespeare, the Holy Grail, the Ark of the Covenant. Every generation of diggers has had a preferred answer, and none has been found.

What the record actually shows

  • Nothing has ever been recovered. Not a coin, not a chest, not an inscription verified in situ. The famous "90-foot stone" has never been produced for examination.
  • Every generation has destroyed the evidence the next one needed. Shafts were dug, flooded, collapsed, re-dug, and in places dynamited. The original feature is gone.
  • The "flood tunnels" have natural explanations. Oak Island is karst-like terrain in a tidal bay; seawater intrusion into excavations is exactly what the geology predicts.
  • The finds are ambiguous. Coconut fibre and old wood have been reported and dated to periods earlier than the diggers — interesting, but consistent with shipwreck debris, ballast, or later contamination of disturbed ground.
Why the legend survives anyway

Because it has the perfect structure for an endless story: a specific place, a promise, a technical puzzle, and a reason why each failure does not count. The money pit is unfalsifiable in practice — every collapse is "the trap working", every empty shaft is "we were close".

Add a reality-television economy that rewards new theories, and you have a machine that has run for two centuries. The Tartaria dossier describes the same engine applied to buildings.

The honest verdict

There may be something buried on Oak Island — people bury things. But the specific claim, that an engineered treasure vault with booby-trapped flood tunnels sits under the island, has had 230 years of testing and produced no treasure, no structure, and no document. Under this archive's standard that is a failed claim, not an open one.

The genuinely interesting history is the digging itself: the companies, the investors, the presidents and actors who bought in, and the way a local story became an industry. That is documented, and it is stranger than the treasure.

Who Wrote Shakespeare?

Debunked — Consensus stands

The question

William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon — actor, shareholder in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, son of a glove-maker — is credited on the title pages of the plays published in his lifetime, and named by contemporaries as their author. The "authorship question" holds that this is a front, and that the real author was someone with the education, travel and court connections the plays seem to require.

The candidates have included Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe (dead in 1593, which requires a conspiracy of remarkable efficiency), Edward de Vere the 17th Earl of Oxford (dead in 1604, which requires plays written after his death), the 6th Earl of Derby, and Mary Sidney.

What the evidence actually is

  • Title pages. Printed plays of the period name "William Shakespeare" as author. Attribution in the theatre was a commercial matter, not a secret.
  • Contemporary testimony. Ben Jonson's poem in the First Folio (1623) addresses Shakespeare directly; the Folio's editors were his fellow actors, who had performed the plays.
  • Local documents. Stratford records, the purchase of New Place, a share in the Globe's tithes, the 1616 will, the monument — an ordinary successful professional life, documented in the way such lives were.
  • Stylometry. Computational analyses of function words, verse habits and spelling patterns consistently cluster the canon with Shakespeare and not with the candidates. Modern studies also show collaboration — with Fletcher, Middleton, Peele — which is exactly what a working playwright's career looks like.
  • Hand D. The manuscript of Sir Thomas More contains three pages in a hand that palaeographers identify as Shakespeare's, writing a scene of the kind the canon contains.
Why the question persists

It began as an argument from class. Delia Bacon's 1857 book assumed a Stratford tradesman could not have the learning on display. That assumption is the engine of the whole tradition, and it has not aged well.

It is unfalsifiable in the direction it needs. Any document naming Shakespeare is explained as part of the cover; any gap in his biography is explained as proof. That is the same structure as phantom time.

It is more interesting than the truth. A nobleman with a secret is a better story than a jobbing actor who wrote fast, collaborated, and made money — which is what the record shows.

Where the sceptics have a fair point

We do not have a single surviving literary manuscript of a Shakespeare play in his hand, and the biographical record is thin by modern standards. That is a real gap and worth saying plainly. It is also true of almost every playwright of the period — the theatre was a collaborative, disposable business, and paper was reused.

The honest statement is: the evidence is strong, documentary and convergent, and it does not depend on trusting a single source. That is more than can be said for any of the alternatives.

Did Hitler Escape?

Debunked — Refuted

What is documented

By late April 1945 the Red Army was in Berlin. Hitler married Eva Braun on 29 April, dictated a will, and died on 30 April in the Führerbunker. The bodies were carried outside, burned in a shell crater, and buried nearby.

Soviet forces found the remains within days. The identification rested on dental work: Hitler's dentist and his assistant were located and reconstructed his bridge and teeth from memory and X-rays, and the match was accepted in a Soviet report of 1945. The jawbone and a skull fragment were retained.

In 1970 the remains were exhumed again and destroyed, with the jawbone kept in Moscow. In 2009 a DNA study of the skull fragment found it belonged to a woman, and was probably not Hitler's — a genuine correction that conspiracy writers seized on. It changes nothing about the dental identification, which is the actual evidence.

The escape story

The strong version: Hitler and Braun left Berlin in the last days, travelled via U-boat (or aircraft to Spain, then by ship) to Argentina, and lived quietly, with sightings reported for decades. A 2018 book by a journalist and a 2022 History Channel series repeated versions of it.

Supporting claims typically include: the FBI investigated and its files are "proof" (they are records of tips, not findings), Argentina's postwar tolerance of Nazis (real, and well documented), and the confusion of the final days (also real).

Why the escape fails

The identification is dental, and it was corroborated twice. Two independent dentists reconstructed his unusual bridgework from memory and from X-rays; the recovered jaw matched. That is strong forensic evidence, and it was obtained by people with every incentive to be certain.

The route is not physically plausible. Berlin was encircled; the airfields were under fire; the harbour exits were watched. Getting a recognisable dictator and his companion out through that, then across an ocean, would require a level of coordination that left no trace in Allied signals intelligence — which was reading a great deal of German traffic in 1945.

Submarine veterans kept records. The U-boat force's movements in May 1945 are documented by both sides, including the surrender operations. No unexplained long-range voyage appears.

No positive evidence exists. Decades of searches, including Argentine and Brazilian police work, produced no documents, graves or confirmed associates. The claim is maintained by anomalies, not by finds — the same structure as Oak Island.

Why it persists

Two reasons, both worth naming. First, the war's end was genuinely chaotic, and the Western Allies had an interest in not publicising a Soviet identification they could not verify — a gap that invites speculation. Second, the escape narrative is a way of refusing closure on a figure people would prefer to imagine still standing trial.

The comparison is with the Anastasia case: in both, a story about a survivor outlived the forensic identification of the remains, and in both, DNA ended the question for anyone willing to read it.

Did Anastasia Survive?

Debunked — Ended by DNA

The execution

In the early hours of 17 July 1918, Nicholas II, Alexandra, their five children and four servants were shot in the cellar of the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg. The bodies were taken to a mineshaft, then moved and buried under railway sleepers. The Soviet state admitted the execution but never disclosed the burial site.

That gap — an official story with no graves — is what made the survival stories possible. For seventy years, "the remains were never found" was literally true.

Anna Anderson

In 1920 a woman was pulled from a Berlin canal and admitted to an asylum. She eventually claimed to be Grand Duchess Anastasia, and spent the rest of her life in litigation and publicity, supported by some Romanov relatives and rejected by others. She died in 1984.

Her case was always weak on specifics: she spoke no Russian, her knowledge of the family was patchy, and her account changed. But she had a remarkable resemblance, and the absence of graves meant nothing could be checked.

What settled it

The graves were found in 1991. Nine sets of remains were excavated near Yekaterinburg and identified through dental work, bone measurements and DNA. Two bodies were missing — Alexei and one daughter — which kept the story alive for another sixteen years.

Anna Anderson was not a Romanov. In 1994 mitochondrial DNA from a tissue sample was compared with Prince Philip, a great-nephew of Alexandra, and with the remains: she did not match. She was later linked to a Polish factory worker, Franziska Schanzkowska.

The missing two were found in 2007. A second burial site produced the remains of Alexei and a daughter, identified by DNA. All seven family members are now accounted for.

Why the story still circulates

Because it is a good story about escape, and because the Soviet state's secrecy gave it decades of oxygen. It also attaches to something real: several impostors did emerge, and some were believed by people who wanted the family to have survived.

The archive's interest is in the method. This is a case where a claim was not defeated by argument but by identification — the same kind of closure that the Hitler escape story resists, and that phantom time cannot accept at all.

The Lost Colony

Live debate — Mystery mostly explained

The sequence

In 1587 John White led a group of about 115 settlers to Roanoke Island, off what is now North Carolina. White sailed back to England for supplies and was unable to return for three years — England was at war with Spain, and every ship was needed against the Armada.

When he finally reached Roanoke in August 1590, the settlement was dismantled. The houses had been taken apart, not destroyed. On a post was carved the word CROATOAN; on a nearby tree, CRO. White had agreed with the colonists that if they moved they would carve the name of their destination, and that if they were in danger they would carve a cross. There was no cross.

White wanted to search Croatoan Island (modern Hatteras) immediately. Bad weather and a damaged ship forced the expedition back to England, and he never returned.

The evidence for assimilation

  • The settlement was taken down carefully. That indicates a planned move, not a massacre or a panicked flight.
  • The destination was named. Croatoan was the island of the Croatoan people, whose leader Manteo had travelled to England and was an ally.
  • Later reports. English expeditions in the 1600s were told by local peoples of Europeans living inland, and of people with blue eyes and grey eyes among the Tuscarora and other groups. These are second-hand, but they are consistent.
  • The map. In 2012 researchers at the British Museum found a patch on White's 1590 map concealing a symbol for a fort, further inland at the head of Albemarle Sound, in an area the colonists had discussed moving to. Excavations at that site ("Site X") have produced late-sixteenth-century English and Native artefacts together.
What is not claimed

Nobody has proved the colonists' fate in detail, and the "Site X" work is suggestive rather than conclusive. The honest position is that a planned relocation toward the Croatoan, followed by absorption into local communities over years, fits every piece of evidence — the dismantled houses, the carved destination, the absence of a danger sign, and the later reports.

The "vanished colony" is a later framing, and it required ignoring the colonists' own message. Compare lost continents: a real place, renamed by people who were not there.

Why the story became supernatural

Because a disappearance is a better story than a merger. Roanoke entered American folklore as an eerie blank, and the blanks attract explanations — pirates, Spanish raiders, a storm, disease, the "lost" tribe. Some are possible; none is needed to explain what the colonists themselves wrote down.

The lesson is one this archive keeps returning to: the primary source usually answers the question, and it is usually less exciting than the legend.

The Bosnian Pyramids

Debunked — Geology, not architecture

The claim

In 2005 the Bosnian-American businessman Semir Osmanagić announced that a group of hills near Visoko — principally Visočica — were in fact pyramids built by an unknown civilisation around 12,000 years ago. He named them the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon, the Pyramid of the Dragon, and so on, and reported tunnels, concrete-like blocks and ancient inscriptions.

The claim found a large audience, a foundation, and a tourist economy. It has also produced years of excavation, some of it damaging genuine archaeological sites.

What geologists found

  • The "pyramid" faces are bedding planes. Visočica is a hill of layered sedimentary rock — breccia and conglomerate — tilted and eroded into a roughly pyramidal shape. The regular "steps" are the layers, not courses of masonry.
  • The "blocks" are natural. The angular slabs are fractured bedrock and tectonic blocks, a common feature of the local geology.
  • The "tunnels" are old mines. The passages under Visoko are documented medieval and later mining galleries, not a prehistoric complex.
  • The dating is not supported. There is no archaeological assemblage, no inscription in situ, and no structure that requires builders.
The professional response

In 2006 the European Association of Archaeologists issued a statement calling the project pseudoarchaeology and expressing concern about the destruction of real medieval and earlier remains. Individual geologists and archaeologists — including specialists sent by Bosnian institutions — reached the same conclusion independently.

Osmanagić's response has been that the experts are defending a closed paradigm. That is a familiar move in this archive: it converts the absence of evidence into evidence of a cover-up, the same shape as Tartaria and phantom time.

Why it worked

Because the hills look like pyramids from certain angles, the country had a hard recent history and wanted a grand ancient identity, and the claim arrived with a photogenic story, a visitor centre and a budget. Tourism is a real force in pseudoarchaeology, and it is not a small one.

The honest comparison is Devils Tower: a natural formation with a striking, regular geometry that looks designed. Geology produces regular shapes constantly — columns, layers, joints — and the test is always the same: is there anything that could only have been made?

Lead and Crime

Live debate — Strong correlation, contested cause

The claim

Children exposed to lead — from petrol additive, paint, water pipes and industrial dust — show measurable effects on impulse control, attention and aggression. If a whole generation was exposed and then a whole generation was not, violent crime should rise and then fall about twenty years later, when each cohort reaches its peak offending age.

The hypothesis was pushed hardest by Rick Nevin, an economist, and by Jessica Wolpaw Reyes, whose 2007 paper in Environmental Research found that childhood lead exposure explained a substantial share of the variation in violent crime across US states, with the expected lag.

The timing is striking. Lead was removed from American petrol between 1975 and 1986; violent crime peaked around 1991–1993 and fell steeply for two decades. The same pattern appears, with different timings, in many other countries.

Where the science is strong

  • Individual-level effects are well established. Cohort studies link childhood lead exposure to lower IQ, attention problems, and behavioural measures associated with impulsivity. The dose–response relationship is consistent.
  • Natural experiments support it. The Flint water crisis produced documented rises in children's blood lead and measurable developmental effects. Communities with abrupt exposure changes show corresponding changes.
  • Mechanism is plausible. Lead disrupts neurotransmitter systems and brain development in ways that could plausibly affect self-regulation.
Where it is contested

Ecological fallacy. Population-level correlation between lead and crime does not prove that the individuals committing crimes were the exposed ones.

Confounding. The same decades saw abortion legalisation, policing changes, demographic shifts, crack's rise and fall, and economic restructuring. A single variable explaining a large share of a complex trend is a strong claim.

Cross-national inconsistency. Some countries with different lead timelines do not fit the model neatly, and replication has been mixed.

The effect size is disputed. Estimates range from "a major driver" to "one contributor among many". The literature has not converged.

The honest verdict

This is genuinely a live scientific debate, not a conspiracy and not settled. The strongest defensible statement is that lead exposure is a real cause of neurological and behavioural harm, that removing it was one of the great public-health wins of the century, and that it plausibly contributed to the crime decline — with the size of that contribution still argued.

What makes it valuable to this archive is the contrast with documented corporate concealment: the lead industry's own history of suppressing evidence is well documented, and the harm is not in doubt. The uncertainty is about the crime statistics, not about whether lead was dangerous.

Secret Tests

Documented — Declassified

1. Operation Sea-Spray, 1950

In September 1950 the US Navy released clouds of Serratia marcescens and other bacteria from a ship in San Francisco Bay, to test how a city might be exposed in a biological attack. The tests were secret. Eleven people were later identified as having been exposed, and one died of a Serratia infection — though whether the spray caused it has been debated by specialists.

It was revealed in Senate hearings in 1977, alongside a set of similar military tests in American cities and subway systems. The government apologised.

2. Project Sunshine, 1953 onwards

The Atomic Energy Commission collected thousands of human tissue and bone samples — including from dead infants and stillbirths — from around the world, without consent, to measure strontium-90 from atmospheric nuclear tests. The project's existence became public in the 1990s through declassified files and journalism.

It is the clearest example of the pattern: a programme that was scientifically serious, ethically indefensible, and entirely hidden until the archive opened.

3. Acoustic Kitty

The CIA spent several years and a reported $20 million trying to turn a cat into a listening device, implanting a microphone and transmitter and wiring the animal's nervous system. The project was declassified in 2001. It failed for a simple reason: cats do not take direction, and the first field test reportedly ended with the cat being hit by a taxi.

4. The heart-attack gun

In 1975 the Church Committee was shown a CIA device that fired a tiny dart coated with a toxin — saxitoxin or a shellfish poison — designed to produce a heart attack that would be hard to attribute. It was never confirmed to have been used on a person, and the agency's own stockpiles were ordered destroyed.

5. The "gay bomb"

In 1994 a laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base submitted a proposal for a "harassment" weapon using strong pheromones to make enemy soldiers sexually irresistible to one another. It was a funding proposal, never built, and was withdrawn after publicity. It is often cited as evidence of military absurdity; it is better read as evidence of what a bad idea looks like on paper.

What these cases teach

Secret programmes are documented, not inferred. Every item above has a file, a hearing or a declassification date. That is the standard Proven Conspiracies applies to everything else in this archive.

The ethical failure is usually consent. Sea-Spray and Sunshine were not secret because the science was dubious; they were secret because the public was not asked.

Capability is not intent. A programme that built a device is not evidence of its use — a distinction conspiracy literature routinely collapses.

The line to draw

The existence of these programmes is a legitimate reason to distrust official denials. It is not a reason to believe any specific claim about present-day activity, which still needs its own evidence. The archive's rule holds: the fact that they did it before is a prior, not a proof.

Unknown Mysteries

Live debate — Explained, mostly

The Bermuda Triangle

The Triangle is a region of the western North Atlantic, loosely bounded by Miami, Bermuda and Puerto Rico, in which ships, aircraft and people are said to have vanished without explanation. It is the model case for this archive because its construction is fully documented.

How the story was built

  • 1950

    An Associated Press story by Edward Van Winkle Jones clusters several losses in the region — the first press treatment.

  • 1964

    Vincent Gaddis publishes “The Deadly Bermuda Triangle” in Argosy, giving the region its name.

  • 1974

    Charles Berlitz’s bestseller The Bermuda Triangle turns it into an international industry, complete with Atlantis and lost technology.

  • 1975

    Larry Kusche publishes The Bermuda Triangle Mystery — Solved, checking each incident against the original reports. He finds them inaccurate, exaggerated or unverified, and finds no excess of losses compared with any other heavily travelled ocean region.

What actually explains the losses

NOAA’s own fact page is refreshingly flat about it. The majority of Atlantic tropical storms and hurricanes pass through the area, and before modern forecasting those storms sank ships routinely. The Gulf Stream produces rapid and sometimes violent weather changes. The Caribbean has many islands and large areas of shallow, treacherous water. And the region sits near the agonic line, where magnetic north and true north align — which historically confused compass navigation.

Flight 19 — five Navy torpedo bombers lost in December 1945 — is real and remains a genuine tragedy. It is also a case of a flight leader becoming disoriented, refusing to switch to a backup compass, and leading the group out to sea, followed by a rescue seaplane lost in bad weather.

The popular “methane bubbles capsize ships” idea is a real physical phenomenon in principle, but as BBC Science Focus notes, USGS studies record no significant methane releases in the area in the past 15,000 years.

The two structural tricks

A loose definition. A boundary that can be redrawn lets any incident be included. A vessel lost near the Azores, or north of Bermuda, can be pulled in after the fact.

Base-rate blindness. The Triangle is one of the busiest shipping and flying corridors on Earth. More traffic will always produce more losses. The correct comparison is losses per vessel-mile, and when that comparison is made, the anomaly disappears.

The Nazca Lines

The geoglyphs of the Nazca Desert in southern Peru — hundreds of figures, lines and trapezoids scraped into the desert pavement — are genuinely mysterious in the sense that their purpose is still argued. They are not mysterious in the sense that they require aliens.

What they probably were

  • Water and fertility ritual. The strongest scholarly reading, associated with Johan Reinhard, is that the lines led to places where rituals were performed to obtain water and agricultural fertility. Many of the animal figures are motifs associated with rain and water, and appear on Nazca pottery too.
  • Paths and gathering places. A 2026 study argues that earlier hillside geoglyphs sit on trails and were visible from long distances — markers for routes and camps, which later became places for gathering and feasting.
  • Astronomical alignment. Proposed by Paul Kosok in 1941 and developed by Maria Reiche over forty years. A 2021 re-analysis found that only a small number of geoglyphs had plausible alignments to a star or solstice — not enough to support the calendar hypothesis as a whole.
  • Not aliens. Gerald Hawkins and others examined and rejected the ancient-astronaut interpretations in the late 1960s and early 1970s.

The honest position is that several purposes probably coexisted over centuries: processional paths, water rituals, markers, and designs meant to be seen by deities from above rather than by people.

Genuinely open cases

It would be a mistake to conclude that everything is solved. There are real artefacts and events with no consensus explanation — the Voynich manuscript’s script and language, the 1959 Dyatlov Pass deaths, the fate of the Roanoke colony. Each has a substantial literature and competing hypotheses.

The distinction that matters is not “explained vs. unexplained”. It is “explained vs. unexplainable”. Most mysteries in this archive are the first. The ones that stay open are open because the evidence is genuinely insufficient — not because a force is at work.

The rule this page teaches

Before accepting that something is unexplained, check three things: whether the primary reports say what the retelling says; whether the comparison group is fair; and whether the boundary was fixed before or after the data. Almost every celebrated mystery fails at least one.

The Hubble Tension

Live debate

Two ways to weigh the same universe

The early-universe route reads the cosmic microwave background — the afterglow of the Big Bang — and fits a cosmological model to its ripples. Planck's 2018 result gives about 67.4 km/s per megaparsec. Because the CMB is a snapshot at 380,000 years, this route extrapolates across all of cosmic history using the standard model.

The local route builds a distance ladder: parallax in the Milky Way, then Cepheid variables in nearby galaxies, then Type Ia supernovae further out. The SH0ES team's answer is about 73 km/s per megaparsec. It measures the expansion here and now, with far fewer model assumptions.

The disagreement is not between two opinions; it is between two measurements. If both are right, the standard cosmological model is incomplete — which is why the phrase 'new physics' keeps appearing.

Why it has not gone away

The gap has survived a decade of attacks on systematics, and has grown as the error bars have shrunk. The obvious suspects have been checked: Cepheid crowding, dust, the calibration of the distance ladder, the handling of the CMB's foregrounds.

The James Webb Space Telescope was the decisive test many expected. If the Cepheid measurements were contaminated by crowding in Hubble's images, JWST's sharper infrared view would show it. Instead the JWST calibrations broadly reproduced the local ladder, leaving the tension roughly where it was.

That result is why the field now treats the tension as a real feature of the data rather than a mistake waiting to be found.

What could actually resolve it

Early dark energy. A component that briefly dominated before recombination would shrink the sound horizon and raise the inferred present-day rate. It fits, and it is contrived: the same mechanism tends to spoil other successes of the model.

A revised distance ladder. A systematic in the Cepheid calibration that has escaped every audit so far. Possible, but the burden of proof is now on this explanation.

Something else entirely. Interacting dark matter, a varying equation of state, extra relativistic species. All are constrained, none is excluded, and each fixes one number while disturbing others.

The honest status

This is the cleanest example in modern physics of a measurement problem that may be a discovery. Five sigma is the conventional threshold for claiming an effect; the tension has crossed it, which does not mean new physics — it means the probability that both measurements are correct within the standard model is small enough to demand an answer.

The resolution will not be rhetorical. Either a new component is found that fits the CMB and the ladder together, or a systematic is found that moves one of the numbers. Until then, the two values stay on the page, side by side, which is exactly how a live debate should look.

MOND

Live debate

The observation that would not go away

In the 1970s, Vera Rubin and others measured how fast galaxies rotate. The outer parts move as if there were far more mass than the stars and gas can account for. The standard answer is dark matter — an invisible halo holding the disk in.

In 1983, Mordehai Milgrom proposed a different reading: the rotation curves are not evidence of missing mass but of a modified force law. Below a characteristic acceleration a₀, the pull of gravity falls off as 1/r rather than 1/r². Flat rotation curves follow immediately, with one parameter and no per-galaxy tuning.

Where it works remarkably well

The radial acceleration relation is the strongest evidence. Across hundreds of galaxies, the observed acceleration tracks the predicted one with very little scatter, over five orders of magnitude. That is a regularity dark-matter simulations had to be tuned to reproduce.

MOND also predicted, before observation, that low-surface-brightness galaxies would rotate faster than they appear to warrant, and it anticipated features of the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation. Predictions that come true before the data are the currency of a good theory.

Where it fails

Clusters of galaxies. MOND still needs roughly twice the mass it accounts for in cluster cores. Dark matter handles clusters without extra parts.

The Bullet Cluster. The mass, mapped by gravitational lensing, sits apart from the hot gas that collided. That separation is natural if the mass is dark matter and awkward if gravity is the only thing being modified.

The cosmic microwave background. The acoustic peaks fit a dark-matter model closely; MOND requires additional components to match them.

Relativistic completion. MOND is a non-relativistic law. TeVeS and similar extensions exist, and are heavily constrained by gravitational-wave speed and lensing data.

Why it is still worth taking seriously

Because the alternative has its own embarrassments, and because MOND's successes are not decorative. A theory that predicts galaxy-scale regularities with one constant is telling you something about the data, even if it is not the final law.

The most likely resolution is a hybrid: dark matter on cluster and cosmic scales, with a modified or emergent gravitational behaviour appearing in the low-acceleration regime. That is not elegant, but neither is the current standoff.

Dark Matter

Live debate

The evidence is not one measurement

Galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing by clusters, the temperature pattern of the cosmic microwave background, the formation of large-scale structure, and the dynamics of colliding clusters all point the same way: about five-sixths of the matter is not the matter we can see.

The CMB is the strongest single argument. Its acoustic peaks encode the ratio of ordinary to total matter, and the fit requires dark matter to be cold — slow-moving — and to interact weakly or not at all with light.

The candidates, and their scoresheets

WIMPs were the favourite for thirty years: heavy, weakly interacting, thermally produced in the early universe, and detectable in deep underground detectors. LUX, XENONnT, PandaX and others have pushed sensitivity down by orders of magnitude and found nothing. The simplest models are now strongly constrained.

Axions are ultra-light and were introduced to solve a different problem — why the strong force preserves a symmetry it need not. ADMX and haloscope experiments are searching in the plausible mass range. No detection yet, and the parameter space remains large.

Sterile neutrinos would be a fourth neutrino, heavier and non-interacting except through mixing. Some oscillation anomalies hinted at one; most have since been explained by detector effects.

Primordial black holes formed in the first second could cover part of the mass range. Microlensing surveys exclude them at many masses, but an asteroid-mass window survives — and LIGO's black-hole mergers keep the idea alive.

The persistent worry

Four decades of null results is not proof that dark matter is wrong, but it is a signal that the field's favourite guess may have been the wrong shape. The phrase 'dark matter' describes a set of gravitational facts; it does not name a particle.

That distinction matters, because it is easy to argue against a particle nobody has found while ignoring the lensing maps that require it. Modified gravity is a serious competitor at galaxy scales, and it fails at cluster scales — which is itself informative.

What would settle it

A direct detection, a laboratory production of a dark-matter candidate, or an astrophysical signature that distinguishes particle dark matter from modified gravity. The next generation of detectors, and the next generation of sky surveys, are aimed at all three.

Until then the honest position is: the phenomenon is documented, the explanation is open, and the most popular explanation has been losing ground for a decade.

Planet Nine

Live debate

The clustering

In 2016, Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown pointed at a set of extreme trans-Neptunian objects whose orbits share an argument of perihelion — they swing closest to the Sun in the same direction, tilted the same way. For six objects drawn from a supposed random distribution, the alignment is unlikely at roughly the 0.1% level.

Their explanation is a planet of five to ten Earth masses on an eccentric orbit hundreds of astronomical units out, inclined about 30 degrees to the plane. Simulations with such a planet reproduce the alignment and predict additional populations — some perpendicular orbits, some retrograde — which have since been partially observed.

The alternatives

Observational bias. We find objects where we look, and surveys have not covered the sky uniformly. A clustering in the discovery data can be a clustering in the telescopes.

A self-gravitating disk. A population of smaller bodies on inclined orbits can maintain the alignment collectively, without a planet — a proposal that has gained traction since 2023.

The galactic tide. The Milky Way's gravitational field stretches the outer solar system, and can imprint alignments that a planet is then invoked to explain.

Why it is not found yet

The predicted orbit is far away and slow: a planet at 400–800 AU takes ten thousand years or more to complete an orbit, and is faint in reflected light. Most of the sky has not been surveyed to the necessary depth.

The Vera Rubin Observatory's repeated all-sky imaging is the first survey capable of covering the search space systematically. If Planet Nine exists and is not absurdly dark, the next few years should find it — or the non-detection will constrain the hypothesis sharply.

The honest status

This is a live debate in the good sense: a specific, testable prediction, made publicly, with a defined observation that would settle it. That is rarer than it sounds.

Two cautions. First, 'Planet Nine' is not Nibiru — there is no connection to the collision myth, no 3,600-year orbit crossing the inner solar system, and no role in any doomsday claim. Second, the clustering evidence has weakened as more objects are found, which is exactly how a hypothesis should be treated: the sample grew, and the signal needs re-testing.

‘Oumuamua

Live debate

What was actually observed

1I/2017 U1 was discovered by Pan-STARRS in October 2017, already leaving. Its trajectory was hyperbolic — it came from interstellar space and will not return. It brightened and dimmed in a way suggesting an elongated, tumbling body, and spectroscopy showed a reddish surface without the usual cometary coma.

The key anomaly is small and real: a non-gravitational acceleration, about 10⁻⁴ m/s², consistent with outgassing — except no gas was detected, and the object's brightness variation implies an extreme shape (very elongated, or a flat sheet).

The natural explanations

A hydrogen iceberg. A body of frozen hydrogen would sublimate at exactly the right rate and produce no visible dust. The proposed formation route — in the dense cores of giant molecular clouds — is plausible, and the model fits the acceleration.

A nitrogen-ice shard. Stripped from the surface of a Pluto-like body, nitrogen ice would also sublimate invisibly and explain the flat, bright shape.

A dust-covered comet or a fractal aggregate, where the outgassing is real but faint, and the odd brightness comes from an unusual geometry.

The lightsail claim

Avi Loeb argued that a thin artificial sail could produce the same acceleration from radiation pressure alone, without any outgassing. It is a legitimate hypothesis in the narrow sense: it fits some of the data.

It is not the best explanation. It requires an artefact, its predictions were not made in advance, and the natural models that have been developed since fit the same anomaly with known physics. An extraordinary claim needs to beat the alternatives, and it has not.

The lasting value of the episode is procedural: it showed how quickly a small anomaly becomes a story, and how much careful modelling it takes to say 'probably a rock'. The archive's frontier index lists it as a live debate because the composition is genuinely unsettled — not because the artefact reading is.

What would settle it

Nothing can: the object is gone. That is the central frustration. The resolution has to come from statistics — if interstellar objects are common, the next ones can be characterised better. Rubin Observatory is expected to find many more, and a future dedicated intercept mission has been proposed.

So the correct status is: an anomaly with several viable natural explanations, no decisive data, and a famous minority claim that has outrun its evidence.

Phosphine on Venus

Live debate

The claim

In September 2020, a team led by Jane Greaves reported phosphine in Venus's cloud decks, detected in the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope and ALMA data at about 20 parts per billion. On Earth, phosphine is produced by anaerobic microbes and industry; on Venus, no known chemistry makes it in those quantities.

The result was carefully hedged by its authors — a possible biosignature, not evidence of life — and it was reported far less carefully by everyone else.

The takedown

The immediate objection was spectroscopic: the phosphine line sits close to a sulfur dioxide absorption feature, and the ALMA data were processed in a way that may have introduced a false signal. Reanalyses found the detection significance dropping sharply, in some cases to nothing.

The original team published a revised analysis with a much weaker claim. Subsequent work has argued both ways — some independent groups report a residual signal in reprocessed data, others find the line explained entirely by SO₂ and calibration effects.

Why it is still a live question

Because Venus's clouds are the most habitable place in the solar system outside Earth: 30–60 km up, the pressure and temperature are close to terrestrial, and the sulfuric acid droplets are a plausible solvent for exotic chemistry.

And because the underlying puzzle has not gone away. Even at reduced significance, the reported abundances are hard to explain with known Venus chemistry, which is why the argument is about measurement rather than about what would follow if it were true.

The honest label is 'live debate' — the detection is contested, the interpretation is speculative, and nobody has produced a decisive measurement either way. NASA's DAVINCI and VERITAS missions, and ESA's EnVision, will make the atmospheric measurements that matter.

What would settle it

A direct atmospheric probe with a mass spectrometer — not remote sensing — measuring phosphine and its isotopes in situ. Isotopic ratios would distinguish biological from geological production, if anything is there at all.

Until then: a single contested line, a lot of careful spectroscopy, and a planet that has been misread before. Venus was once described as a swamp; the lesson of that error is that remote inference about Venus is hard.

Primordial Black Holes

Live debate

The idea

Stephen Hawking pointed out in 1971 that density fluctuations in the very early universe could collapse directly into black holes, without going through a star. Their masses would depend on when they formed: tiny ones from the earliest moments, asteroid-mass ones later, solar-mass ones later still.

The appeal for dark matter is obvious. Black holes interact only gravitationally, they are cold, and they are not invented for the purpose. If enough formed, they solve the missing-mass problem without any new particle.

The constraints

Microlensing. Surveys watching millions of stars for brief brightening events constrain compact objects in the mass range from about a lunar mass to tens of solar masses. The EROS and OGLE results exclude primordial black holes as all of dark matter across much of that range.

The cosmic microwave background. Accreting primordial black holes would inject energy and distort the CMB; the measured spectrum limits how much mass they can carry.

LIGO. Merging black holes of 30 solar masses were a surprise, and the idea that they are primordial has not been excluded — it is one of the few windows still open.

An asteroid-mass window around 10¹⁷ grams survives, because such holes are too small to lens effectively and too faint to accrete visibly. It is the last large hiding place.

Why it matters more than it sounds

If primordial black holes are dark matter, then dark matter is not a new particle and the search programme for WIMPs and axions is looking in the wrong place. That would be the most consequential negative result in the field.

Primordial black holes also give a natural explanation for the black-hole mergers LIGO sees, and for the existence of massive black holes very early in cosmic history — a problem the James Webb Space Telescope has made sharper.

The counterweight is that no positive detection exists. Every claim to date has been either a constraint or a fit, never a measurement of a primordial hole.

The honest status

A serious hypothesis, squeezed at both ends, with one window still open and a clean observational test: find a population of asteroid-mass lenses, or a sub-solar-mass merger, or a statistical signature in the CMB.

The archive labels it 'live debate' rather than 'fringe' because the physics is mainstream and the constraints are real. What is missing is the object.

The Holographic Principle

Live debate

The idea

Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking showed that a black hole's entropy scales with the area of its event horizon, not its volume. Gerard 't Hooft and Leonard Susskind turned that into a principle: the maximum information in a region is bounded by its surface area, so a three-dimensional world could be a complete description of physics on a two-dimensional boundary.

In 1997, Juan Maldacena made it concrete. Type IIB string theory in anti-de Sitter space is exactly equivalent to a conformal field theory on its boundary. Two theories, different dimensions, same physics — a duality.

What has actually been achieved

AdS/CFT is not speculation in the sense that matters: it is a calculational tool that has been checked in many limits, and it has been used to compute properties of strongly interacting plasmas that match experiment.

It also gave the field its most productive metaphors: entanglement entropy as geometry, the Ryu–Takayanagi formula, ER=EPR, and the black-hole information paradox reframed as a question about how information is encoded in the boundary.

The leap that is not supported

AdS is not our universe. Anti-de Sitter space has a negative cosmological constant; ours has a small positive one, which means our cosmos is closer to de Sitter space. There is no established holographic dual for de Sitter space.

'We live in a hologram' is a different claim. It requires the duality to hold for our universe, which nobody has shown. The mathematics supports the principle in a model; it does not establish that the model is reality.

Area scaling is suggestive, not decisive. The entropy bound is a real result. Turning it into 'reality is a projection' is an interpretation, and it is not the only one.

Why it is worth understanding anyway

Because it changes what physicists mean by 'fundamental'. In a duality there is no fact about which side is real — the two descriptions are the same theory in different variables, and that is a genuinely new kind of physical statement.

It is the best current example of the archive's rule: a beautiful mathematical result, widely used, frequently over-claimed in popular accounts. The dossier on quantum oddities covers the related habit of reading interpretations as discoveries.

White Holes

Live debate

The mathematics

The Schwarzschild solution, written in full, contains four regions: the exterior, the black-hole interior, a parallel exterior, and a white-hole interior. The white hole is the time reverse of the black hole — a singularity in the past rather than the future.

Because general relativity is time-symmetric, these solutions are as legitimate as the black-hole ones. The problem is not the equations; it is the initial conditions. A white hole requires an extraordinarily fine-tuned past singularity, which is why macroscopic ones are not expected to form.

Where they reappear

Black-hole evaporation. If a black hole evaporates completely, some descriptions say the end state is a white hole — a long, slow explosion rather than a disappearance. This is speculative and tied to the information paradox.

Loop quantum cosmology. A bouncing model replaces the Big Bang singularity with a transition from a collapsing phase, which behaves like a white hole in some constructions.

Gamma-ray bursts. Occasional papers propose that some bursts are white-hole events. None has been confirmed, and the ordinary explanations — collapsing massive stars, neutron-star mergers — fit the data better.

Why the archive calls it 'live debate' and not 'debunked'

Because the object has not been ruled out; it has simply not been found, and the theoretical case for macroscopic white holes is weak. Those are different situations.

What would count as evidence: a transient that emits matter and radiation with no progenitor, showing a horizon that nothing crosses inward. No such event is in the catalogue.

The idea is best understood as a consistency check on general relativity — a reminder that the theory permits more than the universe uses. That is a useful thing to know about a theory, and it is not a claim that white holes are out there.

The lesson

A solution to an equation is not a discovery. This is the same mistake that produces time-travel paradoxes treated as physics: the equations admit closed timelike curves, and the universe does not appear to contain them.

White holes are in the archive because they are interesting, respected, and unobserved — a clean test case for how to talk about a mathematical possibility.

The Great Filter

Live debate

The argument

Robin Hanson's 1998 formulation is an accounting trick. Take the chain from simple chemistry to a civilisation that colonises its galaxy. Each step has some probability. If the product of those probabilities is not extremely small, the galaxy should be full — so at least one step must be very improbable, and that step is the filter.

The question is not whether there is a filter but where it sits. Behind us: abiogenesis, eukaryotes, multicellularity, intelligence. Ahead: nuclear war, engineered pandemics, misaligned AI, ecological collapse.

Why the placement matters

If the filter is behind us, the implication is cheerful: the hard part is done, and we are rare and lucky. If it is ahead, every civilisation that reaches our stage tends to destroy itself, and the silence is a warning rather than an accident.

The uncomfortable corollary is that finding life elsewhere is bad news. Simple life on Mars would push abiogenesis into the 'easy' column, which moves the filter closer to us. Finding a fossil of complex life would be worse, because it would suggest that complexity is common and the deadly step is later.

The problems with the argument

It rests on one data point. We have a sample size of one biosphere, and no independent estimate of any probability in the chain. The inference is about our ignorance, formalised.

The premises are not settled. Whether civilisations expand galactically is an assumption about motivation; whether they last long enough is an assumption about stability. Both are empirical questions with no data.

It assumes we would notice. A galaxy full of quiet, efficient civilisations using little energy would look much like an empty one.

How to hold it

The Great Filter is best used as a bookkeeping device: it forces you to say which step you think is improbable, and it makes the consequences of that choice explicit. It is not evidence for any particular danger, and it has been used to support almost every position in the debate.

Its companion ideas are in the archive's frontier index — the dark forest, the zoo hypothesis, grabby aliens — all attempts to fill the same silence with a different story about motives.
