Market Efficiency

Live debate

Three claims, not one

Eugene Fama's 1970 review distinguished three forms. The weak form says past prices are already reflected, so chart-reading cannot work. The semi-strong form says all public information is priced, so reading the news cannot work. The strong form says even private information is priced, so insiders cannot profit — and that one is false, which is why insider trading is illegal and occasionally prosecuted.

The remaining two forms are supported well enough that index funds beat most active managers over long periods, a result replicated across countries and decades. The average active manager underperforms after fees by roughly the fee.

The Grossman–Stiglitz paradox sharpens the point: if prices were perfectly efficient, nobody would be paid to gather information, so nobody would gather it, so prices could not be efficient. Some inefficiency is the price of the information that removes it.

The anomalies and the joint hypothesis

Momentum — buying recent winners and selling losers — has survived decades of out-of-sample testing. Post-earnings-announcement drift persisted long after it was published. The value premium, small-cap effects and the low-volatility anomaly are all documented patterns that a strict reading does not predict.

Fama's answer is the joint hypothesis problem: any test of efficiency is also a test of the asset-pricing model used to define 'abnormal' returns. If your model is wrong, your anomaly is a modelling error rather than free money. That is not a dodge — it is a genuine identification problem, and it means efficiency is partly unfalsifiable as usually stated.

The practical resolution is that anomalies shrink after publication, which is exactly what efficiency predicts: the opportunity is real until enough people know about it.

Where the argument actually stands

Weak form: strongly supported. Simple technical rules do not produce reliable risk-adjusted returns.

Semi-strong form: broadly supported, with documented exceptions that are small, unstable and costly to trade.

Strong form: clearly false, and nobody serious defends it.

Behavioural finance accepts most of this and explains the exceptions through limits to arbitrage, not through investor stupidity — which is why the two camps have converged more than the headlines suggest.

The archive labels this live debate because the dispute is about the size and persistence of mispricing, not about whether markets are efficient in some absolute sense.

Why it is in the archive

Because 'the market is efficient' is used both as a serious scientific claim and as a slogan for deregulation, and the difference is what this page is for.

Related: bitcoin as digital gold, black swans.

The Space Elevator

Live debate

Why it works on paper

Put a counterweight beyond geostationary orbit and hang a cable down to the equator. At 35,786 kilometres the cable is in orbital sync with the ground; above that it is held outward by centrifugal effect, below it hangs. Climbers then ascend without rockets, and the energy cost falls to roughly the theoretical minimum.

The tension is highest at geostationary altitude, where the cable must support its own weight below and the counterweight's pull above. The required specific strength — strength divided by density — is around 50 gigapascals per gram per cubic centimetre at the minimum, and designers want a safety factor of two or more.

Steel is out by a factor of thirty. Kevlar and carbon fibre are out by a factor of ten. Carbon nanotubes and graphene have the theoretical numbers, which is why the idea moved from science fiction to NASA studies in the 2000s.

Where the material problem actually sits

The gap is not between theory and experiment in the usual sense; it is between a single perfect nanotube and a fibre long enough to span a continent. Measured tensile strength of macroscopic carbon-nanotube yarns is in the single-digit gigapascals, and the longest individual nanotubes are centimetres, not kilometres.

Defects dominate. A cable is a chain of billions of links, and its strength is set by its worst segment — a statistical problem that gets worse with length, which is exactly the direction the design needs to go. Graphene ribbons and boron-nitride nanotubes are candidate alternatives with the same issue.

The other engineering constraints are real but solvable in principle: avoiding low-Earth-orbit debris, surviving lightning and wind at the base, managing the climber's power supply, and the fact that the base must be on the equator, which puts it in the Pacific, in a storm belt, or in a country with the relevant politics.

The honest state of play

Physics: fine. Nothing in the concept violates a conservation law or a material limit known to physics.

Materials: the blocking problem. No process makes a metre of fibre, let alone 100,000 kilometres, at the required strength.

Cost: estimates assume a material that does not exist; the $10 billion figures in the literature are not forecasts.

The quieter alternative is a rotating skyhook or an orbital ring, which need less extreme materials and more infrastructure — neither has been built either.

The archive labels this live debate because the argument is entirely about a materials-science question that has a definite answer, and it has not arrived.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the standard example of a proposal that is correct in principle, impossible in practice, and constantly reported as nearly ready.

Related: hyperloop feasibility, Kardashev bottlenecks.

Kardashev Bottlenecks

Live debate

The scale and the arithmetic

Nikolai Kardashev's 1964 classification ranks civilisations by power: a type I uses the energy incident on its planet, about 1016 watts; type II the output of its star, about 1026; type III the output of its galaxy, around 1036. Earth is currently around 0.73 on a logarithmic interpolation.

The relevant observation is not the scale but the doubling time. Energy use has historically doubled every few decades. Even at a modest rate, a civilisation that keeps growing crosses from type I to type III in something like a hundred thousand to ten million years — a geological instant, and far less than the age of the galaxy.

So either growth stops, or civilisations are rare, or something about the galaxy is quieter than we expect. Each of those is a bottleneck claim, and they have different observable consequences.

The physical candidates

Thermodynamics is the hardest constraint. Computation and work generate waste heat, and a galaxy-spanning civilisation would be visible in the mid-infrared — which is precisely what a Dyson swarm search looks for. The absence of an infrared excess in most surveyed galaxies is a real bound.

Coordination is the second. A type III civilisation spans 100,000 light years, so any central authority is a hundred millennia behind on every decision. That does not prevent expansion — it prevents central control, which suggests a patchwork rather than an empire.

Resources are a third, and the least binding: the asteroid belt contains enough material for habitats with the area of thousands of Earths, and the Sun's output is 1013 times human consumption. Scarcity is not what stops growth; the speed of light and the second law are.

The behavioural candidates, which are not physics

They stay home. If most civilisations choose stability over expansion — the 'aestivation hypothesis' and various post-scarcity arguments — the galaxy stays empty without any physical limit.

They are short-lived. If the median technological civilisation lasts a few centuries, the galaxy is mostly empty most of the time and the silence needs no exotic explanation.

Expansion is not selected for. Evolutionary arguments about competition apply to biology on one planet; there is no reason to think a mature civilisation optimises for territory.

The archive labels this live debate because the thermodynamic limits are real and calculable, while the behavioural ones are unfalsifiable in practice — and the two are constantly mixed together in the literature.

Why it is in the archive

Because it converts a vague question — where is everybody? — into a set of quantitative bounds, and then shows that the bounds do not decide the answer.

Related: Dyson swarms, the Great Filter, the zoo hypothesis.

The Lindy Effect

Live debate

The claim in its strong form

For non-perishable things — ideas, technologies, institutions, books — the expected additional lifespan is proportional to current age. A technology that has survived a century has an expected future of about a century; double its age and you double the forecast.

Mandelbrot noticed the pattern in a 1964 paper and named it after the deli. Nassim Taleb made it a principle in Antifragile (2012), using it against forecasts that a thing is about to die because it is old.

The mechanism is a decreasing hazard rate: the longer something has survived, the lower its per-period chance of dying becomes, because the things that kill it have already been survived. That is plausible for ideas and institutions and false for light bulbs.

Where the reasoning gets loose

The strong proportional form is not a theorem; it is a special case. It holds exactly when survival times follow a power law with exponent one, or equivalently when the hazard rate falls as one over age. Nothing guarantees that, and the empirical literature on technology and institution survival does not show a universal exponent.

Selection is the second problem. We observe the survivors, so any sample of long-lived things is biased by construction — the same reason a century of successful companies tells you little about the next century's.

There is also a category error in much of the popular use. The effect applies to non-perishable things; a car, a person, a star and a hard drive all have increasing hazard rates, and applying Lindy to them is straightforwardly wrong. Taleb says so explicitly, and the caveat is usually dropped in retelling.

What it is good for

As a prior: a technology that has been in use for 2,000 years is a better bet for the next century than one launched last year, absent specific information. That is a reasonable Bayesian prior, not a law.

As a corrective: it punctures the reflex that old means obsolete, and it predicts that most futuristic predictions about the death of institutions will fail.

As a trap: it also predicts survival for things that deserve to die, and it has no way to distinguish a durable idea from a persistent one. Horses lasted millennia and then did not.

The archive labels this live debate because the intuition is sound, the mathematics is contingent, and almost every popular statement of it is stronger than the evidence supports.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a rule of thumb that is genuinely useful and routinely over-applied, and because the difference between a prior and a law is the point of this whole collection.

Related: black swans, the doomsday argument.

Black Swans

Live debate

The definition and the three properties

Taleb's 2007 book defines a black swan as an event with three properties: it is an outlier relative to past expectations, it carries extreme impact, and human beings produce explanations for it after the fact as though it had been predictable.

The name comes from the European assumption that all swans are white, falsified by the first sighting in Australia. The point is epistemic: the observation that had never occurred is the one that changes the theory.

The practical programme that follows is not prediction but robustness: build systems that survive being wrong, prefer insurance to forecasts, and be suspicious of any model whose tail is thin because nobody has seen a fat one yet.

Where the concept is strongest and weakest

It is strongest as a description of financial and historical data, where returns and event sizes are genuinely fat-tailed and normal-distribution risk models systematically understate extremes. The 2008 crisis and the failures of Gaussian copula models are the canonical case.

It is weakest when used as a universal solvent. Some domains have thin tails and predictable distributions; a bridge has a load rating because the physics of bridges is well behaved. Calling every wide confidence interval a black swan turns a statistical statement into a rhetorical one.

There is also a falsifiability problem. If black swans are by definition unpredictable, then the claim that forecasting is futile cannot be tested and cannot fail — which is precisely the structure the book warns about elsewhere.

What the research actually says

Expert forecasting: Philip Tetlock's long study found experts barely beat chance on long-range political forecasts, but a subset — his superforecasters — did substantially better, with small teams, base rates and frequent updating. That is evidence against fatalism, not for it.

Tail risk is real: the empirical case that financial returns are fat-tailed is not seriously disputed, and risk models that assume normality are wrong in a measurable direction.

Hindsight: the robust finding is the narrative fallacy — the ease with which we construct stories that make past surprises seem inevitable. That is a fact about cognition, and it survives regardless of how the forecasting argument is settled.

The archive labels this live debate because the phenomenon is real, the response is contested, and 'nobody could have known' is often true and often a convenient excuse.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is used both as a serious critique of statistical modelling and as a way to avoid accountability, and the two uses are hard to tell apart from the outside.

Related: the Lindy effect, market efficiency.

Dunbar's Number

Live debate

Where the number comes from

Robin Dunbar's 1992 paper used the correlation between neocortex ratio and mean group size in primates, then extrapolated the human point. The result was roughly 150, and it appeared to match company sizes, military unit structures, Christmas-card lists and the ethnographic record of village sizes.

Dunbar later described layers: about 5 intimate ties, 15 close, 50, 150, 500 and 1,500, each a band of decreasing emotional closeness. Mobile-phone and social-network data seemed to show the same bands in call frequencies.

The supporting argument is about time and grooming. Primates maintain relationships by grooming, which is expensive; language may have evolved as cheap grooming at distance, allowing larger groups. The ceiling is a budget, not a hard wall.

The reanalysis and the internet

A 2021 reanalysis by Lindenfors and colleagues, published in Biology Letters, redid the comparative statistics with modern methods and reported a 95 per cent confidence interval from about 2 to about 520. The point estimate remained near 150, but the interval is so wide that it cannot bear the weight usually placed on it.

Part of the problem is that the primate sample is small, the group-size measures are inconsistent, and the extrapolation assumes humans sit on the same regression line as other primates — an assumption that language and institutions directly challenge.

Online, the test is unavoidable. Average Facebook friend counts run in the hundreds, but the number of contacts people actually interact with regularly stays near the predicted layers. Dunbar's own 2016 analysis of 30 million users found the structure persisted — a smaller active network nested inside a larger passive one.

What survives and what does not

Survives: human relationships are layered by closeness and limited by maintenance cost; there is a small intimate circle and a wider active one, and that structure shows up in phones, firms and villages.

Does not survive: the precision of 150 as a cognitive limit. The confidence interval does not support a specific number, and the primate comparative base is thin.

Wrong framing: 'Dunbar's number says you cannot have more than 150 friends' is a misreading. It is about the number of relationships whose quality can be maintained, not the number of names you know.

The archive labels this live debate because the layered structure is well supported and the famous number is much weaker than its fame implies.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is one of the most cited numbers in popular science and one of the least certain, and because the online version of the question is genuinely open.

Related: echo chambers, the contact hypothesis.

The Contact Hypothesis

Live debate

The theory and its conditions

Gordon Allport's The Nature of Prejudice (1954) argued that contact between groups reduces prejudice only under four conditions: equal status within the situation, common goals, intergroup cooperation, and support from authorities or custom.

Without them, contact can reinforce stereotypes — a competitive, unequal encounter gives each side evidence for what it already believed. This is why the theory is not simply 'exposure fixes bias', which is how it is often summarised.

Pettigrew and Tropp's 2006 meta-analysis of 515 studies found a reliable negative relationship between contact and prejudice, and found that the effect appeared even in studies that did not meet all four conditions — but was stronger where they were met.

The methodological fights

Selection is the central problem. People who are less prejudiced may seek out contact, producing the correlation without the causal direction claimed. Longitudinal studies and natural experiments — desegregation orders, randomised roommate assignment, refugee placement — reduce but do not eliminate this.

Generalisation is the second. Does a good interaction with one member of a group change attitudes to the group? The evidence says yes, through friendship and through changed perceptions of group norms, but the effect sizes are modest and decay without reinforcement.

A 2005 critique by Dixon, Durrheim and Tredoux argued that the literature systematically studies harmonious contact and ignores the political conditions that make inequality durable — that contact research can end up prescribing better attitudes instead of structural change.

What the field agrees on

Contact works: the meta-analytic effect is robust across countries, age groups and target groups, and it is one of the better-replicated findings in the discipline.

Friendship is the mechanism: cross-group friendship is consistently the strongest predictor, more than casual exposure.

Conditions matter: cooperative, equal-status, institutionally supported contact outperforms unstructured mixing.

Scale is not settled: whether many small positive encounters add up to less structural discrimination is an open empirical and political question.

The archive labels this live debate because the psychological effect is well established while the policy inference from it is contested.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a rare case where a social-psychological finding is both robust and genuinely difficult to apply, and the gap between the two is instructive.

Related: Dunbar’s number, echo chambers.

Rational Choice Voting

Live debate

The paradox

Anthony Downs's An Economic Theory of Democracy set out the problem: the benefit of voting is the value of your preferred outcome multiplied by the probability your vote is decisive, minus the cost of voting. In any large election that probability is around one in tens of millions.

Riker and Ordeshook added a term for the satisfaction of performing a civic duty, which makes the equation fit the data by construction. That is the standard move, and it is also the standard criticism: a free parameter that absorbs whatever the model gets wrong.

The empirical regularity is that turnout responds to cost in exactly the way the model predicts — rain, distance to the polling station and registration deadlines all move it — while the level of turnout is far above what pure instrumentality implies.

The four families of explanation

Expressive voting (Brennan and Lomasky) treats the ballot as a way to express identity or values, at near-zero cost, because it will not change anything. On this account voters are not badly informed by accident; they are uninformed because the act is not instrumental.

Altruistic or pivotal voting (Edlin, Gelman and Kaplan) argues that a vote has social value even when it is not decisive, because it marginally raises the chance of the better outcome for everyone — so a small probability of a large benefit can justify the cost.

Group-based models treat turnout as a cooperative act within a group, where social rewards and sanctions operate and where the individual calculus is the wrong unit of analysis.

Behavioural accounts emphasise habit, norms and the doorstep conversation — the fact that turnout is sticky across a life and contagious within a household.

What the evidence supports

Cost matters: the strongest causal evidence comes from natural experiments — rain on election day reduces turnout, especially among marginal voters, and same-day registration raises it.

Habit matters: voting in one election strongly predicts voting in the next, which no single-shot cost-benefit model explains.

Duty is real but measured badly: self-reported civic duty correlates with turnout, but it is also the kind of variable that can explain any result after the fact.

Policy stakes: because marginal voters differ systematically from habitual ones, who turns out changes who wins — which is why the paradox is not merely academic.

The archive labels this live debate because the phenomenon is well measured and the explanation is genuinely unresolved.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest case of a rational-choice model failing at its own game, and because the failure has real consequences for how democracies are designed.

Related: the median voter theorem, superrationality.

The Median Voter Theorem

Live debate

The result

Assume voters have single-peaked preferences along one dimension — each has a most-preferred point and prefers options closer to it. Assume two parties, each wanting to win, and full turnout. Then both parties locate at the median voter's ideal point, because any other position can be beaten by moving toward the median.

The logic is spatial and it is robust within its assumptions: it does not require voters to be informed, only to have preferences of the right shape, and it does not require parties to care about policy at all.

Black proved the underlying majority-rule result; Downs drew out the party-competition implication. Together they produced the textbook expectation that two-party systems converge on the centre.

Where the assumptions break

Multidimensionality destroys it. With two or more issues, majority rule generally has no equilibrium at all — the chaos results of McKelvey and Schofield — unless preferences are restricted in ways real electorates do not satisfy.

Turnout and primaries change who the median voter is. If a party's candidate is chosen by a low-turnout primary electorate, the relevant median is that electorate's, not the general election's, and the two can be far apart.

Abstention is the third break: if mobilising your base is more effective than persuading the centre, a party can profit by moving away from the median. That is a strategic calculation, not an error.

What the evidence says

Convergence happens in low-salience elections and in systems with closed primaries and high turnout — the theorem's conditions.

Divergence happens where polarisation is asymmetric and where the parties' supporters are geographically sorted, which is a structural change the model has no room for.

The theorem is still useful as a baseline: it tells you which deviations need explaining, and the explanations — primaries, turnout, sorting, multidimensionality — are all testable.

The archive labels this live debate because the mathematics is settled under its assumptions and the empirical fit is contested, and the two are often confused in commentary.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a precise, provable claim whose failure in the world is much more informative than a vague assertion that politicians chase the centre.

Related: rational choice voting, democratic peace.

Democratic Peace

Live debate

The finding

The claim is dyadic, not absolute: pairs of democracies are much less likely to go to war with each other than other pairs. Democracies fight non-democracies at least as often as autocracies do, which is why the slogan 'democracies are peaceful' is a different and false claim.

The finding survived the coding disputes of the 1990s and is among the most replicated regularities in the field. Kant's 1795 essay on perpetual peace — republican constitutions, a federation of states, cosmopolitan hospitality — is the intellectual ancestor.

Candidate mechanisms divide into three: normative (democracies externalise the compromise and non-violence of domestic politics), institutional (leaders who must win elections bear audience costs and are slower to escalate), and interest-based (democracies trade and ally with each other, so they have less to fight about).

The critiques

Farber and Gowa argued that the effect is largely confined to the Cold War period and reflects shared security interests rather than regime type — that the democratic peace is a coincidence of alliance structure.

Rosato's critique is that the normative and institutional mechanisms do not survive scrutiny: democracies have fought each other's proxies, have planned for war against each other, and public opinion does not reliably restrain escalation.

Measurement is the third issue. 'Democracy' is coded by indices with thresholds, and the joint democracy cases — pairs that were both partly free — are exactly where the classification decides the result. Several apparent exceptions sit near that boundary.

What is reasonably secure

The pattern is real in the standard datasets, and it is not an artefact of one coding scheme.

The mechanisms are not established. Norms, institutions and trade all predict the pattern and are hard to separate, because they correlate.

Policy inference is contested. 'Promote democracy to get peace' assumes the causal direction and the mechanism, and the record of democracy promotion is mixed at best.

The 2022 invasion of Ukraine is a reminder of the absolute claim's limits: the dyadic finding says nothing about democracies versus autocracies, which is where most wars actually happen.

The archive labels this live debate because the regularity is well documented and the explanation is not.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most policy-consequential finding in international relations and one of the most disputed, and because the distinction between the dyadic claim and the slogan is usually lost.

Related: the Thucydides trap, MAD stability.

The Thucydides Trap

Live debate

The claim

Graham Allison's Belfer Center project identified sixteen cases since 1500 in which a rising power threatened to displace a ruling one, and found that twelve ended in war. The framing is deliberately deterministic: the structural pressure, not the intentions of leaders, is what makes the trap.

The named cases include Portugal versus Spain, the Netherlands versus Britain, France versus Britain, the rise of Germany against Britain, and the United States against Britain — the last being one of the four that did not end in war.

The policy use is almost always about the United States and China, where the analogy is presented as a warning that conscious management is required to escape a structural pattern.

Why historians push back

Case selection is the main objection. The cases were chosen because they are famous great-power confrontations, which guarantees that a high proportion ended badly; transitions that were managed quietly are less likely to be in the dataset at all.

Coding is the second. 'Rising power', 'ruling power' and 'war' each involve judgement calls, and several cases — the Anglo-American transition, the Spanish-Portuguese case — are included on generous definitions. Reclassify a few and the ratio moves a long way.

The causal story is the third. Power transition theory (Organski) is a serious research programme, but it predicts war when a dissatisfied challenger overtakes a satisfied hegemon — a narrower condition than 'a rising power exists', and one that makes the outcome depend on satisfaction, which is exactly what the trap metaphor omits.

Where the analogy is useful and where it is not

Useful: as a checklist of the mechanisms that make confrontations escalate — security dilemmas, honour, domestic pressure, misperception of the other side's resolve.

Not useful: as a probability estimate. A 12-in-16 figure computed from selected cases is not a base rate for any real pair of states.

The self-fulfilling risk: if both sides believe the trap is inevitable, they prepare for war, which is a mechanism the theory creates rather than describes.

What it gets right: structural pressure is real, and the peaceful cases — Britain handing over to the United States — required deliberate choices, which is the opposite of determinism.

The archive labels this live debate because the historical pattern is a genuine object of study and the popular use of it is closer to prophecy than to analysis.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where a quotation from Thucydides, a small historical dataset and a policy slogan are routinely treated as one thing.

Related: democratic peace, MAD stability.

The Zoo Hypothesis

Fringe claim — Fringe

The proposal

John Ball's paper in Icarus in 1973 set out what he called the zoo hypothesis: extraterrestrial intelligence is common, but it follows a policy of non-interference with emerging civilisations, so that we observe nothing.

The hypothesis is a solution to the Fermi paradox that accepts the premises — abundant life, capable civilisations, a galaxy old enough for them to have spread — and explains the absence of evidence as a choice rather than a scarcity.

Variants include the 'interdict' scenario, in which a local advanced civilisation enforces quarantine, and the laboratory hypothesis, in which Earth is an experiment. All share the structure: the silence is deliberate.

Why it is hard to defend

The coordination problem is severe. A policy of non-contact would have to be adopted and maintained by every civilisation in the galaxy, independently, for billions of years — across species with different biologies, values and expansion pressures. One defector, one curious probe, and the hypothesis fails.

It is also close to unfalsifiable. Any absence of evidence is consistent with it, and so is almost any future evidence: a detection could be read as the zoo opening, a continued silence as the policy holding. A hypothesis that predicts nothing in particular is cheap.

There is a testable edge, though. A strict non-interference policy need not mean invisibility: waste heat, probes, and artefacts in the solar system would all be detectable, and searches for them have found nothing so far. That is weak evidence against the strong form.

How it sits with the other answers

Compared with the Great Filter, the zoo hypothesis is optimistic: it says civilisations survive and multiply, and choose restraint. The Filter says they mostly do not survive.

Compared with dark forest, it is the opposite conclusion from similar premises: silence as courtesy rather than as concealment.

Its strongest argument is that it needs no unknown physics — only a policy, which is the kind of thing civilisations can have.

Its weakest point is the same thing: a universal policy sustained without enforcement is not a mechanism, it is a hope.

The archive labels this fringe because it is a serious published proposal with no evidence for it and no clear way to test it — an entry in the solution space, not a finding.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most humane of the Fermi solutions and the least constrained by evidence, and because the difference between those two facts is worth seeing clearly.

Related: Kardashev bottlenecks, the Great Filter, dark forest strategy.

Substrate Independence

Live debate

The argument for

Hilary Putnam's multiple realizability argument (1967) observed that the same mental state — pain, say — is realised by different physical states in different species. If what makes it pain is the functional role rather than the chemistry, then the chemistry is not essential.

Computationalism adds that cognition is computation over representations, and computation is substrate neutral by definition: a program is defined by its formal structure, not by the machinery that implements it. This is the assumption behind whole-brain emulation research and most of the philosophy of AI.

The practical version is the strongest: if you can reproduce the causal organisation of a brain closely enough, behaviour follows, and if behaviour follows then whatever we care about in minds is probably preserved. Sandberg and Bostrom's 2008 roadmap treats this as an engineering question.

The argument against

Searle's biological naturalism is the direct denial: consciousness is a biological phenomenon caused by specific processes in specific tissue, in the way digestion is caused by a stomach. Simulating digestion does not digest, and simulating a brain would not think.

The hard problem sharpens it. Even a perfect functional duplicate leaves open why there is something it is like to be it. If experience is not exhausted by function, then function is not enough, and the substrate question is reopened.

A third line comes from embodied and enactive cognition: minds may be constituted partly by a body's sensorimotor coupling with an environment, in which case a disembodied program is missing a constitutive part rather than merely a convenient one.

What would settle it, and why we cannot do it yet

The test is obvious in principle: build a system that behaves like a mind, then determine whether it is one. The second half is the problem — we have no independent measure of consciousness, only reports.

Integrated information theory makes a specific claim that substrate matters in a measurable way (the causal structure of the system), which is the rare case of a testable version of the dispute.

Current AI provides no evidence either way: language models are functionally impressive and their internal organisation is unlike a brain's, so neither camp gets what it needs from them.

The archive labels this live debate because it is a philosophical dispute with engineering consequences, and neither side has an experiment that decides it.

Why it is in the archive

Because whole-brain emulation, mind uploading and the moral status of AI systems all rest on this claim, and it is usually assumed rather than argued.

Related: the Chinese room, integrated information theory.

Algorithmic Fairness

Live debate

The impossibility results

Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, and independently Chouldechova, showed that when groups have different base rates, a predictor cannot simultaneously satisfy calibration within groups, equal false positive rates and equal false negative rates.

The three properties are each individually compelling. Calibration says a score of 0.7 means a 70 per cent chance for everyone. Equal false positive rates say innocent people are wrongly flagged at the same rate in each group. Equal false negative rates say the same for missed cases. Pick two.

Hardt, Price and Srebro's equalised odds framework made the trade-off explicit and computable: you can adjust a classifier's thresholds post hoc to equalise error rates, at a cost in overall accuracy.

The COMPAS case

ProPublica's 2016 analysis of the COMPAS recidivism tool found that Black defendants were more likely than white defendants to be falsely flagged as high risk, and white defendants more likely to be falsely cleared.

Northpointe, the vendor, replied that the tool was calibrated: among defendants with the same score, the reoffending rate was similar across groups. Both analyses were correct, which is exactly the theorem.

The case is the canonical illustration because it shows that the dispute was never about arithmetic. It was about which error is worse, and that is a normative question the data cannot answer.

What the field now agrees on

The impossibility is proven under stated assumptions, and it is not a limitation of current methods — it follows from the statistics.

Choosing a definition is a policy decision, and it should be made by the institution accountable for the harm, not left to the vendor's default.

Measurement matters: the label a model predicts is often a proxy — arrests rather than crimes — and the proxy's bias is upstream of any fairness constraint.

No definition is neutral. Demographic parity ignores base rates; calibration can entrench them. Each encodes a view about what equal treatment means.

The archive labels this live debate because the mathematics is settled and the ethics and law are not.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where a rigorous result killed a naive hope — that there is a technical fix for a political problem — and the field has mostly absorbed that honestly.

Related: open versus closed models, echo chambers.

Open versus Closed Models

Live debate

The case for open weights

Scientific audit is the strongest argument. A model whose weights are public can be examined, benchmarked and attacked by anyone; one behind an API can only be probed through a filter the provider controls, and its reported evaluations cannot be independently reproduced.

Competition and sovereignty follow. Open weights let universities, small companies and states without frontier compute build on the capability, which is the argument that produced OLMo, Pythia and the Llama releases, and which the EU's AI Act partially accommodates.

Safety research needs the artefacts. Most work on interpretability, unlearning and red-teaming is done on open models precisely because closed ones cannot be studied at the parameter level.

The case against

Fine-tuning removes safety training. Qi and colleagues showed in 2023 that a small amount of adversarial fine-tuning on an aligned model restores harmful capability, and that the effect is cheap and requires no special access to the original training data. You cannot patch a downloaded file.

Capability diffusion is the second argument: the frontier moves fast, and an open release at the frontier is a permanent transfer of a capability to every actor, including ones that will use it for cyber operations or biosecurity. The 'it will be available soon anyway' reply is an empirical claim about lag, and the lag has been short.

The third is the monitoring asymmetry: closed providers can log, rate-limit and revoke. None of those controls survives publication.

What the evidence actually shows

Established: safety training is removable by fine-tuning; open weights are irreversible; closed models cannot be independently audited at the parameter level.

Contested: whether open releases accelerate dangerous capability by months or years, and whether the marginal risk exceeds the auditability benefit.

Policy divergence: the EU AI Act imposes obligations on general-purpose models with some accommodation for open source; the US has relied more on voluntary commitments; the UK has taken a research-heavy line. None of these is settled.

The honest framing: this is a trade between concentrated, revocable control and distributed, irreversible access. Neither is obviously safer in the abstract; which is safer depends on which failure you fear.

The archive labels this live debate because both sides' factual claims are largely correct and the disagreement is about values and risk estimates.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest current example of a policy argument where the empirical premises are shared and the conclusion is not.

Related: algorithmic fairness, AI existential risk.

The Omega Point

Fringe claim — Fringe

Two very different claims

Teilhard's Omega Point, developed in the 1920s and published in The Phenomenon of Man (1955), is a theological vision: evolution tends toward increasing complexity and consciousness, converging on a final unity that is also a person. It is not a physical theory and does not pretend to be testable.

Frank Tipler's 1994 The Physics of Immortality is a physical argument. In a closed, collapsing universe, intelligent life could in principle harvest the available free energy and compute at ever higher rates as the final singularity approaches, achieving in the last moments an infinite amount of subjective time and information.

The two are often conflated because they share a name and a shape. They share nothing else: one is metaphysics, the other is a conditional claim about general relativity and thermodynamics.

Why the physical version fails

The scenario requires a closed universe that recollapses. In 1998 the discovery of accelerating expansion, confirmed repeatedly since, pointed to a universe that will not recollapse — removing the final singularity the argument needs.

Even in a collapsing universe, the calculation is fragile. Anisotropy and inhomogeneity grow during contraction, and BKL-type chaos tends to make the approach to the singularity irregular in a way that destroys the ordered computation the scenario requires. Later work found narrower conditions under which some version survives, but they are special cases, not the generic case.

There is also an information-theoretic objection: the total entropy bound means the available free energy in a collapsing universe is finite, and whether infinite subjective time can be extracted depends on the details of the collapse in ways nobody can test.

What this page is doing here

Teilhard's version is a work of religious philosophy that has been influential in popular science writing and has no empirical content. It is included because it is the origin of the idea, not because it is a hypothesis.

Tipler's version was a legitimate, falsifiable physical proposal. It made a prediction — a closed universe — and the prediction failed. That is how the process is supposed to work.

The general pattern is worth noting: teleological arguments about the endpoint of the universe tend to acquire their conclusions from their premises, and to lose those premises when the cosmology changes.

The archive labels this fringe because the theological form is unfalsifiable and the physical form has been overtaken by observation — the label is a statement about the evidence, not about the sincerity of the authors.

Why it is in the archive

Because it closes the 200, and because it is a clean example of an idea that was scientifically respectable and then stopped being so when the data arrived.

Related: Dyson swarms, the Boltzmann brain, Kardashev bottlenecks.

Cold Fusion

Fringe claim

Two electrochemists announced tabletop fusion on 23 March 1989. Within six months the effect had failed to replicate, and thirty-seven years later there is still a conference, a journal and no accepted mechanism.

The announcement

Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons, electrochemists at the University of Utah, held a press conference before their paper had been reviewed. They reported that electrolysing heavy water over a palladium cathode produced more heat than the electrical input could account for, and that the excess was large enough to require a nuclear explanation. A fusion reaction between deuterium nuclei would release energy and leave behind neutrons, tritium and helium-4.

The claim was extraordinary in the specific sense that matters: it was cheap to test. Palladium, heavy water and a calorimeter cost less than a graduate student's year. Hundreds of labs tried within weeks.

What replication showed

Some groups reported excess heat. Others reported nothing. Almost none reported the full signature: a heat excess that scaled with the neutron flux, the tritium produced and the helium-4 detected. The measurements that were easiest to make — neutrons above background — mostly came back at background, sometimes at levels that would have been lethal if the claimed heat were nuclear in origin.

The calorimetry itself was the weak point. Fleischmann and Pons used a cell that ran at varying temperature, and their calculation assumed all the recombination heat was recovered. A cell that partially boils is a cell whose energy balance is unknown. When calorimetry was improved, the effect shrank.

What the reviews found

1989, US Department of Energy: a panel chaired by John Huizenga found no convincing evidence of cold fusion and no theory that could accommodate it.

2004, a second DOE review: the same conclusion, with a recommendation that a small, focused programme might be funded. It was not.

2019, a Google-funded replication: a multi-lab programme published in Nature after two years of careful calorimetry found no excess heat in palladium–deuterium cells. It did produce better calorimeters, which was the useful part.

The standing exception: the field still meets (ICCF), still publishes, and still points to a handful of positive replications. None has produced the by-product ratio the claim requires, in a calorimeter another lab could reproduce.

Why the claim will not die

Because the failure mode is boring and the promise is enormous. A negative result is a paper about calorimetry; a positive one is free energy. The archive labels it a fringe claim rather than a hoax because the original authors were not fabricating — they were measuring badly, and then defending a measurement instead of a hypothesis. That is a common and human failure, and it is not the same as fraud.

It also sits next to a real result that gets confused with it: sonoluminescence, where a collapsing bubble really does produce a flash of light and, in some experiments, temperatures of thousands of kelvin. Bubble fusion claimed the same route to the same prize and failed the same test.

What would settle it

One cell, sealed, with the heat measured by two independent methods and the gas analysed for helium-4, tritium and neutrons in the same run, replicated by a lab that expects it to fail. That experiment has been attempted; the ratio never appears.

The Placebo Effect

Live debate

The placebo effect is real, modest, and much narrower than either its critics or its enthusiasts claim. It works best on symptoms you have to report and worst on outcomes a machine measures.

Two different things

A placebo-controlled trial compares a treatment against a sham. The placebo response is everything that happens in the sham arm — including the disease getting better on its own, regression to the mean, and the reporting behaviour of people who know they are being watched. The placebo effect is only the part caused by expectation, and it is the smaller of the two.

Most popular writing on placebos conflates them, which is how a natural recovery becomes evidence that the mind heals the body.

Where it is largest

Pain, nausea, fatigue, depression scores, asthma symptoms — anything measured by asking the patient how they feel. In these, sham treatments reliably beat no treatment, and the size is often a fifth to a third of the response to the real drug. The mechanism has been partly mapped: expectation of relief releases endogenous opioids, and the effect is reversed by naloxone in some experiments.

Where it disappears

A 2001 meta-analysis of 114 trials found little evidence of a placebo effect on binary or objective outcomes — blood pressure, infection, tumour size, blood counts. Patients felt better on placebo, but their bodies did not measurably change. Later reviews have argued about the size, not about the direction: the effect is real for experience, thin for physiology.

Asthma gives the cleanest demonstration. In a 2005 study, sham inhalers and sham acupuncture produced large improvements in what patients reported and almost none in forced expiratory volume, the number the machine measures.

The one result that should change your mind

Open-label placebos work, slightly. Kaptchuk and colleagues gave irritable bowel patients sugar pills in a bottle labelled “placebo” and told them so. Symptoms improved more than in the no-treatment group. The effect is small and the mechanism contested, but it means the effect is not simply deception.

Nocebo is the mirror. Expectation of harm produces real symptoms — nausea, headache, pain — and accounts for a measurable share of the side effects reported in trials of statins and vaccines.

What it is not: a treatment for cancer, infection, fracture or anything with an objective trajectory. A placebo can change how a disease feels. It has never been shown to change what a disease does.

Why it belongs in this archive

Because it is the honest version of the claim that belief shapes the body. Something real is happening, it is measurable, and it is far smaller than the claims made for it — the same shape as half the material on this site, except that here the phenomenon survives the test.

Learning Styles

Debunked

The idea that children learn better when taught in their preferred mode — visual, auditory, kinaesthetic — is one of the most widely held beliefs in education and one of the most thoroughly tested negatives in psychology.

The claim, stated fairly

People differ in how they prefer to take in information. The pedagogical claim goes further: matching the teaching method to a student's preferred modality improves how much they learn. This is the meshing hypothesis, and it is the part that has been tested.

What a valid test requires

Three things at once. Students must be sorted by style using a validated instrument. They must then be taught the same material in two different ways. And the outcome must show a crossover: the visual learners do better with the visual lesson, the auditory learners better with the auditory one, in a pattern that cannot be produced by general ability.

Almost no study does all three. A 2008 review commissioned by the Association for Psychological Science found a handful that came close, and none that produced the crossover. Where the design was sound, the interaction disappeared.

Why the belief survives

It feels true, because people do have preferences, and preferences are easy to observe. It is also commercially useful: the VARK questionnaire and its relatives are sold to schools, and a teacher who has spent a training day on it has a stake in the answer. In one survey of teachers in five countries, more than nine in ten endorsed matching instruction to learning styles.

The preference is real. The benefit of matching it is not. Those are different sentences and only the first is supported.

What does work instead

Retrieval practice: testing yourself on material, rather than rereading it. Among the largest and most replicated effects in the learning literature.

Spacing: the same study time distributed across days beats the same time in one block.

Interleaving: mixing problem types forces the learner to choose a method, not just apply one.

Dual coding: pairing words with a relevant diagram helps almost everyone — which is not the same as matching a style, and is often mistaken for it.

The lesson for the archive

A debunked idea is not a stupid one. Learning styles were a reasonable guess about individual difference, and they were killed by a specific experimental requirement rather than by ridicule. That is how the four labels here are supposed to work.

Growth Mindset

Live debate

Believing that ability can grow is a defensible idea with a small, real effect. Believing it is a lever that raises attainment for everyone is a claim that failed its largest test.

The claim

Carol Dweck's work distinguishes a fixed mindset — intelligence is a quantity you have — from a growth mindset — intelligence is a capacity you build. The educational claim is that teaching children the second belief improves their achievement, particularly after failure.

It became one of the most widely adopted ideas in schooling worldwide, appearing in national curricula, teacher training and a great many motivational posters.

What the meta-analysis found

A 2018 meta-analysis pooled 129 studies and around 400,000 students. The correlation between mindset and academic achievement was small, and the effect of interventions was smaller again — an effect size near 0.08, roughly a hundredth of the variance. The authors also found signs of publication bias in the literature, meaning the true figure is probably lower than the published average.

What the large trial found

A 2019 national experiment in the United States randomised about 12,000 ninth-graders to a short online growth-mindset programme or a control. The average effect on grades was near zero. There was a real effect for one subgroup — lower-attaining students — and it was modest: a few grade points, in some schools, under some conditions.

That is not nothing. It is also not a scalable policy lever, and the difference between those two statements is where most of the argument now sits.

How to hold both halves

Beliefs about ability do matter — for how a student responds to a hard problem, and for whether they interpret difficulty as a signal to stop.

The intervention does not generalise — a 45-minute online module does not restructure a school, and the trials that worked had supportive contexts that are hard to ship.

The replication record is the story — original effects were inflated, the meta-analytic effect is tiny, and the field has mostly accepted this rather than defended it. That is what a working science looks like.

Why it is filed as live debate

Because the strong claim is dead and the weak claim is alive: mindset predicts something, interventions help a little in some places, and the disagreement is now about size and context rather than existence. Compare ego depletion, where the effect largely evaporated, and learning styles, where the mechanism was never there.

The Aquatic Ape

Fringe claim

A human ancestor that took to the water would explain hairlessness, upright posture and the diving reflex in one stroke. The fossil record, the comparative anatomy and the genetics each say otherwise, and the charitable version of the idea is a different claim.

The claim

Alister Hardy proposed in 1960 that a branch of apes was pushed by competition into coastal and shallow-water foraging, and that a period of semi-aquatic life left marks on human anatomy: loss of body hair, a layer of subcutaneous fat, bipedalism, voluntary breath control, the diving reflex, and the shape of the nose and hand.

Elaine Morgan made the case for a general reader in The Descent of Woman (1972) and again in The Aquatic Ape Hypothesis (1997). Morgan's argument was also a feminist one: she noted that the savannah narratives of the 1960s were stories about male hunters, and offered a different story. The critique landed. The hypothesis did not.

The problems, in order of weight

There is no fossil evidence of an aquatic phase: no hominin with flipper-like limbs, no marine-associated hominin sites of the right age with the right anatomy. Body hair loss is not unique to humans among mammals, and the human pattern — fine, short, densely follicled — is not what an aquatic mammal has. Subcutaneous fat is shared with many terrestrial mammals, including other primates. Bipedalism appears in the fossil record before any plausible coastal adaptation, in Orrorin and Ardipithecus, in woodland settings.

The comparative argument is the strongest one against: animals that return to the water converge — whales, seals, sirenians, otters — and the convergence is unmistakable in the skeleton. Humans show none of it.

The version that survives

Waterside life is real. Coastal sites in South Africa show shellfish harvesting around 164,000 years ago, and the capacity to cross water is documented at least 50,000 years ago in Australia and much earlier at Flores. Wading, swimming and shore foraging were part of the human repertoire. That is the waterside hypothesis, and it is a claim about diet and range, not about a semi-aquatic ancestor.

Where the label lands

Fringe, not hoax. The hypothesis was proposed in good faith, published in a scientific journal in 1960, and defended for decades. It has not been supported.

The distinction matters. Palaeoanthropology rejected it on evidence — the same evidence that later confirmed the waterside version.

What would revive it: a hominin fossil assemblage from a marine setting, with anatomy that converges on other secondarily aquatic mammals, in the right stratigraphic window. Nothing like it has been found.

Why it is here

Because it is the archive's best example of a claim that is more appealing than the consensus and less supported than it looks, and because the reason it failed — no fossil, no convergence, better explanations already in hand — is a reusable test for every other origin story on this site.

Snowball Earth

Documented

Twice in the Neoproterozoic, ice reached sea level in the tropics. The evidence is in the rocks and is not seriously disputed; how the planet got out again is still argued about.

The evidence that forced the idea

Neoproterozoic rocks contain tillites — lithified glacial deposits — interbedded with rocks that only form in warm water. Some of those tillites sit in units whose palaeomagnetic signature places them within about 10° of the equator. Dropstones, striated pavements and varves appear at those latitudes. Ice sheets at sea level in the tropics is not a small claim, and it is the claim the rocks make.

Above the glacial deposits, almost everywhere the sequence is exposed, lies a distinctive dolostone — a “cap carbonate” — often with odd sedimentary structures and a strongly negative carbon-isotope signature just below it. The pattern repeats across continents and across two separate glaciations.

The mechanism

Ice reflects sunlight. More ice means a colder planet means more ice. Joseph Kirschvink, who coined the term in 1992, pointed out that this feedback has a runaway branch: once ice reaches about 30° latitude, the albedo change can carry it to the equator and the planet stops being able to melt itself.

Getting out requires the other half of the story. With the surface frozen, volcanic carbon dioxide has nowhere to go — no weathering, no photosynthesis — so it accumulates. Over millions of years it reaches the tens of thousands of parts per million needed to break the albedo, and the planet thaws in a geological instant. That is the same CO₂ that then forms the cap carbonates.

The hard part

Life survived, and it survived in a world with no open ocean for millions of years. Proposals include refugia around hydrothermal vents, thin-ice “slushball” states with open water at the equator, and a frozen but not globally sealed ocean. The debate is over how hard the snowball was, not whether the glaciations happened.

Where it stands

Documented: low-latitude glaciations in the Cryogenian, around 717–660 Ma (Sturtian) and 650–635 Ma (Marinoan), with cap carbonates above both.

Contested: whether the ocean was globally ice-covered (“hard snowball”) or had an open equatorial band (“slushball”).

Cause: the breakup of Rodinia, increased weathering and a drop in atmospheric CO₂ are the leading candidates for triggering it.

Consequence: the second glaciation is followed, within a few tens of millions of years, by the Ediacaran organisms and then the Cambrian explosion. Whether the freeze caused the animals is unresolved.

Why it belongs here

Because it is the counter-example the archive needs: a claim that sounded like catastrophism, was resisted for that reason, and then turned out to be written in the rock. The site collects hidden-world theories; this is what it looks like when one is true.

The Dinosaur Extinction

Documented

An asteroid hit the Yucatán 66 million years ago and three quarters of species died. The argument about whether the impact or the Deccan volcanoes did it is now mostly an argument about timing, and the timing has been measured.

The anomaly

In 1980, Luis and Walter Alvarez and colleagues reported that a thin clay layer at the Cretaceous–Palaeogene boundary at Gubbio, Italy, contained iridium at concentrations tens of times the normal crustal value. Iridium is rare on Earth's surface and common in meteorites. The same layer, with the same enrichment, was found in Denmark and New Zealand.

Their proposal — a 10-kilometre asteroid — was resisted for a decade, partly because no crater of the right age was known. In 1991 the Chicxulub structure under the Yucatán was identified as a buried impact crater about 180 kilometres across, dated to the boundary.

What the crater confirms

The impact hypothesis makes predictions that a volcano hypothesis does not: shocked quartz, melt spherules, a worldwide ejecta layer, a tsunami deposit around the Gulf, and an iridium anomaly that decays with distance from the crater. All are present. A 2010 review of 20 years of evidence concluded the impact was the cause of the extinction.

The Deccan Traps

The other candidate is the Deccan Traps flood volcanism in India, which erupted around the same time and would have released sulphur and carbon dioxide over hundreds of thousands of years. The eruptions began before the impact and continued after it. High-precision dating suggests the fastest eruption rates came after the boundary, which weakens the claim that volcanism alone caused the extinction — and strengthens the idea that the impact may have accelerated the eruptions.

How the labels stack

Documented: a large impact at 66.0 Ma, the Chicxulub crater, and a mass extinction at the same boundary. The coincidence is not in doubt.

Documented: the Deccan eruptions also happened, and contributed environmental stress before and after.

Still argued: the relative contribution of each, and whether the Deccan eruptions alone would have caused a mass extinction.

Settled against: the claim that the extinction was gradual and the impact irrelevant. The boundary is abrupt in the highest-resolution marine records.

What died, and what did not

Every non-avian dinosaur, the marine reptiles, the ammonites, most planktonic foraminifera. Birds, mammals, crocodilians, turtles and frogs survived. Size and food chain position predicted survival better than anything else: large terrestrial animals and animals dependent on photosynthesis at the base of the food web went first, which is what a months-long shutdown of sunlight produces.

Why it matters here

Because it is the archive's cleanest case of a catastrophic claim that was mocked and then confirmed by a crater, and because the public argument — volcanoes or asteroid — is now a technical argument about dates rather than a fight about whether the evidence exists.

Panpsychism

Live debate

The view that experience is a basic feature of matter, not something that emerges from complexity. It is taken seriously by a minority of philosophers, has no test, and is not the same as saying rocks are conscious.

The claim

Panpsychism holds that consciousness, or something like it — proto-experience, intrinsic nature — is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of the physical world. Complex minds are built out of simpler experiential parts, the way molecules are built out of atoms. It is not the claim that a rock is conscious in the way you are, and it is not vitalism.

The modern argument is usually framed by the hard problem. Physics describes structure and relations: mass, charge, spin. It does not describe what it is like to be anything. If experience is not derivable from structure, one option is that experience was never absent — it is the intrinsic nature of the physical.

The strongest objection

The combination problem. If micro-experiences exist, how do they combine into a single unified subject? Two subjects cannot simply be added, the way two masses can. Nothing in the panpsychist toolkit explains why a hundred billion tiny experiences would produce one experience of reading this sentence.

A second objection is empirical rather than logical: panpsychism predicts nothing. There is no observation that would count for or against it, which is why it lives in philosophy departments and not in neuroscience labs.

What it is not

It is not integrated information theory, though the two are often mentioned together. IIT is a mathematical theory that makes testable claims about which systems are conscious and is a scientific hypothesis with a contested empirical record. Panpsychism is a metaphysical position about what the world is made of. Related but distinct: Russellian monism, cosmopsychism, and illusionism, which denies the hard problem outright.

How to read it honestly

Respectable, not established: panpsychism appears in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and in mainstream academic presses. That is a statement about its standing as philosophy, not about evidence.

No test exists: nothing in the position constrains an experiment, so it cannot be labelled documented or debunked — only argued.

The honest comparison: the archive files it as live debate because the argument is unresolved, not because both sides have equal support.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most common philosophical idea that reaches popular writing as a scientific one. Claims that “quantum physics proves consciousness creates reality” borrow its vocabulary and none of its care, and this page exists to mark where the careful version stops.

The Free Energy Principle

Live debate

A single mathematical principle is said to explain perception, action, learning and life itself. Its defenders call it the closest thing neuroscience has to a unifying law; its critics call it unfalsifiable, and both have a point.

The claim

Karl Friston's free energy principle starts from a fact about persistence. Anything that continues to exist must, statistically, keep itself within a limited set of states — a body stays at a temperature, a cell keeps its ion balance, an organism stays alive. The principle formalises this as minimising variational free energy, a quantity from statistical mechanics that bounds surprise.

From that, the framework derives perception as inference about the causes of sensory input, action as changing the world to fit the prediction, and learning as updating the model. Predictive processing is the psychological cousin; active inference is the engineering one.

Why it is attractive

It is one formalism for many phenomena. The same equation is claimed to cover vision, motor control, dopamine signalling, psychosis as aberrant precision, and the behaviour of single cells. It also connects to established mathematics — variational Bayes, the evidence lower bound, control theory — rather than inventing notation.

The objection that sticks

A principle that everything living must satisfy cannot distinguish between hypotheses about how a particular brain works. Critics argue the framework is close to a tautology: if persistence requires staying in a low-surprise region, then systems that persist minimise surprise, and the theory is true by construction. Friston's reply is that the interesting content is in the specific generative models, not in the principle — but those models are usually built by hand for each experiment, which is where the falsifiable work actually happens.

The practical test is whether it has produced findings that would not have been found otherwise. Active inference has produced useful engineering results and some striking neuroscience predictions; it has not produced a decisive experiment that killed a rival.

Where the label sits

Not fringe: the mathematics is mainstream, published in Nature Reviews Neuroscience, and used in real experiments.

Not settled: the claim that it is the unifying principle of brain function is contested by people who work on the same problems.

The useful distinction: predictive processing as a family of models is well supported. The stronger claim that all biological self-organisation is free-energy minimisation is a metaphysical bet with a mathematical costume.

Why it is here

Because it is what a grand unified theory looks like from the inside: elegant, generative, and impossible to falsify at the level where it is stated most broadly. The archive treats it the same way it treats the multiverse — serious, and not yet evidence.

Polyvagal Theory

A three-state model of the autonomic nervous system is taught in trauma training worldwide and rests on comparative anatomy that specialists say is wrong. It is the clearest case in this archive of a clinical framework outrunning its evidence.

The claim

Stephen Porges proposed in the 1990s that the mammalian autonomic nervous system has three hierarchical states rather than two: a ventral vagal state of safety and social engagement, a sympathetic state of mobilisation (fight or flight), and a dorsal vagal state of shutdown and immobilisation. Trauma, on this account, is a nervous system stuck in the lower two, and therapy is the business of restoring ventral vagal tone.

The theory is widely used in trauma-informed practice, in polyvagal-informed therapy training, and in popular books about the nervous system. Its vocabulary — “regulated”, “dysregulated”, “stuck in dorsal” — has spread well beyond the clinical literature.

The anatomical problem

The theory's central anatomical claim is that a myelinated ventral vagal pathway is a mammalian innovation that supports social engagement, and that the dorsal vagus is an older, unmyelinated system. Comparative work finds myelinated vagal fibres in fish, amphibians and reptiles, and the dorsal/ventral division does not map onto the proposed evolutionary hierarchy. The “vagal brake” — respiratory sinus arrhythmia as an index of parasympathetic tone — is real, but it does not require the three-state architecture.

A 2007 critique in Biological Psychology argued that the theory's physiological predictions are not supported and that its evidence is largely indirect. Later reviews have been blunter: the model is not a validated account of autonomic function.

What is nonetheless true

The autonomic nervous system does have distinct states, and they do relate to threat, safety and social behaviour. Heart-rate variability does track parasympathetic activity, imperfectly. Breathing practices, safe relationships and predictability do help people who are traumatised. None of that depends on polyvagal theory being correct, and this is the important distinction: the clinical practices can work while the theory that motivates them is unsupported.

Why the label is fringe and not debunked

Fringe: widely taught, weak anatomical basis, limited independent empirical support, and a mechanism that specialists dispute.

Not debunked: parts of it overlap with accepted physiology, and the clinical observations it tries to explain are real. A wrong model of a real phenomenon is not the same as a hoax.

The risk: the vocabulary has become a way of explaining any behaviour after the fact, which is the same failure mode as Freudian drives — unfalsifiable, and therefore unhelpful when a patient does not improve.

The test the archive applies

Does the framework generate predictions that could fail? For polyvagal theory, the honest answer is that the anatomical prediction did fail, and the clinical predictions have not been tested in trials that could distinguish the model from the therapy. That is enough to file it here, and not enough to tell anyone to stop breathing slowly.

Fast Radio Bursts

Documented

Millisecond flashes of radio energy from other galaxies, first dismissed as a microwave oven and now observed in their thousands. The phenomenon is documented; the source of most of them is still open.

The discovery, and the retraction

In 2007, Duncan Lorimer and colleagues reported a 5-millisecond radio pulse in archival data from the Parkes telescope in Australia, with a dispersion measure far larger than any Galactic source could produce. The dispersion measure is the delay between high and low frequencies caused by free electrons along the line of sight — a distance proxy. Their burst implied an extragalactic origin.

Six years later, a paper reported sixteen similar bursts from Parkes and concluded they were cosmological. Within months, the same group retracted: the signals were coming from an open microwave oven in the observatory kitchen, opened while the receiver was pointing at it. The original Lorimer burst survived. The lesson — check your local environment before claiming the universe — is now standard practice.

What settled it

Localisation. In 2017, a repeating burst (FRB 121102) was pinpointed to a dwarf galaxy about 3 billion light years away, using interferometry with the VLA and the European VLBI network. Since then, hundreds have been localised, and the Canadian CHIME telescope — a fixed array that sees a huge fraction of the sky — has catalogued thousands. Most appear in star-forming regions of other galaxies.

What causes them

At least some come from magnetars, the ultra-magnetic neutron stars. In 2020, a burst from the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154 was detected simultaneously in radio and X-rays, with a radio energy far below extragalactic FRBs but with the right signature. Whether magnetars explain all of them, and what produces the repeaters as opposed to the one-off bursts, is unresolved.

Where the evidence stands

Documented: the bursts exist, are extragalactic, last milliseconds, and carry dispersion and Faraday rotation that make them probes of intergalactic plasma.

Documented: magnetars can produce them — the 2020 Galactic event is direct evidence.

Open: the engine for the brightest extragalactic bursts, and why only a few percent repeat.

Why it matters: the dispersion measure counts electrons across billions of light years, so FRBs are one of the few ways to weigh the “missing” baryons in the intergalactic medium.

Why it belongs in a hidden-world archive

Because it is the honest version of a story the fringe tells constantly: a signal from outside, initially dismissed, later confirmed. The difference is that the confirmation came from a second instrument, an identified host galaxy and a Galactic counterpart — not from a reinterpretation of the same noisy data.

Magnetoreception

Documented

Animals navigate by the Earth's magnetic field. That much is settled by decades of behavioural experiments. How a biological cell measures a field a hundred thousand times weaker than a fridge magnet is not.

The behaviour

The evidence is behavioural and old. European robins orient in the right direction under a magnetic field of the correct inclination, and stop doing so when the field is rotated by a magnet. Newts, sea turtles, salmon, honeybees, monarch butterflies, mole rats and some bacteria all show magnetic responses in controlled experiments. The behaviour is robust, replicated across labs, and not seriously disputed.

The complication is that the avian compass appears to be light-dependent and to fail under certain radio-frequency noise — which is a clue about mechanism, and an awkward one for the simplest explanations.

The candidate mechanisms

First, magnetite: crystals of iron oxide in tissue, acting as tiny compass needles coupled to a nerve. Magnetic crystals have been found in many organisms, but the sensory cells in bird beaks once claimed to house them turned out to be iron-rich macrophages, part of the immune system, which badly weakened the strongest version of this account.

Second, the radical pair: a photochemical reaction in the retina in which a magnetic field alters the spin state of a transient pair of radicals, changing the yield of a signalling product. The candidate protein is cryptochrome 4, found in migratory birds' retinas, and in 2021 a team showed that the zebra finch version is magnetically sensitive in vitro. That is a mechanism, not yet a demonstrated sense.

Third, induction: in marine animals, the field generated by swimming through a conductor — seawater — could be detected electrically. Plausible for sharks and rays, which have electroreceptors, and not applicable to a bird.

What is and is not settled

Documented: magnetic orientation behaviour in dozens of species, replicated and robust.

Strong evidence: a light-dependent, cryptochrome-based mechanism in migratory birds, demonstrated in vitro.

Not settled: which cells transduce the signal in vivo, and how a chemical signal becomes a neural one.

Debunked: the specific claim that iron crystals in the pigeon beak are the magnetoreceptors.

Why it is here

Because it is a case where the phenomenon is certain and the explanation is partial, and because popular accounts routinely present the mechanism as solved. It also explains something the archive gets asked about: whether humans have a magnetic sense. The evidence is weak and contested, and no one has demonstrated a behavioural effect that survives replication.
