Tardigrades Between Planets

Documented

A millimetre-long animal that survives vacuum, radiation and decades without water is real. The claim built on top of it — that life travels between planets — is a different proposition, and the experiments that get quoted do not support it.

The animal

Tardigrades were described in 1773 by Johann August Ephraim Goeze, who called them kleiner Wasserbär — little water bear. They are eight-legged animals a fraction of a millimetre long, and there are more than a thousand described species. They live in moss, soil, lake sediment and the sea, which is unremarkable. What made them famous is what happens when the water goes.

Cryptobiosis

A desiccated tardigrade contracts into a tun: a barrel-shaped state in which metabolism falls below the level anyone can measure, the cell replaces water with trehalose and specific proteins, and DNA damage is repaired on rehydration. In that state they have survived years of vacuum, temperatures from near absolute zero to above 100 °C, pressures of hundreds of megapascals, and doses of ionising radiation hundreds of times what would kill a human.

Two results get quoted more than the rest. In 2007, a European team launched dehydrated tardigrades into low Earth orbit for ten days; animals exposed to vacuum and solar radiation survived, and some reproduced after return. In 2019, an Israeli lunar lander carrying a library of human DNA and dried tardigrades crashed on the Moon — which produced headlines about life on the Moon, and no evidence of it.

What the evidence supports

Documented: cryptobiosis, and survival of space vacuum and radiation in the tun state, demonstrated in orbit.

Not shown: that tardigrades are active or metabolising in space. The survival is of a dormant state, not of a living animal doing anything.

Not shown: panspermia. That life could survive a journey says nothing about whether it made one, and the radiation dose over a multi-year transit inside a rock is far above what the orbit experiment tested.

Retracted, not repeated: the 2015 claim that a sixth of the tardigrade genome is bacterial, from horizontal transfer. Re-analysis in 2016 found contamination, and the figure collapsed to about one percent.

Why the claim survives the evidence

Because the real animal is extraordinary enough that the exaggeration is unnecessary. A creature that can be dried to powder, kept in a drawer for years, and then rehydrated and walk away is a better story than one that colonises planets, and it has the advantage of being true.

The archive keeps this page because it is the cleanest example of a pattern worth recognising: a real, measured, remarkable capability, with an unmeasured inference attached to it. The capability is documented. The inference is not.

The Cambrian Explosion

Live debate

Almost every major animal group appears in the fossil record within about twenty million years. Whether that is an explosion of life or an explosion of fossils is the argument, and it has been running since Darwin apologised for it.

The pattern

Below the Cambrian, the fossil record is thin: the Ediacaran organisms, soft-bodied and mostly unlike anything alive, and before them almost nothing but microfossils and trace marks. Within the Cambrian, beginning around 539 million years ago, the record fills with shells, spines, mouths and limbs. Trilobites, brachiopods, molluscs, worms and the armoured predators of the Burgess Shale appear over roughly twenty to twenty-five million years — a fifth of the time since, and an instant in the history of life.

Darwin knew this was a problem. On the Origin of Species devotes a section to the imperfection of the geological record, arguing that the apparent suddenness was an artefact of missing rock. That argument has been tested for a century and a half, and both halves of it have turned out to be partly right.

What makes it look like an explosion

Three things happened close together. Oxygen rose, allowing larger bodies and active predation. Mineralised skeletons evolved — which is what makes the Cambrian visible in the first place. And the animals themselves diversified into the body plans that still exist. The last of these is real: the Cambrian is where the major phyla first appear, and no phylum has appeared since.

What makes it look like a record

Preservation is not uniform. The Burgess Shale and Chengjiang are Lagerstätten: sites where fine mud preserved soft tissue, which is rare. Molecular clocks, calibrated on the DNA of living animals, put the origin of animal groups tens to hundreds of millions of years earlier than their first fossils, in the Ediacaran or Cryogenian. If those clocks are right, the groups existed before the Cambrian and simply were not fossilised until they evolved shells.

Where the argument sits

Documented: the Cambrian radiation of skeletal animals, the appearance of the major phyla, and the rise in oxygen.

Contested: whether the diversification was as fast as the fossil record suggests, or whether it began much earlier and became visible when animals started building hard parts.

Not supported: the creationist reading that the Cambrian shows animals appearing without ancestors. The trace fossils and the Ediacaran biota are the ancestors, and they are in the rock below.

The honest summary: an unusually fast radiation, made to look faster by an unusually good fossil record.

Why it is here

Because it is the archive's best case of a genuine scientific puzzle that gets quoted by both sides of an argument it does not belong to. The explosion is real. What it means is not settled, and the people who say it is are usually selling something.

Earthquake Prediction

Live debate

Nobody can say where and when a large earthquake will happen. A great deal of money and a long list of methods have gone into trying, and the failures are more instructive than the successes.

The difference between three things

Prediction is a statement that an earthquake of a given size will occur in a given place within a stated window. Forecasting is a probability over a longer window and a wider region. Early warning is the seconds between the first fast waves and the damaging ones. Only the last works reliably, and it works because the earthquake has already started.

Most public argument about prediction confuses the three, which is how a successful early-warning system becomes evidence that someone can predict.

The attempts, and what happened

The 1970s produced the dilatancy-diffusion model: rocks about to fail supposedly swell, changing the speed of seismic waves and the level of the water table. It made predictions, and the predictions failed. The Parkfield experiment in California went further — a section of the San Andreas that had ruptured roughly every 22 years — and instrumented it heavily in 1985 to catch the next one. The earthquake came in 2004, nineteen years later, without a precursor anyone could recognise.

Two Chinese cases are quoted on both sides. Haicheng in 1975 was evacuated on the basis of foreshocks and animal behaviour, and is counted as a success. Tangshan in 1976 killed hundreds of thousands with no warning at all. A method that works once and not the next time is not a method.

What actually exists

Operational: aftershock forecasting, which is statistical and works; long-term probabilistic hazard maps; and early warning, which gives seconds to tens of seconds.

Contested: the VAN method, which claimed to detect seismic electrical signals in Greece. It has been argued about for forty years without resolution, largely because the predictions were not stated in a form that could be scored.

Unproven: animal precursors, radon anomalies, cloud patterns and thermal anomalies. Each has a literature; none has produced a prediction that survived a blind test.

The structural problem: for a rare event, a method that raises alarms often will appear to succeed by chance, and the cost of false alarms is paid by someone else.

What would settle it

A pre-registered protocol: a region, a magnitude threshold, a time window, and a published list of alarms issued before the events. Score it against the rate expected without the method. No claimant has yet published such a score, which is itself the answer to why the field looks the way it does.

Aphantasia

Documented

Some people close their eyes and see nothing. The condition was described in 1880, named in 2015, and is now the best-studied example of how differently ordinary minds are furnished.

What it is

Aphantasia is the absence, or near-absence, of voluntary mental imagery. Asked to picture an apple, most people report something apple-like; a person with aphantasia reports nothing, or knows the facts about an apple without seeing one. It is not a memory deficit, not a failure of recognition, and not blindness. People with it recognise faces, navigate cities and describe scenes — they do it without the picture.

Francis Galton described the variation in 1880, in a survey of mental imagery that found, to his surprise, that some scientists reported none at all. The thread was dropped for a century. In 2015 Adam Zeman's group published a case series of people who lost imagery after surgery or stroke, and coined the term; the congenital form turned out to be far more common.

How common, and how it is measured

Estimates cluster around 1–4% of the population, measured with the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire, in which people rate the vividness of imagined scenes. Self-report is the weak point: you cannot check someone's imagery from outside, and the questionnaire measures the confidence of the report as much as the experience behind it.

Objective measures are catching up. Binocular rivalry, in which two images compete for awareness, is biased by imagining one of them — an effect that is reduced or absent in aphantasia. Pupil dilation tracks imagined brightness in most people. Brain imaging shows weaker connectivity between frontal control regions and visual cortex when people try to imagine, though the picture is not a clean on/off switch.

What is established, and what is not

Documented: congenital aphantasia exists, is not rare, and does not impair most everyday function.

Documented: imagery is not one thing. Some people lack visual imagery but have auditory or spatial imagery; some have vivid dreams and no waking imagery.

Open: what it means for memory, creativity and clinical treatment, where imagery-based therapies assume a picture the patient may not have.

Not supported: the claim that people with aphantasia have no imagination. They have no voluntary imagery. The two words are not synonyms, and conflating them is the commonest error in the popular writing.

Why it belongs here

Because it is the counterweight to every claim on this site that treats the mind as a single thing with a standard setting. The variation is real, measurable, and invisible from outside — which is also why the archive is cautious about first-person reports in both directions.

Multiple Intelligences

Debunked

The claim that intelligence comes in eight or nine independent kinds reshaped classrooms worldwide. As a description of how abilities are organised it does not survive the data, and the theory was never built to be tested.

The claim

Howard Gardner's Frames of Mind (1983) argued that the mind is not one general capacity but a set of relatively independent ones: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, and later naturalistic. The argument drew on evidence from prodigies, savants, brain injury and cross-cultural skill, and it was aimed partly at the narrowing effect of IQ tests.

The educational claim came later and is the one that spread: that schools should identify each child's profile and teach to it. The theory itself did not specify how to do that, and Gardner has objected to the way it was turned into tests and labels.

What the evidence says

Psychometrics finds a general factor that predicts performance across dissimilar tasks, plus narrower abilities. That structure is one of the most replicated findings in psychology, and it is not what a theory of eight independent intelligences predicts. Abilities are correlated: people good at one tend to be somewhat good at others, and the correlations are not small.

The stronger problem is that the eight intelligences were not derived from data and do not generate predictions that could fail. Gardner's criteria — prodigies, savants, brain localisation, an evolutionary history — are consistent with the taxonomy, not tests of it. A framework that can accommodate any pattern of ability is not a rival to the general-factor model; it is a different kind of object.

What is true, and what is not

True: abilities are uneven. A child can be musically exceptional and struggle with arithmetic.

True: teaching that uses music, movement and drawing reaches more children than a lecture does.

Not supported: that there are eight or nine separable intelligences with equal standing.

Not supported: that matching instruction to a child's strongest intelligence improves learning. That is the learning-styles claim wearing a different hat, and it has the same problem: no crossover effect.

Why the label is debunked and not fringe

Because the theory was proposed by a serious scholar in good faith, and parts of its motivation — that IQ tests measure less than a person is — are defensible. What failed is the specific structure: a list of independent faculties, presented as an alternative to the general factor, that no study has found. The archive files it here because it changed curricula for forty years on the strength of being attractive.

The Anthropocene

Documented

Humans have changed the rock record. Whether that deserves a place in the geological timescale was put to a vote in 2024 and lost — and the vote is more interesting than the answer.

The proposal

Paul Crutzen and Eugene Stoermer proposed the term in 2000, arguing that human activity had become a geological force. The Anthropocene Working Group, convened in 2009, spent fifteen years on the question of whether it should be a formal unit of the geological timescale — an epoch, following the Holocene — and if so, where its base should be.

In 2016 the group voted for a mid-twentieth-century start, tied to the Great Acceleration: the sharp rise in population, energy use, fertiliser, plastics and carbon dioxide after 1950. The marker would be plutonium fallout from atmospheric nuclear tests, which appears worldwide in sediments and ice and did not exist before 1945.

The vote

In March 2024 the proposal was rejected by the International Union of Geological Sciences. The reason was not that the evidence is weak. It was procedural and definitional: a geological epoch is defined by a synchronous global boundary in rock, and the Anthropocene's boundary is not synchronous — it arrives at different times in different places, and much of the evidence is in sediments that will not survive to become rock.

The working group's alternative is to treat it as an event rather than an epoch, which is how geology handles things like the Great Oxidation Event: a period of change recorded in the rock, without a formal line.

What is settled and what is not

Documented: humans have altered the physical record — radionuclides, plastics, concrete, technofossils, altered sediment transport, a changed carbon cycle.

Documented: the changes accelerated sharply around 1950.

Rejected: the formal epoch, on stratigraphic rather than evidential grounds.

Still argued: the start date. Proposals include 1610 (a dip in atmospheric CO₂ after the Americas were depopulated), the Industrial Revolution, and 1950.

The honest position: the phenomenon is real and the naming is politics. A word that describes a fact and a word that defines a boundary are not the same word.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the rare case where the contested part is the label rather than the evidence, and where the scientists who proposed it lost the vote and accepted the result. It is what a live debate looks like when the participants follow the rules.

Synesthesia

Documented

For some people, letters have colours and sounds have tastes, consistently, for a lifetime. It is one of the few claims in this archive that a laboratory can check in an afternoon.

The experience

Synesthesia is a stable, involuntary cross-linking of senses or concepts: digits printed in black that carry a colour, music that has a taste, words that sit at a position in space. Estimates of prevalence run from 1% to 4%, with grapheme–colour the most commonly reported form.

The critical word is stable. A synaesthete's colour for the digit 7 does not drift. Ask twice, a year apart, and the answer is the same or nearly so — and that consistency is what turned a curiosity into a research subject.

How it is tested

The standard test is a consistency check: the same stimuli presented months apart, scored for agreement. A second is interference: show a grapheme in the wrong colour and synaesthetes are slower to name it, which is a Stroop effect produced by an experience the experimenter cannot see. A third is perceptual: some forms show measurable effects on visual search or on binocular rivalry, where the synaesthetic colour behaves a little like a real one.

The tests matter because the alternative explanation is metaphor. Everyone associates colours with things loosely; the claim is that for some people the association is automatic, stable and percept-like. Consistency plus interference is what separates the two.

What is settled and what is not

Documented: grapheme–colour synesthesia exists, is stable over years, and produces measurable interference.

Documented: it runs in families, and the specific pairings do not — relatives share the tendency, not the colours.

Contested: whether it is a distinct condition or the extreme end of a continuum that everyone sits on.

Contested: the mechanism. The leading account is reduced pruning of cross-modal connections in infancy; the evidence is suggestive rather than decisive.

Not supported: the popular claim that synaesthesia and creativity are linked. The association is reported, is small, and is confounded by who volunteers for studies.

Why it belongs in this archive

Because it is the counter-example to the archive's usual subject. Here is an extraordinary-sounding claim — that some people see sounds — which turns out to be true, testable, and unremarkable to the people who have it. It is a reminder that 'extraordinary' and 'unevidenced' are different words.

Lucid Dreaming

Documented

People can know they are dreaming while asleep, and say so from inside the dream. That was verified with eye movements in 1980, which makes it one of the few dream claims with a laboratory receipt.

The claim, and the problem with it

A lucid dream is one in which the dreamer knows they are dreaming. The report is entirely first-person, from a state in which the reporter cannot move, and dreams are notoriously unreliable to recall. For most of the twentieth century the claim was therefore untestable, and mostly dismissed.

The verification

In 1980 Stephen LaBerge and colleagues found the way through. During REM sleep the eye muscles are not paralysed, so a sleeper can move their eyes voluntarily. They agreed a code in advance: look left-right-left-right for a signal, or move the eyes in a pattern counting from one. Sleepers in verified REM produced the agreed pattern from inside the dream, and reported a lucid dream on waking.

The technique has been repeated many times since, and extended: lucid dreamers have been asked to perform a sequence of eye movements corresponding to a physical task, and their breathing or muscle twitches timed against it. The phenomenon is real and the method is sound.

How common, and whether it can be trained

About half of people report at least one lucid dream; roughly a fifth report them monthly or more. Several techniques claim to increase the rate — reality testing during the day, waking after five hours and returning to sleep with the intention to notice (MILD, WBTB), and external stimulation. A meta-analysis of the induction studies found effects that are real but modest, and the studies are small, which is the usual caveat in this literature.

What is established

Documented: lucid dreaming occurs, is verifiable by pre-agreed eye signals during REM, and can be induced with training, weakly.

Not the same as dream control: knowing you are dreaming and being able to change the dream are different abilities, and the second is much less reliable.

Not established: the therapeutic claims. Lucid dreaming has been trialled for nightmares with promising early results, and for other conditions with much weaker evidence.

Not established: that it is a doorway to anything other than a dream.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clean case of a claim that sounded mystical, was dismissed as such, and turned out to be checkable by anyone with a sleep lab and a cooperative volunteer. The archive files it as documented and notes how thin the popular literature on it still is.

Near-Death Experiences

Live debate

People brought back from cardiac arrest report tunnels, light, life review and calm. The reports are real and consistent enough to study. What they mean about death is the part that is not.

The report

A near-death experience is the account given by someone who came close to death, or believed they did, and returned. The core features were catalogued by Bruce Greyson into a scale: a sense of peace, separation from the body, a tunnel or darkness, light, meeting figures, a life review, and a decision or barrier that ends it. Between 10% and 20% of cardiac-arrest survivors report something in that family.

The accounts are not random. They cluster, they are reported across cultures, and the people who have them usually describe them as more real than ordinary experience. That consistency is what makes them worth studying rather than dismissing.

The problem

The brain during cardiac arrest is not idle: it is hypoxic, acidotic and undergoing a chaotic cascade. Any explanation has to account for vivid, structured, remembered experience during a period when cortical activity is grossly abnormal — and for the fact that most survivors report nothing at all.

The leading accounts are physiological: hypoxia and hypercapnia, surges of neurotransmitters during reperfusion, temporal-lobe activity, and REM intrusion into a failing brain. None of them explains every feature, and none has been demonstrated to produce the full syndrome in a controlled setting. The fact that ketamine and some seizures produce similar experiences is evidence about mechanism, not about what is on the other side.

What the evidence supports

Documented: the experiences occur, cluster into recognisable features, and are reported across cultures.

Not established: veridical perception. The AWARE study placed hidden images in resuscitation rooms; the one widely publicised case of a patient reporting a target was not confirmed as a hit.

Not established: that the experiences are of anything outside the brain. No test has yet distinguished a dying-brain account from a survival account, and the burden of proof sits with the stronger claim.

Culturally shaped: the content tracks the culture — tunnels and light in the West, judgement and ancestors elsewhere — which is what a constructed experience would do.

Why it is filed as live debate

Because the phenomenon is documented and the interpretation is not, and because the honest position — this is a real experience of a brain under extreme stress, whose content we cannot yet fully explain — is uncomfortable for both camps. The archive does not pretend the question is closed in either direction.

The Mpemba Effect

Live debate

Hot water sometimes freezes faster than cold. It was reported by a Tanzanian schoolboy in 1963, dismissed by his teacher, and is still argued about by physicists with better equipment and no agreement on what would count as an answer.

The story

In 1963 a Tanzanian schoolboy, Erasto Mpemba, noticed that warm ice-cream mix froze faster than cold in the same tray. His physics teacher told him he was confusing the question with the answer; he persisted, and in 1969 he and Denis Osborne published a short paper in Physics Education reporting the effect and naming it.

The paper is careful and the observations are ordinary. What followed is a fifty-year argument about whether the phenomenon exists, and if it does, what it is.

Why it is so hard to settle

Freezing is not one process. Water can cool to 0 °C, supercool below it, nucleate at different points depending on the container and its dissolved gas, and freeze from the outside in while convection mixes the interior. A container of hot water starts with convection that cold water does not, loses mass by evaporation, holds less dissolved gas, and may nucleate differently.

So 'hot freezes faster' can mean five different things: reaching 0 °C sooner, starting to freeze sooner, finishing freezing sooner, supercooling to a lower temperature, or having less ice at a given time. Experiments that define it differently get different answers, and reviews have found the positive results are sensitive to every one of those choices.

Where it stands

Reported: many times, including by professional physicists, under controlled conditions.

Not robust: the effect disappears when the protocol is standardised across labs. A 2016 review concluded that the published evidence is consistent with several ordinary mechanisms rather than one anomaly.

Explanations on the table: evaporation, convection, dissolved gases, supercooling, thermal contact with the container, and hydrogen-bonding structure in the 2020 proposal that got the most press.

What would settle it: one agreed definition, one protocol, several labs, and a result that survives. Nobody has run that experiment.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's clearest case of a claim that may well be true and is certainly not established — and where the interesting failure is not the claim but the reporting. A schoolboy's careful observation became a headline about physicists being wrong, when the physicists were mostly arguing about definitions.

Ball Lightning

Live debate

Glowing spheres that drift through rooms during thunderstorms have been reported for four centuries, filmed once, and measured spectroscopically in a handful of cases. The reports are too consistent to dismiss and too rare to pin down.

The reports

Ball lightning is described as a luminous sphere, usually 10–30 centimetres across, lasting seconds, drifting or hovering, sometimes passing through a window or a wall, and often ending in a small explosion or a silent fade. Reports go back to the seventeenth century and are unusually consistent across countries and centuries, which is the main reason physicists have kept taking them seriously.

The weaknesses are equally clear. Witnesses are startled, the events last seconds, and they happen close to the observer — which is the worst possible setup for a measurement.

The measurements

Two things changed the picture. In 2012 and 2014, Chinese researchers recorded a luminous ball during a thunderstorm with a spectrograph, and the spectrum showed silicon, iron and calcium — soil elements — rather than nitrogen and oxygen from air. That fits a model proposed in 2000: a lightning strike vaporises soil, the vapour condenses into nanoparticles, and the cloud of particles oxidises slowly, glowing.

The other line of work is laboratory: microwave discharges and vapourised silicon can produce glowing, floating structures that look like the descriptions. Neither has produced the thing itself on demand.

Where the evidence stands

Reported: consistently, for four centuries, by many witnesses including scientists.

Measured: at least one spectroscopic record consistent with vaporised soil.

Reproduced: laboratory analogues that resemble the reports, not the phenomenon itself.

Not explained: the reported persistence, the passage through solid surfaces, and the energy budget — a glowing ball lasting seconds needs a source nobody has identified for certain.

The honest label: a real observation without an accepted mechanism. Closer to 'unexplained' than to 'debunked'.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is what a genuine anomaly looks like before it is solved: too rare to study properly, too consistent to dismiss, and surrounded by a fringe literature that has attached everything from aliens to plasma life to it. The archive keeps the reports and drops the attachments.

The Flynn Effect

Documented

Measured intelligence rose by about three points a decade through the twentieth century, in every country with good data. Then, in several of them, it stopped. Both halves of that sentence are strange.

The finding

In the 1980s James Flynn noticed something hiding in plain sight. Every time a standardised test was restandardised, the new sample scored higher than the old one on the old norms — by about three IQ points a decade. Across the twentieth century that compounds to roughly fifteen to twenty points, or about a standard deviation.

The name 'Flynn effect' was coined by others; Flynn himself preferred to describe it as a puzzle about what intelligence tests actually measure. The finding is not in dispute. Its causes are.

What kind of gain it is

The gains are not uniform across subtests, and that is the clue. They are largest on tests of abstract reasoning — matrices, similarities, classification — and near zero on tests of vocabulary, arithmetic and general knowledge. If people had simply become smarter in a general sense, the gains would be spread evenly.

Flynn's own reading was that the twentieth century changed how people think rather than how much: from a world of concrete particulars to one of abstractions, categories and hypotheticals, which is exactly what the tests reward. Schooling, nutrition, health, smaller families, urbanisation and a visually richer environment are all candidate contributors, and none has been isolated as the main one.

The reversal

Since the 1990s, several countries — Norway, Denmark, the UK, France, the Netherlands — have reported the trend flattening or reversing on some tests. The size of the reversal is small, the data are patchy, and the explanations are contested: changes in immigration, in test coaching, in schooling, or a ceiling effect from a measure that was never designed to track a century of change.

What is established and what is not

Documented: large gains in measured IQ across birth cohorts in the twentieth century, concentrated on abstract reasoning.

Documented: a flattening or reversal in several rich countries since the 1990s on some tests.

Not established: the cause. Every candidate is plausible, none is decisive, and they are not mutually exclusive.

Not supported: the reading that the twentieth century made people genetically more intelligent. A change that fast, and that specific to particular subtests, is environmental by default.

Why it matters: any claim that intelligence is falling, or rising, has to say which test, which country and which decade — and most do not.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the fact that makes every argument about IQ harder. If the measure moves by a standard deviation in a century, then the measure is not measuring a fixed thing, and any claim built on it — about race, about schooling, about a generation — has to explain the movement before it uses the number.

Why Zebras Have Stripes

Live debate

Camouflage, confusion, cooling and social signalling have all been proposed. The hypothesis with the best experimental support is the least romantic one: flies.

The candidates

Darwin, Wallace and generations of naturalists proposed that stripes break up the outline, confuse predators, or help animals recognise each other. The thermoregulation hypothesis came later: black stripes absorb heat, white ones reflect it, and the difference might drive convection. The fly hypothesis is the most recent and the least intuitive — biting flies, particularly tsetse and tabanids, appear to avoid landing on striped surfaces.

Each hypothesis makes a different prediction about where stripes should be, how many there should be, and what should happen when a fly approaches.

The evidence

The biogeographic test is the strongest. Analyses mapping stripe presence and intensity against climate, predators and fly ranges across equid species find the best predictor is the range of biting flies, not predator density and not temperature. Zebras with the boldest stripes live where the flies are worst.

The experimental test followed. In 2019 a team dressed horses in striped coats — black-and-white, and controls in single colours — and counted fly landings. Striped coats attracted markedly fewer. A 2023 study extended this to full-body patterns and found the same direction of effect. This is rare in behavioural ecology: a hypothesis with a controlled experiment behind it, in a field that mostly runs on correlation.

Where the argument stands

Best supported: fly avoidance. Biogeography and at least two controlled experiments point the same way.

Weakly supported: thermoregulation. There is a measurable effect of stripe pattern on surface temperature, and it is small.

Poorly supported: predator confusion. The evidence is theoretical and the pattern does not obviously help against the predators that actually hunt zebras.

Not supported: the idea that stripes are for individual recognition. Zebras recognise each other perfectly well without them.

The honest position: one mechanism with real evidence, several with suggestive evidence, and no reason to think only one is at work.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's pleasantest example of science working as advertised: a question everyone has an intuition about, several competing explanations, and an experiment that discriminated between them. It also shows how a good hypothesis can be dull — the answer is flies, not majesty.

The Giraffe's Neck

Live debate

Lamarck's favourite example is not a Lamarckian one. The neck has seven vertebrae, like yours, and the best explanation is not that giraffes stretched.

The example everyone knows

Lamarck used the giraffe to explain inheritance of acquired characteristics: ancestors stretched for high leaves, the neck lengthened, and the lengthening was passed on. The story is intuitive, memorable, and wrong in its mechanism — there is no known route by which stretching an animal's neck alters the genes it gives its offspring.

What is less well known is how strange the anatomy is. A giraffe has seven cervical vertebrae. So do you, and so does a mouse. The neck is long because each vertebra is hugely elongated, not because there are more of them — and the constraint that keeps the count at seven is one of the more interesting open questions in vertebrate palaeontology.

The competing explanations

The feeding hypothesis says longer necks reach higher browse during competition. The sexual-selection hypothesis, revived by Simmons and Scheepers in 1996, points out that males use their necks as weapons in fights and that neck length is more sexually dimorphic than the feeding hypothesis needs. The thermoregulation hypothesis notes the neck's surface area and the animal's heat budget.

The evidence is mixed. Giraffes often feed below their maximum reach, which weakens the feeding story; males feed higher than females, which supports it partly. Neck growth in males continues past sexual maturity, which supports the sexual-selection account. The fossil record is thin, and the closest relatives — Samotherium and others — show intermediate neck lengths, which tells us the transition was gradual but not why it happened.

What the evidence supports

Documented: seven cervical vertebrae, each elongated; a gradual fossil transition from shorter necks.

Well supported: sexual selection on males, as at least a major contributor.

Partially supported: feeding competition, probably as a secondary pressure.

Not supported: Lamarckian inheritance. Stretching does not write to the genome, in giraffes or anything else.

Open: why the vertebral count is fixed at seven, and what the actual selective pressure was at each step.

Why it belongs here

Because it is the most-quoted example of a mechanism that does not work, attached to an animal whose real anatomy is stranger than the story. The archive keeps it as a reminder that the famous version of an evolutionary explanation is usually the least accurate one.

Whale Strandings

Live debate

Hundreds of whales beach themselves together, and the explanations on offer range from sonar to solar storms. Some of them have been demonstrated. Most have not.

What happens

A single whale can strand because it is sick, injured or old. A mass stranding is different: dozens or hundreds of animals, often of one species, often in a tight group, often on a shallow sloping beach. Pilot whales and sperm whales are the commonest, and the pattern has been recorded for centuries.

The animals are usually not all sick. Necropsies often find one or two with disease or injury and the rest apparently healthy, which points at the social structure rather than at individual pathology.

The explanations

The strongest social account is simple: these are highly cohesive animals that follow a leader or a pod-mate. If one navigates into trouble, the rest follow, and the refloating instinct works against them because they stay together in shallow water.

The strongest environmental account involves naval sonar. In 2000, beaked whales stranded across the Bahamas during a US Navy exercise using mid-frequency sonar; necropsies found gas-bubble lesions consistent with decompression, and the link has been supported by subsequent events and by controlled exposure studies. This is a documented human cause of strandings, not a hypothesis.

Beyond those two, the evidence thins. Geomagnetic anomalies are proposed because some species may navigate magnetically; the correlations are weak and the mechanism is unproven. Solar storms, seismic activity and pollutant loads have all been suggested, none has been demonstrated.

What is settled and what is not

Documented: mass strandings occur, are dominated by a few social species, and often involve apparently healthy animals.

Documented: mid-frequency naval sonar has caused strandings, with post-mortem evidence.

Well supported: social cohesion as the mechanism that turns one animal's error into a pod's death.

Unproven: geomagnetic disturbance, solar activity, and most of the other environmental correlations.

The honest position: a real phenomenon with at least two well-supported causes and a large fringe literature attached to it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the fringe explanation and the real one look similar from outside — both involve invisible forces acting on animals that navigate — and only one of them has a necropsy and a controlled exposure experiment behind it.

Abiogenic Petroleum

Fringe claim

Oil is not made from fossils in the way schoolbooks imply — but it is organic. The claim that it forms abiotically in the mantle has been tested for a century and has produced no commercial field.

The claim

Abiogenic petroleum theory holds that hydrocarbons are primordial or mantle-derived, migrating upward through faults rather than forming from buried organic matter. It was proposed in various forms from the nineteenth century, argued at length by the Soviet geologist Nikolai Kudryavtsev, and popularised in English by Thomas Gold in The Deep Hot Biosphere (1999). Gold also proposed that a deep microbial biosphere feeds on such hydrocarbons.

The appeal is real. It would explain why oil appears in places that are not obviously source-rock basins, and it would mean the supply is not finite in the way the organic theory implies. That second implication is why the theory is popular in some political writing.

The evidence against

The chemistry is decisive. Petroleum contains biomarkers — molecules whose carbon skeletons are unmistakably derived from specific biological precursors, such as steranes from eukaryotic sterols and hopanes from bacterial lipids. It is optically active, meaning it rotates polarised light, which is a signature of biological synthesis. Its carbon isotope ratios match organic matter, not mantle carbon.

The geology is nearly as decisive. Commercial accumulations occur in sedimentary basins with organic-rich source rocks, at temperatures in the oil window, and not in crystalline basement or in mantle-derived rocks. Where hydrocarbons do occur in basement, they are almost always explained by migration from adjacent sediments.

What is true, and what is not

True: abiotic hydrocarbons exist. Methane is produced by serpentinisation in mantle rocks, and it is found in some hydrothermal systems.

True: the 'fossil fuel' shorthand is misleading. Oil forms from buried microbial and algal matter, not from dinosaurs.

False: that commercial oil and gas accumulations are abiogenic. The biomarker and isotope evidence rules it out for every field tested.

False: that the theory has been suppressed. It has been tested: companies have drilled on its predictions, and the predictions have not produced a commercial field.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a genuinely scientific-sounding alternative with a real literature behind it, and the way it fails is instructive: not on rhetoric but on molecules that could only have come from living things. The archive labels it fringe rather than debunked because abiotic methane is real — it is the commercial-oil claim that fails.

The Great Oxidation Event

Documented

About 2.4 billion years ago the atmosphere filled with oxygen, the planet froze, and most of the life then living died. The evidence is in rocks that record the moment the air changed.

The evidence

Banded iron formations are the most visible sign. Iron dissolves in anoxic water and precipitates when it meets oxygen, so a world with abundant dissolved iron is a world without much oxygen. These formations are common in the early Precambrian and essentially stop afterwards.

The sharper evidence is isotopic. Sulphur has four stable isotopes, and in rocks older than about 2.45 billion years their abundances deviate from the expected mass-dependent pattern — mass-independent fractionation, produced by photochemical reactions in an atmosphere without an ozone shield. After that date, the anomaly disappears. Something changed in the atmosphere, and it changed irreversibly.

The cause and the consequences

The cause is cyanobacteria: photosynthesis that splits water and releases oxygen, which evolved at least 2.7 billion years ago and took hundreds of millions of years to overwhelm the sinks — dissolved iron, volcanic gases, and reduced minerals — that consumed it. Oxygen only accumulates once the sinks are full.

The consequences were severe. Methane, a greenhouse gas, is destroyed by oxygen, and the loss of it plausibly triggered the Huronian glaciations — evidence of glaciation at low latitudes around the same time. For most existing life, oxygen was a poison, and the fossil record of that period is thin enough that the die-off is inferred rather than counted.

What is established

Documented: the loss of mass-independent sulphur fractionation around 2.45–2.32 billion years ago — the atmosphere changed.

Documented: the rise of oxygen, from cyanobacterial photosynthesis, over hundreds of millions of years.

Documented: glaciations in the same window, plausibly triggered by methane collapse.

Contested: how high oxygen actually got, and whether it stayed there. Estimates for the mid-Proterozoic run from 0.1% to several percent of the modern level.

Why it matters: it is the largest biological change to the planet's chemistry, and the only one we know of that was caused by a single metabolic innovation.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's deepest-time example of a claim that sounded like a story and turned out to be written in isotopes. The oxygen catastrophe is what happens when a microbe invents something and the planet has to live with it — which is a fair description of several pages in this collection.

  • Wikipedia, “Huronian glaciation” — the freeze that followeden.wikipedia.org

The Inner Core's Spin

Live debate

The solid iron ball at the centre of the planet may rotate slightly differently from the rest of it. The claim rests on subtle differences between earthquake waves recorded decades apart, and the disagreement is about the data as much as the physics.

The claim

In 1996, Song and Richards reported that seismic waves travelling through the inner core arrived slightly earlier or later depending on when the earthquake occurred, and interpreted the difference as the inner core rotating faster than the mantle — a 'super-rotation' of a few degrees per year. The inner core is solid iron, surrounded by liquid iron, so differential rotation is physically plausible.

The method depends on repeating earthquakes: events in the same place, recorded at the same station, years apart. If the core has moved, the path through it changes and so does the arrival time.

The argument

The signal is small, the repeating earthquakes are few, and the assumption that two earthquakes in the same place produce identical source signals is a strong one. Subsequent studies using different datasets and different methods produced a range of answers: fast super-rotation, slow super-rotation, oscillation, and no resolvable rotation at all.

In 2023 a pair of papers reported that the inner core's rotation had slowed, possibly pausing or reversing relative to the mantle — an oscillation rather than a steady spin. Other seismologists argued the data could not distinguish that from noise. The disagreement is not about whether the inner core can rotate; it is about whether the measurements are good enough to say it does.

Where the evidence stands

Documented: the inner core exists, is solid, and is decoupled from the mantle by a liquid outer core.

Contested: whether it rotates differentially, and if so how fast and in which direction.

The core problem: few repeating sources, small travel-time differences, and source effects that can mimic rotation.

What would settle it: a much denser set of repeating earthquakes, or a different observable — such as core-sensitive normal modes or a longer instrumental record.

The honest position: a real physical possibility, with a signal at the edge of what the data can resolve.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the disagreement is entirely about measurement, and the participants say so. There is no fringe here, no motive, and no hidden claim: just a hard problem at the limit of the instruments, which is what most live debates in geophysics look like.

The Baghdad Battery

Debunked

A clay jar with a copper cylinder and an iron rod will produce a voltage if you fill it with vinegar. Whether anyone in Parthian Iraq did that is a different question, and the answer is almost certainly no.

The object

In 1936 workers near Khujut Rabu, outside Baghdad, found a set of small clay jars. One held a rolled copper cylinder, an iron rod down the middle, and an asphalt plug holding the rod in place. Wilhelm König, then director of the Iraq Museum, described them in 1938 and suggested that filled with an acidic liquid — vinegar, or wine — they would have worked as galvanic cells.

Replicas do produce a voltage, usually between half a volt and two volts, and several can be wired in series to give more. That much is not in dispute.

Why the battery reading fails

The archaeology is the problem. No wires, conductors or terminals have been found with the jars. No object from the period shows electroplated metal, which is the use the hypothesis needs. The jars resemble other Parthian vessels that held scrolls, and the asphalt seal is consistent with storage rather than with a cell that would need to be filled and emptied.

The electroplating claim is the weakest part. It requires a current source, a conductive solution, a cathode and a knowledge of the process — and no ancient Iraqi object shows the thin, uniform plating that electrodeposition produces. König's original paper speculated; later popular writing turned the speculation into a claim.

What the evidence supports

Documented: the jars exist, with those components, from the Parthian period.

Documented: the arrangement works as a galvanic cell if filled with acid.

Not documented: any use as a cell — no wires, no electrolyte residue, no plated objects.

More likely: a scroll container, of a type known from the same region and period.

Why the label is debunked: not because the object is ordinary, but because the specific claim — that it was a battery in use — has no evidence and a better alternative.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the model of an out-of-place artefact claim: a real object, a real physical effect, and an inference that outruns both. The archive's rule applies exactly here — a claim and its evidence are different things, and the second one is missing.

The Piri Reis Map

Debunked

A 1513 Ottoman map of the Atlantic is genuinely remarkable. The claim that it shows an ice-free Antarctica surveyed by an unknown civilisation rests on a misreading of one coastline.

The map

Piri Reis was an Ottoman admiral and cartographer. His 1513 world map survives as a fragment on gazelle skin, showing the Atlantic Ocean, the coasts of South America and West Africa, and a southern landmass along the left edge. It was rediscovered in the Topkapı Palace in 1929, and it is genuinely impressive: the Caribbean is drawn with recognisable detail, and Piri Reis's own notes say he used charts captured from Columbus.

That provenance is the first thing to understand. The map is a compilation, openly declared as such, of Portuguese and Spanish charts plus older sources — which is exactly what a competent sixteenth-century cartographer would produce.

The Antarctica claim

In 1966 Charles Hapgood argued that the southern portion of the map depicts the Antarctic coast under the ice, surveyed before it froze — which would require an unknown civilisation with seagoing capability, and an ice-free Antarctica, which last existed millions of years ago.

The reading does not survive inspection. The southern landmass on the map is continuous with South America, drawn as though the continent extends eastward — a common error in early sixteenth-century maps, and one consistent with Ptolemaic ideas about a southern landmass balancing the northern continents. Detailed comparisons find no correspondence between the map's southern coast and the actual subglacial topography of Antarctica. Hapgood's method involved rotating and rescaling the map until features aligned, which is the cartographic equivalent of fitting a curve to noise.

What is established

Documented: the map is genuine, dates to 1513, and draws on Columbus-era charts.

Documented: it is an unusually accurate Atlantic chart for its date.

Not supported: that it shows Antarctica, ice-free or otherwise.

Not supported: that it required a lost civilisation. Its declared sources explain what it contains.

The honest reading: a fine piece of sixteenth-century compilation, with the errors of its time, described in its own marginal notes.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most attractive of the map claims, and the one where the refutation is available in the object itself: Piri Reis wrote down where his information came from. The mystery is manufactured by not reading the annotations.

The Kensington Runestone

Debunked

A Minnesota farmer found a stone in 1898 claiming a Norse expedition reached the American interior in 1362. Runologists have been unanimous for a century that the inscription is nineteenth-century Swedish.

The find

In 1898 Olof Öhman, a Swedish immigrant farmer in Kensington, Minnesota, found a slab of greywacke tangled in the roots of an aspen. The inscription, in runes, purported to record a party of eight Goths and twenty-two Norwegians who had reached that place in 1362, and whose members had been killed while the survivors were out fishing.

The claim is not absurd on its face: the Norse reached Newfoundland around 1000, and a fourteenth-century expedition inland is not physically impossible. That is why the stone has defenders.

The linguistic evidence

The decisive objections are philological. The inscription uses runic forms and spellings that belong to nineteenth-century Dalecarlian and to modern Swedish, not to fourteenth-century Norse. Several words are anachronistic; the grammar shows constructions that appear in later Swedish; and the rune forms themselves include characters that were not in use in 1362.

The historical context is equally suggestive. The stone appeared at a moment when Scandinavian-Americans were arguing for a Norse claim on the continent, and Öhman had both the runic knowledge and the motive. A 2003 investigation by Swedish linguists found the inscription consistent with a nineteenth-century forger working from an almanac.

Where scholarship stands

Documented: the stone was found in 1898 and bears an inscription in runes.

Documented: its language, orthography and rune forms are nineteenth-century Swedish, not fourteenth-century Norse.

Not supported: the 1362 expedition. No other artefact, site or document supports it.

Defenders: a small amateur literature continues to argue for authenticity; no peer-reviewed runologist supports it.

Why it matters: it is the clearest case of a forgery that would be harmless if it were not used to argue about who belongs where.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows what a debunked claim looks like when the debunking is technical rather than dramatic: no confession, no court case, just a hundred years of specialists agreeing about grammar while a popular literature continues to cite the stone.

The Philadelphia Experiment

Debunked

A destroyer escort is said to have vanished from a Philadelphia shipyard in 1943 and reappeared in Norfolk. The story comes from letters written by one man in 1955, and the ship's own deck logs contradict it.

The story

The claim is that in October 1943 the US Navy made the destroyer escort USS Eldridge invisible at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard, and that it teleported to Norfolk, Virginia and back, with crew members fused into the hull and others driven mad. It became a fixture of UFO and conspiracy literature through the 1979 film The Philadelphia Experiment and its sequels.

The source

The story originates in letters sent in 1955 to the writer Morris Jessup by a man signing himself Carlos Miguel Allende — later identified as Carl Meredith Allen, who had served in the merchant marine, not the Navy. Jessup had published a book on UFOs; Allen wrote to him about invisibility experiments and the Eldridge. The letters are the sole primary source, and Allen's biography includes a court-martial and a documented history of fabrication.

There is no corroboration. The Navy has no record of such an experiment. The Eldridge's deck logs place the ship on convoy duty in the Atlantic and Mediterranean during the period in question, and the ship's war diary does not put it in Philadelphia. No crew member's testimony supports the account before 1955.

The plausible kernel

Two real programmes get pulled in. Degaussing — wrapping a steel ship in cables to cancel its magnetic signature against mines — was real, secret, and visible as a strange hum and glow to sailors who did not know what it was. And the Navy did work on radar invisibility, in the sense of stealth and countermeasures. Neither involves teleportation, and neither is classified today.

What is established

Documented: the Eldridge existed, and served on convoy duty in 1943–44.

Documented: degaussing was real, secret and physically strange to observe.

Not documented: any invisibility or teleportation experiment; no records, no logs, no witnesses before 1955.

The source: one correspondent with a record of invention, writing to a UFO author.

Why it persists: because a real secret programme provides the texture, and a film provided the plot.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the template for a whole genre: a real classified programme, a single unreliable source, a film, and forty years of retelling in which the film becomes the evidence. The archive keeps it as the worked example of how a modern legend is assembled.

The Crystal Skulls

Debunked

A dozen quartz skulls were said to be pre-Columbian, and one was said to be the work of aliens or Atlanteans. Microscopy found nineteenth-century lapidary tools on every one that has been examined.

The objects

Around a dozen large crystal skulls are known. They were said to be Aztec or Maya, and were popularised from the 1920s by the explorer F. A. Mitchell-Hedges, who claimed his daughter had found one in a Maya ruin in British Honduras in 1924. The skulls became a fixture of New Age writing, with claims that they were Atlantean, alien, or capable of storing information.

The examinations

The British Museum and the Smithsonian submitted their skulls to examination in 1996 and 2005. The British Museum's skull and the Smithsonian's were found to be carved from Brazilian quartz — not a material used by Mesoamerican lapidaries — with tool marks from a rotary cutting wheel and abrasive paste. Those techniques are nineteenth-century European, not pre-Columbian. The Smithsonian's skull was traced to a Mexico City dealer in the 1880s.

The Mitchell-Hedges skull, the most famous, has never been independently examined and has no documented provenance before the 1920s. Its claimed discovery in a ruin is contradicted by the excavation records of the site.

What is established

Documented: the skulls exist and are skilfully carved.

Documented: every skull examined by a museum shows nineteenth-century lapidary tool marks and non-Mesoamerican quartz.

Not documented: any pre-Columbian origin, any provenance before the nineteenth century.

Not documented: any effect. The claims about light, energy and information storage have never been tested under controlled conditions, and the one study of 'energy' effects found nothing.

The remaining uncertainty: the Mitchell-Hedges skull, which is unexamined — and which the burden of proof has always been on.

Why it is in the archive

Because the debunking is not rhetorical: it is a microscope, a crystal-origin analysis and a dealer's invoice. The skulls are beautiful objects; the claim about them is a nineteenth-century market with a twentieth-century mythology attached.

Stonehenge Acoustics

Live debate

A replica of Stonehenge has been built and measured. The stones do affect sound in ways that would matter for speech, music and drumming — and the site is a ruin, which is the problem with every claim about how it sounded.

The claim

Archaeoacoustics asks what a site sounded like and what that meant. For Stonehenge the proposals are specific: that the circle's geometry would have produced reverberation and interference patterns, that certain positions were acoustically favoured for speech or ritual sound, and that the monument's design was partly an acoustic one.

The most cited work is a 1999 study by Watson and Keating, who measured a half-scale replica in the USA and reported reverberation and echo effects inside the circle. A 2012 project at the University of Salford built a full-scale temporary replica and measured speech intelligibility, music and drumming inside it.

What the measurements show

The replica studies agree on the general picture: a stone circle is a reverberant space, with reflections and some focusing effects, and it changes the character of sound relative to open ground. Whether those effects were intended, exploited, or even noticed is a separate question, and it is the one the evidence does not answer.

The ruin problem is fundamental. Stonehenge today is missing roughly half its stones; the sarsen circle is incomplete, the bluestone horseshoe is partly gone, and we do not know what was on top. Every acoustic model has to assume a reconstruction, and different reconstructions give different answers. The site was also modified repeatedly over more than a thousand years, so 'the acoustics of Stonehenge' describes no single moment.

Where the evidence stands

Documented: a stone circle measurably alters sound, with reverberation and reflections.

Documented: replica measurements exist, including a full-scale temporary build.

Contested: whether any of it was intended, and whether the design was acoustic rather than structural or astronomical.

The limit: the monument is a ruin, so the object measured is a hypothesis about the past, not the past itself.

The honest position: a real physical effect, an unresolved question of intent, and a site too damaged to settle it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most careful of the 'ancient wisdom' claims — it uses real measurement, real replicas and published results — and it still cannot get past the same wall every claim in this collection hits: the evidence that would settle it no longer exists.

The Shroud as a Radiation Flash

Fringe claim

The Shroud of Turin is a fourteenth-century linen cloth. The claim that its image was burned in by a burst of radiation at the resurrection explains the image and contradicts the dating, which is the wrong way round.

The claim

The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth bearing a faint double image of a bearded man, front and back. The radiation hypothesis says the image was formed by a burst of energy — light, protons, neutrons — at the moment of resurrection, and that this flash also reset the cloth's radiocarbon clock, which is why three independent laboratories dated it to 1260–1390.

The second half of that claim exists to explain away the first half's problem. Radiocarbon dating of the Shroud, published in Nature in 1989, was a blind test across three accelerator laboratories with control samples; the result was consistent and unambiguous.

What the image actually is

The image behaves like a painting or a contact transfer: it sits on the surface of the fibres, it is more intense where the cloth would touch a body, and it lacks the geometric distortion a projected image would produce. It also has anatomical errors — the hair, the proportions of the face, the position of the hands — that a real body would not produce.

No physical mechanism has been demonstrated that would produce this image on this cloth and leave no other trace. The radiation proposals are computer models fitted to the image, not experiments that generate it.

What the evidence supports

Documented: the cloth is medieval, dated by three laboratories in a blind protocol.

Documented: the image is a surface phenomenon with painting-like characteristics.

Not demonstrated: any radiation mechanism that produces the image.

Circular: the claim that the flash reset the radiocarbon date has no independent evidence — it is inferred from the date it is meant to explain.

The honest label: fringe. The image is unexplained in detail; the resurrection-flash explanation is unevidenced and requires the dating to be wrong for a reason nobody has shown.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best example of an explanation that is built backwards from a conclusion. Everything in it is designed to protect the conclusion from the measurement, which is the opposite of how the rest of these pages are argued.

Nessie as a Giant Eel

Live debate

Environmental DNA sampling of Loch Ness found eel DNA in most samples and no reptilian DNA at all. The eel hypothesis is the most parsimonious one on offer, which is not the same as evidence for a giant eel.

The claim

In 2019 a team led by Neil Gemmell sampled environmental DNA from Loch Ness — the fragments of genetic material every organism sheds into water — and sequenced what was there. They reported no DNA from reptiles, no DNA from a large unknown vertebrate, and eel DNA at almost every site.

The popular reading was that Nessie is a giant eel. The paper said something more careful: eels are abundant in the loch, and the data cannot rule out an unusually large one.

What the method can and cannot do

eDNA is powerful for presence and rough abundance, and it is a genuine advance on sonar and photographs. It is weak on size: a DNA sequence does not tell you whether the eel that shed it was 30 cm or 3 m. It is also weak on rarity — a population of a handful of animals may shed too little DNA to detect, and absence of detection is not proof of absence.

So the result does two things at once. It makes a large unknown reptile unlikely, since a breeding population would leave DNA. And it leaves the eel idea alive without supporting it.

Where the evidence stands

Documented: the loch is eel-rich; no reptilian eDNA was recovered.

Documented: the sampling was systematic and the method is sound for presence.

Not established: that a giant eel exists. Size is not recoverable from the data.

Not established: absence of anything else, because rare animals are hard to detect this way.

The honest position: the most plausible of the surviving explanations, on the weakest kind of evidence — and still far better than a plesiosaur, which the data argue against.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows a real scientific technique applied to a folklore question, producing a result that is genuinely informative and is then over-read in both directions — by believers as vindication and by sceptics as a debunk. The archive labels it live debate because the question is open and the method is honest about its limits.

Baalbek and the Giants

Debunked

The Roman temple platform at Baalbek contains three stones of about 800 tonnes each. They were quarried, moved and set by Roman engineers, and the claim that only giants could have done it is an argument from incredulity with a documented answer.

The stones

The podium of the temple of Jupiter at Baalbek, in Lebanon, includes the trilithon: three limestone blocks of roughly 800 tonnes each, set side by side in a course about 5 metres high. A fourth stone still in the nearby quarry, the Stone of the Pregnant Woman, is heavier still at around 1,000 tonnes.

They are, by a wide margin, the largest blocks used in classical antiquity, which is why the site attracts the claim that no ancient people could have moved them.

The documented answer

The quarry is adjacent, the stone is local, and the blocks carry quarry marks and unfinished edges that show how they were cut. Roman engineering used levers, rollers, sledges, ramps and large teams; experiments with replicas have moved comparable masses with those methods. The trilithon sits in a Roman temple complex with inscriptions, a plan and a construction sequence.

The giant claim has no independent evidence: no bones, no tools of unusual size, no ancient text describing giants as builders. It is an argument from the observer's surprise, and surprise is not a datum.

What the evidence supports

Documented: the stones exist, are Roman-period, and were quarried metres away.

Documented: the methods available to Roman engineers can move masses of that order.

Not documented: any involvement of giants, or any culture other than the Roman one.

The reasoning error: 'I cannot imagine how' is not evidence that nobody could.

Why it persists: because the stones are genuinely astonishing, and astonishment is a better story than a ramp.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest case of the argument from incredulity in the whole collection, and because the answer is not a dismissal — the Romans really did do something extraordinary here, and the quarry marks are still visible.

Geopolymer Pyramids

Live debate

A French chemist proposed that the pyramid's blocks were cast from a limestone geopolymer rather than quarried. The idea explains some odd features and is contradicted by others, and the argument has been running for forty years.

The claim

Joseph Davidovits argued from the late 1970s that the blocks of the Great Pyramid were not cut and hauled but cast in place from a limestone-based geopolymer — a slurry of crushed limestone, lime and sodium carbonate that sets hard. On this account the blocks are artificial stone, poured into moulds.

The appeal is that it dissolves the hardest logistics problem: moving 2.3 million blocks of 2.5 tonnes average becomes moving sacks of aggregate.

The evidence on each side

For casting: the blocks are unusually regular, some show what look like mould lines, and there are thin layers of material between courses. Against casting: petrographic analysis finds fossil shells and sedimentary structures continuous across block boundaries, which a cast block would not preserve; the quarry sites at Giza and Tura are extensive and match the block lithology; and the blocks show tool marks consistent with chisels and copper saws.

The strongest recent work is microscopy and X-ray diffraction on the blocks, which finds natural limestone textures rather than a set cement matrix. Casting advocates reply that a geopolymer of crushed limestone would preserve the fossils of the source rock — which is true, and is why the argument has not closed.

Where it stands

Documented: extensive quarries, tool marks, and natural sedimentary fabric in the blocks.

Documented: the blocks are more regular than a naive hand-quarrying picture suggests.

Contested: whether any blocks are cast. A minority of researchers argue yes; the mainstream reads the evidence as quarried.

Not in dispute: the builders, the date, or the purpose. This is a claim about technique, not about aliens.

The honest position: an interesting minority hypothesis that has not overturned the quarrying account.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a fringe-adjacent claim made by a real chemist with real analyses, and it is filed as live debate rather than fringe for that reason. It is also a useful reminder that 'mainstream' is a description of the weight of evidence, not a slur.

Tutankhamun's Meteorite Dagger

Documented

A dagger buried with Tutankhamun was made of iron that fell from the sky. It took ninety years and an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer to prove what the nickel content had hinted at.

The object

Howard Carter found two daggers on the mummy in 1925. One had a gold blade; the other, with a gold handle and a rock-crystal pommel, had an iron blade. In the fourteenth century BC, smelted iron was not yet in use in Egypt, so the blade was either a rare import or meteoritic.

The blade's nickel content — high for terrestrial iron of the period — was noted early. The confirmation came in 2016, when a team used portable X-ray fluorescence to measure the blade without removing it from the museum, and found a composition matching an octahedrite meteorite.

Why it matters

It is a small object that fixes a large point: iron before the Iron Age came from the sky, and ancient metalworkers knew it, worked it, and valued it. The word for iron in Egyptian texts has been argued to mean 'metal of heaven', and the dagger is the physical case.

What is established

Documented: the blade is meteoritic iron, by composition (Ni, Co, and trace elements).

Documented: it was made by low-temperature working, not smelting — consistent with meteoritic metal.

Documented: the object was buried with the king around 1323 BC.

Not claimed: that the dagger is magic, alien, or evidence of lost technology. It is evidence of good craft and a rare material.

Why it is in the archive: because it is the counter-example to the out-of-place-artefact genre — a genuinely surprising object whose surprise has a measurement behind it.

Why it is here

The archive collects claims that look impossible and turn out to be ordinary, and claims that look ordinary and turn out to be remarkable. This is the second kind, and it is filed as documented because the spectrometer said so.

Water Erosion on the Sphinx

Live debate

The Sphinx's enclosure shows deep vertical weathering. Whether that pattern is rain, salt, wind or groundwater decides how old the monument is, and the argument has been running since 1979.

The claim

In 1979 the geologist Robert Schoch argued that the vertical fissuring and undulating profile of the Sphinx enclosure were produced by rainfall runoff, which would place the carving thousands of years before the conventional date of about 2500 BC, when the Giza plateau was much wetter.

The claim does not require any lost civilisation, and Schoch has been careful about that. It requires only that the erosion is older than the conventional date.

The counter-evidence

The mainstream reading is that the enclosure's weathering is dominated by salt exfoliation and wind, with groundwater and flash floods contributing. The Sphinx sits in a limestone quarry; the enclosure walls expose beds of differing hardness, and the vertical fissures follow the joints in the rock rather than a rainfall pattern.

The decisive difficulty is that the monument has been repaired, re-carved and buried in sand for most of its history — it was excavated repeatedly, and the body has been stabilised with modern masonry. The original surface is largely gone, so any reading of 'the' weathering profile is a reading of a palimpsest.

Where it stands

Documented: the enclosure shows deep, complex weathering; the body has been repaired many times.

Documented: the limestone beds differ in hardness, and the fissures follow jointing.

Contested: how much of the pattern is rain rather than salt, wind and groundwater.

Not established: a pre-2500 BC date. The geological argument is a minority reading, and it does not require a lost civilisation to be interesting.

What would settle it: a systematic survey of the enclosure distinguishing original surfaces from repairs, which has not been published.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real geological argument, made by a real geologist, that is usually reported as either proof of Atlantis or a crank claim. Neither is right: it is an unresolved reading of a badly damaged surface.

The Vinland Map

Debunked

A fifteenth-century map showing Vinland looked like proof that the Norse reached America before Columbus. The ink turned out to contain a pigment that was not manufactured until the 1920s.

The object

The Vinland Map surfaced in 1957 and was published by Yale in 1965 as a fifteenth-century manuscript — a world map including a landmass west of Greenland labelled 'Vinlandia Insula', apparently confirming Norse contact before Columbus. It was valued partly as a document and partly as an object lesson in how much a map can prove.

The ink

Doubts were raised immediately about the ink. In 1974, Walter McCrone reported that the yellow line outlining Vinland contained anatase — titanium dioxide — in a form not manufactured until the 1920s. Yale defended the map for decades, arguing contamination.

In 2021, Yale's own conservation scientists published a definitive analysis: the anatase in the ink is in the specific form produced by industrial pigment manufacture from the 1920s onward, and the map's ink differs in composition from the genuine medieval manuscript it was bound with. Yale announced the map was a forgery.

What is established

Documented: the parchment is medieval; the ink is twentieth-century.

Documented: the anatase is the industrial form, not a natural contaminant.

Documented: Yale's own scientists published the result in 2021.

Not established: who made it. The forger has never been identified.

What it does not affect: the Norse reached Newfoundland around 1000. That is established by the L'Anse aux Meadows site, not by this map.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the institution holding the object did the work that destroyed its value, and said so. The archive collects claims; this is what it looks like when a claim is withdrawn by the people who had the most to lose from withdrawing it.

The Cottingley Fairies

Debunked

Two girls photographed fairies in a Yorkshire garden, and Sherlock Holmes's creator believed them. Sixty years later they admitted the fairies were paper cut-outs pinned to a bush.

The photographs

In 1917 Elsie Wright, sixteen, and Frances Griffiths, nine, produced photographs taken in the garden at Cottingley, near Bradford, showing small winged figures among the leaves. In 1920 the images reached Arthur Conan Doyle, who was a spiritualist, and he published them in The Strand as evidence of a real phenomenon.

The photographs were defended for decades by believers, including Doyle, who took them as proof that the spirit world was photographable. The girls maintained the story into adulthood.

The admission

In 1983, Elsie and Frances admitted the fairies were paper cut-outs — traced from a book, painted, and pinned to the foliage with hatpins. The photographs are sharper than the fairy figures, which are flat and evenly lit, and the figures cast no shadow that matches the scene.

One of the five photographs has never been fully explained to everyone's satisfaction — the last one, which shows a blur of gauze. That gap is the part believers cite, and it is a gap about one image, not about the series.

What is established

Documented: four of the five photographs were faked with paper cut-outs; the makers said so.

Documented: Conan Doyle published them as genuine, in good faith.

Disputed: the fifth photograph, which the sisters described differently at different times.

The lesson: a sincere, intelligent, motivated witness is not evidence — Doyle wanted the photographs to be true, and that is why they were believed.

Not claimed: that the girls were fraudsters. They were children who made a joke that adults turned into a movement.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best illustration of how belief propagates through credentials. The photographs are unremarkable; the fact that a famous author vouched for them is what made them evidence, and that is exactly the error the four labels exist to catch.
