The Mozart Effect

Debunked

Listening to Mozart was said to raise IQ. It raises arousal for about fifteen minutes, and the IQ claim was a press release that outlived the paper.

The study

In 1993 Frances Rauscher and colleagues published a short paper in Nature reporting that students who listened to a Mozart sonata for ten minutes performed better on a spatial reasoning task than students who sat in silence. The improvement was about eight or nine points on a standardised scale, and it lasted around ten to fifteen minutes.

The paper said nothing about intelligence, and nothing about children. The press coverage said both, and the governor of Georgia proposed a budget line for classical music CDs for new mothers.

The replications

The effect replicates — as an arousal effect. Any enjoyable or stimulating activity produces a comparable short-term boost, including listening to a preferred genre of pop music, and the effect disappears when arousal is controlled for. A meta-analysis in 2010 found an effect on spatial tasks that was small and best explained by arousal and mood.

The long-term claim — that music makes children smarter — has been tested in randomised trials of music lessons, which find small improvements in some cognitive measures and none in general intelligence.

What is established

Documented: the original study, and its narrow scope.

Replicated: a short-term arousal effect, not specific to Mozart.

Not supported: any lasting increase in intelligence.

Not supported: any special property of classical music.

The lesson: a real, small, transient finding became a policy and an industry through one sentence of interpretation.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest case of a finding being inflated at the press-release stage, and because the corrected version — music is arousing, and arousal helps briefly — is both true and unexciting.

Why Ten Per Cent Are Left-Handed

Live debate

Hand preference is stable, partly heritable, and not explained. Identical twins disagree about a third of the time, which rules out a simple genetic account.

The pattern

About one in ten people is left-handed, the proportion is stable across cultures and centuries, and it is higher in men than in women. Hand preference appears early — thumb-sucking preference in the womb predicts it — and it is remarkably stable over a life.

The explanations

There is a genetic component: left-handedness runs in families, and several genes have been associated with it, including LRRTM1. But the heritability is modest, and monozygotic twins are discordant for handedness in roughly a quarter to a third of pairs. Identical genes, different hands.

That discordance points to developmental noise — random variation in the developing brain, perhaps in the timing of lateralisation — rather than a deterministic programme. Handedness looks like a threshold trait: many small influences, a cut-off, and randomness at the boundary.

The evolutionary question is why left-handers persist at all. The leading suggestion is a frequency-dependent advantage in combat or sport, where a minority of left-handers has an advantage that disappears if the minority grows.

Where it stands

Documented: the prevalence, the early onset, the stability and the sex difference.

Documented: a genetic contribution, and discordance in identical twins.

Not established: a single cause, or a complete model.

Contested: the advantage that maintains the minority.

The honest label: live debate — a well-measured phenomenon with no settled explanation.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the everyday version of the archive's recurring lesson: a trait that looks like it must have one cause, and turns out to have several, one of which is chance.

Dunning–Kruger

Documented

Low performers overestimate their ability. The effect is real and the popular version — a graph with a peak of confidence on a mountain of stupidity — is not what the paper showed.

The study

Kruger and Dunning (1999) asked participants to rate their own performance on tests of grammar, logic and humour, and compared those ratings with their actual scores. The lowest scorers overestimated their percentile rank substantially; the highest scorers underestimated theirs slightly. The explanation offered was metacognitive: to know you are doing badly, you need the skill you lack.

The corrections

Later statistical work showed that much of the pattern follows from two ordinary effects: regression to the mean, and the fact that self-assessment is noisy. If everyone is uncertain and the low performers have nowhere to go but up in their estimates, you get a version of the graph without any metacognitive story.

The effect survives in a weaker form: low performers are overconfident relative to their performance, and this has been replicated. The 'Mount Stupid' curve — a peak of confidence at low skill, a trough at moderate skill, and a slow rise at high skill — is a cartoon that the original data do not support.

What is established

Documented: the original studies, and the overestimation by low performers.

Replicated: a calibration gap between low and high performers, in weaker form.

Explained in part: by regression to the mean and measurement noise.

Not supported: the three-act curve that circulates as 'the Dunning–Kruger effect'.

The honest label: documented as a phenomenon, with the popular graph being a distortion.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most misused finding in internet argument, and because the correction is a good example of how a real effect can be inflated into a meme by removing its statistics.

Why We Sleep

Live debate

Sleep restores something, and after a century of research nobody can say precisely what. The candidates are all supported and none is sufficient.

The candidates

The restorative theory says sleep repairs what waking wears out — but the repair is not localised, and the body does much of it while awake. Synaptic homeostasis (Tononi and colleagues) says sleep renormalises synaptic strength, which is supported by molecular and electrophysiological evidence and explains why learning increases sleep need.

The glymphatic hypothesis says the brain clears metabolic waste faster during sleep, which has been demonstrated in rodents and is harder to measure in humans. The immune theory notes the tight coupling between sleep and immune function. The adaptive theories say sleep keeps animals still and safe when being active is unprofitable.

What is agreed

Sleep is necessary: total deprivation is fatal in animals, and chronic restriction degrades cognition, mood and metabolic health. What is not agreed is the function, and the field is honest about it in review articles even when popular books are not.

Where it stands

Documented: sleep is necessary; deprivation has measurable costs.

Supported: synaptic renormalisation, glymphatic clearance, immune coupling.

Not established: a single function that explains sleep.

Contested: how the functions relate, and which is primary.

The honest label: live debate — one of biology's large open questions.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most ordinary unexplained thing about us, and because the confident popular books about it are a good test of whether a reader can tell a mechanism from a hypothesis.

Why We Dream

Live debate

Dreams are vivid, emotional, remembered badly, and unexplained. The leading theories disagree about whether they do anything at all.

The theories

Hobson's activation-synthesis model treats dreams as the cortex making sense of random brainstem activity during REM — a by-product, not a function. Revonsuo's threat simulation theory argues that dreams rehearse dangers, which would be adaptive. Memory-consolidation accounts note that sleep consolidates, and that dream content often reflects recent experience. Social simulation theories say dreams rehearse relationships.

The evidence

Each has support and none is decisive. Threat simulation predicts more threatening dreams in people exposed to danger, which has been found in some studies and not others. Memory accounts fit the incorporation of recent experience into dreams, which is well documented. The by-product account is hard to falsify and hard to rule out.

The methodological problem is fundamental: dream content is known only from waking reports, which are reconstructions subject to forgetting and expectation.

Where it stands

Documented: dreams occur, mostly in REM, and incorporate recent experience.

Supported: memory-related content; emotional salience.

Contested: whether dreams have a function at all.

Not established: any single function, or any predictive content.

The honest label: live debate, with the by-product hypothesis as the null.

Why it is in the archive

Because dreaming is where the archive's fringe claims (prophecy, shared dreams, astral travel) attach, and the honest scientific position is that the basic function is still unknown.

Why We Yawn

Live debate

Yawning is contagious, appears before birth, and has no agreed function. The brain-cooling account is the best supported; the social account explains the contagion.

The phenomenon

Yawning is a reflex — mouth opening, deep inhalation, stretching — found in mammals and birds, and present in fetuses from about eleven weeks. In humans it is contagious: seeing, hearing or reading about a yawn makes one more likely, and the contagion is stronger for people you know and weaker for strangers.

The theories

The brain-cooling hypothesis (Gallup and colleagues) says a yawn thermoregulates: it draws cool air in and increases blood flow, and yawning is more frequent when ambient temperature is in a comfortable range and less frequent at extremes. The arousal hypothesis says yawning is a state change that increases alertness. The social hypothesis says contagious yawning is a synchronisation signal.

The evidence is mixed and the field is small. The cooling account has the best experimental support; the contagion is real and correlates with empathy measures, but the correlation is modest and does not establish the function.

Where it stands

Documented: the reflex, its prenatal presence, and its contagion in humans.

Supported: the brain-cooling account, in some experimental settings.

Contested: whether contagion reflects empathy, and what it is for.

Not established: any single function.

The honest label: live debate — a universal behaviour with no agreed explanation.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the smallest possible open question, and because reading this page will probably make you yawn — which is the phenomenon doing its own demonstration.

Why We Lost Our Fur

Live debate

Humans are the naked ape: hairless, sweaty, and able to run in heat. The three leading explanations are thermoregulation, parasites and sexual selection, and the fossil evidence does not choose between them.

The facts

Humans have much sparser body hair than any other primate, with the same density of hair follicles but much finer, shorter hairs. The loss appears to predate the genus Homo, or at least to be early in it. Clothing is much later: the body louse, which lives in clothing, diverged from the head louse roughly 100,000 years ago, which gives a date for regular clothing.

The explanations

The thermoregulation hypothesis, developed by Bramble and Lieberman, links hairlessness to sweating and endurance running: a furred animal cannot dump heat fast enough to run long distances in the heat, and eccrine sweating requires exposed skin. The parasite hypothesis says fur is a habitat, and losing it reduced the load. The sexual-selection hypothesis says hairlessness was selected as a signal.

Each explains part of the pattern. None explains the timing, which is poorly constrained, and the fossil record does not preserve hair.

Where it stands

Documented: reduced hair density, eccrine sweating, and the louse date for clothing.

Well supported: thermoregulation, as at least a major pressure.

Plausible: parasite load and sexual selection as contributors.

Not established: a single cause or a reliable date for the loss.

The honest label: live debate — a real anatomical fact with three good explanations and no decisive test.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the question every child asks about humans, and because the answer is a set of competing pressures rather than a story — which is what most of evolutionary biology actually looks like.

Serotonin and Depression

Live debate

The story that depression is caused by low serotonin is the most repeated claim in mental health. A 2022 review found no consistent evidence for it, and the argument since has been about what that means for the drugs.

The hypothesis

The monoamine hypothesis, proposed in the 1960s, held that depression results from a deficiency of serotonin (and noradrenaline). It was supported by the action of the first antidepressants, and it became the standard explanation given to patients.

The 2022 review

Moncrieff and colleagues published an umbrella review in Molecular Psychiatry in 2022 examining the evidence for lowered serotonin activity in depression. They found no consistent evidence of reduced serotonin, of altered receptor levels, or of a link between serotonin depletion and low mood in healthy volunteers, and concluded that the hypothesis is not supported.

The review was criticised — for the studies it excluded, for the heterogeneity of depression, and for the implication that antidepressants therefore do not work. The drugs do work, better than placebo for moderate and severe depression, by mechanisms that are not fully understood and that are not the same as the hypothesis.

What is established

Documented: antidepressants are more effective than placebo in moderate to severe depression.

Not supported: the simple claim that depression is caused by low serotonin.

Contested: what the drugs actually do, and over what timescale.

Not established: a single neurotransmitter explanation of depression.

The honest position: the mechanism is unknown, the treatment is real, and the popular explanation was a simplification that became a fact by repetition.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where a simplified explanation did real harm — to patients who were told their illness was a chemical imbalance — and where the correction is easy to misread as 'the drugs do not work'.

Mirror Neurons

Live debate

Neurons that fire both when a monkey acts and when it watches the same action. They were found in macaques, and the human claims built on them — empathy, language, autism — are much larger than the evidence.

The finding

In the early 1990s Rizzolatti's group recorded from premotor neurons in macaques and found cells that fired both when the monkey grasped an object and when it watched a human do the same. They were named mirror neurons. Similar responses have since been reported in other regions and species.

The extrapolation

The popular literature extended the finding to human empathy, imitation, language evolution and autism. The human evidence is indirect — fMRI adaptation, TMS, EEG — because single-unit recording in healthy humans is not done. Critics, notably Hickok, have argued that the human 'mirror system' is a motor system with sensory associations, and that the strong claims outrun the data.

The autism claim in particular has not held up: predictions about mirror neuron dysfunction in autistic people have not been consistently confirmed, and the theory has been largely abandoned in that field.

Where it stands

Documented: mirror neurons in macaques; sensorimotor matching responses in humans.

Plausible: a role in action understanding and imitation.

Overstated: the claims about empathy, language origins and autism.

Contested: how much of human social cognition depends on them.

The honest label: live debate — a real finding with a large speculative literature attached.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a single-cell finding being asked to explain the whole of human social life, and because the correction came from within neuroscience rather than from outside it.

Hygiene or Old Friends

Live debate

Allergies and autoimmune disease rose through the twentieth century in rich countries. The explanation is not dirt, and the leading version — that we have lost contact with old microbial companions — has good evidence and no complete mechanism.

The observation

Allergic and autoimmune diseases increased sharply in the twentieth century in industrialised countries, and the increase is not explained by better diagnosis alone. Strachan's 1989 'hygiene hypothesis' proposed that smaller families and less childhood infection left the immune system uneducated.

The modern version, the 'old friends' hypothesis (Rook), is different in an important way: the relevant exposures are not infections but the harmless microbes and helminths with which mammals co-evolved. Losing them leaves the immune system's regulatory arm underdeveloped.

The evidence

The strongest support is epidemiological: farm upbringing, larger households, pet exposure and helminth prevalence all correlate with lower allergy rates, and the farm effect has been replicated across countries. Trials of deliberate helminth exposure for inflammatory disease have produced mixed results, with some benefit in small studies and no consistent effect in larger ones.

The confounders are serious: farming families differ in diet, income and genetics as well as microbes, and 'hygiene' in the popular sense is not the variable being measured.

Where it stands

Documented: the rise in allergic and autoimmune disease; the farm and household associations.

Supported: a role for early microbial exposure in immune regulation.

Mixed: helminth therapy trials.

Not established: a complete mechanism, or a prescription.

The honest label: live debate — a good epidemiological signal with an incomplete mechanistic story.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the rare case where the popular version ('we are too clean') is directionally right and mechanistically wrong, and because the correction matters for parents deciding what to do.

The Grandmother Hypothesis

Live debate

Human females live decades past childbearing, which is rare among mammals. The proposal is that grandmothers helped feed weaned children, and that this is why menopause exists.

The puzzle

Human females are unusual in living well past the end of fertility — decades, in a species where most mammals reproduce until death. Menopause is not obviously adaptive, since natural selection is usually indifferent to what happens after reproduction stops.

The proposal

Kristen Hawkes and colleagues proposed in the 1990s that post-reproductive women increased their grandchildren's survival by provisioning weaned children, allowing mothers to wean earlier and have the next child sooner. Fieldwork with the Hadza in Tanzania found that grandmothers' foraging contributed to grandchildren's nutrition, and that the presence of a grandmother correlated with grandchildren's weight.

The alternative explanation is the 'patriarchal transfer' of resources, or simply that longevity is a by-product of other adaptations, and that grandmothering is a consequence rather than a cause. Data from other populations have been mixed: some find grandmother effects, others do not, and the effect may depend on residence patterns and on which grandmother.

Where it stands

Documented: human post-reproductive longevity, and its rarity.

Supported: grandmother provisioning in some populations, with measurable effects.

Contested: whether grandmothering caused menopause or followed it.

Mixed: cross-cultural evidence, dependent on residence and ecology.

The honest label: live debate — a well-formed hypothesis with real field data and no consensus.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the evolutionary story is testable with field data, and where the data have been collected — which is rarer than the number of evolutionary stories suggests.

Why We Age

Live debate

Ageing is not one process. Several mechanisms are well described, no single one explains it, and the interventions that extend lifespan in mice have mostly failed to translate.

The theories

Mutation accumulation (Medawar) says selection is weak after reproduction, so deleterious mutations that act late accumulate. Antagonistic pleiotropy (Williams) says some genes are beneficial early and harmful late, and selection favours the early benefit. The disposable soma theory (Kirkwood) says organisms trade investment in repair against reproduction, and ageing is the accumulated damage from that trade.

On top of those sit the mechanistic hallmarks: genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alteration, loss of proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion and altered intercellular communication.

The interventions

Caloric restriction extends lifespan in rodents and is being tested in primates with mixed results. Rapamycin, senolytics and metformin are under study in humans, with no demonstrated lifespan effect yet. The mouse results that generate headlines have a poor record of translating to humans.

Where it stands

Documented: the hallmarks, and the trade-off framework.

Well supported: ageing as accumulated damage with several contributing processes.

Contested: which process is primary, and whether any is a drug target.

Not established: any intervention that extends human lifespan.

The honest label: live debate — one of biology's largest open problems, with a great deal of confident marketing around it.

Why it is in the archive

Because the longevity industry makes claims that the science does not support, and because the honest position — several overlapping mechanisms, no lever — is more interesting than the supplement advertisements.

Cancer's Origin

Live debate

Cancer is not one disease but a process: cells evolving inside a body, escaping the controls that make multicellular life possible. That framing explains more than any single cause does.

The framing

Cancer is best understood as somatic evolution: a cell acquires mutations, its descendants compete for space and resources, and selection favours lineages that proliferate, invade and survive treatment. Hanahan and Weinberg's 'hallmarks of cancer' (2000, updated 2011) catalogued the capabilities a tumour must acquire — sustained proliferation, evasion of growth suppression, resistance to death, replicative immortality, angiogenesis, invasion, and metabolic reprogramming.

What that explains

It explains why cancer is many diseases with different mutations and different drug responses; why resistance to targeted therapy emerges; and why the same pathway can be involved in unrelated tumours. It also explains Peto's paradox: large, long-lived animals should have far more cancer than they do, and the answer appears to be additional tumour-suppression mechanisms evolved in those lineages.

What it does not explain is why a particular person gets a particular cancer. Risk factors — smoking, radiation, infection, inherited variants — raise mutation rates or remove safeguards, but most cancers arise without a single identifiable cause.

Where it stands

Documented: the hallmarks, the evolutionary dynamics, and therapy resistance.

Documented: the major risk factors and inherited syndromes.

Contested: the relative weight of mutation versus tissue environment.

Not established: a general cause, or a general cure.

The honest label: live debate about mechanism, with the framing itself well established.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where 'one disease' framing does real harm — in research funding, in patient expectations, and in the supplement market — and where the evolutionary account is the honest one.

Amyloid and Alzheimer's

Live debate

The amyloid cascade hypothesis has driven thirty years of Alzheimer's research. Two drugs now remove amyloid and slow decline slightly; whether that vindicates the hypothesis is still argued.

The hypothesis

The amyloid cascade hypothesis holds that the accumulation of amyloid-beta peptides — the plaques found in Alzheimer's brains since Alois Alzheimer's case of 1906 — initiates a cascade that leads to tau tangles, synaptic loss and dementia. It has been the dominant framework for three decades and the main target for drug development.

The drugs

Lecanemab and donanemab, both antibodies against amyloid, were approved in the United States in 2023 and 2024. Trials showed a slowing of cognitive decline of roughly a quarter to a third on standard scales over eighteen months, alongside brain swelling and bleeding in a minority of patients. That is a real effect and a modest one.

Critics note that the effect size is small, that the correlation between plaque removal and benefit is weak, and that the field spent decades on a target that has produced only marginal results. Defenders note that a disease-modifying treatment now exists, which was not true a decade ago, and that tau and inflammation remain targets.

Where it stands

Documented: the plaques, the tangles, the clinical course.

Documented: antibodies remove amyloid and slow decline modestly.

Contested: whether amyloid is the cause or a marker.

Contested: whether the effect size justifies the cost and risk.

The honest label: live debate — with the important caveat that a small real effect has been measured, which is more than the field had before.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the highest-stakes live debate in medicine, and because both the hype and the backlash have outrun the numbers.

Quantum Coherence in Photosynthesis

Live debate

Light-harvesting complexes were reported to sustain quantum coherence for hundreds of femtoseconds. Whether that coherence helps, or is a by-product, is the argument.

The finding

In 2007 Gregory Engel and colleagues reported two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy of a photosynthetic complex from green sulphur bacteria, showing oscillatory signals interpreted as electronic coherence lasting several hundred femtoseconds — far longer than expected in a warm, wet protein at room temperature.

The suggestion was that coherence might allow the excitation to sample multiple pathways simultaneously, improving the efficiency of energy transfer. The claim became a flagship example of 'quantum biology'.

The corrections

Subsequent work argued that much of the long-lived oscillation was vibrational rather than electronic — nuclear motion in the protein, not a superposition of electronic states. Later experiments at physiological temperatures found shorter electronic coherence than the original reports. The current consensus is that coherence exists but is brief, and that its contribution to transfer efficiency is unclear and probably small.

The transfer itself is remarkably efficient, and that efficiency is real; whether quantum coherence is the explanation is the open question.

Where it stands

Documented: the spectroscopy, and the oscillations.

Revised: long-lived electronic coherence; much is vibrational.

Documented: high efficiency of energy transfer.

Contested: whether coherence contributes to that efficiency.

The honest label: live debate — a real quantum effect in biology, with the functional claim downgraded since 2007.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the legitimate quantum-biology result that the 'quantum healing' pages borrow their authority from, and the two are worth reading together.

Plant Neurobiology

Fringe claim

Plants signal, remember in a loose sense, and respond to damage. The claim that they have nervous systems, or brains, is where the metaphor stops being useful.

What is real

Plants have electrical signalling: action potentials in the Venus flytrap and in Mimosa, propagated through the phloem, and slower calcium waves. They have auxin gradients that carry information about light and gravity. They respond to damage with systemic signals, and some show priming effects that resemble memory.

This is a genuine field — plant electrophysiology and plant signalling — with real results.

The claim that overreaches

Plant neurobiology, as a named programme from 2005, argued that plants have a nervous system in a meaningful sense: synapse-like structures, neurotransmitter analogues, and a 'brain-like' command centre in the root apex. Critics replied that analogy is not homology: plants have no neurons, no synapses, and no evidence of a central integrating organ, and that the vocabulary imports claims the data do not support.

Where it stands

Documented: electrical and chemical signalling in plants, and adaptive responses.

Documented: action potentials, calcium waves, auxin transport.

Not established: neurons, synapses, or a plant brain.

Contested: whether the vocabulary of neuroscience is illuminating or misleading here.

The honest label: fringe — a real biology with a metaphor that has been promoted to a claim.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a metaphor doing the work of a finding, and because the underlying biology is more interesting than the claim built on it.

Linguistic Relativity

Live debate

Does the language you speak shape what you can think? The strong version is dead; the weak version has small, replicated effects that are easy to overstate.

The claim

The Sapir–Whorf hypothesis holds that language shapes thought. The strong form — that you cannot think what you cannot say — has been rejected: people without colour terms can discriminate colours, and translation works. The weak form — that language influences attention, memory and categorisation — has experimental support.

The evidence

Colour: speakers of languages with a single term for blue and green show different patterns in discrimination tasks, though the effect is small and depends on the task. Space: languages that use absolute directions (north/south) rather than relative ones (left/right) produce speakers who track orientation differently. Time: languages that describe time vertically or horizontally produce different gesture patterns and different performance on temporal tasks.

The effects are real, replicated in several cases, and modest. They are effects of attention and habit, not of the boundaries of thought.

Where it stands

Rejected: the strong form — language as a limit on thought.

Supported: small effects of language on attention, memory and categorisation.

Contested: the size of the effects and their generality.

Not supported: the claim that a language makes some thoughts impossible.

The honest label: live debate — with the interesting action in the weak version.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most quoted idea in the humanities and the most overquoted in popular science, and because the corrected version — language nudges thought — is both true and less exciting.

Facial Feedback

Live debate

Holding a pen in your teeth makes cartoons funnier, according to a 1988 study. A 17-lab replication failed to find it, and the argument since has been about what that means.

The hypothesis

Darwin and William James both suggested that the experience of emotion is partly the perception of one's own bodily state. The facial feedback hypothesis makes that concrete: adopting an expression should modulate the corresponding feeling. Strack, Martin and Stepper (1988) tested it with a pen held in the teeth (forcing a smile) or the lips (preventing one), and found that the teeth condition rated cartoons funnier.

The replication

In 2016 a large multi-lab replication — seventeen laboratories, nearly two thousand participants — found an effect in the same direction but too small to be conclusive, and the original result was outside the confidence interval. The authors of the replication concluded that the effect, if it exists, is much smaller than reported.

The original study's design also came under scrutiny for the pen-in-mouth manipulation, which may have been confounded by difficulty and discomfort. Later meta-analyses with better methods find a small but real effect, which is where the field currently sits.

Where it stands

Documented: the hypothesis, and the original study.

Not replicated at the original size: the 17-lab study found a much smaller effect.

Supported: a small effect in later meta-analyses.

Contested: the mechanism — proprioception, effort, or demand characteristics.

The honest label: live debate — a famous result that shrank under replication, which is the normal fate of famous results.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's clearest illustration of what replication does to a well-loved finding, and because the corrected version — small effect, uncertain mechanism — is the honest one.

Split-Brain Consciousness

Live debate

Severing the connection between the hemispheres produced patients whose two halves seemed to know different things. Whether that means two minds is still argued.

The surgery and the findings

Commissurotomy — cutting the corpus callosum — was performed on a small number of patients with severe epilepsy from the 1940s. Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga studied them from the 1960s and found striking dissociations: a stimulus presented to the right visual field (left hemisphere) could be named, while the same stimulus in the left field (right hemisphere) could be used correctly but not described.

The interpretation was that the left hemisphere is verbal and the right is not, and that with the connection cut, each hemisphere processes its own information.

The argument

The stronger claim — that the patients have two streams of consciousness — is contested. Gazzaniga himself argued for a single left-hemisphere 'interpreter' that constructs a unified narrative after the fact, which is a claim about a unified self rather than two. Others read the same data as evidence of dual consciousness. The patients themselves report feeling unified.

Where it stands

Documented: the dissociations, replicated many times.

Documented: hemispheric specialisation for language and visuospatial tasks.

Contested: whether there are two consciousnesses or one plus a narrator.

Not established: any conclusion about consciousness in general.

The honest label: live debate — the data are solid and the interpretation is philosophy.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is where neurology and the philosophy of mind meet with real patients, and because the 'two minds' headline is a good test of whether a reader can separate a finding from its interpretation.

Catharsis

Live debate

The idea that venting anger relieves it. The evidence says the opposite: rehearsal makes anger more accessible, and the studies that tested it found venting increases aggression.

The claim

Catharsis comes from Aristotle's account of tragedy and from Freud and Breuer's early work: strong emotion, if expressed, is discharged, and the discharge is therapeutic. In its popular form it says that venting anger — shouting, hitting something, venting online — reduces it.

The evidence

The direct tests are unkind to the hypothesis. Bushman's work in the 2000s found that participants who hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who angered them became more aggressive, not less, compared with those who sat quietly. A meta-analysis found that venting reduces neither anger nor aggression and can increase both.

What does help is different: distraction, reappraisal, and in some cases writing about the experience — which is expressive disclosure, not catharsis. The distinction matters because both get called 'getting it out'.

Where it stands

Documented: the hypothesis and its history.

Not supported: venting as a way to reduce anger.

Found instead: rehearsal increases accessibility and aggression.

Supported: distraction, reappraisal and expressive writing.

The honest label: live debate in the literature, but the popular version is debunked by the direct tests.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most widely believed piece of psychological advice that the evidence contradicts, and because the correction is practical: stop rehearsing, start doing something else.

The Wet-Bulb Threshold

Documented

At a wet-bulb temperature of about 35 °C, sweat stops cooling the body and a healthy adult dies within hours, even in the shade. It is a hard physical limit, and parts of the world are approaching it.

What the number means

Wet-bulb temperature is measured with a thermometer wrapped in wet cloth: it is the lowest temperature reachable by evaporation. Human cooling depends almost entirely on sweating, so the wet-bulb temperature sets a ceiling on how much heat a body can dump.

At a wet-bulb of 35 °C — roughly 35 °C at 100% humidity, or 46 °C at 50% — the theoretical limit is reached: sweat cannot cool the skin below air temperature, core temperature rises, and death follows within hours even at rest in the shade.

The evidence

The 35 °C figure comes from Sherwood and Huber (2010) and is a theoretical limit for a healthy adult at rest. Later work suggests lower thresholds for older people and for those doing physical work, and modelling studies find that brief exceedances have already occurred in South Asia and the Persian Gulf.

The threshold is not a climate projection; it is thermodynamics. What is projected is how often and where it will be reached.

What is established

Documented: the physical limit, and its dependence on humidity.

Documented: brief exceedances in some regions already recorded.

Documented: lower tolerance in the elderly and in physical work.

Projected: increasing frequency in South Asia, the Gulf and parts of Africa.

The honest label: documented — a measured physical constraint, not a forecast.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a number that is not disputed by anyone competent and is not acted on at the scale the number implies — which is a different kind of failure from the ones the rest of this archive documents.

Kessler Syndrome

Live debate

Enough collisions in low orbit could produce a cascade that makes the region unusable for centuries. The mechanism is real; whether the cascade has started is argued.

The mechanism

Donald Kessler proposed in 1978 that a sufficiently dense population of orbital debris would begin a self-sustaining cascade: each collision creates fragments that raise the chance of further collisions. Above a threshold, the process continues without any new launches.

The physics is not in doubt. A fleck of paint at orbital velocity carries the energy of a bullet, and a collision between two intact satellites produces thousands of trackable fragments.

The evidence

The 2007 Chinese anti-satellite test and the 2009 Iridium–Cosmos collision each added thousands of trackable objects, and the population has grown since. Modelling suggests parts of low orbit are already in a slow cascade for some size classes, and that mitigation — deorbiting satellites within 25 years, then 5 — can stabilise the environment if it is done consistently.

The megaconstellation era complicates the arithmetic: thousands of satellites raise both the collision risk and the operational incentive to deorbit them.

Where it stands

Documented: the mechanism, the growth in debris, and the collision events.

Documented: mitigation can stabilise the environment if applied.

Contested: whether a cascade has already begun in some orbits.

Contested: how megaconstellations change the risk.

The honest label: live debate — a real mechanism with a threshold nobody can measure precisely.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim about a threshold that is neither alarmism nor reassurance, and because the numbers are public in a way that most of the archive's subjects are not.

Solar Geoengineering

Live debate

Cooling the planet by reflecting sunlight — sulphate aerosols in the stratosphere, or brighter clouds. The physics is understood, the governance is not, and the termination problem is the argument against.

The proposals

Solar radiation management aims to reflect a fraction of incoming sunlight. The leading proposal is stratospheric aerosol injection: dispersing sulphate particles high enough to persist for a year or two, mimicking the cooling after a large volcanic eruption. The 1991 Pinatubo eruption lowered global temperatures by about half a degree for a year, which is the natural experiment the idea rests on.

Alternatives include marine cloud brightening and cirrus thinning. None has been deployed, and the research has been small-scale and contested: a Harvard stratospheric experiment was cancelled in 2021 and again in 2024, largely over governance rather than physics.

The arguments

Supporters argue that the physical risk of overshoot justifies research, and that cooling is cheap and fast. Critics argue three things: it does nothing about ocean acidification; it creates a moral hazard that weakens emissions cuts; and the termination problem — a sudden stop after deployment would cause very rapid warming.

The governance problem is the deepest. Any state or wealthy actor could deploy unilaterally, and there is no mechanism to decide whether, how much, or who stops.

Where it stands

Documented: the physics, and the volcanic analogue.

Documented: the termination risk and the acidification gap.

Not deployed: no stratospheric deployment has occurred.

Contested: whether research should proceed, and under whose rules.

The honest label: live debate — a real physical option with an unresolved political problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the rare case where the scientific claim is solid and the objection is entirely political, and the archive should be clear about which is which.

De-Extinction

Live debate

Bringing back the mammoth, the thylacine or the passenger pigeon. The genetics is progressing, the ecology is harder, and no de-extincted animal exists yet.

The proposals

De-extinction uses ancient DNA, gene editing and surrogate species to produce animals resembling extinct ones. The best-funded project aims at a cold-adapted elephant edited with mammoth genes; others target the thylacine and the passenger pigeon. Ancient DNA is fragmentary, so the approach is editing a living relative rather than cloning the extinct animal.

What has been achieved

No de-extincted animal exists. The closest results are cellular: induced pluripotent stem cells from an endangered rhino, and the cloning of a black-footed ferret from frozen tissue — a conservation success, not a de-extinction. The mammoth project has published gene edits in cells, not animals.

The ecological objections are substantial: an edited elephant needs a herd, a habitat and a microbiome, and the Arctic it would inhabit no longer exists in its Pleistocene form. The conservation objection is that the money and attention would be better spent on species that are still alive.

Where it stands

Documented: ancient DNA recovery; gene editing; the project plans.

Documented: cellular progress in related conservation work.

Not achieved: any de-extincted organism.

Contested: whether a proxy species counts as restoration.

The honest label: live debate — a real research programme with a large gap between the press releases and the animals.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the headline ('the mammoth returns by 2027') and the state of the science are furthest apart, and because the ethics are genuinely arguable rather than obviously wrong.

Xenotransplantation

Documented

Transplanting pig organs into people. The first living recipients survived weeks to months, which is both a real advance and a long way from a treatment.

The idea

Xenotransplantation uses animal organs — almost always pig — for human transplant, to address the shortage of donor organs. Pigs are used because their organs are a similar size and they breed quickly. The barrier is immunological: the human immune system rejects pig tissue violently, and pigs carry endogenous retroviruses that must be edited out.

The results

In 2022 and 2024, gene-edited pig hearts and kidneys were transplanted into a small number of living patients in the United States, under compassionate-use arrangements. The first recipients died within about two months; a later kidney recipient lived longer. Two brain-dead patients were also used for short studies.

These are genuine firsts and they are not a therapy. The survival times are short, the patients were critically ill, and the trials were not controlled.

What is established

Documented: pig-to-human transplants have been performed, with gene-edited organs.

Documented: survival for weeks to months in a handful of cases.

Not established: a reliable, durable treatment.

Contested: the risk of cross-species infection, and the ethics of compassionate use.

The honest label: documented as an experimental procedure, not as a treatment.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real medical frontier where the honest description — a handful of compassionate-use cases — is much less exciting than the coverage, and the coverage is what most people will remember.

Epigenetic Inheritance of Trauma

Live debate

The claim that trauma leaves chemical marks on DNA that pass to children and grandchildren. The human studies are small and confounded; the mechanism is real in animals and unproven in people.

The claim

Epigenetic inheritance holds that environmental experience — famine, stress, trauma — alters DNA methylation or histone marks in a way that is transmitted to offspring, changing their physiology or behaviour without changing their genes. The Dutch Hunger Winter and the descendants of Holocaust survivors are the most cited human cases.

The evidence

The animal evidence is stronger: in mice, odour-fear conditioning and stress paradigms have produced effects in offspring, with some molecular correlates. The human evidence is weaker. The Dutch Hunger Winter cohort shows health differences by gestational timing, which is real; the methylation differences reported in descendants come from small samples and have not been consistently replicated.

The central biological problem is germline reprogramming: mammalian embryos erase most epigenetic marks shortly after fertilisation, which is why transgenerational inheritance of acquired marks is hard to explain mechanistically.

Where it stands

Documented: epigenetic marks respond to environment within a lifetime.

Documented: some transgenerational effects in animals.

Contested: transgenerational effects in humans; small, confounded studies.

Not established: a mechanism that survives germline reprogramming in humans.

The honest label: live debate — a real mechanism with an over-extended human claim.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is one of the most emotionally compelling scientific claims of the last twenty years, and the evidence does not yet carry the weight the writing puts on it.

The Momo Panic

Debunked

A bird-woman image was said to be contacting children on WhatsApp and instructing them to harm themselves. It was a sculpture, a hoax, and a lesson in how a panic travels.

The panic

In 2018 a story spread that a character called Momo was appearing in children's videos and on WhatsApp, threatening them and urging self-harm. Schools sent letters home; police forces issued warnings; newspapers ran the story in dozens of countries.

The image was a photograph of a sculpture by the Japanese artist Keisuke Aiso, made in 2016 and not connected to any of it. The WhatsApp number in the story belonged to unrelated people, some of whom were harassed. No case of harm was traced to the character.

How it spread

The mechanism is well studied: a threat to children, an unfamiliar image, an authority (school, police) repeating it, and a platform that rewards engagement. The warnings themselves were the vector — each one made the story more credible to the next school.

Comparable panics followed: the Blue Whale challenge, the Slender Man case, the Momo variants. Each has the same structure and the same absence of a verified victim.

What is established

Documented: the sculpture, the hoax, and the wave of official warnings.

Documented: no verified case of harm linked to the character.

Documented: the amplification mechanism, including the warnings.

Not established: any organised campaign targeting children.

The lesson: a safety warning is a transmission channel, and can be the thing that spreads the harm it warns about.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's clearest case of a hoax that worked through institutions rather than around them, and because the correct response — don't forward it — is the opposite of what feels responsible.

John Titor

Debunked

A forum poster in 2000 claimed to be a time traveller from 2036. His predictions failed, his physics did not work, and the posts have been traced to a group of people.

The posts

Between 2000 and 2001, a poster calling himself John Titor appeared on several internet forums, claiming to be a soldier from 2036 sent back to retrieve an IBM computer for a legacy system. He described a civil war in the United States, a changed constitution, and a device for creating miniature black holes. He also posted photographs of what he said was his time machine.

The failures

The predictions were specific and did not happen: no civil war in 2004–2015, no constitutional change of the kind described. The physics — a portable micro-singularity generator — is not consistent with known physics, and the photographs show an ordinary appliance.

Later investigation traced the posts to a group of people, one of whom was connected to a legal dispute over the character. That is a mundane explanation, and the failure of the dated predictions is independent of it.

What is established

Documented: the posts, their dates, and their content.

Documented: the specific predictions, and their failure.

Documented: the physical implausibility of the described device.

Likely: an origin in a small group of people, not a time traveller.

The lesson: dated predictions are checkable, and this is what happens when they are checked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the internet's founding time-travel story, and because it is a clean case of a claim that gave itself a deadline and missed it.

Randonautica

Debunked

An app that generates a random coordinate and sends you there, promising 'anomalies'. In 2020 two teenagers following one found a suitcase containing human remains, and the app became famous for the wrong reason.

The app

Randonautica generates coordinates near the user — 'attractors', 'voids', 'anomalies' — using a random number generator seeded in part by the user's intention. Users walk to the point and report what they find. The framing borrows from quantum randomness and the observer effect.

What happened

In 2020, two teenagers in Washington state followed a coordinate into a wooded area and found a suitcase containing human remains, which led to a murder investigation and a great deal of coverage about the app's 'accuracy'. The coordinates are random; a random point in a populated area will sometimes contain something.

The statistics are the answer. Millions of walks have been generated; the number of notable finds is what you would expect from chance plus selection — the finds get posted, the empty walks do not.

What is established

Documented: the app, its random generation, and the 2020 case.

Documented: the mechanism is chance plus selection.

Not established: any link between intention and outcome.

Not established: any 'anomaly' beyond ordinary finds.

The lesson: a random destination is a good way to notice your surroundings, and a bad way to test a hypothesis.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the frequency illusion with a map attached, and because it produced one genuinely useful outcome — a solved case — from a mechanism that explains nothing.

Reality Shifting

Debunked

A practice, spread on TikTok, of moving consciousness to another reality by relaxing into sleep. It is a description of dreaming with a different vocabulary and a stronger claim.

The practice

Reality shifting became widespread on TikTok around 2020. Practitioners describe lying still, relaxing deeply, and 'shifting' to a desired reality — a fictional world, a different life, a version of the past — where they live for hours or years before returning. Techniques have names (the Raven method, the pillow method) and there are large communities sharing 'shifting stories'.

What it actually is

The reports are consistent with immersive, lucid or vivid dreaming: a relaxed body, an intention, a constructed scenario, and a narrative that feels continuous. The phenomenological descriptions overlap heavily with lucid dreaming and with hypnagogic imagery.

There is no evidence of travel to another reality, and no test that could distinguish a vivid dream from one — which is the structural problem. The claims that shifting is dangerous, or that it is a form of dissociation, are also unevidenced; the practice appears to be harmless for most people and disappointing for many.

What is established

Documented: the practice, its techniques and its communities.

Documented: the overlap with lucid and vivid dreaming.

Not established: travel to another reality.

Not established: the harms claimed by some critics.

The honest label: debunked as a claim about reality, while the experience it produces is real and is dreaming.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the newest form of an old claim — that the mind can go somewhere else — and because the debunking is not dismissive: what the practitioners describe is a real and interesting dream phenomenon with an inflated cosmology.

Havana Syndrome

Live debate

Diplomats in Havana reported headaches, dizziness and cognitive problems, and some heard a sound. Eight years of investigation have produced two rival explanations and no confirmed cause.

The cases

From late 2016, US and Canadian diplomats in Havana reported sudden onset of headaches, dizziness, nausea, tinnitus and cognitive difficulties, sometimes with a directional sound. Similar reports followed from other posts — China, Cuba, Vienna, and Washington itself — and the condition acquired the name 'Havana syndrome'.

Some patients showed measurable abnormalities on balance and eye-movement testing, and a 2024 study reported brain imaging differences in a small cohort. Others showed nothing, and the case definitions varied between studies, which is a large part of the problem.

The two explanations

The directed-energy hypothesis proposes a microwave or acoustic device causing tissue damage. It has been supported by some government-funded studies and by a 2024 study from the University of Pennsylvania, and it has not produced a device, a mechanism, or a dose-response relationship.

The mass psychogenic illness hypothesis proposes that symptoms spread within a stressed community, as they have in documented outbreaks for centuries. A 2021 CIA interim assessment reportedly leaned this way for most cases, and the recorded 'sonic attack' was later matched to the call of a local cricket.

Where it stands

Documented: the cluster of symptoms, and the political consequences.

Documented: some objective findings in subsets of patients.

Contested: whether a directed-energy device exists and was used.

Contested: whether mass psychogenic illness explains most cases.

The honest label: live debate — with the strong caveat that the two explanations are not mutually exclusive, and that no cause has been established.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the symptom is documented, the cause is not, and the interpretation has become a matter of institutional position — which is where the archive's labels earn their keep.

Non-Human Biologics

Fringe claim

A 2023 congressional hearing was told the United States holds craft and biological material of non-human origin. The claim is consequential, the evidence has not been produced, and the official investigations have found nothing to support it.

The testimony

In July 2023 a former intelligence officer, David Grusch, told a House subcommittee that the US government had run a multi-decade programme recovering craft of non-human origin, and that 'non-human biologics' had been recovered with them. He testified under oath, and said his information was second-hand, from witnesses.

Two other witnesses described personal experiences — a pilot who saw an object off the US coast, and a former Navy officer who described a 2004 encounter. Neither presented material evidence.

The investigations

The All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, established in 2022, reported in 2024 that it had found no evidence of extraterrestrial technology, and that most resolved cases were balloons, drones, aircraft or sensor artefacts. Its historical review found no evidence that the government had concealed recovered craft.

The claim is not thereby disproved — a negative finding from an office with limited access is not a proof of absence — but the burden is on the claim, and the objects have not been produced.

Where it stands

Documented: the testimony, and the political process around it.

Documented: the official investigations and their findings.

Not produced: any craft, material or biological sample.

Not established: the existence of a recovery programme.

The honest label: fringe — a claim by named people, without the evidence that would make it more than a claim.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the highest-profile version of the archive's oldest question, and because 'under oath' is being used as a substitute for evidence in most of the coverage.

The Shadow Biosphere

Fringe claim

The proposal that life with a different biochemistry exists on Earth, undetected because our methods assume ours. It is a serious hypothesis with one famous failed test.

The proposal

A shadow biosphere would be life that shares the planet but not our biochemistry — a different genetic alphabet, different amino acids, different solvents. It would be invisible to standard assays, which look for DNA and proteins of the kind we know.

The idea was developed by astrobiologists including Carol Cleland and Paul Davies as a way to think about the origin of life: if life began more than once, descendants of a different origin might still be here.

The test that failed

In 2010 a team reported a bacterium, GFAJ-1, from Mono Lake, that appeared to substitute arsenic for phosphorus in its DNA. It was the closest thing to a shadow-biosphere result, and it was heavily publicised. Within two years, two independent reanalyses found that the arsenic was not in the DNA and that the organism was simply tolerating arsenic while scavenging trace phosphorus.

No other candidate has survived. The hypothesis remains unfalsified in principle and unsupported in practice, and the methods that would find it are not obviously available.

Where it stands

Documented: the hypothesis, and the reasoning behind it.

Failed: the arsenic-life claim, on reanalysis.

Not found: any organism with a demonstrably different biochemistry.

Not excluded: in principle.

The honest label: fringe — a well-posed question with no positive evidence and one prominent retraction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's most respectable 'we might be missing something' claim, and because the arsenic story is a model of how a dramatic result is dismantled by careful chemistry.

The CE5 Contact Protocol

Debunked

Paid events where groups meditate to summon UFOs. Participants report lights in the sky; the lights are usually identifiable, and the protocol has never produced an object anyone could examine.

The protocol

CE5 — close encounter of the fifth kind — is a term popularised by Steven Greer, an American physician and UFO campaigner, for human-initiated contact. Participants gather at night, meditate, and attempt to signal craft with lights or thought. Events are commercial, and some are expensive.

What happens

Participants report lights appearing, moving, and responding to signals. The reports are consistent, and the identification rate is not. Analyses of CE5 footage have repeatedly matched the lights to aircraft, satellites, lanterns, flares and, in several cases, to drones flown by other participants or by the organisers.

The pattern is the same as the Starlink panics: a large dark sky, a motivated observer, and a low bar for what counts as a response. The protocol has never produced an object that could be examined, tracked by radar, or photographed at resolution.

What is established

Documented: the events, the protocol and the reports.

Documented: many of the reported lights have mundane identifications.

Not established: any contact, or any craft.

Not established: that the lights respond to signals.

The honest label: debunked as a contact method, while the experience of the participants is real and is a night in a dark place looking up.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the commercial form of the archive's oldest subject, and because the debunking is not about the sincerity of the participants but about the identification of the lights.

Starlink and UFO Panics

Documented

A train of bright lights crosses the sky, and a town reports a UFO. It is a line of satellites catching the sun, and the reports are now a routine part of astronomy outreach.

The phenomenon

Starlink satellites are launched in batches and released in a line, spreading out over weeks. Shortly after deployment, while still low and catching sunlight after sunset, they appear as a moving chain of bright points. The same effect has been produced by other constellations and, historically, by re-entering spacecraft and by aircraft in formation.

The reports

Since 2019, UFO reporting services have recorded spikes that coincide with Starlink launches, and astronomers have documented the same pattern. The objects are tracked, their orbits are public, and identification is usually a matter of checking a launch schedule.

The episodes are a useful natural experiment in how unidentified objects become identified: the same sky, the same observers, and a catalogue that resolves them.

What is established

Documented: the satellites, their appearance, and the timing of the reports.

Documented: the correlation between launches and reporting spikes.

Documented: the identifications, which are public and repeatable.

Not established: that any of these events involved anything other than satellites.

The lesson: most unidentified objects are unidentified because the observer lacks the catalogue, not because the object is anomalous.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's cheapest demonstration of its own method, and because the same episode will recur with every new constellation.

The Elisa Lam Tapes

Live debate

A student died in a Los Angeles hotel in 2013, and the elevator footage of her last hours became one of the internet's most analysed videos. The official finding is an accidental drowning; the theories have not stopped.

The case

Elisa Lam, a Canadian student, was found dead in a water tank on the roof of the Cecil Hotel in February 2013, nineteen days after she was reported missing. The coroner recorded accidental drowning, with bipolar disorder as a contributing factor.

The elevator footage released by police shows her entering, pressing buttons, stepping out and back, and making unusual gestures. It became the most analysed video of its kind, with theories ranging from foul play to supernatural explanations.

The explanations

The mundane account fits the record: a young woman in a psychiatric crisis, behaving in ways consistent with it; a hotel with a history of poor security; a roof access that was not secured; a water tank that was accessible. The toxicology and the coroner's finding are on the record.

The 'strangeness' of the footage is largely the strangeness of watching someone in distress without context, in a low frame-rate clip that was edited for release.

Where it stands

Documented: the death, the coroner's finding, the footage, the hotel's condition.

Documented: a history of safety problems at the hotel.

Not established: foul play; no evidence has been produced.

Not established: any paranormal element.

The honest label: live debate in public, but a closed case in law, and the archive files it as a case where the internet's need for a mystery outlasted the evidence.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archetype of the internet true-crime case: a real death, a strange video, a documented explanation, and an audience that prefers the version without one.

Elsagate

Documented

Children's videos on YouTube were infiltrated by content with inappropriate themes, surfaced by recommendation. The scandal was real, the platform response was documented, and the underlying problem has not gone away.

The scandal

In 2017, researchers and journalists documented a category of videos on YouTube and YouTube Kids that used characters from children's media in content involving violence, medical procedures, and sexualised situations. The videos were not marginal: recommendation systems surfaced them alongside legitimate children's content.

The name came from a Reddit thread. The coverage led to advertiser withdrawals, a platform response including restricted mode changes, age restrictions and removed channels, and a broader debate about automated moderation at scale.

What it showed

The mechanism was the recommendation engine optimising for watch time, with children as a captive audience and a content farm ecosystem producing whatever held attention. The platform's moderation was reactive, and the categories of content were not obviously illegal, which is why they survived automated filters.

What is established

Documented: the content, its scale, and the recommendation pathway.

Documented: the platform response and the advertiser withdrawals.

Documented: the difficulty of moderating at scale.

Not established: that the problem was solved; later reporting has found variants.

The lesson: an engagement-optimised feed will find the edge of what is permitted, and children are the least able to report it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest documented case of a recommendation system doing exactly what it was built to do, with an outcome nobody designing it would have chosen.

Sad Satan

Live debate

A 2015 horror game distributed through the deep web, said to contain illegal material. The claims are unverified, the game has been examined, and its authorship is unknown.

The story

In 2015 a YouTube channel described a horror game called Sad Satan, supposedly found on the deep web, containing disturbing imagery and hidden material. The videos were unsettling and the story spread quickly.

The game files were later distributed and examined. They contain crude assets, distorted imagery and audio, and references that appear to be assembled from other sources. Several analyses found no evidence of the illegal content claimed, and the authorship remains unknown.

What it is

The most plausible reading is that Sad Satan is an art project or a hoax built to generate exactly the reaction it generated: a disturbing file, an untraceable origin, and a story about what it might contain. That is not a debunking of the file's existence — it exists — but of the claims about its contents.

Where it stands

Documented: the game, the videos, and the circulation of the files.

Examined: by several people, who found no illegal material.

Unknown: who made it, and why.

Not established: the deep-web provenance and the content claims.

The honest label: live debate — a real artefact with a manufactured mystery around it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the purest example of a creepypasta that produced a physical artefact, and because the artefact was less interesting than the story told about it.

SCP-096

Fiction

A fictional creature that becomes violently distressed when its face is seen. It is one entry in a collaborative writing project with thousands of them, and it is labelled fiction everywhere it appears.

The fiction

The SCP Foundation is a collaborative writing wiki, founded in 2007, in which contributors write clinical-style documents about anomalous objects and creatures. SCP-096, 'The Shy Guy', is a humanoid that will pursue and kill anyone who sees its face, including in a photograph.

The format is the appeal: containment procedures, a description, and interview logs, written as bureaucracy. It is one of the largest collaborative fiction projects on the internet.

Why it is here

Because the archive collects claims and the SCP project is explicit that it is fiction — the wiki states it, the licence states it, and the community states it. The page exists to mark the boundary: this is what an honestly labelled invented thing looks like, next to the pages where an invented thing is presented as a finding.

What is established

Documented: the fiction, its format, and its community.

Labelled: as fiction by its authors, in every context.

Not a claim: about the world, and never presented as one.

The contrast: compare the pages here where a fiction is treated as evidence.

The label: fiction — which in this archive is a compliment to the authors, not a criticism.

Why it is in the archive

Because a collection of claims needs a category for honest invention, and because the SCP wiki is the best example of it on the internet.

The Backrooms Levels

Fiction

An endless maze of yellow rooms, invented in a 2019 forum post, expanded by thousands of writers and filmmakers. It is fiction, it is labelled, and it has become one of the defining images of the internet's sense of place.

The origin

In May 2019 an anonymous post on 4chan asked for images that felt 'wrong and unsettling', and offered a photograph of an empty yellow room as an example. The image — a fluorescent-lit space with damp carpet — became the Backrooms, described as the space you fall into when you clip out of reality.

The idea was expanded into 'levels': a taxonomy of spaces with their own rules, entities and communities. A 2022 video series by Kane Pixels brought it to a wider audience with a found-footage aesthetic, and it has since been adapted by other filmmakers.

Why it works

The Backrooms are a liminal space: familiar architecture with the people removed. That is a well-documented aesthetic category, and it explains why the image landed. Nothing in the fiction claims to be real, and the community is explicit about it.

What is established

Documented: the origin, the expansion, and the adaptations.

Labelled: as fiction throughout.

Analysed: as liminal-space horror, a recognised aesthetic.

Not a claim: about the world.

The label: fiction — the archive's category for invention that does not pretend otherwise.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the internet's most successful piece of original horror in a decade, and because it shows what the same imaginative machinery does when it is honestly labelled — compared with the pages here where it is not.

The Wandjina

Debunked

Rock art from the Kimberley shows figures with large white faces and haloes. They were read as astronauts in helmets. They are ancestral beings, painted by the people who still paint them.

The art

Wandjina figures appear in rock art and bark paintings across the Kimberley region of Western Australia. They are depicted with large white faces, dark eyes and a halo or headdress, and they are ancestral beings associated with rain and with the creation of the landscape. The tradition is living: the paintings are repainted in ceremony by the Ngarinyin, Wunambal and Worora peoples.

The claim

In the ancient-astronaut literature the figures were read as astronauts in helmets or as visitors in spacesuits. The reading requires ignoring the tradition that explains them and the artists who maintain it.

The 'helmet' is a headdress or halo; the 'goggles' are the eyes of a being associated with cloud and rain; and the white pigment is kaolin, used for its ritual significance. The interpretation is not uncertain — it is documented by the people whose heritage it is.

What is established

Documented: the art, its antiquity, and its continuing tradition.

Documented: the meaning, from the communities who paint it.

Not established: any connection to astronauts or spacesuits.

The error: reading an unfamiliar iconography through a modern visual vocabulary.

The harm: the claim strips the art from the people who made it and gives it to outsiders.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case in this collection where the debunking is not only factual but ethical: the explanation was available from the artists all along.

Dogū as Astronauts

Debunked

Clay figurines from Jōmon Japan have goggle-like eyes and patterned bodies. They were read as space suits. They are stylised figures, mostly female, and many were deliberately broken.

The objects

Dogū are clay figurines from the Jōmon period of Japan, made from roughly 14,000 to 300 BC. They are small, usually 10–30 cm, with exaggerated eyes, patterned surfaces and unusual proportions. They are found in domestic and burial contexts, and many are deliberately broken.

The claim

The ancient-astronaut literature read them as figures in space suits, with goggles and breathing apparatus. The reading is a modern projection onto a stylised form: the 'goggles' are the goggle-eyed style of Jōmon depiction, the 'suit' is incised pattern, and the 'helmet' is a hairstyle or headdress.

The archaeological reading is that most are female, that they relate to fertility, childbirth and the household, and that the deliberate breakage is part of their use — a pattern seen in many figurine traditions.

What is established

Documented: the figurines, their dates, their contexts and their breakage.

Supported: a fertility and household association, with most figures female.

Not established: any connection to space travel.

The error: recognising a modern shape in a stylised ancient form.

The pattern: the same one as the Saqqara bird and the Quimbaya figures.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the Japanese entry in a genre that appears on every continent, and because the objects are genuinely strange without needing to be alien.

The Quimbaya Aeroplanes

Debunked

Small gold figurines from Colombia have triangular wings and a vertical tail. Replicas have been flown as gliders, which is the argument, and the argument is backwards.

The objects

The Quimbaya culture of Colombia produced gold figurines, some of which are flat, triangular and have a vertical element at one end. They date to roughly 1000 AD and are part of a wider tradition of stylised animal and human pendants.

The claim

The claim is that they depict aircraft or gliders: the triangular form is a delta wing, the vertical element is a tail fin, and the objects are aerodynamically shaped. Enthusiasts have built replicas that glide, which is presented as proof.

The replicas glide because they were built as gliders — with the body thinned, the wings enlarged and a stabiliser added. The original is a stylised bird or flying creature, part of a zoomorphic tradition, and many of the 'aircraft' features are common in insect and bird depictions of the region.

What is established

Documented: the figurines, their date and their cultural context.

Documented: the replicas, and the modifications made to them.

Not established: that the originals are aircraft.

The logical error: modifying an object until it flies, then claiming it was designed to.

The honest label: debunked — the argument fails on its own method.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the test was performed and the test was rigged, and because the rigging is visible in the replicas.

Babel as a Spaceport

Debunked

The Tower of Babel is a story about language. A modern reading makes it a rocket launch facility, which requires ignoring what the text says and what Babylon actually built.

The text

Genesis 11 describes a city and a tower built to reach the heavens, and the confusion of languages as the consequence. It is a story about human ambition and the origin of linguistic diversity, set in a Mesopotamian landscape of ziggurats.

The reading

The literal structure it refers to is the Mesopotamian ziggurat — stepped temple towers, of which Etemenanki at Babylon is the best-known candidate. They were real, they were tall, and their name in Akkadian means 'house of the foundation of heaven and earth'.

The spaceport reading requires a launch facility, propellant, and a purpose — none of which appears in the text, the archaeology or the Mesopotamian record. It also requires the story to be a report rather than a narrative, which is not how it is read by anyone who studies it.

What is established

Documented: the text, its genre and its setting.

Documented: Mesopotamian ziggurats, including Etemenanki.

Not established: any spaceport, or any technology.

The error: treating an etiological narrative as a technical report.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archetypal misreading of a text whose genre is the answer, and because Bruegel's painting is doing most of the visual work in the claim.

The Manna Machine

Fringe claim

A 1978 book argued that the manna of Exodus was produced by a machine the Israelites carried. The argument is built on a medieval mystical text, and there is no machine in the archaeological record.

The claim

In 1978 George Sassoon and Rodney Dale published The Manna Machine, arguing that the manna described in Exodus was produced by a machine — a device that grew algae, specifically chlorella, to feed the Israelites in the desert. The reconstruction was based on their reading of the Zohar, the medieval kabbalistic text.

The argument treats the Zohar's description of a divine apparatus as a description of a physical device, and then engineers the device from that reading.

The problems

The Zohar is a thirteenth-century mystical work, not a technical manual, and its descriptions are symbolic. The machine has never been found, and the logistics — a device producing food for a population for forty years — would leave traces, fuel requirements and maintenance records that do not exist.

The natural explanations for manna have their own literature: a secretion of scale insects on tamarisk, still harvested in the region, which appears seasonally and does not keep.

Where it stands

Documented: the book, its argument and its source.

Documented: the natural candidates for manna.

Not established: any machine.

The methodological error: reading a mystical text as an engineering spec.

The honest label: fringe — an inventive reconstruction with no archaeological support.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most elaborate example of a genre that runs through the collection: taking a text written to mean one thing and reading it as a technical document.
