The Ark as a Capacitor

Fringe claim

The Ark of the Covenant was a gold-plated box that killed a man who touched it. The claim is that it was an electrical capacitor. The description fits a capacitor; the rest does not.

The claim

The Ark is described in Exodus as a box of acacia wood overlaid with gold, with a gold lid and two cherubim, carried on poles and kept in the inner sanctum. In 2 Samuel, Uzzah touches it to steady it and dies. The claim is that the Ark was a capacitor: gold plates as conductors, wood as dielectric, and the death as electrocution.

The problems

The construction fits a capacitor in the loosest sense — two conductors separated by an insulator — and does not fit in any functional sense. There is no charging mechanism, no circuit, no evidence of electrical knowledge in the ancient Near East, and no repeatable effect. A static charge of the kind a person could accumulate would not kill.

The narrative explanation is available in the text itself: the Ark is holy, touching it is prohibited, and the death is a demonstration of that prohibition. That is a theological claim, and it is what the passage is about.

Where it stands

Documented: the description of the Ark, and the Uzzah narrative.

Not established: any electrical function.

Not plausible: a lethal static discharge from that construction.

The methodological error: fitting a modern device to a description and declaring an identity.

The honest label: fringe — a coincidence of materials, promoted to a mechanism.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest example of the 'it fits a modern object' fallacy, and because the text gives its own explanation in the same chapter.

Sodom and the Airburst

Live debate

A 2021 paper argued that a site in Jordan was destroyed by a Tunguska-like airburst around 1650 BC, and linked it to Sodom. The claim is contested on chronology, geology and identification.

The claim

Tall el-Hammam, a Bronze Age site in the southern Jordan valley, has a destruction layer with evidence of intense heat, shattered building material and possible shocked quartz. In 2021 a team published a paper in Scientific Reports arguing that a cosmic airburst, comparable to Tunguska in 1908, destroyed the city around 1650 BC, and suggested a link to the Sodom narrative.

The objections

The criticisms are specific: the chronology is disputed and does not match the conventional date for the Sodom story; the evidence for an airburst — shocked quartz, high-temperature minerals — has been challenged as consistent with ordinary destruction and post-depositional processes; and the identification of the site with Sodom is not accepted by most archaeologists.

The paper's authors have defended the analysis. The debate is ongoing and technical, and the biblical identification is the weakest link in the chain: even if the airburst happened, the link to the text is an interpretation.

Where it stands

Documented: a destruction layer at Tall el-Hammam.

Contested: the airburst interpretation of the evidence.

Contested: the chronology and its fit with the narrative.

Not accepted: the identification with Sodom.

The honest label: live debate — with three separate claims bundled into one story, and each of them weaker than the last.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a recent, real, peer-reviewed claim that has been over-read in public, and because separating the three claims is exactly the work the archive exists to do.

The Star of Bethlehem

Fringe claim

Matthew mentions a star that led the Magi to Bethlehem. Astronomy has offered conjunctions, comets and supernovae, and none of them fits the text without strain.

The text

The star appears only in Matthew. It is said to have risen, to have been interpreted by the Magi as a royal sign, and to have gone before them and stopped over the place where the child was. That last behaviour — a star that moves, leads and stops — is not how any astronomical object behaves.

The candidates

Proposed identifications include a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in 7 BC, Jupiter and Venus in 2 BC, a comet (Halley's was in 12 BC), a supernova, and an occultation. Each fits one element of the story and fails others: conjunctions do not lead and stop, comets are not royal signs in the right way, and no supernova in the relevant period has been identified.

The dating problem is separate: Herod died in 4 BC, which constrains the nativity to before that, and the gospel's own chronology is not internally consistent with Luke's.

Where it stands

Documented: the text, and its uniqueness to Matthew.

Documented: the astronomical candidates and their problems.

Not identified: any object that fits the described behaviour.

Contested: whether the account is astronomical at all, or literary.

The honest label: fringe — a real question with no candidate that survives the description.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most popular astronomy-and-scripture question, and because the text's own description rules out most of the answers offered.

The Great Martian God

Debunked

A 1976 Viking image showed a face on Mars. Higher-resolution images showed a mesa. The claim survived the picture, which is the interesting part.

The image

In 1976 the Viking 1 orbiter photographed the Cydonia region of Mars, and a hill with what looked like a face appeared in the frame. The image was low resolution, taken at a particular sun angle, and the 'face' was an artefact of shadow and pixelation.

The claim, developed in the 1980s and 1990s, was that the face was artificial — part of a complex including pyramids and a 'city'. It became a fixture of Mars conspiracy literature.

The resolution

Mars Global Surveyor imaged the region in 1998 and 2001 at far higher resolution, and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's HiRISE followed. The face is a natural mesa, and the 'pyramids' are ordinary landforms. The later images were published by NASA and are freely available.

The claim did not disappear. It moved to 'the later images were doctored', which is unfalsifiable and is the standard end state of a claim that has been photographed out of existence.

What is established

Documented: the 1976 image, and its resolution.

Documented: the later images, at a hundred times the resolution.

Documented: the mesa interpretation.

Not established: any artificial structure.

The lesson: pareidolia plus low resolution produces a face, and better data removes it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest case of a claim being tested by better data and surviving only as an accusation about the data.

Kubrick Confessed to the Moon Hoax

Debunked

A video appears to show Stanley Kubrick confessing to faking the Moon landings. The video is a hoax, the interview is real and unrelated, and the claim has been circulating since 2015.

The claim

The Moon-landing hoax claim holds that NASA filmed the landings in a studio, and a variant names Stanley Kubrick as the director — because of 2001: A Space Odyssey and because he was known for technical precision. In 2015 a video circulated in which Kubrick appeared to confess, in an interview, to having staged the landings.

The video

The footage is real: it comes from an interview Kubrick gave in 1979, and the 'confession' is a re-edit with audio altered and a different voice. The original interview is available, and the relevant passage is about something else entirely.

The wider claim has been addressed many times: the landing sites have been photographed from orbit by independent spacecraft, the retroreflectors left on the surface are used by observatories, and the Apollo programme's scale — 400,000 people — is the standard objection to any conspiracy.

What is established

Documented: the 2015 video, and that it is an edit.

Documented: the original interview, which contains no confession.

Documented: independent imaging of the landing sites; the retroreflectors.

Not established: any hoax.

The lesson: a fabricated confession is the strongest-looking evidence a conspiracy can have, and the easiest to check.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most-watched piece of forged evidence in the collection, and because checking it takes one search and settles it.

The Klerksdorp Spheres

Debunked

Grooved stone spheres from a South African mine, three billion years old, were said to be manufactured. They are concretions, and the grooves are where crystals grew.

The objects

The Klerksdorp spheres come from pyrophyllite deposits near Ottosdal in South Africa, in rock around three billion years old. They are small — a few centimetres across — and some have parallel grooves around the middle. Mineralogists have known them since the 1970s, and they are sold to tourists.

The claim and the answer

The claim is that they are manufactured: too spherical, too regular, with grooves that look machined. The answer is that they are concretions — mineral masses that form by accretion around a nucleus in sedimentary rock — and that the grooves are where crystals of a harder mineral grew and later weathered out, or where the concretion grew in a layered environment.

The surfaces are not as regular as they look in photographs, the 'balance' claims do not survive measurement, and there is no evidence of tooling: no concentric lathe marks, no consistent dimensions.

What is established

Documented: the objects, their age, their locality and their mineralogy.

Documented: the concretion mechanism, and the crystal-groove explanation.

Not established: manufacture, or any precision beyond the natural range.

The error: judging regularity from photographs and anecdotes rather than measurement.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archetype of the genre: an object that is genuinely odd, genuinely old, and genuinely natural, with a photograph that makes it look otherwise.

The Coso Artifact

Debunked

A 'geode' from California was found to contain a spark plug. It was said to be half a million years old. It is a 1920s Champion spark plug in a concretion.

The find

In 1961 a group collecting minerals near Olancha, California, found a nodule that appeared to be a geode. When it was cut open, it contained what looked like a spark plug, along with a metal washer and a nail-like object. The story, published in a treasure-hunting magazine, dated the nodule to around half a million years.

The identification

Spark plug collectors identified the object as a Champion spark plug of a type made from the 1920s onward, with a design that matches a specific model. The 'geode' is a concretion — a mass of iron-rich sediment that had formed around the object, which is exactly how such nodules form around debris in wet ground.

The dating came from the assumption that the nodule was a geode formed in ancient rock, not from any measurement of the object. Once the object is identified, the age follows from the object, not the nodule.

What is established

Documented: the object, its find and its identification as a 1920s spark plug.

Documented: the concretion mechanism that encased it.

Not established: any ancient origin.

The error: dating the container and attributing the date to the contents.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest example of the container-versus-contents error, which appears in several pages here, and because the identification took a specialist collector ten minutes.

The Betz Sphere

Debunked

A steel sphere found after a forest fire was said to move on its own, hum, and resist investigation. It is a ball bearing from industrial machinery.

The object

In 1974 a family in Florida found a metal sphere about 20 cm across in the aftermath of a forest fire on their property. They reported that it moved on its own, that it hummed, and that it behaved oddly when placed on a glass table. It was covered widely, including by newspapers and a television programme.

The identification

The sphere was examined and identified as a stainless steel ball — a large ball bearing of a kind used in industrial machinery, with a manufacturing seam. Analyses found no mechanism, no power source and no anomaly. The movement reports were consistent with a heavy sphere on an uneven or vibrating surface, and with the expectations of the people watching it.

The sphere was later reported lost or stolen, which is the usual afterlife of an object whose mystery has run out.

What is established

Documented: the object, and its identification as an industrial ball bearing.

Documented: the absence of any mechanism or power source.

Not established: any anomalous behaviour under controlled conditions.

The error: reports of motion treated as measurements.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the 1970s version of a viral object, and because the debunking is a single sentence: it is a ball bearing.

The Dorchester Pot

Debunked

A brass vessel was found in rock in 1852 and dated to the deep past. It is a nineteenth-century ornament, and the 'rock' is a conglomerate that formed around it.

The find

In 1852, workers in Dorchester, Massachusetts, reported finding a bell-shaped metal vessel in rock that was said to be ancient — variously described as Precambrian or as part of a great deposit. The object was reported in a local scientific journal, and has been cited ever since as an out-of-place artefact.

The identification

The vessel resembles a nineteenth-century decorative object — a finial or a bedpost fitting, in a style in production at the time — and the rock is a conglomerate, a sedimentary rock made of cemented fragments, which can form around an object relatively quickly. The original report's geological description has been questioned since the nineteenth century.

The object is in a private collection and has not been re-examined with modern methods, which is a common feature of this genre.

What is established

Documented: the find, the report and the object's description.

Documented: the resemblance to a nineteenth-century fitting.

Documented: conglomerates form around objects.

Not established: any ancient origin.

The honest label: debunked, on style and geology rather than on a modern measurement.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is one of the oldest entries in the genre, and because the answer was available in 1852 to anyone who looked at the object's style.

The Aiud Wedge

Debunked

An aluminium wedge was found in Romania in 1973 alongside bones, and was said to be ancient. Aluminium of that kind was not made before the nineteenth century, and the object is probably wartime debris.

The find

In 1973 workers near Aiud in Romania found a wedge-shaped metal object in a sand pit, reportedly alongside bones of an extinct animal. The object was described as aluminium, and the claim followed that it was ancient — sometimes with a date in the thousands of years.

The metallurgy

Aluminium is difficult to smelt; it was first isolated in the 1820s and only became cheap after the Hall–Héroult process in the 1880s. An aluminium object in a prehistoric context is therefore a contradiction, and the analyses of the wedge are consistent with modern industrial aluminium, with a composition typical of the twentieth century.

The most plausible identification is a piece of aircraft or machinery debris from the Second World War, when the region was heavily bombed, buried in sand alongside unrelated fossil bones.

What is established

Documented: the object, its find, and its composition.

Documented: the industrial history of aluminium.

Not established: an ancient origin; the 'bones' association is unverified.

The error: treating co-occurrence in a sand pit as a shared date.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case where the material itself dates the object, and because wartime debris is the most common answer to this class of find.

The Wolfsegg Iron

Debunked

An iron block with a groove was found inside a lignite seam in Austria in 1885 and dated to millions of years. It is a piece of nineteenth-century mining equipment.

The find

In 1885 a block of iron was found in a lignite (brown coal) seam at Wolfsegg in Upper Austria, and was reported as being of great antiquity because of the age of the seam. It is roughly a cube with a groove around it, and it has been exhibited as an out-of-place artefact.

The identification

The block is consistent with nineteenth-century mining or milling equipment — a component that fell or was discarded into the working face. The groove is a functional feature, and the metal is of a kind produced industrially. The 'ancient' date comes from the seam, not from the object, which is the same error as the Coso artifact.

Objects falling into workings and being incorporated into the deposit is routine in mining geology, and it is why mine finds need independent dating.

What is established

Documented: the find, the locality and the object's appearance.

Documented: the industrial character of the metal and the groove.

Not established: an ancient origin.

The error: dating the seam and applying the date to the object.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the Austrian twin of the Coso artifact, and because the two together make the container-versus-contents error impossible to miss.

The Dropa Stones

Debunked

Stone discs with spiral grooves, said to have been found in a Chinese cave with the remains of a dwarf people, and said to record an alien crash. No museum has them and no archaeologist saw them.

The story

The Dropa stones are said to be about 700 discs, 30 cm across, with double spiral grooves, found in 1938 in caves near the Bayan Har mountains on the China–Tibet border, along with the remains of a small-statured people. The discs were said to carry a script, which was later 'deciphered' as an account of a crash landing by beings from another star.

The problems

There is no archaeological record: no site report, no excavation, no museum holding the discs, and no scholar who examined them. The story was assembled in the 1970s and 1980s from a 1960s report about the discovery of a small-statured population in the region, with the discs and the crash added afterwards. The 'decipherment' was produced by people with no training in the scripts concerned.

The region does have a real archaeological record, and small-statured human remains have been documented in the area; neither is connected to the discs.

What is established

Documented: the story, its sources and its growth.

Documented: a real report of a small-statured population in the region.

Not established: the discs; no object has been produced or catalogued.

Not established: the crash, the script or the decipherment.

The honest label: debunked — the strongest case in the archive for 'no evidence' as the finding.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the genre's purest example: a claim with a date, a place, a number of objects and a translation, and not one object.

The Watchers of Enoch

Fringe claim

The Book of Enoch describes 200 angels who descended, taught forbidden knowledge and fathered giants. It is apocalyptic literature, and the reading that makes them extraterrestrials is a twentieth-century one.

The text

1 Enoch is a collection of apocalyptic texts, composed over several centuries before the Common Era, and preserved complete only in Ge'ez, the liturgical language of Ethiopia. Its opening section, the Book of the Watchers, describes 200 angels who descend to earth, take human wives, teach forbidden arts — metallurgy, cosmetics, astrology, weapon-making — and father the giants called Nephilim.

The reading

The text is in the genre of apocalyptic revelation: it explains the origin of evil, the corruption of the world and the coming judgement. The 'forbidden knowledge' motif is a theological statement about the boundaries between the human and the divine, not a report of a technology transfer.

The extraterrestrial reading treats the Watchers as visitors and their teachings as technology. It has to discard the genre, the demonology and the moral structure of the text to do so.

Where it stands

Documented: the text, its languages, its genre and its influence.

Documented: the Watchers tradition in Second Temple literature.

Not established: any historical event behind the narrative.

The error: reading apocalyptic symbolism as reportage.

The honest label: fringe — a real ancient text with a modern reading imposed on it.

Why it is in the archive

Because 1 Enoch is the single most-cited ancient text in the ancient-astronaut literature, and because the genre it belongs to is the answer.

The Nephilim

Fiction

Genesis mentions giants called Nephilim in a handful of verses. The enormous literature built on them — bloodlines, hybrids, modern sightings — is later, and the verses are not a description of a species.

The text

The Nephilim appear in Genesis 6:4, in the report of the spies in Numbers 13:33, and in a related form in Ezekiel. Genesis says they were on the earth in those days and afterwards, when the sons of God came to the daughters of men; Numbers has the spies describing them as giants. The passages are brief and their translation is disputed.

The Hebrew word is of uncertain etymology, and the texts are concerned with the corruption of the world before the flood, not with a species. The 'sons of God' are a motif from the wider ancient Near Eastern literature.

The literature

The modern edifice — a surviving bloodline, hybrid beings, giant skeletons, ongoing sightings — is built from a few verses, later apocalyptic texts, nineteenth-century American newspaper hoaxes about giant skeletons, and twentieth-century paperback publishing. None of it is in Genesis.

What is established

Documented: the verses, and the difficulty of translating them.

Documented: the later literature that developed the idea.

Documented: the nineteenth-century 'giant skeleton' newspaper hoaxes.

Not established: any physical evidence of a giant race.

The label: fiction — the archive's category for a literary figure that has been presented as a historical one.

Why it is in the archive

Because the gap between three verses and a publishing industry is the largest in this collection, and because the giant-skeleton hoaxes are a documented, dated, checkable origin for the modern form.

Oannes

Fiction

A Babylonian priest described a fish-man who came out of the sea and taught civilisation. It is a myth recorded centuries after the fact, and it has become a fixture of the ancient-astronaut literature.

The source

Oannes appears in the Babyloniaca of Berossus, a Babylonian priest writing in Greek in the third century BC. He describes a being with a fish's body and a human head who emerged from the sea, taught writing, mathematics, agriculture and law, and returned to the sea at night. The account is a summary of Babylonian tradition written long after the period it describes.

The tradition

The figure belongs to the Mesopotamian tradition of the apkallu — seven sages, often shown with fish cloaks, who brought the arts of civilisation. They are mythological, depicted in Assyrian reliefs, and their function is to explain where knowledge came from.

The extraterrestrial reading treats Oannes as a visitor who taught humanity. It requires discarding the genre, the iconography and the function of the figure in Mesopotamian thought.

What is established

Documented: the text, its author and its date.

Documented: the apkallu tradition and its iconography.

Not established: any historical being behind the myth.

The error: reading a culture-bringer myth as contact reportage.

The label: fiction — the archive's category for myth presented as history.

Why it is in the archive

Because Oannes is the oldest 'teacher from elsewhere' in the literature, and because the Mesopotamian tradition that explains him is displayed in the same museums as the reliefs the claims use.

The Gate of the Sun

Fringe claim

A monolithic gate at Tiwanaku carries a carved figure holding staffs, surrounded by winged attendants. It is a real monument with a documented iconography, and it has been read as a calendar, a portal and a record of visitors.

The object

The Gate of the Sun stands at Tiwanaku in Bolivia, carved from a single block of andesite about three metres wide. Its frieze shows a central figure with a rayed headdress holding two staffs, flanked by rows of winged attendants, all in a style found elsewhere at the site. It dates to roughly 500–950 AD.

The central figure is usually identified as a deity — the 'Staff God' — and the composition has been read as a cosmological statement. The gate is incomplete: it is a fragment of a larger structure, and the lower part of the carving is missing.

The readings

Proposals have included an astronomical calendar, a portal, and a record of contact with outsiders. The calendar reading is the most studied: the carvings have been claimed to align with solstice positions, and the evidence is suggestive rather than decisive. The portal and visitor readings have no evidence at all.

Where it stands

Documented: the monument, its date and its iconography.

Supported: a religious and cosmological function, by comparison with the site.

Contested: whether the carving encodes astronomical observation.

Not supported: any portal or contact reading.

The honest label: fringe — a real monument with an over-read frieze.

Why it is in the archive

Because the frieze is dense, unfamiliar and genuinely astronomical in flavour, which is exactly the combination that attracts readings with no evidence behind them.

Chavín's Psychedelic Gods

Documented

The stone carvings at Chavín de Huántar show fanged deities, serpents and transformations. The visionary imagery is real, and the argument that the site's rituals used hallucinogens is supported by archaeological finds.

The site

Chavín de Huántar is a ceremonial centre in the Peruvian Andes, occupied from about 900 BC. Its stone carvings show composite beings — human and feline and serpent — with fangs, snakes for hair, and bodies that transform into one another. The most famous is the Lanzón, a granite monolith in an internal gallery.

The evidence

The site's galleries are a maze of narrow corridors with channels for water and air, which would have produced sound and light effects for anyone inside. Archaeological work has found remains of psychoactive plants, including the San Pedro cactus, in contexts associated with ritual.

The interpretation — that Chavín's authority rested on altered states, engineered acoustics and visionary art — is now mainstream, and it is an argument about ritual practice rather than about contact with anything else.

What is established

Documented: the carvings, the galleries, and the psychoactive plant remains.

Supported: ritual use of altered states, and engineered sensory effects.

Interpreted: the iconography as visionary rather than descriptive.

Not established: the details of the ritual.

The label: documented — a case where the strange imagery has an evidenced explanation.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the counter-example to the ancient-astronaut pages: visionary art that turns out to be about vision, and the archaeology says so.

Quetzalcoatl the Visitor

Debunked

A feathered serpent god was recast in the twentieth century as a pale-skinned teacher from overseas. The evidence for the visitor is a sixteenth-century text read backwards.

The god

Quetzalcoatl is a Mesoamerican deity — feathered serpent, wind, learning, and in some traditions a legendary ruler of Tollan. The iconography is ancient and widespread, from Teotihuacan to the Aztec capital.

The visitor

The claim that Quetzalcoatl was a bearded, pale-skinned foreigner who came to teach civilisation rests on sixteenth-century Spanish accounts written after the conquest, some of them by friars interpreting local tradition through their own expectations. The 'return of Quetzalcoatl' story, used to explain Moctezuma's response to Cortés, is now widely regarded by historians as at least partly a post-conquest construction.

Mesoamerican depictions of the god do not show a bearded European, and the traditions describe a deity and a legendary king, not a visitor from elsewhere.

What is established

Documented: the deity, its iconography, and its antiquity.

Documented: the sixteenth-century sources and their context.

Contested: how much of the 'return' story is pre-conquest.

Not established: any foreign teacher, or any visitor.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows how a colonial-era reading became an ancient-astronaut staple, and because the correction comes from the same sources the claim uses.

The Hopi Ant People

Fiction

Hopi tradition describes ancestors sheltering underground with the Ant People during a world's destruction. It is a sacred narrative, and the reading that makes it an account of extraterrestrial rescue is an outsider's.

The tradition

Hopi emergence narratives describe previous worlds destroyed for their corruption, and ancestors who survived by sheltering underground with the Ant People, who taught them survival skills. The story is part of a living religious tradition, told in specific contexts and with restrictions.

The claim

The ancient-astronaut literature reads the Ant People as extraterrestrials and the underground shelters as bases or craft. That reading requires removing the narrative from its religious frame — where the Ant People are a category of being with their own role in the cosmology — and treating it as a report.

Hopi communities have objected to the use of their traditions in this way, which is a point the literature rarely mentions.

What is established

Documented: the narrative, its place in Hopi tradition, and its restrictions.

Documented: the objections of Hopi people to its use in fringe literature.

Not established: any extraterrestrial or subterranean base.

The error: reading a sacred narrative as history and ignoring its owners.

The label: fiction — invention about a tradition, not a finding.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case where the fringe reading takes something that is not for sale, and because the ethics and the facts point the same way.

The Brahmastra

Fiction

The Mahabharata describes celestial weapons of enormous destructive power. They have been read as nuclear bombs. They are literary devices in a poem about dharma.

The text

The Mahabharata and the Ramayana describe astras — weapons invoked with a mantra and associated with a deity — including the brahmastra, said to be capable of destroying the world. The descriptions include blinding light, thunder, and devastation of the land.

The epics are vast poetic works composed and transmitted over centuries, in a genre where scale is a literary instrument: heroes are larger, battles are bigger, and weapons are cosmic.

The claim

The nuclear reading points to the light, the blast and the aftermath, and to passages about land that is barren and water that is poisoned. It requires reading hyperbole as technical description, and it requires ignoring the rest of the epic's imagery, which is equally extreme and equally symbolic.

There is no archaeological, radiological or textual evidence of a nuclear event in the relevant period, and the dating of the epics is centuries wide.

What is established

Documented: the texts, their genre, and their composition history.

Documented: the astras as divine weapons in a literary cosmology.

Not established: any nuclear event, or any technology.

The error: reading a poetic convention as a technical report.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most popular ancient-technology claim in India after the Iron Pillar, and because the answer is the genre, not the physics.

Prometheus the Rebel

Fiction

A Titan stole fire for humanity and was punished. The story has been read as an account of a visitor who gave technology to humans. It is a myth about knowledge and its cost.

The myth

Prometheus appears in Hesiod and Aeschylus: a Titan who steals fire from the gods, gives it to humans, and is punished by being bound while an eagle eats his liver. In some versions he also teaches crafts and trickery.

The claim

The ancient-astronaut reading makes Prometheus a visitor who brought technology. It treats the fire as a device and the punishment as a response by other visitors.

The myth is a theodicy — an explanation of why human life is hard and why knowledge costs — and it is one of the most interpreted stories in Western literature, from Aeschylus to Shelley. None of that interpretation requires a visitor, and none of the ancient sources describes one.

What is established

Documented: the myth, its sources and its interpretations.

Documented: its function as a story about knowledge and its cost.

Not established: any historical figure, or any visitor.

The error: reading an etiological myth as a report.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest example of a myth that is already about exactly the thing the fringe reading claims to have discovered, and says something better.

The Yellow Emperor's Dragon

Fiction

The Yellow Emperor is said to have ascended to heaven on a dragon, taking seventy officials with him. It is a foundation myth of Chinese civilisation, and it has been read as a spacecraft.

The tradition

Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, is a culture hero and a legendary sage-king in Chinese tradition, associated with the origins of medicine, writing and statecraft. In the Shiji and in later accounts, at the end of his reign a dragon descends, he mounts it, and a group of officials follows him to heaven.

The claim

The spacecraft reading treats the dragon as a vehicle and the ascent as a departure. It has to ignore the role of the dragon in Chinese cosmology — a symbol of the sovereign, of rain, of the cosmos — and the convention by which sage-kings ascend rather than die.

The ascent motif is widespread in Chinese legendary history, and it functions to mark a reign as complete and legitimate.

What is established

Documented: the tradition, its sources and its motifs.

Documented: the dragon as a cosmic and imperial symbol.

Not established: any vehicle, or any departure.

The error: reading a legitimacy motif as a transport report.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows how a symbol with a documented meaning becomes a machine when the meaning is removed.

The Apkallu

Fiction

Assyrian reliefs show fish-cloaked and bird-headed sages who brought the arts to humanity. They are the Mesopotamian originals behind Oannes, and they are mythological advisers, not visitors.

The figures

The apkallu are seven sages of Mesopotamian tradition, often shown in Assyrian reliefs as human figures with fish cloaks or bird heads, holding a bucket and a cone — the equipment of ritual purification. They are associated with wisdom, with the arts of civilisation, and with the protection of the king.

The claim

The fringe reading makes them extraterrestrials in suits, and the fish cloak a helmet or breathing apparatus. The iconography has a documented meaning: the fish cloak identifies the figure with the primordial waters and with Ea, the god of wisdom.

The bucket and cone are ritual implements, used in depictions of purification, and they are held by kings and priests as well as sages.

What is established

Documented: the figures, their iconography and their function.

Documented: the ritual meaning of the cloak, bucket and cone.

Not established: any visitor, or any equipment.

The error: reading ritual iconography as technical apparatus.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because the apkallu are the origin of the Oannes story, and because the bucket and cone have been read as everything from a weapon to a power tool.

The Crystal Palaces

Fiction

The Crystal Palace was a glass and iron building of unprecedented scale, and the idea of a 'crystal palace' became a utopian image. It has been read as evidence of lost technology rather than of Victorian engineering.

The building

The Crystal Palace was built in Hyde Park for the Great Exhibition of 1851: a modular structure of cast iron and glass, designed by Joseph Paxton, covering about 92,000 square metres and assembled in months. It was dismantled and rebuilt in south London, where it burned in 1936.

The claim

The 'crystal palace' image recurs in utopian literature — Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground argues with it, and it appears in socialist and architectural writing as an image of a rational future. The fringe reading treats the image as a memory of an ancient glass civilisation.

The building is documented in photographs, drawings, contracts and visitor accounts. There is nothing lost about it.

What is established

Documented: the building, its construction and its destruction.

Documented: its influence on architecture and utopian writing.

Not established: any ancient glass civilisation.

The error: reading a metaphor as a memory.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the Victorian engineering is more impressive than the myth, and because the myth depends on not knowing when the building was put up.

The Cosmic Web and the Brain

Fringe claim

A 2020 paper compared the distribution of galaxies to the network of neurons in a brain, and found them quantitatively similar. The comparison is a real result about structure, not about consciousness.

The comparison

In 2020 Franco Vazza and Alberto Feletti compared the cosmic web — the large-scale distribution of matter — with the neural network of the human brain. They found that the two share statistical properties: both are networks with a similar ratio of nodes to connections, similar clustering, and similar distributions of connection lengths.

What it does not show

The result is about geometry and network statistics, and it is genuinely interesting: it suggests that similar organising processes — gravitational collapse on one side, neural development on the other — produce similar structures.

It does not show that the universe is conscious, or that the resemblance is anything more than structural. The fringe reading takes the paper's title and skips its content, which is a common pattern.

Where it stands

Documented: the statistical similarity, in a peer-reviewed paper.

Not established: any functional similarity.

Not established: any consciousness in the cosmic web.

The error: treating a structural analogy as an identity.

The honest label: fringe — a real result with a claim attached that the result does not support.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a good example of how a legitimate paper becomes a mystical claim, and because the paper is worth reading on its own terms.

The Quantum Biology of the Bird Compass

Documented

Migratory birds navigate using the Earth's magnetic field, and the leading explanation involves quantum entanglement in a protein in the retina. It is one of the best-supported examples of quantum biology.

The phenomenon

Many migratory birds can detect the direction of the Earth's magnetic field, and the sense depends on light: in the 1970s, experiments showed that the orientation of European robins under artificial magnetic fields broke down when the wavelength of light changed, and that the effect was in the right eye.

The mechanism

The leading model is the radical-pair mechanism. When light strikes a protein called cryptochrome in the retina, it creates a pair of radicals whose spins are quantum-entangled; the Earth's field alters the interconversion between spin states, and the resulting chemical signal depends on the field's direction.

The evidence is now substantial: the light dependence, the magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome in vitro, and 2021 work showing that the protein responds to magnetic fields in a way consistent with the model. Whether the bird's nervous system reads that signal is the remaining question.

What is established

Documented: magnetic orientation in birds, and its light dependence.

Supported: the radical-pair mechanism in cryptochrome.

Contested: the exact neural readout.

Not established: the complete pathway.

The label: documented — a real quantum effect in a real behaviour.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the legitimate end of quantum biology, and because the 'quantum' pages that follow it in this collection are borrowing its credibility.

Quantum Tunnelling in Smell

Live debate

The claim that we smell by detecting molecular vibrations through quantum tunnelling, rather than by shape. The evidence is mixed and the debate is live.

The idea

The standard account of smell is shape-based: molecules fit receptors, and the fit determines the odour. In 1996 Luca Turin proposed a vibration-based alternative: the receptor detects the vibrational frequency of the molecule through inelastic electron tunnelling, which would explain why molecules with similar shapes but different vibrations smell different.

The tests

The critical test uses isotopes: a molecule with deuterium instead of hydrogen has almost the same shape but a different vibrational frequency. If smell is vibration-based, the two should smell different. Some experiments found a difference in flies and humans; others found none, and the results have been contested on both sides.

The consensus is that shape does most of the work and that a vibrational contribution is possible but unproven.

Where it stands

Documented: the shape-based account, which explains most of the data.

Proposed: the tunnelling account, with a specific test.

Contested: the isotope experiments, in both directions.

Not established: a vibrational mechanism in human olfaction.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a rare case of a fringe-sounding idea from a serious scientist being tested properly, and remaining undecided.

Microplastics and Hormones

Live debate

Microplastics are everywhere, including in blood and placentas. Whether they act as endocrine disruptors in people is a question the exposure data cannot yet answer.

What is established

Microplastics — fragments under five millimetres — have been found in oceans, soils, air, bottled water, human blood, lung tissue and placentas. The measurement methods have improved sharply since 2004, and the exposure is now well documented.

What is contested

Some plastics contain or leach chemicals that are endocrine-active in laboratory assays — bisphenols, phthalates, and additives. The question is whether the doses that reach human tissue produce effects. The evidence is mostly from cell and animal studies at concentrations above environmental levels, plus epidemiological associations that cannot establish causation.

The honest position is that the exposure is real, the mechanism is plausible, and the human effect size is unknown.

Where it stands

Documented: widespread human exposure.

Documented: endocrine activity of some plastic chemicals in the lab.

Contested: whether environmental doses produce human effects.

Not established: a causal link to hormonal disease.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the exposure is undeniable and the consequence is unknown, and most writing collapses the two.

The Holobiont Human

Documented

You are a habitat: trillions of microbes, thousands of species, and a genome many times larger than yours. The holobiont concept treats the human and its microbes as one unit, and it is now standard.

The concept

A holobiont is a host and its associated microbes considered as a unit. The human microbiome contains roughly as many microbial cells as human cells — the old 'ten to one' ratio has been revised to closer to one to one — and a gene count many times larger than the human genome.

What it explains

The microbiome is involved in digestion, vitamin synthesis, immune development, colonisation resistance and the gut-brain axis. Germ-free animals show measurable differences in immune and neural development, and faecal transplants are an established treatment for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection.

The concept's risk is overreach: 'the microbiome causes' is now attached to obesity, depression, autism and more, on evidence that is usually correlational.

What is established

Documented: the composition and function of the microbiome.

Documented: causal roles in digestion, immunity, and C. difficile treatment.

Contested: roles in most other conditions.

Overreached: 'microbiome causes X' claims.

The label: documented — with a large correlational literature attached.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest version of the 'we are not one thing' claim, and because it is true without being the explanation for everything.

AMOC Collapse

Live debate

The Atlantic overturning circulation could weaken or collapse as the climate warms. The models disagree about when, and the observations are short.

The system

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation carries warm surface water north, where it cools, sinks and returns south at depth. It shapes the climate of Europe and the tropics. Its strength depends on temperature and salinity, so freshwater input from melting ice can weaken it.

The evidence

Direct observations began in 2004 and show variability but not a clear trend. Proxy reconstructions suggest a weakening over the twentieth century, with wide uncertainty. Models project weakening, and a minority project collapse this century; the disagreement is large and the mechanisms are not fully resolved.

Some studies have argued for early-warning signals in the data; others have found the statistical approach unreliable.

Where it stands

Documented: the circulation, and its sensitivity to freshwater.

Documented: weakening in most projections.

Contested: whether collapse is likely this century.

Contested: whether early-warning signals exist.

The honest label: live debate, with the risk real and the date unknown.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a high-consequence claim where the honest answer is a range, and the public argument treats it as a date.

Polyvagal Theory

Fringe claim

A theory that the vagus nerve supports three hierarchical states — social engagement, fight-or-flight, shutdown — and that trauma traps people in the lower ones. It is enormously popular in therapy and weakly supported in physiology.

The theory

Stephen Porges proposed polyvagal theory in 1994. It holds that the mammalian vagus has two branches: a myelinated ventral branch supporting social engagement, and an unmyelinated dorsal branch associated with shutdown, with the sympathetic system's fight-or-flight between them. Trauma is said to leave people stuck in the lower states.

The criticism

Comparative anatomists have challenged the core claim: the 'two vagal systems' distinction is not supported by the anatomy of the vagus across vertebrates, and the evolutionary story attached to it does not match the evidence. The theory's clinical vocabulary — 'dorsal vagal shutdown' — is widely used but not operationalised.

Therapists report that the model is useful for talking about states of arousal, which may be true regardless of whether the physiology holds.

Where it stands

Documented: the vagus nerve and its roles in heart rate and digestion.

Contested: the two-branch hierarchy.

Not supported: the evolutionary account, per comparative anatomy.

Useful clinically: as a metaphor, according to practitioners.

The honest label: fringe — popular, useful to some, and not supported physiologically.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most influential theory in trauma therapy that most physiologists do not accept, and because the distinction between a useful metaphor and a mechanism matters.

Orch-OR

Fringe claim

The claim that consciousness arises from quantum computation in microtubules inside neurons. It has a testable prediction, one experiment that claimed to support it, and no replication.

The proposal

Orchestrated objective reduction, proposed by Roger Penrose and Stuart Hameroff in 1994, holds that consciousness arises from quantum state reductions in microtubules — protein structures inside neurons — rather than from neural network activity. The 'orchestration' is the biological part; the 'objective reduction' is Penrose's proposed quantum-gravity mechanism.

The problems

The decoherence objection is the main one: quantum states in warm, wet tissue collapse in around 10⁻²⁰ seconds, far too fast for the millisecond timescales of neural processing. The theory's answer is that microtubules provide shielding, which is a claim rather than a demonstration.

A 2022 experiment reported anaesthetic effects on microtubules in rats that were interpreted as support; it has not been replicated independently, and the interpretation has been disputed.

Where it stands

Documented: the theory, and its specific predictions.

Contested: the decoherence objection and the shielding answer.

Unreplicated: the 2022 anaesthetic result.

Not established: any quantum role in consciousness.

The honest label: fringe — a serious, specific, unevidenced proposal.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most respectable quantum-consciousness theory, and because its specific predictions make it more falsifiable than most of the genre.

Embodied Cognition

Live debate

The claim that thinking is shaped by having a body — that concepts are grounded in sensorimotor experience. It is well supported in some domains and over-claimed in others.

The claim

Embodied cognition holds that cognitive processes are shaped by the body's form and its interactions with the environment, rather than being computations run on abstract symbols in the brain. Concepts are grounded in sensorimotor experience; gestures and bodily states affect thought.

The evidence

Support comes from several directions: action-perception coupling, the way gesture supports learning, the effects of bodily posture on emotion and judgement, and the difficulty of grounding abstract concepts without bodily metaphor. The effects are real and often modest.

The over-claims are the strong versions: that the body does the thinking, or that the brain is not the locus of cognition. Those are philosophical positions rather than findings.

Where it stands

Supported: bodily states and actions influence cognition.

Supported: gesture and sensorimotor grounding in learning.

Contested: how far the influence extends.

Over-claimed: strong versions that displace the brain.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a mainstream position that is often stated in its strongest form, and the evidence supports the middle.

Terror Management Theory

Live debate

The claim that awareness of death drives people toward cultural worldviews and self-esteem. It has hundreds of studies behind it, a replication problem, and a large theoretical apparatus.

The theory

Terror management theory, developed by Jeff Greenberg, Tom Pyszczynski and Sheldon Solomon from 1986, draws on Becker and on cultural anthropology: awareness of inevitable death creates existential terror, which is managed by commitment to a cultural worldview and by self-esteem. The experimental manipulation is 'mortality salience' — writing about one's own death.

The evidence

Hundreds of studies reported that mortality salience increases worldview defence, in-group favouritism and punishment of norm violators. Then came the replication crisis: several large pre-registered replications found much smaller effects or none, and a 2023 multi-lab effort reported effects that were inconsistent across measures.

The theory's defenders argue that the replications tested a narrow version and that the broader framework stands.

Where it stands

Documented: the theory, and the original body of studies.

Contested: whether the effect replicates at the reported size.

Contested: the causal role of death awareness.

Unsettled: the current status after replication failures.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a large, influential research programme meeting the replication crisis head-on.

Repressed Memory

Live debate

The claim that traumatic memories can be pushed out of awareness and recovered later, often in therapy. The evidence for the mechanism is weak, and the recovered memories have produced both convictions and miscarriages of justice.

The claim

Repression, from Freud, holds that threatening material is pushed out of consciousness and can be recovered. In the 1980s and 1990s, therapists used techniques — hypnosis, guided imagery, suggestion — to 'recover' memories of abuse, and a wave of accusations followed.

The evidence

Memory research supports forgetting, and supports the malleability of memory under suggestion. It does not support a mechanism that reliably buries a traumatic event and later restores it intact. Laboratory studies show that suggestions can produce confident false memories, including of events that never happened.

Trauma can be poorly remembered, and some forgetting is documented; the contested claim is that a recovered memory is more likely to be true than a constructed one. Several convictions based on recovered memories have been overturned.

Where it stands

Documented: forgetting, and the power of suggestion.

Documented: false memories can be created in the lab.

Contested: whether repression is a real mechanism.

Not established: that recovered memories are reliable.

The honest label: live debate, with serious legal consequences.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where a psychological theory changed lives and courtrooms, and where the evidence moved against the theory.

Universal Grammar

Live debate

The claim that children are born with an innate language faculty that constrains the possible grammars. It reshaped linguistics, and the evidence for the strong version has weakened.

The claim

Chomsky's universal grammar holds that the human capacity for language is innate and structured: children are not taught grammar, they acquire it from limited input, so there must be an inborn faculty constraining the space of possible grammars.

The evidence

Support comes from the poverty of the stimulus argument, from the uniformity of acquisition despite varied input, and from the existence of creoles with consistent structure. The objections are substantial: the languages of the world vary more than the theory predicted, construction-based and usage-based accounts explain acquisition without an innate grammar, and the 'language organ' has no identified neural or genetic basis.

The debate is live, and the field has partly moved on: the strong nativist version is defended by some and abandoned by many.

Where it stands

Documented: rapid acquisition from limited input.

Contested: whether an innate grammar is required.

Contested: the extent of cross-linguistic universals.

Not identified: a neural or genetic basis for the faculty.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is one of the most consequential theories in the humanities, and because its strongest form is now contested from inside the field.

Gesture or Voice First

Live debate

Did language begin in the hands or the mouth? The evidence is indirect, and the debate has moved with discoveries about mirror systems, sign languages and ape gestures.

The question

Language leaves no fossil record, so the question of whether gesture or speech came first has to be answered indirectly. The gesture-first hypothesis proposes that manual communication preceded vocal language, and that speech took over later. The voice-first hypothesis proposes that vocal calls were the substrate from the start.

The evidence

Support for gesture-first includes the manual gestures of great apes, the structure of sign languages (which show the full properties of language), the role of gesture in child development, and the overlap between gesture and speech in the brain. Support for voice-first includes the antiquity of vocal control, the anatomy of the vocal tract, and the difficulty of using hands while making tools.

Both sides rely on indirect evidence, and the field is divided.

Where it stands

Documented: ape gesture, sign language structure, gesture-speech coupling.

Documented: vocal anatomy and control in humans and ancestors.

Contested: which came first.

Not established: any direct evidence of the order.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a major scientific question with no direct evidence, which is a useful contrast with the pages where the absence of evidence is the finding.

Evolutionary Modularity

Live debate

The claim that the mind is a collection of specialised modules shaped by Pleistocene selection. It is productive and contested, and the evidence for specific modules is thinner than the framework.

The claim

Evolutionary psychology proposes that the mind consists of many domain-specific mechanisms — modules for detecting cheaters, for theory of mind, for language, for fear of snakes — each shaped by selection in ancestral environments. Massive modularity is the strong version: there is no general-purpose processor.

The evidence

Support comes from dissociations, from developmental evidence for domain-specific learning, and from cross-cultural regularities. The criticisms are that many proposed modules rest on laboratory tasks with alternative explanations, that the Pleistocene environment is unknown in the detail the theory needs, and that neural evidence for the modules is scarce.

The framework has been productive — it generates testable hypotheses — and many of its specific claims have not survived testing.

Where it stands

Supported: domain-specific mechanisms exist for some functions.

Contested: massive modularity.

Contested: most specific module claims.

Productive: as a research framework.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the field most often used to give scientific authority to stories about human nature, and the stories outrun the evidence.

Conformal Cyclic Cosmology

Live debate

Penrose's proposal that the universe repeats, with each aeon's end becoming the next one's beginning. It makes a specific prediction about the microwave background, and the searches for it have not found it.

The proposal

Roger Penrose's conformal cyclic cosmology (2005) proposes that the universe is a sequence of 'aeons'. At the end of an aeon, all matter has decayed and only massless radiation remains; because massless particles do not experience time or scale, the infinite future of one aeon is conformally identical to the singularity of the next. The geometry connects, and a new aeon begins.

The test

The theory makes a striking prediction: gravitational radiation from the previous aeon should leave concentric circles in the cosmic microwave background, of a specific temperature signature. Searches were reported in 2010 and again in 2013 as detections; independent reanalyses found that the circles were consistent with chance in the noise, and the claimed significance did not survive.

Penrose and colleagues have defended the analysis. The theory is mathematically serious and observationally unsupported.

Where it stands

Documented: the theory and its specific prediction.

Reported: circle detections in the CMB, in 2010 and 2013.

Not replicated: independent analyses find chance-level circles.

Not excluded: the theory, which survives on other fronts.

The honest label: live debate, with the only test to date coming back negative.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where a theorist made a falsifiable prediction and it failed — which is worth showing, since the collection is full of claims that avoid that risk.

The Ekpyrotic Universe

Live debate

A model in which the Big Bang is the collision of two branes in a higher-dimensional space. It replaces inflation with a collision, and the two make different predictions.

The model

The ekpyrotic model, proposed by Paul Steinhardt and Neil Turok in 2001, places the visible universe on one of two branes in a higher-dimensional bulk. The branes approach, collide, and the collision appears to us as a hot Big Bang; the process can repeat, producing a cyclic universe.

The test

The motivation was to explain the same puzzles inflation explains — flatness, homogeneity — without an inflaton field. The two models differ in their predictions for primordial gravitational waves and for non-Gaussianity in the microwave background. Planck's measurements have constrained both, and the simplest ekpyrotic models are under pressure, while variants survive.

The debate is technical and unresolved. Inflation remains the majority view, partly because it has more free parameters with which to accommodate the data.

Where it stands

Documented: the model and its predictions.

Constrained: by Planck's non-Gaussianity limits.

Contested: whether any version survives comfortably.

Not excluded: the class of models.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a serious rival to the standard account, and because the argument between them is about predictions rather than about evidence for either.

Holographic Noise

Live debate

If space is a hologram, it should jitter at the Planck scale. A purpose-built interferometer looked for the jitter and found nothing, which ruled out some versions of the idea.

The idea

The holographic principle suggests that the information in a volume of space is encoded on its boundary. Craig Hogan argued that this would produce a fundamental 'holographic noise' — a jitter in the positions of objects at the Planck scale, detectable as correlated fluctuations in the light paths of an interferometer.

The experiment

The Holometer at Fermilab was built for this: two 40-metre interferometers, cross-correlated to look for the predicted jitter. Results published in 2015 found no holographic noise at the predicted level, ruling out Hogan's original model in its simplest form.

That is a clean negative result on a testable prediction, which is rarer in fundamental physics than it should be. Later work has refined the bounds.

Where it stands

Documented: the hypothesis and its predicted signal.

Built: the Holometer, at Fermilab.

Result: no signal at the predicted level.

Ruled out: the simplest version of the model.

The honest label: live debate that a purpose-built experiment has narrowed decisively.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best example here of a claim that was tested properly and came back negative, with the negative published and accepted.

A White Dwarf as a Weapon

Fringe claim

The claim that a stellar remnant could be steered, or used, as a weapon. It appears in science fiction and in UFO lore; the physics of moving a star is the objection.

The claim

The idea appears in two forms: science fiction, where stellar remnants are engineered into weapons, and UFO literature, where a white dwarf — often Sirius B — is said to have been used or threatened. The claim is that a sufficiently advanced civilisation could accelerate a white dwarf and direct it at a target.

The physics

A white dwarf has roughly the mass of the Sun compressed into an Earth-sized body. Changing its velocity requires momentum, and momentum requires either ejecting mass at high speed or an external force; both require energy on a scale that no known process supplies at the required rate. The object is also a star, with its own orbital dynamics and a galaxy of objects to interact with.

There is no observation of an anomalous white dwarf trajectory, and no mechanism proposed beyond assertion.

Where it stands

Documented: white dwarfs, their masses and their dynamics.

Not established: any means of steering one.

Not observed: any anomalous stellar trajectory.

Not testable: as stated.

The honest label: fringe — fiction and lore with a physics objection attached.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the largest object anyone has proposed as a weapon, and because the objection is a momentum budget rather than a mystery.

Grabby Aliens

Fringe claim

A model in which civilisations expand at a fixed speed and announce themselves, and the fact that we see none constrains when they appear. It explains the Fermi paradox by predicting we are early.

The model

Robin Hanson, Daniel Martin and Jonathan McCarter proposed 'grabby aliens' in 2021. The assumptions: civilisations appear at some rate, expand at a fraction of light speed, and visibly transform the volumes they occupy — so a volume that has been settled looks different. Since we see no such volume, we must be early, and the model can be fitted to the observed absence.

What it predicts

The model makes a quantitative prediction: given the observed sky, the most likely time until a grabby civilisation arrives in our volume, and the fraction of the universe already taken. The numbers that fit best put the arrival in the far future, which is consistent with what we see.

The criticism is that the model has enough free parameters to fit almost any observation, and that its predictions are about a single event — arrival — that we cannot test.

Where it stands

Documented: the model and its fit to the observations.

Contested: whether it is falsifiable.

Not tested: the arrival prediction.

Useful: as a framework for the Fermi paradox.

The honest label: fringe — a well-posed model with no test available.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most quantitative of the Fermi paradox answers, and because being quantitative is not the same as being testable.

Nessie as a Plesiosaur

Fringe claim

The Loch Ness Monster is usually drawn as a plesiosaur. That identification has a specific problem: a breeding population of large air-breathing reptiles in a cold lake would leave traces, and none has been found.

The sightings

Reports of a creature in Loch Ness became a public phenomenon in 1933, after a new road opened along the shore. The most famous image, the 'Surgeon's Photograph' of 1934, was admitted as a hoax in 1994 by one of the men involved.

The plesiosaur problem

A plesiosaur is a marine reptile that breathed air and gave birth to live young. A surviving population in a freshwater lake would need to be large enough to breed — dozens of individuals — and would surface to breathe regularly, which ninety years of observation has not recorded.

Surveys have included sonar, submersibles, and environmental DNA sampling in 2018, which recovered DNA from fish, birds, plants and mammals but no reptile. The lake's biomass is also too small to support a population of large predators.

Where it stands

Documented: the sightings, the hoax, and the surveys.

Not found: any reptile DNA, carcass, or verified photograph.

Not plausible: a breeding population of large reptiles in the lake.

Not excluded: large fish, seals, or misidentification.

The honest label: fringe — a claim tested by every available method, with no positive result.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most thoroughly investigated cryptid, and the investigation is the interesting part: the more methods were applied, the less there was.

The Chupacabra

Debunked

A creature that drains livestock of blood, first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995. Every carcass that has been tested has turned out to be a coyote or dog with mange.

The reports

The chupacabra — 'goat sucker' — was first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995, after a series of livestock deaths. The original description was a bipedal creature with spines and large eyes; it spread across Latin America and the southern United States.

The carcasses

Since the 2000s, people have produced carcasses identified as chupacabras. DNA testing on specimens from Texas, Michigan and elsewhere has identified them as coyotes, dogs and raccoons, often with severe mange — a condition that causes hair loss, thickened skin and a gaunt appearance that matches the descriptions.

The livestock deaths are real; the interpretation is not. The original 1995 reports were never supported by a specimen.

What is established

Documented: the reports, and the carcasses.

Documented: DNA identification of the carcasses as known animals with mange.

Not established: any unknown species.

Explained: the sightings, by a common disease on common animals.

The honest label: debunked — the specimens were tested, and they answered.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest cryptid case where physical evidence existed and settled the question, and the settlement was unglamorous.

Mokele-mbembe

Fringe claim

A large animal said to live in the Congo basin, often described as a sauropod dinosaur. Expeditions have been going for a century and have produced stories, not specimens.

The reports

Mokele-mbembe appears in accounts from the Congo basin from the early twentieth century, notably after the 1909 Hagenbeck expedition. Descriptions vary: a large animal with a long neck, a hippo-sized body, said to live in rivers and swamps. Local traditions describe a being that is not necessarily a dinosaur.

The expeditions

There have been many, including several in the 2000s and 2010s. None has produced a specimen, a photograph, a carcass or a clear track. The region's fauna is well documented by biologists working there, and a breeding population of large animals would leave droppings, trails and bones.

The strongest version of the claim relies on the forest's size, which is an argument from absence of survey rather than evidence of an animal.

Where it stands

Documented: the reports and the expeditions.

Documented: the region's known fauna.

Not found: any physical evidence.

Not plausible: a sauropod surviving 66 million years unnoticed.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cryptid most often tied to a specific extinct group, and because the century of searching is itself the evidence.

The Mongolian Death Worm

Fringe claim

A worm said to live in the Gobi, capable of spitting venom or electricity. The reports come from travellers, and no specimen has ever been produced.

The reports

The creature entered Western literature through Roy Chapman Andrews's 1926 book on Central Asia, which reported the local belief in a worm that could kill at a distance. Later accounts described a red, metre-long worm that spits a corrosive fluid or discharges electricity, and that emerges after rain.

The searches

Expeditions in 2005, 2009 and later searched the Gobi and interviewed herders. They found no specimen and no verified account. The Gobi's fauna is not well surveyed, but a metre-long animal with a distinctive defence would be notable.

The 'electric' element has no known biological precedent at that scale, and the venom claim would require a delivery system that no one has described.

Where it stands

Documented: the reports, and the expeditions.

Not found: any specimen, photograph or track.

Not established: the venom or electrical claims.

Not plausible: electrical discharge in a worm of that size.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a cryptid whose defining features are physical claims that could be tested, and have not been.

Raining Animals

Documented

Reports of fish, frogs and other animals falling from the sky are documented across centuries. The mechanism is meteorological, and it is well understood.

The reports

Accounts of animals falling from the sky appear in historical records across many countries, most often fish, frogs and small birds. The reports cluster in storms, and they are documented well enough that meteorological services treat them as a real phenomenon.

The mechanism

Strong updrafts — tornadoes and waterspouts — can lift small aquatic animals from ponds and shallow water, carry them some distance, and drop them when the wind weakens. The animals are usually a single species from a single nearby water body, which is consistent with a local lift.

The reports are exaggerated in transmission, and 'raining frogs' rarely means a heavy fall; it usually means a scattering of stunned animals found after a storm.

What is established

Documented: the reports, across centuries and countries.

Documented: the meteorological mechanism.

Consistent: single-species falls near water bodies.

Not established: any case of a large fall of healthy animals.

The label: documented — a strange-sounding phenomenon with an ordinary cause.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archive's best case of a genuinely weird event that turned out to be weather, and because the reports were right even when the explanations were not.

The Sailing Stones

Documented

Rocks on a dry lake bed leave long tracks, apparently moving on their own. The explanation — ice sheets pushed by light wind — was confirmed with GPS and time-lapse in 2014.

The phenomenon

On the Racetrack Playa in Death Valley, stones leave trails in the dry mud, some tens of metres long. Nobody had seen them move, and the trails persist for years. The phenomenon was documented from 1915 and investigated for decades.

The solution

In 2014 Richard Norris and colleagues instrumented the playa with GPS-tracked rocks and time-lapse cameras. They recorded movement in winter, when a thin layer of water freezes at night into ice sheets; as the ice breaks up and a light wind pushes the floating sheets, the rocks are dragged along, leaving the trails.

The movement is slow — a few metres per minute at most — and rare, which is why nobody saw it for a century.

What is established

Documented: the trails, over a century.

Documented: the mechanism, filmed and measured in 2014.

Required conditions: water, freezing nights, light wind.

Not mysterious: the phenomenon is solved.

The label: documented — and one of the few on this shelf with a complete answer.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best case of a mystery that was solved by instrumenting it, and because the solution is more interesting than the folklore.

Lake Nyos

Documented

A crater lake in Cameroon released a cloud of carbon dioxide that killed about 1,700 people overnight. It is the clearest documented case of a limnic eruption.

The event

On 21 August 1986, Lake Nyos in Cameroon released a large volume of carbon dioxide. The gas, denser than air, flowed down the valleys and suffocated people and livestock in nearby villages — around 1,700 deaths, with survivors found unconscious.

The mechanism

The lake is volcanic, and its deep water is saturated with CO₂ from below. Normally the layers stay separate; a disturbance — a landslide, a temperature change — can overturn the lake and release the gas catastrophically. A similar event at Lake Monoun in 1984 killed 37 people.

Since 2001, a degassing pipe has been installed at Nyos, venting CO₂ continuously and keeping the deep water below saturation. It is one of the few cases of a natural hazard being engineered out of existence.

What is established

Documented: the event, the deaths and the mechanism.

Documented: the earlier Monoun event.

Documented: the degassing installation and its effect.

Not mysterious: no exotic cause is required.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the rare case of a mass-casualty event with a fully understood cause and a working fix, and because it is often cited in support of claims it does not support.

The Door to Hell

Documented

A gas crater in Turkmenistan has been burning since 1971, and it looks like an entrance to the underworld. It is a collapsed gas cavity, set alight to burn off the gas.

The site

The Darvaza crater in Turkmenistan is about 70 metres across and 30 metres deep. It formed in 1971 when a Soviet drilling rig hit a gas cavity that collapsed beneath it. The gas was set alight, on the assumption that it would burn out in a few weeks.

What happened

It has burned for more than fifty years. The crater is a methane vent, and the fire consumes the gas as it escapes. There is no portal, no bottomless pit, and no supernatural element — it is a well-documented industrial accident with an unusually long afterlife.

The Turkmen government has announced plans to extinguish it several times, on environmental and economic grounds.

What is established

Documented: the collapse, the ignition and the duration.

Documented: the methane source.

Not established: any depth beyond the measured cavity.

Not mysterious: no exotic cause required.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real place whose name promises something the geology does not, and because the name is doing most of the work.

The Crooked Forest

Live debate

About four hundred pines near Gryfino in Poland bend sharply north at their base. They were planted in the 1930s, and nobody knows why they bend.

The trees

The Crooked Forest near Gryfino in western Poland contains roughly 400 pines, planted in the 1930s, whose trunks bend sharply to the north at about 20 cm above the ground, then straighten. The bend is at the same height and in the same direction in every tree, which suggests a single cause applied to all of them.

The explanations

The leading suggestion is human intervention: the trees were deliberately bent, perhaps for furniture, boat ribs or barrel staves, using a technique that involves damaging or weighting the young leader. The forest was planted in the 1930s, when the region was German, and the trees were never harvested.

Other explanations — heavy snow, a landslide, grazing animals — struggle with the uniformity of direction and height, though none is excluded. No documentation of the planting has been found.

Where it stands

Documented: the trees, their age, the uniformity of the bend.

Most likely: deliberate human shaping.

Contested: the purpose, and whether it was deliberate at all.

Not documented: the planting or the technique.

The honest label: live debate, with a good answer and no record.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a genuinely unexplained thing that does not need an exotic explanation, and because the most likely answer is a forgotten craft.
