Star Jelly

Live debate

A gelatinous substance found in fields, traditionally said to fall from the sky during meteor showers. The DNA work has found frog and toad, and the rest is slime mould and bacteria.

The substance

Star jelly — also called astral jelly or, in Welsh, llwyg — is a translucent, gelatinous material found on grass and soil, traditionally associated with meteor showers. Reports go back to the fifteenth century.

The analysis

Analyses have identified several sources. Some samples are the remains of frogs or toads — the jelly around amphibian eggs, or the body fluids of an animal that has been eaten and discarded by a predator, which swell after rain. Others are slime moulds, cyanobacteria colonies, or unfertilised frog spawn.

A 2013 study found frog DNA in samples from a nature reserve. No sample has been shown to be meteoric, and the association with meteor showers is folklore.

Where it stands

Documented: the substance, its history and its analyses.

Identified: amphibian remains, slime moulds, bacterial colonies.

Not established: any meteoric origin.

Explained: the meteor association, as folklore.

The honest label: live debate about which source produced which sample, with no extraterrestrial candidate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the classic case of a natural substance acquiring a celestial story, and because the DNA work settled it in the most ordinary way possible.

The Dancing Plague of 1518

Live debate

In Strasbourg, hundreds of people danced for days without stopping, and some died. The two leading explanations are ergot poisoning and mass psychogenic illness.

The event

In July 1518, a woman in Strasbourg began dancing in the street and did not stop. Within a week, dozens had joined; within a month, according to contemporary accounts, several hundred people were dancing. Some collapsed and a number are said to have died from exhaustion, stroke or heart attack.

The town authorities responded by encouraging the dancing — building a stage and hiring musicians — on the theory that the affliction was a natural excess that had to be danced out.

The explanations

Ergot poisoning is the chemical candidate: ergot alkaloids from contaminated rye can cause convulsions and hallucinations, and the period had seen crop failures. The objection is that ergotism produces gangrene and seizures, not sustained coordinated dancing, and that the outbreak was too localised.

Mass psychogenic illness is the other candidate, supported by the period's extreme stress — famine, disease, and the belief that a saint could inflict a dancing curse.

Where it stands

Documented: the event, the location, the response of the authorities.

Plausible: mass psychogenic illness, given the documented stress and belief context.

Contested: ergot poisoning, on the symptom mismatch.

Not established: a single cause.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-documented historical outbreak of collective behaviour, and because both explanations are still argued by people who know the sources.

Nazca Lines as Runways

Debunked

The lines and figures on the Nazca desert were said to be landing strips for aircraft. They are shallow scrapes in the surface, and the ground beneath them would not support a wheel.

The claim

Erich von Däniken's 1968 book argued that the Nazca lines were runways for spacecraft. The argument rests on their size, their straightness, and their visibility from the air.

The archaeology

The lines were made between roughly 500 BC and 500 AD by removing the dark iron-oxide-coated surface stones to expose the lighter ground beneath. The scrapes are shallow — a few centimetres — and the desert's climate has preserved them. The figures include animals and plants, and the lines are associated with water and with processional routes; many converge on places where water is available.

The 'runway' claim fails on engineering: the surface is soft, the lines are not level, some run into hills, and there is no evidence of any landing gear, fuel or structure.

What is established

Documented: the construction method and the dates.

Documented: the association with water and ritual movement.

Not established: any runway, aircraft or vehicle.

Not plausible: the surface would not support a landing.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most famous ancient-astronaut claim, and because the archaeology is more interesting than the runway.

The Dogon and Sirius B

Debunked

The Dogon of Mali are said to have known that Sirius has a tiny, dense companion with a fifty-year orbit, centuries before telescopes could see it. The fieldwork behind the claim is the problem.

The claim

The Dogon are said to know that Sirius has a companion star, Sirius B — invisible to the naked eye — with an orbital period of about fifty years, and that it is extremely dense. The claim comes from the fieldwork of Marcel Griaule and Germaine Dieterlen in the 1930s–1940s, published in the 1950s.

The problems

Sirius B's orbit and density were established by astronomy in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, so the information was available in print before Griaule's work. The Dogon's own traditions, as recorded by later anthropologists, are more ambiguous than the claim requires, and Griaule's methods — long conversations with a small number of informants, translated and interpreted — have been criticised as leading.

The alternative explanations are contamination from European sources, or a reading imposed by the anthropologist. The extraterrestrial-teacher version requires a third explanation with no evidence.

What is established

Documented: the Dogon's astronomical traditions, as recorded.

Documented: the timing — Sirius B's properties were known in print first.

Contested: how precise the Dogon knowledge actually was.

Not established: any pre-telescopic knowledge, or any teacher.

The honest label: debunked, on the documentary record.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-constructed version of the ancient-knowledge claim, and it fails on a date rather than on a mystery.

The Olmec Heads as Africans

Debunked

The colossal stone heads of the Olmec show faces with broad noses and full lips, and have been said to depict Africans. They depict Olmec rulers, and the stone came from local quarries.

The objects

The Olmec civilisation of the Gulf Coast of Mexico carved more than a dozen colossal heads between roughly 1500 and 400 BC, from basalt. They are up to three metres high and weigh many tonnes, and they were moved from quarries in the Tuxtla mountains, tens of kilometres away.

The claim

The claim that the heads depict Africans rests on the facial features and on the assumption that the Olmec could not have carved them. The archaeological reading is that the heads are portraits of rulers, wearing helmets, in a style consistent with other Olmec sculpture of the same figures.

There is no archaeological evidence of African contact in the period — no trade goods, no settlement, no genetic signal — and the quarrying and transport, while impressive, are documented from local sources.

What is established

Documented: the heads, their dates, their material and their source quarries.

Documented: the interpretation as ruler portraits.

Not established: African contact, or African identity for the figures.

Not supported: the claim that the Olmec could not have carved them.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the claim rests on an assumption about capability, and where the assumption is doing all the work.

Puma Punku Laser Cuts

Debunked

Stone blocks at Tiwanaku have precise right angles and interlocking shapes, said to require lasers. They were cut with stone tools, and the site has been heavily disturbed.

The site

Puma Punku is part of the Tiwanaku complex in Bolivia, built around 500–1000 AD. It contains large blocks of red sandstone and andesite, some with complex interlocking shapes and precise right angles, scattered across the site.

The claim

The claim is that the blocks were cut with a precision and regularity that requires modern machinery — lasers, or diamond tools — and that they are too hard for stone tools. The archaeological evidence contradicts this: the blocks are of moderate hardness, the surfaces show tool marks, and the shapes are consistent with known Andean stone-working techniques using harder stones, abrasives and patient labour.

The site has also been damaged: it was quarried for building material in the colonial period and later, and many blocks were moved or broken, which makes the 'impossible precision' claims harder to assess from what remains.

What is established

Documented: the blocks, their material, and their dates.

Documented: Andean stone-working techniques capable of the shapes.

Documented: the site's later disturbance.

Not established: any powered cutting.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest-looking 'impossible precision' case, and because the answer is craft plus time, which is less exciting than a laser.

D. B. Cooper

Live debate

A man hijacked a passenger jet, took $200,000, and jumped into the night over the Pacific Northwest. He was never found, and the case is the only unsolved hijacking in US history.

The hijacking

On 24 November 1971, a man calling himself Dan Cooper bought a ticket on a Northwest Orient flight from Portland to Seattle, showed a briefcase he said contained a bomb, and demanded $200,000 and parachutes. The passengers were released in Seattle; the aircraft took off again with a small crew, and somewhere over southwestern Washington he jumped.

The search

An extensive search found nothing. In 1980 a boy found $5,800 of the ransom money in river silt near Vancouver, Washington — the only physical trace ever recovered, and its condition suggested it had been in the water for years. The FBI closed the active investigation in 2016.

A copycat, Martin McNally, was caught; the original was not. Suspects have been proposed for fifty years, none established.

Where it stands

Documented: the hijacking, the ransom, the jump, the recovered notes.

Not established: his identity.

Not established: whether he survived the jump.

Not established: any of the proposed suspects.

The honest label: live debate, with the physical evidence exhausted.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real crime with real evidence that has been worked for fifty years without resolution, which is a different thing from a mystery with no evidence at all.

The Lost Dutchman Mine

Fringe claim

A German prospector is said to have found a fabulously rich gold mine in the Superstition Mountains and died without revealing it. People have died looking, and nothing has been found.

The story

Jacob Waltz, a German immigrant, is said to have found a rich gold mine in the Superstition Mountains east of Phoenix and to have kept its location secret until his death in 1891. The story gained detail over decades, with maps, coded directions and a supposed cache.

The record

There is no documentation of the mine, no ore sample of unusual richness traceable to it, and no confirmed find in more than a century of searching. What the story has produced is a long series of expeditions and a number of deaths — from heat, falls and, in several cases, other searchers.

The mountains do contain old prospects and minor mineralisation, which is enough to keep the story alive.

Where it stands

Documented: Waltz's existence; the searches; the deaths.

Not documented: the mine.

Not found: any ore or cache.

Plausible: that Waltz had a small prospect, exaggerated after his death.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the archetypal treasure legend, and because the body count is the part of the record that is not in doubt.

The Yonaguni Monument

Live debate

A submerged rock formation off Japan has flat surfaces, right angles and a stair-like structure. Geologists read it as natural sandstone; others read it as a worked monument.

The formation

The Yonaguni monument lies in about 25 metres of water off Yonaguni island, Japan, discovered in 1986. It is a large structure of sandstone with flat surfaces, apparent steps, and angular features that look constructed.

The readings

Geologists, including those who have surveyed it, describe it as a natural formation: the sandstone has bedding planes and joint sets, and the 'steps' and 'angles' follow those planes. The region is seismically active, and the rock has been fractured and eroded along consistent directions.

The archaeological reading points to the regularity and to a few features that look like tool marks. No artefacts, no datable construction and no associated material have been found, which is the weakness of the claim.

Where it stands

Documented: the formation, its geology and its setting.

Supported: a natural origin, by the geologists who have surveyed it.

Contested: whether some features were modified.

Not found: any artefact or dating evidence.

The honest label: live debate, leaning natural.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-looking underwater 'monument', and because the geological explanation is specific and checkable.

Darth Jar Jar

Fiction

A fan theory that Jar Jar Binks was secretly a Sith lord, whose clownish behaviour was a cover. It is inventive, it is argued from staging and dialogue, and its authors know it is fiction.

The theory

In 2015 a long post argued that Jar Jar Binks, the widely disliked comic character from The Phantom Menace, was in fact a Sith lord using apparent incompetence as cover: his gestures mirror those of Force users, he is present at key moments, and his clumsiness repeatedly produces strategic outcomes.

The evidence

The argument is a reading of staging, framing and dialogue, and it is more careful than most fan theories. It is also not supported by anything the filmmakers have said: George Lucas and later creators have described the character as comic relief, and the theory's own authors have treated it as speculation.

The archive files it as fiction because that is what it is — an inventive reading of a film, offered as such.

What is established

Documented: the theory, its arguments and its reception.

Documented: the filmmakers' statements about the character.

Not established: any intended Sith identity.

The value: a demonstration of how much a careful reading can find.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most entertaining fan theory of the decade, and because it shows the difference between reading a text closely and claiming a fact about it.

Mario 3 Is a Stage Play

Documented

A fan theory holds that Super Mario Bros. 3 is staged as a theatre performance — the curtain, the blocks on stands, the card at the end. It is a reading, and the developers have answered it.

The theory

The theory points to details in Super Mario Bros. 3: the game opens with a curtain rising, the ground blocks appear to be bolted to the backdrop, some platforms hang from the ceiling, and the level ends with a card flip. On this reading, the whole game is a stage performance.

The answer

The observation about staging is accurate — the game's designers used theatrical framing deliberately. The conclusion that the game is therefore a play within a fiction is a reading, not a fact, and the developers have described the aesthetic as a stylistic choice for a game that was already self-consciously theatrical.

The archive files it as documented rather than fiction because the phenomenon — a fan reading of deliberate design — is documented, and the reading is presented as interpretation by its authors.

What is established

Documented: the theatrical design elements.

Documented: the fan theory and its arguments.

Documented: the developers' description of the aesthetic.

Not established: a hidden narrative.

The label: documented, as a reading.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the observation is right and the conclusion is optional, which is the distinction the whole archive runs on.

Chemtrails

Debunked

The claim that aircraft are spraying chemicals to control populations or climate. The trails are ice crystals, they behave exactly as contrail physics predicts, and no sampling has found the chemicals.

The phenomenon

Aircraft engines emit water vapour and particles. At altitude, the air is often cold enough that the vapour condenses and freezes into ice crystals — a contrail. Whether a contrail persists and spreads depends on humidity and temperature: in dry air it evaporates within seconds, in humid air it spreads into cirrus-like sheets and can last hours.

The claim

The chemtrail claim holds that persistent trails are deliberate spraying of aluminium, barium, strontium or biological agents, for weather modification or population control. The evidence offered is the appearance of the trails and the claim that they are new.

The trails are not new — they are documented from the early jet age — and the atmospheric science explains the variation in persistence without any payload. Sampling studies of rainwater, soil and air have not found the claimed materials above background, and the quantities required for a global programme would be enormous and logistically visible.

What is established

Documented: contrails, their formation, and their dependence on humidity and temperature.

Documented: the historical record, from the 1940s onward.

Not found: the claimed chemicals, in any sampling study.

Not plausible: the logistics of a covert global spraying programme.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because the observation is real and the explanation is physics, which makes it the cleanest case of a claim built on not knowing how the sky works.

HAARP Weather Control

Debunked

A research facility in Alaska heats a patch of the upper atmosphere with radio waves. It has been blamed for earthquakes, hurricanes and mind control, and its power output is smaller than a large city's.

The facility

HAARP — the High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program — is an ionospheric research facility at Gakona, Alaska, with a phased array of 180 antennas and a transmitter of about 3.6 megawatts. It heats a patch of the ionosphere to study its physics, including radio propagation and auroral processes.

The claim

The conspiracy literature attributes earthquakes, hurricanes, droughts and mind control to HAARP. The objection is scale: a weather system contains energies many orders of magnitude larger than HAARP's output, and the ionosphere is 100 km up and does not couple to the lower atmosphere in the way the claims require.

The facility's funding was ended in 2013 and it was transferred to the University of Alaska Fairbanks in 2015, which is a strange fate for a supposed global weapon.

What is established

Documented: the facility, its power and its research programme.

Documented: its transfer to a university after funding ended.

Not established: any weather or seismic effect.

Not plausible: the energies required, by orders of magnitude.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where a real facility with a strange name did most of the work, and the numbers finish it.

The Sovereign Strawman

Debunked

The claim that a birth certificate creates a corporate 'strawman' separate from the real person, and that a living soul can escape law by naming it. Courts have rejected it in every jurisdiction that has heard it.

The claim

The sovereign citizen movement holds that the legal person named on a birth certificate is a corporate entity — a 'strawman' — created by the state, and that the real, living person is not bound by its laws, taxes or courts. Adherents attempt to file documents, refuse to give names, and assert that the court has no jurisdiction.

The record

The theory has no basis in statute or common law. Courts in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and elsewhere have rejected it consistently, sometimes with penalties for frivolous filing, and several adherents have been convicted after violence.

The deeper problem is that it is unfalsifiable in the way that matters: when a court rejects it, the rejection is treated as proof of the conspiracy rather than as a test of the theory.

What is established

Documented: the movement, its documents and its arguments.

Documented: the consistent rejection by courts.

Not established: any legal basis for the strawman.

The pattern: an argument that treats losing as evidence.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the purest example of a claim that is decided by procedure rather than evidence, and the procedure has answered.

NESARA and GESARA

Debunked

A claimed law that would cancel all debt, abolish income tax and deliver prosperity packages. It has been 'about to be announced' for thirty years.

The claim

NESARA — the National Economic Security and Reformation Act — is said to be legislation passed in secret in 2000 that would abolish income tax, cancel personal debt, return to a gold standard and distribute 'prosperity packages'. GESARA is the global version. The story spread through channelled messages, internet radio and, later, political conspiracy channels.

The record

No such law exists in any public record. The original source was a Nevada-based figure who claimed to have been contacted by ascended masters; the act was never introduced, let alone passed. Announcement dates have come and gone for decades, and the packages have never been delivered.

The structure — a secret law that will imminently transform the world, blocked by a hidden cabal — is the same as the 'imminent disclosure' pattern in UFO lore.

What is established

Documented: the claim, its sources and its history.

Documented: the absence of any such legislation.

Documented: the repeated failed announcement dates.

Not established: any of it.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the purest example of the 'imminent' claim, and because its thirty-year record of non-arrival is the evidence.

Majestic 12

Debunked

A set of documents supposedly signed by Truman, establishing a secret committee on recovered alien craft. The FBI examined them and called them fake, and the forgery is not subtle.

The documents

In 1984, rolls of film were posted anonymously to UFO researchers, containing what appeared to be classified documents about 'Operation Majestic 12' — a committee supposedly set up in 1947 to manage recovered alien technology, with a memorandum signed by President Truman.

The analysis

The FBI investigated in 1988 and concluded the documents were fabricated. Analysts have found the Truman signature to be a copy of one from a known letter, the typefaces and formats inconsistent with the period, and the filing numbers not matching any record. The documents have no provenance beyond an anonymous envelope.

The MJ-12 papers did more than any other document to create the modern UFO-conspiracy narrative, which is why they are still cited despite being debunked in public.

What is established

Documented: the documents, their arrival and their content.

Documented: the FBI's conclusion that they are fake.

Documented: the signature copy and the format errors.

Not established: any committee, or any recovered craft.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the founding forgery of modern UFO lore, and because the forgery is checkable in an afternoon.

Roswell Was Project Mogul

Documented

The 1947 Roswell debris was a secret balloon array built to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. The US Air Force said so in 1994, and the alien story arrived decades later.

The event

In July 1947 a rancher found debris on a field near Roswell, New Mexico: foil, rubber strips, sticks and tape. The local air base issued a press release describing a 'flying disc', then retracted it the next day, saying it was a weather balloon. The story was forgotten for thirty years.

The explanation

Project Mogul was a classified programme that used long trains of balloons carrying microphones to detect Soviet nuclear tests. The arrays were launched from Alamogordo, and one was lost near Roswell. The materials match the debris description exactly, and the secrecy explains the retraction and the refusal to give details at the time.

A 1994 Air Force report identified the debris as Mogul flight no. 4. The alien bodies and the cover-up narrative entered the literature in the late 1970s and 1980s, after the witnesses had been interviewed repeatedly.

What is established

Documented: the debris, the press release and the retraction.

Documented: Project Mogul, its purpose and its flights.

Documented: the 1994 identification.

Not established: any craft or bodies.

The label: documented — a real secret programme, and not the one claimed.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the conspiracy is real and the subject is wrong: there was a cover-up, of a balloon.

The Montauk Project

Fringe claim

A claimed secret programme at a decommissioned radar station on Long Island: mind control, time travel, and a boy who conjured a monster. The station is real; the programme exists only in books.

The claim

The Montauk Project is described in books by Preston Nichols and others from 1992: a secret programme at Camp Hero, a Second World War radar station on Long Island, involving mind control, teleportation, time travel and contact with extraterrestrials. A related claim ties it to the Philadelphia Experiment.

The record

Camp Hero was a real radar station, decommissioned in 1981 and now a state park. There is no documentary record of a research programme of the kind described, no participant testimony that has been verified, and no physical evidence at the site. The books' authors give differing accounts of the same events.

The pattern — a real military site, a decommissioned facility, and a narrative that arrives decades later — recurs throughout this shelf.

Where it stands

Documented: the radar station, its history and its closure.

Documented: the books and their claims.

Not documented: the programme.

Not found: any physical or documentary trace.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the template for the 'secret base' genre, and because the real site is a pleasant park you can visit.

Die Glocke

Fringe claim

A supposed Nazi secret weapon called 'the Bell': a bell-shaped device said to use exotic physics. It appears in a 2000 book, and there is no contemporary document.

The claim

Die Glocke — 'the Bell' — is described as a Nazi secret device, bell-shaped, several metres tall, using a metallic fuel called 'Xerum 525' and involving high-voltage equipment and exotic effects, tested at a facility in Lower Silesia. The story was popularised by Igor Witkowski in 2000 and by the British writer Nick Cook.

The record

No wartime document, photograph, blueprint or witness statement from the period describes the device. The 'henge' structure at the site is a real industrial cooling tower foundation from a mine. The exotic physics attributed to it is not described in any technical source of the period, and the alleged fuel has no chemistry.

The claim's structure — a secret weapon so advanced it was suppressed, documented only decades later by one researcher — is the same as the Nazi-UFO lore that surrounds it.

Where it stands

Documented: the site and its industrial remains.

Documented: the 2000 book and its influence.

Not documented: the device.

Not established: any of the physics or the fuel.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most-cited 'suppressed technology' of the war, and because a single book is its entire documentary base.

Operation Highjump

Fringe claim

A US naval expedition to Antarctica in 1946–47, with 4,700 men and a carrier. It has been read as a military operation against a hidden Nazi or alien base.

The expedition

Operation Highjump was a US Navy mission to Antarctica in 1946–47, led by Rear Admiral Richard Byrd. It involved about 4,700 personnel, thirteen ships including an aircraft carrier, and aircraft, and its purpose was mapping, training and scientific survey. It was announced publicly in advance.

The claim

The fringe reading holds that the expedition was a military operation against a surviving Nazi base, or against extraterrestrials, and that it was defeated or driven off. The evidence offered is a newspaper interview in which Byrd is said to have warned about hostile aircraft near the pole — a quotation that has been reconstructed and embellished in retellings.

The expedition's records are extensive and public: charts, photographs, reports. There is no mention of combat, and the force was not configured for it.

Where it stands

Documented: the expedition, its size, its purpose and its records.

Documented: the public announcement and the scientific output.

Not documented: any engagement, base or enemy.

Not established: the quotation in the form usually given.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-documented expedition on the shelf and the least mysterious, and the gap between the record and the story is instructive.

Lazar and Element 115

Fringe claim

A man who said he worked on alien craft at Area 51 claimed their fuel was element 115, unknown at the time. Element 115 was synthesised in 2003, and it decays in milliseconds.

The claim

In 1989 Robert Lazar said he had worked at a facility near Area 51 reverse-engineering alien craft, and that their propulsion used element 115 — then an undiscovered element — as a stable fuel. He described the craft's operation and the programme.

The problems

Element 115, moscovium, was first synthesised in 2003 by a Russian–American team. It is highly radioactive, with isotopes that decay in milliseconds, and it cannot be accumulated in the quantities a fuel would require. The 'island of stability' predicted for heavier elements does not extend to moscovium in a usable way.

Lazar's employment and education claims have been checked and not supported: no record at the institutes he named, and no degree at the institutions he cited. He has been convicted of a prostitution-related offence and of illegal chemical disposal, both unrelated to the UFO claim but relevant to credibility.

Where it stands

Documented: the claim, and the subsequent synthesis of element 115.

Documented: moscovium's instability.

Not supported: Lazar's employment and education claims.

Not established: any craft or programme.

The honest label: fringe — a story with one apparent prediction that the chemistry refutes.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most influential piece of Area 51 lore, and because the one checkable prediction was checked.

The Tic Tac

Live debate

A Navy pilot filmed an object off San Diego in 2004 that looked like a tic tac and appeared to move impossibly. It is the best-documented modern UAP case, and it is still unexplained.

The encounter

In November 2004, during exercises off San Diego, the USS Nimitz carrier group tracked objects descending from about 24,000 metres to sea level. A flight of F/A-18s intercepted one; the gun camera recorded a white, tic-tac-shaped object that appeared to accelerate away without visible exhaust.

The analyses

The video is genuine and was released officially. Analyses have proposed several mundane explanations: a parallax effect from the camera's tracking, a distant aircraft or balloon, sensor artefacts, or a classified drone. None has been demonstrated conclusively, and the pilots' accounts of the object's behaviour have not been explained.

The case is significant because of the quality of the data — radar, infrared video, and multiple trained observers — not because it establishes anything.

Where it stands

Documented: the video, the radar tracks and the witness accounts.

Contested: the mundane explanations.

Not established: any exotic craft.

Not established: the object's performance as described.

The honest label: live debate — the best case in the collection for 'unidentified' meaning unidentified.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the one page where the archive's answer is genuinely 'we do not know', and because that is a category worth having.

The Men in Black

Fringe claim

Men in dark suits who visit witnesses and warn them to keep quiet. The stories are consistent, old, and unsupported by a single verified case.

The stories

The Men in Black entered UFO folklore in the 1950s: witnesses reported being visited by men in dark suits, sometimes in groups of three, who warned them to stop talking, produced official-looking identification, and behaved oddly. The most-cited early case is Albert Bender's, who later retracted his account.

The record

No visit has been verified, and the descriptions are inconsistent in detail while consistent in outline — the pattern of a legend rather than of an event. The folklore was shaped by the writer Gray Barker's 1956 book, which is where the image of the men in black suits was fixed in the literature.

Real government agents do visit people, and the air force did have officers interview witnesses; that mundane reality is enough to seed the legend.

Where it stands

Documented: the stories and their literary origin.

Documented: real interviews by real officials.

Not established: any organised intimidation programme.

Not established: any single verified visit.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the folklore has a dated, named origin, and the origin is a book.

The Illuminati

Fringe claim

A Bavarian enlightenment society, banned in 1785, has become the supposed secret government of the world. The real organisation lasted nine years and left a paper trail.

The society

The Order of the Illuminati was founded in Bavaria in 1776 by Adam Weishaupt, a professor of canon law, as an Enlightenment secret society opposed to religious and political obscurantism. It recruited officials and intellectuals, and it was banned by the Bavarian authorities in 1785. Its internal papers were seized and published.

The claim

The modern claim is that the Illuminati survived, went underground, and now controls governments, banks and media. It rests on eighteenth-century anti-Enlightenment polemic — notably the claim that the society caused the French Revolution — and on a set of symbols, including the eye in the pyramid, which comes from Christian iconography and appears on the US dollar bill for unrelated reasons.

There is no documentary evidence of a surviving organisation. The society's own records end with its suppression.

Where it stands

Documented: the society, its founder, its membership and its suppression.

Documented: the publication of its seized papers.

Not established: any survival, or any current control.

The symbol: older than the society and unrelated to it.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most-named secret society in the world and the least documented after 1785, and because the paper trail is the answer.

The D.C. Street Grid

Debunked

Washington's diagonal avenues are said to form a pentagram, a Masonic symbol and a satanic layout. They are baroque city planning, and the geometry does not work.

The claim

The claim is that Pierre L'Enfant's 1791 plan for Washington encodes Masonic or occult geometry: diagonal avenues forming a pentagram, the Capitol and the White House at specific points, and streets laid out to symbolic effect.

The planning

Diagonal avenues over a rectangular grid were standard baroque planning — Versailles, Paris, and many European capitals use the same device, which creates long vistas and traffic routes. L'Enfant's plan was designed to place the Capitol and the President's house on prominent sites with radiating avenues between them.

The pentagram reading requires selecting a subset of intersections and ignoring the rest; the lines do not close, and the angles do not match. Washington does have Masonic connections in its founding era, but the street plan is not evidence of a layout.

What is established

Documented: the plan, its designer and its European precedents.

Documented: the baroque convention of diagonals over a grid.

Not established: any occult encoding.

The method error: selecting points until a shape appears.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best example of pattern-hunting in a map, and because the architectural history is more interesting than the pentagram.

The Georgia Guidestones

Documented

A granite monument in Georgia carried ten commandments for a post-apocalyptic age, in eight languages. It was commissioned anonymously, vandalised repeatedly, and destroyed by a bomb in 2022.

The monument

The Georgia Guidestones were erected in Elberton, Georgia, in 1980: four granite slabs over six metres tall, a central pillar and a capstone, inscribed with ten principles in eight languages, beginning with a call to keep the human population under 500 million and to live in balance with nature. The monument also functioned as an astronomical calendar.

The record

The monument was commissioned by a man using the pseudonym 'R.C. Christian', who left instructions and paid in advance; his identity has never been established. The inscriptions made it a target for conspiracy theories about population control and a 'new world order'.

It was damaged by vandals several times and destroyed by an explosive device in July 2022; the remains were demolished. The county cited public safety.

What is established

Documented: the monument, its inscriptions, its astronomy and its destruction.

Documented: the anonymous commissioning.

Not established: the identity or motive of the commissioner.

Not established: any organisation behind it.

The label: documented — a real monument with a real and unresolved authorship.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the rare case where a conspiracy-shaped object had a mundane explanation (one anonymous donor) and still generated a mythology.

Bilderberg

Documented

An annual off-the-record meeting of politicians, bankers and executives. It is real, it is influential, and it is not secret — the participant list is published every year.

The meeting

The Bilderberg Meeting has been held annually since 1954, bringing together around 120–150 people from politics, finance, industry, academia and media, for three days of off-record discussion. It was founded by a group including Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands, partly to improve transatlantic understanding during the Cold War.

The record

The meeting is private — participants speak under the Chatham House rule — but it is not secret: the attendee list is published on the organisation's website each year, the venue is announced, and journalists cover it. Agendas are published in outline.

The claim that it makes binding decisions is unsupported: the meeting has no formal power, no resolutions and no communiqué. Its influence is real and informal, which is a different thing and harder to measure.

What is established

Documented: the meetings, the participants and the format.

Documented: the published guest lists.

Not established: any decision-making authority.

Real but unmeasured: informal influence.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the 'secret meeting' claim is half right — it is private — and the half that is wrong is checkable in one page of a website.

Fluoride and the Pineal Gland

Debunked

The claim that water fluoridation calcifies the pineal gland and dulls the mind. The studies cited are high-dose animal work, and the doses are orders of magnitude above drinking water.

The claim

The claim is that fluoride in drinking water accumulates in the pineal gland, causing calcification and reducing melatonin, and that this is a deliberate means of dulling the population. It circulates widely in alternative-health and conspiracy media.

The evidence

The pineal gland does calcify with age, in almost everyone, independently of water fluoridation. The studies cited for fluoride effects are typically animal studies at doses far above those in fluoridated water — which is maintained at about 0.7 mg per litre — and the human epidemiological evidence for cognitive effects at those levels is contested and, at best, from areas with naturally high fluoride.

The public-health evidence for fluoridation's benefit to dental health is substantial, and the safety reviews by national bodies have repeatedly found no evidence of harm at regulated levels, while recommending that very high natural levels be reduced.

What is established

Documented: dental benefit at regulated levels.

Documented: pineal calcification with age, independent of fluoride.

Contested: cognitive effects at high natural exposure.

Not established: harm at 0.7 mg/L, or any deliberate purpose.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most durable of the public-health conspiracy claims, and because the honest version — high natural fluoride is a real problem — is more interesting than the version told.

The Water-Powered Car

Debunked

The claim that a car can run on water alone, usually by splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen on board. The electrolysis costs more energy than the hydrogen returns.

The claim

The claim is that water can be used as fuel, typically by electrolysing it on board to produce hydrogen, which is then burned. Versions of it have circulated since the oil crises of the 1970s, with inventors claiming suppressed technology and patents.

The physics

Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen requires at least as much energy as burning the hydrogen releases — in practice more, because of efficiency losses. A car running on water alone would need an external energy source to drive the electrolysis, and if that source is the engine, the loop loses energy at every step.

Hydrogen vehicles are real, but they carry hydrogen produced elsewhere, or use fuel cells. Demonstrations of 'water cars' have repeatedly failed when examined by independent engineers, and several inventors have been convicted of fraud.

What is established

Documented: the claim and its long history.

Documented: the thermodynamics of electrolysis.

Documented: real hydrogen vehicles, using stored hydrogen.

Not established: any water-only vehicle.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest energy claim to test, and because the second law of thermodynamics is not a conspiracy.

Project Azorian

Documented

The CIA built a ship to lift a sunken Soviet submarine from the Pacific floor, and told the world it was mining manganese. It is the most expensive covert engineering project of the Cold War.

The operation

In 1968 the Soviet ballistic-missile submarine K-129 sank in the Pacific, about 3,000 km northwest of Hawaii. The CIA, using acoustic data, located it and decided to attempt a recovery — a feat never attempted at that depth.

The ship Glomar Explorer was built with a cover story: Howard Hughes was said to be mining manganese nodules from the seabed. It carried a giant claw designed to reach 5,000 metres. In 1974 it lifted part of the submarine; the operation was partly successful, and the details remained secret for decades.

The aftermath

The press learned of the attempt in 1975, and the CIA responded with what became known as the 'Glomar response' — neither confirming nor denying. Documents were declassified in 2010, and the recovered material is said to have included codebooks and two nuclear torpedoes.

What is established

Documented: the sinking, the location, the ship and the cover story.

Documented: the recovery attempt and its partial success.

Documented: the declassification, from 2010.

Not established: some details of what was recovered.

The label: documented — a real conspiracy, with a real cover story.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best evidence that real covert operations exist, and that they look nothing like the ones in the rest of this shelf.

Operation Snow White

Documented

The Church of Scientology ran a systematic infiltration of US government offices to remove documents about itself. Eleven senior officials were convicted.

The operation

In the 1970s the Church of Scientology's Guardian's Office ran a programme to infiltrate government agencies and remove or alter documents relating to the church — including the Internal Revenue Service, the Department of Justice and the FBI. The programme was called Operation Snow White; a related operation targeted journalists and critics.

The outcome

The FBI raided Scientology offices in 1977 and recovered documents. Eleven senior officials, including Mary Sue Hubbard, were convicted of offences including conspiracy and theft of government property, and served prison terms. The church itself was named an unindicted co-conspirator.

It remains the largest known infiltration of the US government by a private organisation.

What is established

Documented: the operation, the raids and the convictions.

Documented: the scale, across several agencies.

Not established: any wider reach than the prosecutions established.

Significance: the largest such infiltration on record.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real conspiracy that was prosecuted to conviction, and because the paperwork is the evidence.

Stuxnet

Documented

A computer worm that destroyed uranium centrifuges in Iran by making them spin at the wrong speed while reporting normal operation. It is the first known cyber weapon to cause physical damage.

The worm

Stuxnet was discovered in 2010. It spread through Windows systems, but its payload targeted Siemens industrial controllers of a specific configuration used in uranium enrichment. It recorded normal operating data, replayed it to the monitoring system, and meanwhile drove the centrifuges through damaging speed cycles.

Analyses found that it used four zero-day exploits — unprecedented at the time — and that it was designed to reach one specific facility, widely identified as Natanz in Iran. It is generally attributed to the United States and Israel, though neither has officially confirmed it.

The consequences

The operation damaged or destroyed a substantial number of centrifuges and delayed the programme. It also demonstrated that code could destroy physical equipment, and it changed how governments thought about critical infrastructure.

What is established

Documented: the worm, its payload and its effects.

Documented: the zero-days and the target configuration.

Attributed: to the US and Israel, by reporting rather than by official confirmation.

Documented: physical damage to centrifuges.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a real operation that sounds like fiction, and because the technical detail is public and checkable.

Crypto AG

Documented

A Swiss company sold encryption machines to governments around the world for decades. The CIA and the German BND owned it, and the machines were compromised by design.

The operation

Crypto AG was a Swiss manufacturer of cipher machines, sold to governments, militaries and businesses worldwide from the 1950s. From 1970 the CIA and the West German BND secretly owned the company through a Liechtenstein foundation, and the machines were designed so that the owners could decrypt the traffic.

The operation, code-named Rubicon, gave Western intelligence access to the communications of dozens of countries for decades — including, at times, states that were not adversaries.

The exposure

The story was published in 2020 by the Washington Post, ZDF and Swiss television, based on declassified documents and interviews. The company was sold off in the 1990s, and the Swiss government had known of the arrangement for years without acting.

What is established

Documented: the ownership, the compromised design and the duration.

Documented: the 2020 exposure, with documents.

Documented: the customers, in outline.

Not fully documented: which traffic was read and when.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest possible counter-example to 'they could never keep it secret' — they did, for fifty years.

The Rainbow Warrior

Documented

French intelligence officers sank a Greenpeace ship in Auckland harbour, killing a photographer. France initially denied it, then admitted it.

The attack

On 10 July 1985, two explosive charges sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour, where it was preparing to sail to protest against French nuclear testing at Moruroa. The photographer Fernando Pereira was killed.

The exposure

New Zealand police arrested two French nationals travelling on false Swiss passports; they pleaded guilty to manslaughter and were sentenced, then held on an island before being repatriated. Investigative journalism established that the operation was authorised by the French defence ministry and the DGSE, and that the president knew.

France denied responsibility at first, then admitted it after the evidence became overwhelming; the defence minister resigned. A subsequent French inquiry exonerated the officers involved.

What is established

Documented: the attack, the death, the arrests and the convictions.

Documented: the authorisation at ministerial level.

Documented: the initial denial and later admission.

Not established: some details of the chain of command.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a state conspiracy proven by court record, and because the cover-up lasted weeks, not decades.

Dead Hand

Documented

A Soviet system designed to launch retaliation if the command authority were destroyed — a doomsday machine that actually exists, and is semi-automatic rather than automatic.

The system

Dead Hand — in Russian, Perimetr — was developed by the Soviet Union in the 1980s as a retaliatory system. If sensors detected a nuclear attack and the command authority did not respond within a set time, the system could authorise launch of intercontinental missiles, including by triggering them without a human decision at the top.

It was designed to remove the incentive for a decapitating first strike: even if the leadership were destroyed, retaliation would follow.

The record

Its existence was disclosed after the Cold War by Russian officials and by defectors, and confirmed in interviews. Whether it remains operational is uncertain; Russian statements have suggested it does, in a modified form. Its designers have said it was semi-automatic — it required human initiation to arm, and its logic was constrained.

What is established

Documented: the system, its purpose and its design.

Documented: its disclosure after 1991.

Uncertain: its current status and configuration.

Not established: a fully automatic doomsday machine.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the one 'doomsday machine' claim that turns out to be true, and because the truth is stranger and more constrained than the myth.

Ulcers Are Bacterial

Documented

Stomach ulcers were said to be caused by stress and acid. Two Australian researchers found a bacterium living in the stomach lining, were ignored for a decade, and won the Nobel Prize.

The finding

In 1982 Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, working in Perth, found a spiral bacterium — later named Helicobacter pylori — in stomach biopsies from patients with gastritis and ulcers. The prevailing view was that the stomach was sterile and that ulcers were caused by stress and excess acid.

Their paper was rejected at a conference and then published, and the finding was largely ignored for years. Marshall famously drank a culture of the bacterium in 1984 and developed gastritis, which he then treated with antibiotics.

The outcome

The causal link was established, antibiotic treatment transformed ulcer care, and Marshall and Warren received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005. H. pylori is now recognised as the cause of most peptic ulcers and a major risk factor for gastric cancer.

What is established

Documented: the bacterium, the causal link and the treatment.

Documented: the initial rejection and the decade of resistance.

Documented: the Nobel Prize, 2005.

Not established: that all ulcers are bacterial — some are drug-related.

The label: documented — a case where the establishment was wrong.

Why it is in the archive

Because the archive is mostly about claims that failed, and it needs the cases where the minority view won on evidence.

Batterygate

Documented

Apple slowed down older iPhones to stop them shutting down unexpectedly, and did not tell anyone. It was a reasonable engineering decision and a serious communication failure.

What happened

In December 2017 Apple confirmed that iOS had been throttling processor performance on iPhones with degraded batteries, to prevent the devices from shutting down unexpectedly under peak load. The practice had been introduced in an earlier release without being explained.

Users noticed slower phones after updates and assumed planned obsolescence. Benchmark results showing reduced performance on older devices drove the story, and Apple's confirmation turned a technical fix into a scandal.

The consequences

Apple apologised, cut the price of battery replacements, and added a battery health indicator so users could see the condition of their battery and disable the throttling. Regulators in several countries investigated; France fined the company for not informing consumers.

What is established

Documented: the throttling, and Apple's confirmation of it.

Documented: the engineering rationale — preventing shutdowns.

Documented: the absence of disclosure, and the response.

Not established: planned obsolescence as a motive.

The label: documented — a real practice, honestly named.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where a conspiracy theory was half right: something was being done to the phone, and the reason was mundane.

The Ice Cream Machine

Live debate

McDonald's ice cream machines break constantly, and it is a franchise-wide joke. The machines are made by one company, their error codes are proprietary, and the repair rules are the story.

The phenomenon

The soft-serve machines in McDonald's restaurants are manufactured by Taylor, and they are notoriously prone to being out of service. The machines require a nightly pasteurisation cycle, they throw error codes that staff cannot diagnose, and repairs are restricted to authorised technicians.

The argument

In 2020 a company built a device to read the machines' diagnostic data, and was sued; the dispute became a test case for the right to repair. Investigations found that many outages are caused by cleaning cycles and minor faults that staff could fix if the codes were documented.

The counter-argument is that the machines are food-safety equipment with real constraints, and that unauthorised repair carries genuine risk. Both things are true, which is why the topic is filed as a live debate rather than a scandal.

Where it stands

Documented: the failure rate, the error codes and the repair restrictions.

Documented: the right-to-repair dispute.

Contested: how much of the downtime is avoidable.

Contested: the safety argument for the restrictions.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most ordinary possible example of a systemic problem — and because a joke that everyone makes turned out to have a documented cause.

New Coke as a Trojan Horse

Fringe claim

Coca-Cola replaced its recipe in 1985, the public revolted, and the original returned in 79 days. The claim is that the whole thing was a planned manoeuvre.

The events

In April 1985 Coca-Cola replaced its formula with a sweeter version, 'New Coke', after taste tests showed it beat both Pepsi and the original. The reaction was immediate and hostile; the company restored the original as 'Coca-Cola Classic' in July, seventy-nine days later.

The claim

The conspiracy reading is that the whole episode was planned to reinvigorate the brand and to convert customers from Pepsi back to Coke, and that the backlash was anticipated. It is an attractive story: the company got a huge amount of free publicity and emerged with a stronger position.

The evidence is against it. Internal documents and interviews with executives describe genuine alarm, emergency meetings and a scramble to reverse the decision; the company's stock and sales fell during the period. A planned failure that costs you market share and requires an apology is a strange plan.

Where it stands

Documented: the reformulation, the backlash, the reversal.

Documented: the internal reaction, from documents and interviews.

Not established: any plan to fail.

Contested: how much of the eventual benefit was luck.

The honest label: fringe — a good story with the record against it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best example of a conspiracy theory that would make the world more interesting if it were true, and because the documents are the answer.

The CIA and Modern Art

Documented

The CIA covertly funded abstract expressionist exhibitions and journals during the Cold War, as cultural diplomacy. The paintings were real; the funding was hidden.

The programme

From the late 1940s, the CIA's Congress for Cultural Freedom — a covertly funded organisation — supported journals, concerts and exhibitions across Europe, including abstract expressionist art. The purpose was cultural: to present the United States as a place of artistic freedom, in contrast to Soviet socialist realism.

The record

The funding was secret until 1967, when it was exposed in the press; the Congress for Cultural Freedom had received money from the CIA through private foundations. The scale of the art programme is documented, though the claim that the CIA 'invented' abstract expressionism is not — the artists were working before and independently of the funding.

The distinction matters: covert patronage of an existing movement is documented; the creation of a movement by an intelligence agency is not.

What is established

Documented: the covert funding, its channels and its purpose.

Documented: the 1967 exposure.

Not established: that the CIA created the movement.

The distinction: patronage versus invention.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the real story is stranger than the myth and the myth is more flattering to the conspiracy.

The Guatemala Syphilis Experiments

Documented

US researchers deliberately infected Guatemalan soldiers, prisoners and psychiatric patients with syphilis to test penicillin. The subjects were not told, and the study was hidden for sixty years.

The experiments

Between 1946 and 1948, US Public Health Service researchers, working with Guatemalan authorities, deliberately exposed around 1,300 Guatemalan soldiers, prisoners, sex workers and psychiatric patients to syphilis, gonorrhoea and chancroid, in order to study prophylaxis and treatment with penicillin. The subjects were not informed and did not consent.

The exposure

The study was forgotten until the historian Susan Reverby found the records in 2010 while researching Tuskegee. The US government apologised, and a presidential commission found that the experiments violated ethical standards of the time as well as later ones.

The Guatemalan government called the experiments a crime against humanity, and a lawsuit on behalf of survivors was dismissed on jurisdictional grounds.

What is established

Documented: the experiments, the numbers and the methods.

Documented: the absence of consent.

Documented: the 2010 disclosure and the official apology.

Documented: the presidential commission's findings.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real conspiracy in the sense that matters — concealed, official and harmful — and it is documented in the government's own report.

Operation Fast and Furious

Documented

US agents allowed firearms to be trafficked into Mexico in order to trace them, and lost track of most of them. Two were found at the scene of a Border Patrol agent's killing.

The operation

Operation Fast and Furious was run by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives between 2009 and 2011 in Arizona. Agents allowed suspected straw purchasers to buy firearms and cross into Mexico, in the hope of tracing the weapons to cartel leaders rather than arresting buyers at the border.

The consequences

Around 2,000 firearms were involved, and most were not recovered. Two were found at the scene of the killing of Border Patrol agent Brian Terry in 2010, which brought the operation into public view. Congressional investigations found serious failures of oversight, and the ATF's acting director was reassigned; the attorney general was held in contempt of Congress over documents.

The operation's defenders argue that it was a flawed attempt at a hard problem; its critics that it armed criminals with official sanction.

What is established

Documented: the operation, its method and its scale.

Documented: the recovery failure and the Terry case.

Documented: the congressional findings.

Contested: who authorised what, at which level.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the conspiracy theory — the government let guns walk — turned out to be substantially true, and was admitted.

Iran–Contra

Documented

The US sold arms to Iran and used the proceeds to fund Nicaraguan rebels, in defiance of an embargo and a congressional ban. It was exposed, investigated and pardoned.

The scheme

Between 1985 and 1986, senior officials in the Reagan administration arranged sales of arms to Iran — then subject to an arms embargo — in the hope of securing the release of American hostages in Lebanon. Proceeds from the sales were diverted to the Contras in Nicaragua, in violation of the Boland Amendment, which barred military aid.

The exposure

The scheme unravelled in November 1986 when a Lebanese magazine reported it. A presidential commission, a congressional investigation and an independent counsel followed. Eleven officials were convicted; most convictions were overturned on appeal or vacated, and several were pardoned by the first President Bush.

The affair is the clearest documented case of a covert policy run outside congressional oversight, and its details are in the public record.

What is established

Documented: the arms sales and the diversion.

Documented: the violations of the embargo and the Boland Amendment.

Documented: the investigations and the convictions.

Contested: how far up the chain responsibility reached.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case the conspiracy literature is right about, and it is right because the documents were eventually published.

BCCI

Documented

A bank grew into a global institution by serving dictators, arms dealers and intelligence services, and was closed by regulators in 1991. It is the largest bank fraud prosecuted to that date.

The bank

Bank of Credit and Commerce International was founded in 1972 by Agha Hasan Abedi, with capital from the Gulf and a structure of holding companies that spread its operations across dozens of jurisdictions. It grew quickly by serving customers that mainstream banks avoided: regimes under sanctions, arms traders, drug traffickers and intelligence agencies.

The collapse

Regulators in several countries moved against it in 1991, and it was closed with losses of around $10 billion, much of it from depositors' accounts. Investigations in the US and UK found systematic fraud, false accounting and a deliberate structure designed to frustrate supervision.

Its customers included the CIA and other intelligence services, which had used it as a channel — a fact that complicated the investigations and feeds the conspiracy literature.

What is established

Documented: the fraud, the structure and the closure.

Documented: the scale of the losses.

Documented: the intelligence use of the bank.

Contested: how much of the intelligence use was known to regulators.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the conspiracy literature's instincts were right — the bank was a criminal enterprise — and the reality is more bureaucratic than the myth.

The Lavon Affair

Documented

Israeli military intelligence recruited Egyptian Jews to bomb Western targets in Egypt, in an attempt to damage relations with the West. The operation was exposed, and the political fallout lasted a decade.

The operation

In 1954, Israeli military intelligence recruited a network of Egyptian Jews to carry out bombings against American and British targets in Egypt — cinemas, post offices, a library — in an attempt to damage Egypt's relations with the West and to prevent a British withdrawal. The bombs were timed to cause damage without casualties; one device injured people.

The exposure

The network was rolled up by Egyptian police, several members were tried and convicted, and two were executed. The operation became a political scandal in Israel — the 'Lavon affair', named after the defence minister — with a long dispute over who had authorised it, a resignation, and a political crisis that lasted until 1963.

What is established

Documented: the operation, the network and the trials.

Documented: the political fallout in Israel.

Contested: the exact chain of authorisation.

Documented: the executions of two members.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real false-flag operation — rare, documented, and smaller and messier than the ones imagined in the literature.

CIA Black Sites

Documented

The CIA ran a network of secret prisons in several countries, where detainees were held and subjected to techniques the US government later acknowledged as torture.

The programme

After 2001 the CIA established a network of secret detention facilities — 'black sites' — in several countries, where high-value detainees were held outside normal legal process and subjected to 'enhanced interrogation techniques', including waterboarding, sleep deprivation and confinement in small boxes.

The record

The programme was exposed by journalists in 2005, investigated by the European Parliament and by the US Senate, whose 2014 report found the techniques ineffective as well as brutal. The US government acknowledged the programme and the use of techniques that, in the Senate's words and in the judgment of most legal analysts, constituted torture.

Several European states were found to have hosted or facilitated the programme, and cases continue in the European Court of Human Rights.

What is established

Documented: the programme, the sites and the techniques.

Documented: the Senate report and its findings.

Documented: European complicity, in several cases.

Contested: the legal characterisation, in some jurisdictions.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most consequential documented secret programme of the century, and because it was exposed by the ordinary means the archive relies on: documents and reporting.

Project 112 and SHAD

Documented

The US military tested biological and chemical agents on ships and in the open, sometimes without informing the personnel involved. The programme was disclosed decades later.

The programme

Project 112 was a US Department of Defense programme that ran from 1962 to 1973, testing biological and chemical agents in the open — including at sea, on ships, and in several land locations. A sub-programme, SHAD (Shipboard Hazard and Defense), tested agents on naval vessels with crews aboard, in some cases without telling them what was being released.

The disclosure

The programme was declassified in stages, and a 2002 Pentagon review found that thousands of service members may have been exposed. The department set up a register and contacted veterans; several tests had used live biological agents and simulants.

The scale and the secrecy are documented; the health consequences are harder to establish, which is the ongoing argument.

What is established

Documented: the programme, its tests and its locations.

Documented: the 2002 review and the veteran register.

Contested: the health effects on participants.

Documented: the absence of consent in some tests.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the conspiracy claim — the military tested agents on its own personnel — was substantially correct.

The Green Run

Documented

A secret test released radioactive material over Washington state to see how it would disperse. It was detected 300 km away, and the public was told nothing.

The test

In December 1949, at the Hanford Site in Washington state, the US Atomic Energy Commission conducted a secret test called Green Run: irradiated fuel was processed to release radioactive material — including iodine-131 and xenon-133 — into the atmosphere, to study how it would disperse and to calibrate monitoring for Soviet tests.

The consequences

The plume was detected hundreds of kilometres away, and the release was kept secret for decades. The test is part of the wider record of Hanford's releases, which contaminated the Columbia River and the surrounding area and made the site the largest nuclear cleanup in the United States.

The documents were declassified in the 1980s, and the health effects on downwind communities remain an active subject of study and compensation claims.

What is established

Documented: the test, the release and the detection.

Documented: the secrecy and the later declassification.

Contested: the health effects and their attribution.

Documented: Hanford's wider contamination record.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a deliberate release of radiation over a civilian area, done in secret, and documented in the government's own files.

The FBI and Martin Luther King

Documented

The FBI wiretapped King, bugged his hotel rooms, and sent him an anonymous letter urging suicide. The campaign is documented in the Bureau's own files.

The campaign

From the mid-1950s, the FBI under J. Edgar Hoover monitored Martin Luther King Jr, initially through the Communist Party investigation and then as a target in his own right. The Bureau wiretapped his phones, bugged hotel rooms, and compiled a file on his political and sexual life.

The letter

In 1964, after King received the Nobel Peace Prize, the Bureau sent an anonymous letter to his address, combining surveillance material with a suggestion that he kill himself; King's associates treated it as an attempt at blackmail. The letter was disclosed in the 1970s by the Senate's Church Committee.

The campaign was documented in the Church Committee's 1976 report, which found that the Bureau had sought to 'neutralize' King as a political figure. Hoover's deputy, William Sullivan, later acknowledged the letter's authorship.

What is established

Documented: the surveillance, the files and the letter.

Documented: the authorisation at senior level.

Documented: the Church Committee's findings.

Not established: every purpose behind the campaign.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a state agency using surveillance against a domestic political figure, and because the Bureau's own files are the evidence.

The CIA–Mafia Plots Against Castro

Documented

The CIA recruited mafia figures to kill Fidel Castro, using poison pills, exploding cigars and a contaminated diving suit. The schemes failed, and the Church Committee published them.

The plots

From 1960, the CIA's Directorate of Operations developed a series of plots to assassinate Fidel Castro, working through Cuban exiles and through mafia figures including Sam Giancarlo and Santo Trafficante, who had lost casino interests in Cuba. Methods proposed included poison pills, a contaminated diving suit, exploding cigars and a fungus-infected scuba suit.

The record

The plots were investigated by the Church Committee in 1975 and by the Rockefeller Commission, and the reports were published with the details. The Inspector General's 1967 report, declassified later, catalogued eight distinct plots.

Castro was not killed, and the schemes are remembered for their improbability rather than their effectiveness.

What is established

Documented: the plots, the participants and the methods.

Documented: the Church Committee and IG reports.

Documented: mafia involvement.

Not established: any successful attempt.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case the conspiracy literature cites most often, and the documents are more damning and more ridiculous than the myth.

The Horizon Scandal

Documented

A faulty accounting system made subpostmasters look like thieves. Hundreds were prosecuted, some went to prison, and the Post Office fought the victims for twenty years.

The system

The Post Office's Horizon accounting system, introduced in 1999, recorded shortfalls that subpostmasters could not explain. The Post Office prosecuted hundreds of them for theft and false accounting, based on the system's output, and many were convicted, fined, or imprisoned.

The exposure

Subpostmasters organised, and a 2019 High Court case found that the system contained bugs and errors and that the Post Office's own investigators knew of them. A public inquiry began in 2022, and legislation was introduced to quash convictions automatically.

By 2024 more than a hundred convictions had been overturned, and the inquiry heard evidence that the Post Office had withheld information and treated its own operators as adversaries for years.

What is established

Documented: the system's faults, the prosecutions and the convictions.

Documented: the 2019 judgment and the public inquiry.

Documented: the overturned convictions.

Contested: individual culpability at senior levels.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the institution was the wrongdoer and the evidence was a computer log — and because it took twenty years.

Dieselgate

Documented

Volkswagen fitted cars with software that detected emissions tests and switched on full pollution control only when being tested. On the road, the cars emitted many times the limit.

The fraud

In 2015 the US Environmental Protection Agency found that Volkswagen diesel cars contained 'defeat device' software: it detected when the vehicle was on a test rig, and enabled full emissions control; on the road, the controls were reduced, and nitrogen oxide emissions were up to forty times the legal limit.

The consequences

Volkswagen admitted the use of the software, and the scandal spread to other manufacturers. The company has paid more than €30 billion in fines, settlements and recalls, several executives were charged, and two were imprisoned in the United States. A German court later found that the software was installed with the knowledge of senior management.

What is established

Documented: the software, its function and the emissions.

Documented: the admission and the penalties.

Documented: the convictions of executives.

Documented: the spread to other manufacturers.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the largest deliberate emissions fraud ever admitted, and because the mechanism was software — which is now the usual mechanism.

Enron and California

Documented

California's electricity market was deregulated, and traders found ways to make money by creating scarcity. The state had rolling blackouts, and Enron collapsed.

The market

California deregulated its electricity market in the late 1990s, separating generation from retail supply and creating a spot market. In 2000–2001 the state experienced rolling blackouts and prices that rose by orders of magnitude.

The manipulation

Enron and other traders used strategies with names recorded on tape — 'Fat Boy', 'Death Star', 'Ricochet' — to exploit the market rules: creating the appearance of congestion, scheduling power out of the state and back in, and withholding capacity. Recordings of traders boasting about 'stealing' from California were published in 2005.

Enron collapsed in 2001 in an accounting scandal, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission later found that manipulation had contributed to the crisis, though the extent is still argued.

What is established

Documented: the market design, the strategies and the recordings.

Documented: the blackouts and the price rises.

Documented: Enron's collapse and the regulatory findings.

Contested: how much of the crisis was manipulation versus supply.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the conspiracy was a business model, and the evidence is the traders' own voices.

The P2 Lodge

Documented

A Masonic lodge in Italy recruited generals, ministers and intelligence chiefs, and was exposed in 1981. Its members were involved in the decade's political violence.

The lodge

Propaganda Due — P2 — was a Masonic lodge in Italy that, under Licio Gelli from the 1960s, recruited senior military officers, politicians, civil servants, intelligence chiefs and journalists. It operated as a secret network outside the normal Masonic structure, which had been suspended.

The exposure

In 1981 police found a membership list in a suitcase belonging to Gelli; it included nearly a thousand names, among them senior figures in the armed forces and intelligence services. The lodge was dissolved by law, and a parliamentary commission investigated its role in political violence, including the Bologna bombing.

Gelli was convicted of various offences, escaped custody, and the lodge's activities remain a reference point for Italian conspiracy literature.

What is established

Documented: the lodge, the membership list and the dissolution.

Documented: the parliamentary investigation.

Contested: the lodge's role in specific acts of violence.

Documented: Gelli's convictions.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where a secret society turned out to be exactly as infiltrated as the rumours said, and the evidence was a suitcase.
