The Gleiwitz Incident

Documented

German agents staged an attack on a radio station and blamed Poland, as the pretext for invasion. Prisoners were killed and left as 'casualties'.

The operation

On the night of 31 August 1939, SS personnel under Alfred Naujocks staged an attack on the radio station at Gleiwitz, then in Germany (now Gliwice, Poland). They broadcast a short anti-German message in Polish, left a body on the steps, and presented the event as a Polish provocation.

The record

The operation was part of a wider set of staged incidents along the border, and it was used in Hitler's speech announcing the invasion the next day. At Nuremberg, Naujocks testified to the operation and to the killing of a prisoner — referred to by the code name 'Canned Goods' — to provide a corpse.

The incident is one of the best-documented false flags in history, and it is the standard example used whenever the category is discussed.

What is established

Documented: the operation, the participants and the staging.

Documented: the death of a prisoner to provide a body.

Documented: the Nuremberg testimony.

Documented: the use as a pretext.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the historical false flag that all later claims are measured against, and because it was admitted by its own organiser.

Asbestos and Radon Cover-Ups

Documented

Both asbestos and radon were known hazards long before they were regulated, and in both cases industry documents show the knowledge preceded the action.

Asbestos

The health effects of asbestos were documented in the early twentieth century, and industry-funded research in the 1930s–1960s confirmed the link to asbestosis and mesothelioma while companies suppressed and contested it. Internal documents, disclosed through litigation, show that executives discussed the risks and chose not to warn workers.

Radon

Radon, a radioactive gas from uranium decay, accumulates in buildings and is a leading cause of lung cancer among non-smokers. Its risks were established in the 1950s–1980s through uranium miner studies, and regulation of domestic exposure followed slowly, with industry and some governments resisting remediation costs.

Both cases follow the same pattern: the hazard is established, the evidence is contested for decades, and the regulation arrives after the harm.

What is established

Documented: the hazards, and the dates of the evidence.

Documented: the internal industry documents on asbestos.

Documented: the delayed regulation of both.

Contested: the extent of deliberate concealment in each case.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because these are the clearest cases of a real cover-up that killed people slowly, and because the documents are now public.

Cambridge Analytica

Documented

A political consulting firm obtained Facebook data on millions of users through a personality quiz app, and used it for targeted advertising. The scandal changed how the platform handled data.

The harvesting

In 2014 a researcher at Cambridge University built a Facebook quiz app that collected data not only from users who installed it but from their friends — a feature the platform then allowed. The data covered tens of millions of profiles and was passed to Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm.

The exposure

The arrangement was reported in 2018 by the Guardian and the New York Times, with testimony from a former employee. Facebook suspended the firm, apologised, and later paid penalties in the US and UK; the firm collapsed. Investigations found the platform's data controls had been inadequate and its disclosures misleading.

What remains contested is the effect: the firm claimed its 'psychographic' targeting was decisive, and the evidence for that claim is weak.

What is established

Documented: the data harvesting, its scale and the transfer.

Documented: the platform's inadequate controls.

Documented: the penalties and the firm's collapse.

Contested: the effectiveness of the targeting.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real scandal whose most dramatic claim — that it swung an election — is the part with the least evidence.

Zero-Click Search Extinction

Live debate

More searches now end without a click, because the answer appears on the results page or in an AI summary. Whether that is the death of the open web or an ordinary shift is argued.

The claim

The argument is that search engines and AI assistants increasingly answer questions directly — featured snippets, knowledge panels, and now generated summaries — so users do not click through to publishers. On this reading, the referral traffic that funds independent publishing is being withdrawn.

The evidence

Studies of search behaviour have found that a large share of queries end without a click, and publishers report declining referral traffic. The measurement is contested because the platforms do not publish the data, and because 'zero-click' includes queries that never had a clickable answer.

The structural point is not in dispute: if the answer is on the results page, the publisher does not get the visit. Whether that ends the open web or simply changes its business model is the argument.

Where it stands

Documented: the shift to direct answers.

Documented: declining referral traffic, in publisher reports.

Contested: the scale, and the definition of a zero-click search.

Contested: the long-term effect on publishing.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim about the internet's economics made almost entirely from data held by the companies being described.

Short-Form Video and Attention

Live debate

The claim that short-form video has shortened attention spans. The evidence is mixed, the definition of attention is contested, and the platforms measure engagement, not cognition.

The claim

The claim is that short-form video — vertical clips of seconds to a few minutes, delivered by an algorithm — reduces attention span, harms concentration and impairs learning, especially in young people.

The evidence

The evidence is mixed. Some studies find associations between heavy short-video use and self-reported attention difficulties; others find small or null effects, and the direction of causation is unclear — people with attention difficulties may use the format more. Standardised attention tests show no clear population-level decline, and the historical record shows the same panic attached to novels, radio, television and the walkman.

What is well documented is that the format is designed to maximise engagement, that it displaces other activities, and that displacement has measurable effects on sleep and study time.

Where it stands

Documented: the design for engagement, and displacement effects.

Contested: effects on attention as measured by tests.

Contested: causality.

Documented: the historical pattern of the panic.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the current version of a two-century-old claim, and because the honest answer — displacement is real, cognitive damage is unproven — is rarely the one given.

The NPC Theory

Fringe claim

The joke-theory that most people are non-player characters with no inner life. It began as a meme, and a survey found a surprising number of people willing to say they doubted others' consciousness.

The meme

The NPC meme, from 2016, depicts people as non-player characters — game characters with scripted dialogue and no inner life — and was used as an insult in online argument. It developed into a half-serious 'theory' that some proportion of people lack consciousness.

The survey

A 2023 paper reported that a substantial minority of respondents said they believed it possible that some people they interact with are not conscious, or that the people around them lack inner experience — figures that surprised the researchers and prompted a debate about how the questions were understood.

The philosophical ancestor is the problem of other minds, which is a genuine and unsolved question. The meme is not a contribution to it, and the survey may be measuring a joke taken literally.

Where it stands

Documented: the meme and its spread.

Documented: the survey and its reported figures.

Contested: what the survey respondents meant.

Serious ancestor: the problem of other minds.

The honest label: fringe — a joke with a philosophical shadow.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the only page here where the claim is about the reader's neighbours, and because it shows a meme becoming a belief.

Avril Lavigne Was Replaced

Debunked

A claim that the singer died in 2003 and was replaced by a body double named Melissa. The evidence is photographs, and the photographs are of the same person at different ages.

The claim

The claim, circulating since around 2005, is that the Canadian singer Avril Lavigne died in 2003 and was replaced by a lookalike named Melissa Vandella, who has continued her career. The evidence offered is comparison of photographs before and after the alleged date: differences in facial proportions, height and style.

The problems

The photographs span years during which a person's face, weight, hair and makeup change normally, and the comparison relies on selecting images that support the claim. Lavigne has continued to perform, record and give interviews, and there is no documentary, medical or legal evidence of a death and substitution.

The claim is a well-known example of a 'celebrity death replacement' legend, a genre that also attaches to other figures.

What is established

Documented: the claim and its comparison photographs.

Documented: the normal changes the photographs show.

Not established: any death or substitution.

The method: selection of images to fit a conclusion.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the purest photographic claim in the collection, and because the method is the same one used in earnest on much older objects.

Goodhart's Law

Documented

When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The law is a one-line summary of a century of institutional failure, and it is demonstrated every year.

The law

Charles Goodhart formulated it in 1975 about monetary aggregates: any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed on it for control purposes. Marilyn Strathern's 1997 paraphrase is the one everyone quotes: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

The examples

The pattern is old and well documented. Soviet factories given targets in tonnes produced heavy furniture; given targets in nails, they produced useless tiny ones. Wells Fargo's sales targets produced millions of fraudulent accounts and a $3 billion settlement. British hospital waiting-time targets produced gaming of the clock; police crime-recording targets produced downgrading of offences.

The mechanism is not stupidity. It is that a target creates an incentive to optimise the number rather than the thing the number was supposed to represent, and the people closest to the number are best placed to do it.

What is established

Documented: the law, its origin and its paraphrase.

Documented: the case history, across sectors and decades.

The mechanism: incentive applied to a proxy measure.

Not a law of nature: it is a pattern, not a theorem.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most useful single sentence in the collection, and because every institution on the previous shelf was, at bottom, an example of it.

  • Wikipedia, “Perverse incentive” — the mechanismen.wikipedia.org

The Third Place

Live debate

The claim that cafés, bars, parks and barbers are the places where community actually forms, and that they are disappearing. The concept is well formed; the decline is harder to measure.

The concept

Ray Oldenburg's The Great Good Place (1989) argued that functioning societies need 'third places' — neither home nor work — where people meet as equals, regularly and informally. He listed the features: neutral ground, levelling, conversation as the main activity, accessibility, a regular crowd, a low profile, a mood of play.

The claim about decline

The argument that third places are disappearing draws on declining membership of clubs and religious congregations, rising rents in urban areas, and the shift to online interaction. The evidence is mixed: some categories have declined sharply, others — cafés, gyms, co-working spaces — have grown, and the measurement depends on what counts.

The stronger empirical claim is about the loss of places that are free, unstructured and open to anyone, which is narrower and better supported.

Where it stands

Documented: the concept and its features.

Documented: declines in some categories of association.

Contested: whether third places as a whole are declining.

Contested: what counts as one.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim about social life that people recognise instantly and that is very hard to measure — a combination the archive meets constantly.

Male Loneliness

Documented

Surveys find that a substantial share of men report no close friends and rely on a partner for emotional support. The pattern is documented; the explanations are contested.

The finding

Surveys in several countries find that men report fewer close confidants than women, and that a substantial minority — around 15% in a widely cited 2021 US survey — report no close friends at all. Men are also more likely to name a romantic partner as their main source of emotional support, which makes the loss of that relationship a larger shock.

The explanations

Proposed explanations include differences in how friendships are maintained (activity-based rather than conversation-based), norms that discourage disclosure, the decline of institutions that structured male social life, and the way surveys measure intimacy — asking about confiding rather than about companionship.

The health consequence is better established than the cause: social isolation is associated with higher mortality, and the effect is comparable in size to well-known risk factors.

What is established

Documented: the survey findings, across countries.

Documented: the association between isolation and mortality.

Contested: the causes, and the size of any trend.

Contested: whether the measurement captures what it claims.

The label: documented, with a live debate attached.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a social claim with real data behind it and a public argument that outruns the data in both directions.

Shrinkflation and Skimpflation

Documented

Products get smaller or worse while the price stays the same. Both are documented by statistics agencies, and both are hard for a shopper to see.

The practice

Shrinkflation is the reduction of a product's size or quantity while the price stays the same, so the unit price rises without a visible price change. Skimpflation is the reduction of quality — fewer ingredients, cheaper substitutes, less service — with the same effect. Both are documented by statistics agencies, which adjust price indices for quantity changes.

The evidence

The UK's Office for National Statistics has published analyses of shrinkflation across hundreds of products, finding that it affects a small but persistent share of goods, concentrated in food and household products. Consumer bodies document examples and unit-price changes; manufacturers argue that input costs and reformulation drive it.

The practice is not illegal where the net quantity is labelled, which it must be. The harm is informational: shoppers compare prices, not unit prices.

What is established

Documented: the practice, with statistical agency data.

Documented: the unit-price effect.

Contested: the scale relative to ordinary inflation.

Legal: where labelling requirements are met.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real phenomenon that feels like a conspiracy and is actually a labelling problem.

The Peltzman Effect

Live debate

The claim that safety features cause people to take more risks, cancelling out the benefit. The mechanism is real; the size of the effect is disputed.

The claim

Sam Peltzman argued in 1975 that seat-belt laws would reduce deaths among occupants but increase them among pedestrians and cyclists, as drivers felt safer and drove more riskily. The broader idea — risk compensation — holds that people adjust behaviour to a perceived level of safety.

The evidence

Risk compensation is well documented in some settings: drivers with antilock brakes take shorter following distances, skiers with helmets ski faster, and cyclists may ride differently with helmets. Whether it offsets the safety benefit is a different question, and the evidence there is mixed.

For seat belts, the consensus is that the net effect is strongly positive: occupant deaths fell substantially, and the claimed increase in other road users has not been found at the magnitude Peltzman predicted.

Where it stands

Documented: risk compensation as a behaviour.

Contested: its magnitude, and whether it offsets benefits.

Not supported: the strong claim that seat belts are net neutral.

Mixed: the evidence in other domains.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best example of a counter-intuitive claim that is partly true, which is harder to handle than one that is simply false.

The Streisand Effect

Documented

An attempt to suppress information draws attention to it. The name comes from a photograph of a house, and the mechanism is now a standard part of online strategy.

The episode

In 2003 the photographer Kenneth Adelman published aerial photographs of the California coast as part of a coastal survey, including one of Barbra Streisand's house. Her lawyers demanded its removal; the site reported 420,000 visitors in the following month, and the image was widely reproduced. The term was coined by Mike Masnick shortly afterwards.

The mechanism

The effect is not magic. A takedown attempt supplies three things: a signal that the material matters, a story for journalists, and a reason for people to mirror the content. The result is the opposite of the intent, and it is now well enough understood that organisations plan for it.

It is a documented case rather than a universal law: many takedowns succeed quietly, and the effect requires an audience that notices the attempt.

What is established

Documented: the original episode, with traffic figures.

Documented: many subsequent cases.

The mechanism: attention drawn by suppression.

Not universal: most takedowns do not backfire.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a strategy that reliably produces the outcome it was meant to prevent.

Poe's Law

Documented

Without a clear marker of intent, a parody of extremism is indistinguishable from the real thing. It was formulated on a forum and has been demonstrated repeatedly since.

The law

Poe's law states that without a clear indicator of the author's intent, it is impossible to tell the difference between a parody of extremism and the real thing. It was formulated on the Christian Forums site around 2005 by Nathan Poe, in the context of creationist arguments.

The evidence

The demonstrations are abundant. Sincere believers have adopted slogans invented as parody; parody accounts have been taken as genuine by large audiences; and the 'flat earth' and 'birds aren't real' movements each contain participants who are joking and participants who are not, with no reliable way to tell from the content.

The law is a statement about interpretation under conditions of low information, and it explains why the archive insists on provenance: who said it, where, and with what record.

What is established

Documented: the formulation and its origin.

Documented: repeated demonstrations.

The mechanism: absence of intent markers.

Not a law of nature: a heuristic about interpretation.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the reason this archive labels fiction as fiction, and because a reader who does not know it will be fooled by design.

Cunningham's Law

Documented

The fastest way to get the right answer online is to post the wrong one. It is a joke about correction culture, and it is accurate often enough to be useful.

The law

Cunningham's law is usually stated as: the best way to get the right answer on the internet is not to ask a question, it is to post the wrong answer. It is attributed to Ward Cunningham, the inventor of the wiki, though the attribution is informal and the exact origin is not documented.

Why it works

The mechanism is a combination of things that are well documented in online behaviour: people are more motivated to correct an error than to answer a question, corrections are socially rewarded in technical communities, and a confident wrong statement is more visible than a tentative question.

The cost is that the correction may be wrong too, and that the law rewards provocation. It is a heuristic about incentives, not a method for finding truth.

What is established

Documented: the formulation and its informal attribution.

Documented: the behaviour it describes.

Not documented: a specific origin date or statement.

The cost: corrections can be wrong; provocation is rewarded.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it explains a great deal of the archive's subject matter: a confident wrong claim travels further than a careful question.

Brandolini's Law

Documented

The energy needed to refute nonsense is an order of magnitude greater than the energy needed to produce it. It is the reason this archive exists in the form it does.

The law

Brandolini's law, also called the bullshit asymmetry principle, was formulated by the programmer Alberto Brandolini in 2013: the amount of energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude larger than the energy needed to produce it.

Why the asymmetry exists

Producing a claim requires one sentence and no evidence. Refuting it requires locating the source, checking the data, running the analysis, and then explaining the result to an audience that has already moved on. The asymmetry is not a failure of the refuter; it is a property of the medium.

The practical consequences are well documented: corrections travel less far than the original claim, and repetition of a false claim increases belief even when it is corrected.

What is established

Documented: the formulation.

Documented: the asymmetry, in the mechanics of publishing and correction.

Documented: the weaker reach of corrections.

Not a theorem: an observation about incentives and effort.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because the archive's entire design — short pages, sources, labels, no arguing in the comments — is a response to this law.

The Truman Show Delusion

Documented

A delusion in which the patient believes their life is a television show and everyone around them is acting. It is documented, it is rare, and it is named after a film.

The phenomenon

In 2008 the psychiatrists Joel and Ian Gold described a small series of patients who believed their lives were being filmed and broadcast, with the people around them playing roles. The content closely followed the plot of The Truman Show, and the Golds named the presentation after it.

What it is

It is not a new disease. The patients had diagnoses including schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and the delusion is a culturally shaped version of a familiar persecutory belief: that one is being watched, that events are staged, that others are actors. Delusion content has always tracked the available technology — radio in the 1920s, television later, cameras and the internet now.

The value of the description is in what it shows about how delusions take their content from the culture, not in any new mechanism.

What is established

Documented: the case series and the description.

Documented: the underlying diagnoses.

Documented: the cultural shaping of delusion content.

Not established: any new syndrome.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows the mechanism behind a whole class of claims here: a belief that is shaped by the media available to the believer.

Room 641A

Documented

A room in an AT&T switching centre in San Francisco, built for the NSA, where internet traffic was copied. A technician's evidence exposed it in 2006.

The room

Room 641A is a room in an AT&T switching facility at 611 Folsom Street, San Francisco, fitted out from 2003 with equipment that split internet traffic and diverted a copy to a National Security Agency programme. It was described in a 2006 declaration by Mark Klein, a retired AT&T technician.

The record

Klein's evidence, published by Wired and used in litigation, described the hardware and the installation. The US government invoked state secrets privilege to have the case dismissed, and the programme was later confirmed in outline by the 2013 Snowden disclosures.

The room is one of the few pieces of physical infrastructure of a mass surveillance programme to be documented with a site address.

What is established

Documented: the room, the equipment and the whistleblower's declaration.

Documented: the litigation and the state secrets dismissal.

Documented: the programme, confirmed in outline later.

Contested: the scope of the collection.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where a conspiracy theory about the internet was replaced by a documented room, with an address.

Pegasus Zero-Click

Documented

Spyware that infects a phone without any interaction, sold to governments. The 2021 Pegasus Project documented its use against journalists, lawyers and activists.

The software

Pegasus is spyware made by the Israeli firm NSO Group, sold to governments. It infects phones — historically through zero-click exploits in messaging apps — and gives access to messages, calls, location, camera and microphone. The 'zero-click' aspect means the target does nothing to trigger it.

The exposure

In 2021 a consortium of news organisations, the Pegasus Project, analysed a leaked list of more than 50,000 phone numbers selected for possible targeting, and identified journalists, lawyers, activists and politicians. The list indicated selection rather than confirmed infection, which the consortium stated clearly.

NSO has said its product is for fighting crime and terrorism, and that it does not control how clients use it. The US placed the company on an export blacklist in 2021, and litigation continues.

What is established

Documented: the software, its capabilities and its customers.

Documented: the 2021 leak and the targeting of journalists and activists.

Documented: the US export restrictions.

Contested: which specific numbers were infected, as opposed to selected.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a surveillance capability that was sold commercially, and because the reporting was careful about what the list did and did not prove.

Boeing's MCAS

Documented

A software system designed to correct a handling characteristic, fed by a single sensor, brought down two aircraft. 346 people died.

The system

The 737 MAX's larger engines were mounted further forward, which changed the aircraft's pitch behaviour at high angles of attack. Boeing added MCAS — a system that automatically pushed the nose down when it detected a high angle of attack — to make the aircraft handle like earlier 737s, so that pilots would not need simulator training.

The failures

MCAS relied on a single angle-of-attack sensor, with no cross-check against the other one, and its authority was increased during development. In October 2018 and March 2019, faulty sensor readings caused MCAS to repeatedly push the nose down; the crews could not overcome it. Lion Air flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines flight 302 crashed, killing 346 people.

The fleet was grounded worldwide in March 2019 for twenty months. Investigations found design and certification failures, and Boeing paid settlements exceeding $2.5 billion.

What is established

Documented: the system, its single-sensor input and its authority.

Documented: the two crashes and the grounding.

Documented: the certification failures.

Contested: the allocation of responsibility between company and regulator.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a design decision made for commercial reasons that had a body count, and because the documentation is public.

Purdue and OxyContin

Documented

A company marketed an addictive opioid as low-risk, using a claim about its formulation that was not supported. The consequences are measured in deaths.

The marketing

Purdue Pharma launched OxyContin in 1996 and marketed it as less addictive than other opioids, on the basis that its slow-release formulation reduced the rate at which the drug entered the bloodstream. Sales representatives were trained to tell doctors that the risk of addiction was under one per cent, a figure without evidence.

The consequences

The drug was widely prescribed for chronic pain, and misuse rose sharply; the formulation could be defeated by crushing. Purdue pleaded guilty in 2007 to misbranding and paid $635 million. In 2020 the company pleaded guilty to federal criminal charges and agreed to pay $8.3 billion; the Sackler family settled civil claims. The overdose deaths attributed to prescription opioids in the period run to the hundreds of thousands.

The company's bankruptcy settlement, which would have shielded the family, was rejected by the Supreme Court in 2024.

What is established

Documented: the marketing claims and their lack of evidence.

Documented: the pleas, the fines and the settlements.

Documented: the rise in overdose deaths.

Contested: the attribution of the whole crisis to one company.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest documented case of a corporate claim that killed people at scale, and because the documents are court exhibits.

FTX's Backdoor

Documented

An exchange took customer deposits and lent them to a related trading firm, using a hidden exemption in its accounting. It collapsed in days.

The structure

FTX was a cryptocurrency exchange; Alameda Research was a trading firm founded by the same person, Sam Bankman-Fried. Customer deposits were transferred to Alameda, and FTX's systems included a feature that allowed Alameda to maintain a negative balance without triggering the automatic liquidation that would have applied to any other account.

The collapse

In November 2022 a leaked balance sheet showed Alameda's holdings were largely in illiquid tokens, and a rival exchange's decision to sell its FTX token triggered a run. The company collapsed within days; Bankman-Fried was convicted of fraud and conspiracy in 2023 and sentenced to 25 years.

The bankruptcy examiner and the prosecutors documented the backdoor and the commingling in detail. Customer funds were partly recovered.

What is established

Documented: the commingling, the backdoor and the collapse.

Documented: the conviction and sentence.

Documented: the scale of the shortfall.

Contested: the precise allocation of responsibility among executives.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the fastest large fraud in financial history, and because the evidence was a database.

Libor Rigging

Documented

Traders manipulated the interest rate that underpinned trillions in loans and derivatives, by submitting figures that suited their books.

The benchmark

Libor — the London Interbank Offered Rate — was calculated from submissions by major banks estimating the rate at which they could borrow from each other. It underpinned trillions of dollars of loans, mortgages and derivatives.

The manipulation

Investigations from 2008 found that traders had asked colleagues who submitted the rates to adjust them to benefit trading positions, and that during the 2008 crisis some banks submitted artificially low rates to appear healthier. Barclays was fined $450 million in 2012; UBS, RBS and others followed, with total penalties in the billions, and several traders were convicted.

The benchmark was subsequently reformed and is being replaced by risk-free rates; Libor's final settings ended in 2023.

What is established

Documented: the manipulation, the fines and the convictions.

Documented: the two motives — trading profit and appearing healthy.

Documented: the replacement of the benchmark.

Contested: the full extent of the manipulation before 2008.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a conspiracy in the plain sense — coordinated, concealed and profitable — and it is documented in regulatory settlements.

FIFA Bribes

Documented

Senior football officials were indicted in the United States for racketeering and bribery over media and marketing rights. The president resigned.

The indictments

In May 2015 the US Department of Justice indicted fourteen people, including senior FIFA officials, on charges of racketeering, wire fraud and money laundering, over decades of bribes connected to the sale of media and marketing rights for football tournaments in the Americas.

The aftermath

Sepp Blatter resigned as president days after the arrests, and FIFA's ethics committee banned him from the sport for eight years (later reduced). Several officials were convicted, and the organisation was restructured under a new president. Swiss prosecutors also investigated the award of the 2018 and 2022 World Cups; a criminal case over the 2006 German bid collapsed in 2021.

The evidence base is court filings and plea agreements, which is what makes this page a documented case rather than a rumour about a governing body.

What is established

Documented: the indictments, the pleas and the convictions.

Documented: the resignation and the bans.

Documented: the scale of the bribery scheme.

Contested: the extent of corruption in the World Cup awards.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the conspiracy was real, the paper trail was in another country, and the sport's own governance could not have found it.

Monopoly's Anti-Monopoly Origin

Documented

The world's most famous property game was invented to teach that land monopolies are unjust. The irony is documented in patents and in the inventor's own words.

The origin

In 1903 Elizabeth Magie patented 'The Landlord's Game', designed to illustrate the ideas of the economist Henry George — that land value should be taxed and that monopoly ownership is unjust. The game had two rule sets: one in which everyone prospered, and one in which monopolists crushed the others.

The transformation

The game spread through Quaker communities and college campuses, was adapted by Charles Darrow, who sold it to Parker Brothers in 1935 as his own invention, and became Monopoly. Magie received $500 and no royalties. Her game's anti-monopoly intent was lost, and the published version taught the opposite lesson — that winning means bankrupting everyone else.

The history was rediscovered by Ralph Anspach during a trademark lawsuit in the 1970s and 1980s, and is now well documented.

What is established

Documented: Magie's patent, the two rule sets and her intent.

Documented: Darrow's role and the Parker Brothers sale.

Documented: Magie's compensation.

Contested: how much of the design Darrow adapted.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-documented case of a game's meaning being inverted by its publisher, and because the patent settles it.

Dune as Anti-Messiah

Documented

Frank Herbert wrote Dune as a warning about charismatic leaders and the danger of following them. The films and the fandom have often read it as a hero story.

The intent

Herbert described Dune as a study of the messiah pattern: Paul Atreides becomes a religious and political leader, and the consequence is a jihad that kills billions. Herbert wrote sequels — particularly Dune Messiah — specifically to undercut the heroic reading of the first book, and said so in interviews.

The reading

The first novel can be read as a hero's journey because Paul is sympathetic, competent and victorious, and because the warning is structural rather than stated. The sequels make it explicit: the cost of the myth is the point.

The films have taken different positions on this — the 2021 and 2024 adaptations foreground the danger, while earlier versions softened it — and the argument about whether the text is a warning or an adventure is now a small industry.

What is established

Documented: Herbert's stated intent, in interviews and essays.

Documented: the sequels written to undercut the hero reading.

Contested: how clearly the first novel conveys the warning.

Contested: the adaptations' fidelity to it.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the author's intent is on the record and the popular reading has ignored it, which is the reverse of the usual pattern here.

Vault-Tec Started the War

Documented

The Fallout games imply that the corporation behind the survival vaults knew the war was coming, and may have caused it. The evidence is inside the games.

The lore

Fallout is set after a nuclear war between the United States and China in 2077. Vault-Tec built the vaults that sheltered survivors, and the games establish that the vaults were social experiments: each had a different, often lethal, parameter set by the company.

The claim

The claim that Vault-Tec started the war is supported by in-game documents and by the television adaptation, which depicts the company discussing the profitability of the apocalypse. The games are ambiguous about whether the company caused the exchange or merely anticipated it.

The archive files it as documented because the material is in the games' own texts — not because the war happened.

What is established

Documented: the vault experiments, in in-game material.

Documented: the company's foreknowledge, in the adaptation.

Ambiguous: whether Vault-Tec caused the war.

Fiction: the whole setting.

The label: documented, as a reading of a text.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where a fan reading is well supported by the source, and where the source is fiction and says so.

GTA's Two Universes

Documented

The Grand Theft Auto games are split into a 3D universe and an HD universe, with separate continuities. Rockstar confirmed it, and it explains why the same city looks different.

The split

Rockstar has described the series as running in separate continuities: the '3D universe' of GTA III, Vice City and San Andreas, and the 'HD universe' beginning with GTA IV, in which the cities are reimagined and the characters are different people. Radio stations, brands and geography differ between them.

Why it matters

The split explains apparent contradictions that fans spent years trying to reconcile — the same city with different layouts, characters with the same names who are not the same people, and references that do not carry across. It is a deliberate design choice rather than a continuity error, and it is stated by the developer.

The 'two universes' idea is documented by the publisher; the further claim that the games are connected by a hidden timeline is not.

What is established

Documented: the two continuities, as described by Rockstar.

Documented: the differences in cities and characters.

Not established: any hidden overarching timeline.

The value: it explains real contradictions.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the fan question had an official answer, and the answer was simpler than the theories.

Squid Game Card Colours

Debunked

A fan theory holds that the red and blue cards in Squid Game encode the choice between the games and the outside world. The show's creator has described the cards more simply.

The theory

In Squid Game, a recruiter offers a card and a choice, and the series uses red and blue repeatedly. A fan theory holds that the colours encode a systematic meaning — that red means the games and blue the outside world, or that the choice determines a character's fate — and that the pattern can be traced across episodes.

The problems

The colours are used as a motif throughout the series, and motifs do not require a code. Analyses of the theory find that it requires ignoring instances that do not fit, and the creator's comments describe the cards and the colours in thematic terms rather than as a cipher.

The archive files it as debunked rather than fiction because it is presented as a hidden system in the work, and the work does not contain one.

What is established

Documented: the theory and the motif.

Documented: the creator's comments.

Not established: any systematic code.

The method error: ignoring contrary instances.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the commonest form of the pattern-hunting error, applied to a work of fiction rather than to the world.

The Simpsons Time Machine

Debunked

The Simpsons appears to predict events. With nearly 800 episodes over 35 years, some of them will match, and the ones that do are the ones that get posted.

The claim

Lists circulate of events The Simpsons is said to have predicted: the Trump presidency, the 9/11 attacks, the Apple Watch, the pandemic, various disasters. The implication is either foresight or something stranger.

The arithmetic

The show has aired around 780 episodes since 1989, each with multiple scenes and jokes. Any large set of specific, topical gags will contain some that later resemble events, and the ones that do are the ones that are clipped, shared and remembered. The ones that do not — the overwhelming majority — are not.

The claims also rely on loose matching: a scene that vaguely resembles an event is counted as a prediction. The selection and the loose matching together explain the phenomenon without any foresight at all.

What is established

Documented: the episodes, the dates and the matches.

Documented: the selection mechanism — only hits are shared.

Not established: any prediction, or any foresight.

The arithmetic: hundreds of episodes; some matches are certain.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest example of the denominator being invisible, and because the same structure underlies most prophecy claims.

The Mushroom War

Documented

Adventure Time is set a thousand years after a nuclear war, and the show reveals it slowly. The backstory is documented in the episodes, not invented by fans.

The setting

Adventure Time is set in the Land of Ooo, a world of mutants, magic and ruins. The series establishes over its run that Ooo is Earth after a nuclear war — the 'Mushroom War' — around a thousand years earlier, and that the show's magic is a consequence of the aftermath.

The reveal

The backstory is delivered through artefacts, flashbacks and the histories of characters such as the Ice King and Marceline, and it is confirmed in later episodes and in the finale. It is not a fan construction: the show's own writers built the setting on it.

The archive files it as documented because the claim is about what the text contains, and the text contains it.

What is established

Documented: the war, the timeline and the reveal.

Documented: the episodes that establish it.

Not a fan theory: the writers built the setting on it.

Fiction: the setting itself.

The label: documented, as a reading of the show.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where a fan observation turned out to be the intended reading, which is rarer than the reverse.

Dating-App Elo Gating

Fringe claim

The claim that dating apps score users and show them only to people of similar scores. One app did use an Elo-style system, and said it stopped.

The claim

The claim is that dating apps assign each user a hidden attractiveness score — the name comes from the Elo rating system used in chess — and match users within score bands, so that a user's experience is determined by a ranking they cannot see.

The evidence

Tinder confirmed that it used an Elo-style system in its early years, then said in 2019 that it had replaced it with a different algorithm that responds to user behaviour. Other apps do not publish their ranking systems. Patents and job postings describe ranking methods, but not the specifics.

The claim is therefore partly documented and mostly not: one company confirmed a version of it and described its replacement, and the rest is inference from behaviour that users can observe.

Where it stands

Documented: Tinder's early use of an Elo-style score.

Documented: the company's statement that it changed the system.

Not published: current ranking systems.

Inferred: behaviour that users observe.

The honest label: fringe — partly true, mostly unverifiable.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim about an algorithm that is invisible by design, and because the one confirmed case is now history.

Atlantis in Antarctica

Debunked

The claim that Atlantis was Antarctica, shifted to the pole by a crustal displacement. Plate tectonics does not permit it, and the ice cores are older than the claim requires.

The claim

Rand and Rose Flem-Ath proposed in When the Sky Fell (1995) that Atlantis was on Antarctica, and that a rapid displacement of the Earth's crust moved it to the pole around 9,600 BC — the date Plato gives for Atlantis's destruction. The argument combines the Plato text with Charles Hapgood's crustal displacement theory.

The problems

Hapgood's mechanism is not supported by geophysics: the crust does not slide over the mantle in the way required, and plate tectonics explains the evidence differently. The Antarctic ice sheet has been continuous for hundreds of thousands of years, and ice cores record volcanic ash and atmospheric composition without any interruption consistent with a temperate civilisation on the continent.

The claim also requires the Plato text to be a geographical record rather than a philosophical parable, which is not how it is read.

What is established

Documented: the claim and its two components.

Not supported: crustal displacement as a mechanism.

Not supported: any civilisation under the ice.

Documented: the continuity of the ice sheet.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most extreme version of the Atlantis claim, and because the ice cores are the cleanest refutation in the collection.

Atlantis at Doñana

Live debate

A team argued that Atlantis lies under the marshes of Doñana in southern Spain, destroyed by a tsunami. The site has structures, and the identification is not accepted.

The claim

In 2004 a German researcher, Rainer Kühne, and later a team including Richard Freund argued that Atlantis was located in the marshes of Doñana, near Cádiz, and that the concentric rings described by Plato could be seen in satellite imagery. A 2011 National Geographic documentary presented the case, and a tsunami was proposed as the destroyer.

The problems

The 'rings' are consistent with natural and later human features in a wetland, and the structures found by geophysical survey have not been dated to the period required or shown to be a city. Spanish archaeologists working in the area have rejected the identification, and no peer-reviewed case has established it.

The wider problem is the same as with every Atlantis location: the Plato text is a philosophical dialogue, and the search for its setting has produced dozens of candidates, each with a local feature that fits part of the description.

Where it stands

Documented: the claim, the imagery and the survey work.

Not established: the identification with Atlantis.

Contested: the dating and character of the structures.

Rejected: by most archaeologists working in the region.

The honest label: live debate, leaning against.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-argued Atlantis location, and because it shows how a real landscape with real features can absorb a legend.

Atlantis as Thera

Live debate

The Minoan eruption of Santorini destroyed a civilisation, and the parallel with Plato's story is striking. The date is the problem: it is 9,000 years out.

The claim

In 1909 the archaeologist K. T. Frost suggested that the Minoan civilisation was the basis for Plato's Atlantis, and that its destruction by the Thera eruption was the catastrophe behind the story. The eruption, around 1600 BC, was one of the largest in the Holocene; it buried the town of Akrotiri and caused damage and famine on Crete.

The problems

The date is the difficulty: Plato places Atlantis's destruction 9,000 years before Solon, roughly 9,600 BC, and the Thera eruption is about 3,600 years ago. The mismatch is a factor of two and a half, and the proposed explanations — a mistranslation of Egyptian units, or a copying error — are possible but unsupported.

The cultural details also differ: Plato describes a naval empire beyond the Pillars of Hercules, and the Minoans were in the Aegean.

Where it stands

Documented: the eruption, its scale and its effects.

Documented: the Akrotiri destruction.

Contested: whether it inspired the Atlantis story.

Not supported: the date match.

The honest label: live debate, with the chronology against it.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most respectable Atlantis hypothesis, and it fails on a number rather than on a mystery.

Kumari Kandam

Fringe claim

A lost Tamil landmass said to have sunk south of India, sometimes linked to Lemuria. The ocean floor has been mapped, and there is no continent there.

The tradition

Kumari Kandam appears in Tamil literary tradition as a land in the far south, associated with the Pandya kingdom and with a deluge. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries it was connected to Lemuria, a hypothetical land bridge proposed by zoologists to explain the distribution of lemurs, and the combined idea became a Tamil nationalist and later a fringe historical claim.

The geology

Lemuria was abandoned once plate tectonics explained the distributions. The Indian Ocean has been mapped in detail, and there is no submerged continental mass in the position required; the features that exist — the Ninety East Ridge, the Kerguelen Plateau — are volcanic and not a lost civilisation's homeland.

The literary tradition is genuine and worth studying; the geological claim attached to it is not supported.

Where it stands

Documented: the literary tradition and its modern use.

Documented: the abandonment of Lemuria.

Not found: any submerged continent.

Not supported: the geological claim.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a colonial-era scientific hypothesis being adopted by a nationalist tradition, and then outliving the science.

Zealandia

Documented

A continent of five million square kilometres, 94% of it underwater, with New Zealand and New Caledonia above the surface. It is real, and it was formally described in 2017.

The continent

Zealandia — Te Riu-a-Māui in Māori — is a continental mass of about five million square kilometres in the southwest Pacific. About 94% of it is submerged, with New Zealand, New Caledonia and some island groups above water. It has continental crust: thicker, older and less dense than oceanic crust.

The science

The term was coined in 1995, and a 2017 paper by Nick Mortimer and colleagues argued that it meets the criteria for a continent: elevation above the surrounding ocean floor, a wide area of continental crust, and clear boundaries. It separated from Gondwana and then subsided.

The claim is uncontroversial in geology, and its interest for this archive is that it is a genuine lost continent — one that no legend predicted.

What is established

Documented: the crust, the area and the boundaries.

Documented: the 2017 formal description.

Documented: its separation from Gondwana.

Not disputed: in geology.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because a shelf full of imaginary lost continents needs the real one, and because it is more interesting than most of them.

Doggerland

Documented

A landmass in the southern North Sea, drowned between about 8,000 and 7,000 years ago. Trawlers have brought up bones and tools for a century.

The land

Doggerland was a low-lying landmass connecting Britain to continental Europe across the southern North Sea. It was inhabited in the Mesolithic, and it was progressively drowned as sea levels rose after the last glaciation, with a final catastrophic event around 8,200 years ago — the Storegga submarine landslide and tsunami.

The evidence

Trawlers have brought up mammoth bones, antlers, tools and peat for a century, and the name comes from the Dogger Bank. Modern work uses seismic survey, cores and computer reconstruction — the 'Europe's Lost Frontiers' project has mapped river channels and coastlines. Dredged material has produced artefacts including a decorated bone point.

The land is documented; what people did there is being pieced together, and the reconstruction is one of the most active areas of Mesolithic archaeology.

What is established

Documented: the landmass, its extent and its drowning.

Documented: the artefacts and bones recovered.

Documented: the Storegga event.

Being reconstructed: the landscape and its occupation.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real lost land with real finds, and because it shows what the imaginary ones would look like if they existed: peat, bones and tools.

Beringia

Documented

A land bridge between Asia and America, exposed when sea levels fell. It was not just a corridor: people lived on it for thousands of years.

The land

Beringia is the region between northeast Asia and northwest North America, including the shallow continental shelf that was exposed as sea levels fell during glacial periods. The last exposure, from roughly 30,000 to 11,000 years ago, created a land bridge between Siberia and Alaska.

The evidence

The bridge is the standard route for the peopling of the Americas, though coastal migration by boat is also proposed and increasingly favoured. Genetic evidence suggests a period of isolation — a 'standstill' — of several thousand years in Beringia before populations expanded into the Americas, which implies people lived there rather than merely passing through.

The land is now under the Bering and Chukchi seas, and its archaeology comes from both shores.

What is established

Documented: the exposed land and its dates.

Documented: the genetic evidence for a standstill.

Contested: the route — interior bridge versus coastal.

Contested: the timing of the first expansion south.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a lost land that mattered, and because the genetic evidence turned a corridor into a home.

Sundaland

Live debate

A drowned subcontinent in Southeast Asia, exposed at low sea levels, with a coastline the size of Europe's. It is real; what happened on it is the debate.

The land

Sundaland is the continental shelf of Southeast Asia — the Sunda Shelf — which was exposed as dry land during glacial lowstands, joining Sumatra, Java, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula into a single landmass about the size of Europe west of Russia. It was flooded as sea levels rose after the last glacial maximum.

The debate

The land is not in dispute. The argument is about what it means: whether the drowned landscape is where major population movements and cultural developments occurred, and whether its archaeology can be recovered. Underwater survey in the region is difficult, expensive and in its infancy.

Some scholars have proposed that the flooding of Sundaland is the origin of flood myths across the region, which is plausible and untestable in the strong form.

Where it stands

Documented: the shelf, its extent and its flooding.

Contested: the cultural significance of the drowned land.

Underexplored: the underwater archaeology.

Plausible: a role in regional flood traditions.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real lost land whose archaeology is mostly inaccessible, which is the honest version of every sunken-civilisation story.

Tartessos

Live debate

A wealthy kingdom in southern Spain, described by Greek writers, that traded with the Phoenicians and then vanished. Its capital has never been found.

The culture

Tartessos was a culture of the lower Guadalquivir in southern Spain, known from Greek and Roman sources as a wealthy kingdom with a port that traded tin and silver. It appears in the Bible as Tarshish. Archaeology has identified its material culture, its settlements and its trade with the Phoenicians from the ninth century BC.

The lost capital

The capital city has not been identified. Candidates include Huelva, Seville and sites in the marshes; the 2004 Atlantis-at-Doñana claim placed it in the same landscape. The culture declined in the sixth century BC, and the reasons — a Phoenician collapse, internal conflict, or environmental change — are argued.

The distinction matters: the people and their trade are documented; the city and its name are a separate problem.

Where it stands

Documented: the culture, its trade and its dates.

Not identified: the capital.

Contested: the decline's cause.

Plausible: several candidate sites.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a genuinely lost city with written sources, which is rarer and more interesting than the invented ones.

El Dorado

Debunked

The legend of a city of gold began as a ritual: a Muisca chief covered in gold dust, offering at a lake. Expeditions killed thousands looking for a place that was never there.

The origin

El Dorado — 'the gilded one' — began as an account of a Muisca ceremony at Lake Guatavita in the highlands of what is now Colombia: a chief, covered in gold dust, was rowed out and offered gold and emeralds to the lake. Spanish accounts from the 1530s describe the ritual.

The transformation

The story became a city, then an empire, then a destination. Expeditions from the 1530s onwards searched the Orinoco and Amazon basins; Gonzalo Pizarro's and Orellana's expedition lost hundreds of men, and Walter Raleigh made two voyages. Thousands died, and no city was found.

The lake itself has been drained and dredged repeatedly; the gold that was recovered is a fraction of what the legend promised, and the ceremony is documented.

What is established

Documented: the Muisca ritual and its description.

Documented: the expeditions and their cost.

Not found: any city of gold.

Explained: the transformation of a rite into a place.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a real ritual becoming a fictional city, and because the cost of the search is documented.

The Lost City of Z

Documented

A British explorer vanished looking for a civilisation in the Amazon. The civilisation turned out to be real — but not as a city of stone.

The explorer

Percy Fawcett, a British surveyor and explorer, spent years in the Amazon and became convinced that a sophisticated civilisation had existed there — which he called 'Z'. In 1925 he entered the jungle with his son and a companion and never returned; over a hundred people died in subsequent searches.

The archaeology

Fawcett's premise was dismissed for decades, on the grounds that Amazonian soils could not support large populations. From the 2000s, satellite and survey work found extensive earthworks — geoglyphs, causeways and ditched settlements — in the upper Xingu and elsewhere, and evidence of large, settled populations and managed forest. The civilisation was real; it built in earth and wood, not stone, which is why it left no ruins to find.

What is established

Documented: Fawcett's expeditions and disappearance.

Documented: the earthworks and the revised population estimates.

Not found: a city of stone.

Contested: the scale of Amazonian societies.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the rare case where the crank premise contained a real insight, and the real answer was better than the search.

Lyonesse

Fiction

A sunken kingdom off Cornwall, drowned in a single night, from which Tristan came. It is literature, and the sea floor has been surveyed.

The legend

Lyonesse appears in Arthurian romance from the thirteenth century: a kingdom off the coast of Cornwall, ruled by a king whose daughter is Tristan's mother, drowned in a single night along with its towns. The story is closely related to the Breton legend of Ys and to the wider European motif of the sunken city.

The evidence

There is no geological candidate: the sea between Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly is deep and has been mapped, and the only drowned land in the region is the Scilly archipelago's prehistoric lowland, which was flooded gradually over millennia rather than in a night.

The motif is literary and is shared across cultures, which is what makes it interesting rather than evidential.

What is established

Documented: the legend, its sources and its relatives.

Not found: any sunken kingdom.

Documented: the gradual flooding of the Scilly lowland.

Not plausible: a single-night drowning at that scale.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-known sunken-land story in English, and because it is honestly a story.

Dwarka

Live debate

Ruins have been found under the sea off Gujarat, and they are real. The claim that they are the 32,000-year-old city of Krishna is not supported by their dating.

The finds

Marine archaeologists have recorded submerged structures off Dwarka in Gujarat since the 1980s: wall segments, a possible harbour, anchors, pottery and stone objects. The finds are documented in the archaeological literature and are the subject of ongoing survey.

The claims

The claim that these are the city of Krishna described in the Mahabharata, dated by some to more than 30,000 years ago, is not supported by the material. The pottery and structures are consistent with historical periods, and the surviving ruins have been associated with the historical Dwarka of the first millennium BC or later.

The submerged structures are also partly natural: some of the recorded 'walls' have been interpreted as beachrock, a sedimentary formation that can look artificial.

Where it stands

Documented: submerged structures, anchors and pottery.

Documented: the archaeological surveys.

Contested: the dating and the identification with the legendary city.

Not supported: the 30,000-year date.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real underwater site with a legend attached, and because the dating is the whole question.

Thule

Live debate

A Greek navigator described a land six days' sail north of Britain, where the sea became sluggish. Nobody knows which land he meant.

The source

Pytheas of Massalia, around 320 BC, sailed north and wrote an account of a land called Thule, six days' sail north of Britain, near the frozen sea. His own work is lost; we know of it through later writers, including Strabo, who was sceptical, and Pliny.

The candidates

Candidates include Iceland, Norway, the Shetlands, the Faroes, and — in the most speculative reading — a Baltic or North Sea coast. The description of a 'congealed sea' suggests pack ice, which points to the far north; the 'six days' sail' constrains it.

There is no archaeological identification, and the question is a matter of textual interpretation rather than of excavation.

Where it stands

Documented: the account, through later quotations.

Documented: the candidates.

Not established: which land was meant.

Not resolvable: by archaeology.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the oldest lost place in the collection, and because its interest is entirely in the text.

The Seven Cities of Gold

Debunked

Spanish explorers were told of seven golden cities to the north. Coronado found pueblos of stone and mud, and no gold.

The legend

The legend of the Seven Cities — Cíbola — reached the Spanish from Indigenous accounts and from a survivor of an earlier expedition, Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, who reported large settlements to the north. A Franciscan, Marcos de Niza, returned claiming to have seen a wealthy city.

The expedition

In 1540 Francisco Vázquez de Coronado led an expedition north with several hundred men. They reached Zuni pueblos in what is now New Mexico: substantial stone and adobe settlements, but without the gold the accounts promised. The expedition continued east and north for two years and returned bankrupt.

The pueblos were real cities. The gold was not there, and the descriptions had grown in the retelling.

What is established

Documented: the legend, the accounts and the expedition.

Documented: the Zuni pueblos and their wealth in food, not gold.

Not found: any city of gold.

Explained: the growth of the account in transmission.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the same error as El Dorado in a different direction: a real settlement described by someone who wanted it to be rich.

Iram of the Pillars

Live debate

A city in the Qur'an destroyed for its arrogance, and a byword for a lost city in the desert. A site in Oman has been excavated, and the identification is argued.

The tradition

Iram of the Pillars appears in the Qur'an as a city of a people destroyed for their arrogance, and became a byword in Arabic literature for a lost city in the sands — sometimes called Ubar or Wabar. The tradition includes stories of travellers who stumbled on its ruins.

The archaeology

In the early 1990s a team using satellite imagery and local accounts excavated a site at Shisr in Oman, finding a large structure with eight-sided walls, a well and evidence of a caravan stop that had collapsed into a sinkhole. The site was identified with the legendary Ubar/Iram and publicised widely.

The identification is plausible but not settled: the site is a caravan city of the right region and period, and the link to the legendary city is an interpretation.

Where it stands

Documented: the text and the later traditions.

Documented: the excavation at Shisr.

Contested: the identification with Iram/Ubar.

Plausible: a caravan city of the right region.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a legend that produced a real excavation, and because the site is more interesting than the identification.

The Location of Punt

Live debate

Egypt traded with a land called Punt for a thousand years, and its location has never been fixed. The candidates run from Somalia to Yemen.

The evidence

Punt appears in Egyptian records from the Old Kingdom onwards, with the most famous account being the reliefs at Deir el-Bahari from Hatshepsut's expedition around 1470 BC, showing ships returning with myrrh trees, ebony, ivory, gold and live baboons. The Egyptians called it 'God's Land'.

The candidates

The candidates are the Horn of Africa — Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia, and the Sudanese coast — and the Arabian shore of the Red Sea, including Yemen. The flora and fauna in the reliefs (baboons, myrrh) point to the African side, and the sailing times in the texts are consistent with the southern Red Sea.

No site has been conclusively identified as Punt, and the debate is conducted through texts, artefacts and geography.

Where it stands

Documented: the trade, the goods and the expeditions.

Documented: the reliefs and the texts.

Contested: the location.

Favoured: the Horn of Africa, on flora and fauna.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a lost place that traded with a literate civilisation for a millennium and still cannot be located, which is a useful corrective to confident maps.

Linear A

Documented

The script of Minoan Crete, used for accounting and ritual, and never deciphered. Linear B was cracked because a scholar guessed the language; Linear A has no such handle.

The script

Linear A was used on Crete and the Aegean from roughly 1800 to 1450 BC, mostly on clay tablets, along with sealings and stone vessels. About 1,400 inscriptions survive, most of them short accounting records, and the signs are catalogued in a standard syllabary.

The problem

Linear B was deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952 partly because he guessed — correctly — that the language was Greek. For Linear A, the underlying language is unknown, the corpus is small and repetitive, and there is no bilingual text. The signs can be read phonetically in part, but the words do not resolve into a known language.

Proposed identifications include a Minoan language unrelated to Greek, a Luwian-related Anatolian language, and others; none is established.

What is established

Documented: the corpus, the signs and the find contexts.

Documented: the accounting character of most texts.

Not established: the language.

Not deciphered: the script.

The label: documented — a real script and a real open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the honest version of the 'undeciphered script' claim: no aliens, no Atlanteans, just a small corpus and no bilingual.

The Orion Correlation

Fringe claim

The claim that the three pyramids at Giza are laid out to match the belt of Orion. The pattern is approximate, the dates do not line up, and the layout has a simpler explanation.

The claim

Robert Bauval argued in 1994 that the three main pyramids at Giza are positioned to mirror the three stars of Orion's belt, with the Nile standing in for the Milky Way, and that the alignment dates the layout to about 10,500 BC. The claim became central to the 'Giza as a star map' literature.

The problems

The correspondence is approximate: the pyramid positions do not match the star positions closely, and the sizes and orientations have to be explained separately. The pyramids were built around 2550 BC, and the 10,500 BC date refers to a supposed alignment of the layout with the sky at that date, which requires the monuments to have been planned millennia before they were built.

The simpler explanation is that the pyramids are arranged along a diagonal determined by the site's geology and by the sequence of construction, with each king building near his predecessor.

Where it stands

Documented: the layout, the dates and the star positions.

Contested: whether the correspondence is intended.

Not supported: the 10,500 BC planning date.

Simpler explanation: geology and construction sequence.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most influential astronomical claim about the pyramids, and because the method — matching two patterns loosely — is the same one used on every ley-line page.

Acoustic Levitation

Debunked

The claim that sound could have lifted the stones of ancient monuments. Acoustic levitation is real, and it works on objects the size of a grain of rice.

The physics

Acoustic levitation is a real technique: a standing wave of ultrasound creates pressure nodes where small objects can be trapped and held. It is used in laboratories to handle droplets and small particles without contact.

The claim

The claim that ancient builders levitated stone blocks with sound is a staple of the 'lost technology' literature. The obstacle is scale: the force available depends on the acoustic pressure, which falls with the size and mass of the object; levitating a multi-tonne block would require acoustic intensities that would destroy the emitter and the surrounding air, and would be audible and lethal to anyone nearby.

The largest objects levitated acoustically are grams, not tonnes — a difference of six orders of magnitude.

What is established

Documented: acoustic levitation, at laboratory scale.

Documented: the physics of the force available.

Not established: any ancient use.

Not plausible: levitating blocks at any usable scale.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest case of a real phenomenon being attached to an impossible scale, and the arithmetic is decisive.

The Hall of Records

Debunked

A chamber beneath the Sphinx, said to hold the records of Atlantis, predicted by a psychic. Seismic surveys and excavations have found nothing.

The claim

Edgar Cayce, an American psychic, gave readings from the 1920s to the 1940s describing a 'Hall of Records' buried near the Sphinx, containing the archives of Atlantis, to be opened at the end of the twentieth century. The claim became a fixture of Egyptian fringe literature.

The tests

Seismic surveys around the Sphinx in the 1990s were reported by some researchers as showing chambers; the claims were disputed by geophysicists, and subsequent investigation found the anomalies consistent with natural features and with the water table. Excavations and conservation work around the monument have not found a chamber or any archive.

The Sphinx itself has been studied extensively, including the enclosure and the geology of the plateau, and the ground beneath it is well characterised.

What is established

Documented: the prediction and its terms.

Documented: the surveys and the excavations.

Not found: any chamber or archive.

Not supported: the seismic claims.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a psychic prediction that was specific, dated and testable, and it failed on all three.

The Walking Moai

Documented

How were the Easter Island statues moved? A 2012 experiment showed they can be 'walked' upright with ropes, which matches the island's oral tradition.

The question

The moai of Easter Island — hundreds of statues, some weighing tens of tonnes — were moved from the quarry at Rano Raraku to platforms around the island. How they were transported has been argued for decades, with proposals including rollers, sledges and levers.

The experiment

In 2012 Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo tested the 'walking' hypothesis: with a replica statue and three ropes, a team rocked the figure upright and moved it forward by alternating pulls, covering tens of metres in under an hour. The method matches the island's oral tradition that the statues walked, and it explains the shape of the bases and the wear patterns.

The experiment does not prove that this is what happened, but it demonstrates that it could have, without rollers or timber — which matters on a deforested island.

What is established

Documented: the statues, their transport and their platforms.

Demonstrated: that upright rocking works at replica scale.

Documented: the oral tradition of walking statues.

Contested: whether it was the method used.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where an experiment and a tradition agreed, and the answer was more interesting than either the mystery or the myth.

Rongorongo

Documented

A script from Easter Island, carved on wooden tablets, and undeciphered. Only about two dozen objects survive.

The objects

Rongorongo is a system of glyphs carved on wooden tablets and other objects from Easter Island, first reported in the 1860s. About two dozen objects survive, in museums around the world, and the signs — several hundred distinct forms — are catalogued.

The problem

No one can read it. The corpus is very small, the objects are scattered and some are fragmentary, and the tradition of reading was lost in the nineteenth century, when the island's population collapsed and the knowledge died with the carriers. Attempts at decipherment have proposed a script of logographs, a mnemonic system, or a partly syllabic script; none is accepted.

There is also a debate about whether the tablets are readable text at all, or a record-keeping or chanting aid.

What is established

Documented: the objects, the signs and their history.

Documented: the loss of the reading tradition.

Not deciphered: the script.

Contested: whether it is writing in the full sense.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real script that was lost with its readers, which is a more sober story than any of the invented ones.

Gunung Padang

Debunked

A terraced hill in Indonesia was claimed in 2023 to be a 25,000-year-old pyramid. Geologists and archaeologists have challenged the dating and the interpretation.

The site

Gunung Padang is a terraced site in West Java, with stone walls, steps and paved areas built on a hill. It is a genuine megalithic site, and it has been studied by Indonesian archaeologists for over a century.

The claim

In 2023 a paper in a Wiley journal argued, from core samples and radiocarbon dates, that the site was a layered pyramid built in stages beginning 25,000 years ago — which would make it the oldest known pyramid by a wide margin. The paper was widely reported.

The criticism was immediate and technical: the cores were not shown to contain human-made material at the claimed depths, the 'layers' are consistent with natural weathering and soil formation, and the radiocarbon dates were on soil organic matter rather than on construction. The journal investigated the paper, and much of the archaeological community rejects the interpretation.

What is established

Documented: the terraces and the megalithic structures.

Contested: the age and the layered-pyramid interpretation.

Not supported: the 25,000-year construction claim.

Documented: the technical criticism.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most recent example of a real site being over-interpreted in a peer-reviewed journal, and because the correction happened in public.

Coral Castle

Debunked

One man carved and moved over a thousand tonnes of coral rock alone, at night, and refused to say how. The answer is levers, pulleys and patience.

The structure

Coral Castle is a complex of carved oolite limestone at Homestead, Florida, built by Edward Leedskalnin, a Latvian immigrant, between about 1920 and 1951. It includes walls of large blocks, a nine-tonne gate that turns on a central pivot, furniture carved from rock, and a tower. Leedskalnin worked alone, mostly at night, and was secretive.

The claims and the explanation

The claims are that the stones were moved by levitation, magnetism or lost knowledge — Leedskalnin wrote pamphlets about magnetism, which fuelled the idea. The explanation is more ordinary: the rock is relatively soft oolite, easily worked with hand tools, and the blocks were moved with levers, pivots, inclined planes and simple lifting gear.

The gate, which could be pushed with one finger, was found to have worn and was repaired in 1980s; its ease of movement comes from a central shaft bearing, not from anything unexplained.

What is established

Documented: the structure, the builder and the dates.

Documented: the material and the pivot mechanism.

Not established: any levitation or lost technology.

Plausible: levers, pivots and patient labour.

The honest label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a genuine feat of solitary engineering, and the myth has obscured the achievement rather than revealed it.
