Akhenaten's Revolution

Documented

One pharaoh replaced Egypt's gods with a single sun disc, moved the capital, and changed the art. The revolution is documented; why it happened is not.

The change

Akhenaten, who ruled around 1351–1334 BC, promoted the Aten — the sun disc — above the other gods, built a new capital at Amarna, and encouraged an art style that abandoned the formal conventions of Egyptian representation for something more fluid and less idealised. Hymns to the Aten survive, and they are among the most striking religious texts from Egypt.

The questions

Whether this was true monotheism, henotheism, or a political move against the priesthood of Amun is argued. The revolution was reversed within a generation: Tutankhamun restored the old cults, the capital was abandoned, and Akhenaten's name was later erased from monuments.

The evidence is abundant — Amarna was excavated and its archives survive — but the motive is not recorded.

What is established

Documented: the reign, the Aten cult, the capital and the art.

Documented: the reversal under Tutankhamun.

Documented: the erasure of his name.

Contested: the religious and political motive.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a documented religious revolution, and because it shows how much of ancient history is evidence without motive.

Hidden Chambers in Tut's Tomb

Debunked

A claim that Nefertiti's tomb lies behind the walls of Tutankhamun's burial chamber, based on radar scans. The scans were repeated, and the chambers were not there.

The claim

In 2015 Nicholas Reeves argued that high-resolution images of Tutankhamun's tomb showed traces of two sealed doorways, and that one of them could lead to the burial of Nefertiti. The claim was widely reported and raised hopes of a major discovery.

The tests

Radar surveys in 2015 and 2016 produced conflicting results; a further survey in 2017–2018 by a different team found no evidence of chambers or doorways behind the walls. Ground-penetrating radar and thermographic surveys found nothing, and the Egyptian authorities concluded that there were no hidden chambers.

The episode is a clean case of a hypothesis being tested and rejected, and it is worth noting that the original claim was made by an Egyptologist, argued from evidence, and published.

What is established

Documented: the hypothesis and its basis in the imagery.

Documented: the radar and thermographic surveys.

Not found: any hidden chamber.

Rejected: by the subsequent surveys.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows the archive's method working in a live discipline: a good hypothesis, a decisive test, and a negative result.

Cleopatra at Taposiris Magna

Live debate

A temple site west of Alexandria has produced coins and a tunnel, and a claim that it holds Cleopatra's tomb. The excavator believes it; most Egyptologists are cautious.

The site

Taposiris Magna is a temple complex on the coast west of Alexandria, built in the Ptolemaic period. Excavations led by Kathleen Martinez since 2005 have found coins bearing Cleopatra's image, a necropolis, statues, and a large tunnel cut through rock, along with evidence of royal burials.

The claim

Martinez argues that Cleopatra and Mark Antony were buried at the site rather than in Alexandria, based on the coins, the temple's dedication, and the tunnel's scale. Other Egyptologists note that the coins and burials are consistent with an ordinary Ptolemaic temple and necropolis, and that no royal burial has been found.

The site's excavation is real and continuing, and the question could be settled by a find. Until then the identification is a hypothesis.

Where it stands

Documented: the temple, the coins, the tunnel and the necropolis.

Contested: the identification with Cleopatra's tomb.

Not found: any royal burial.

Ongoing: the excavation.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a live archaeological search with real finds and no conclusion, which is what most of this shelf looks like before the answer arrives.

Alexander's Lost Tomb

Live debate

Alexander the Great died in Babylon and his body was taken to Egypt. His tomb was visited for centuries, and it has never been found.

The record

Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BC. His body was taken to Egypt by Ptolemy, and a tomb — the Soma — was built in Alexandria. Roman emperors visited it: Augustus, according to Suetonius, touched the body, and Caracalla left offerings. The tomb's location was known in antiquity.

The search

After antiquity the tomb disappears from the record. Alexandria has been rebuilt repeatedly, the palace quarter is under the modern city and partly under the sea, and no trace has been found. Candidates include the Nebi Daniel mosque area, the Latin cemetery, and sites now underwater.

The search continues, and it is one of the few genuinely plausible lost-tomb problems: the body was real, the tomb was real, and it was in a city whose ancient levels are largely unexcavated.

Where it stands

Documented: the death, the transfer and the tomb's existence.

Documented: the Roman visits.

Not found: the tomb.

Plausible: that it survives under the modern city or the harbour.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real lost tomb rather than an invented one, and because the reason it is lost — a city built on top of itself — is the same reason so much archaeology is impossible.

Qin's Mercury Rivers

Live debate

The First Emperor's tomb is said to contain rivers of mercury under a ceiling of pearls. The soil around the mound shows elevated mercury, and the tomb has never been opened.

The record

The historian Sima Qian, writing about a century after the emperor's death, describes the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang as containing palaces, traps, and rivers and seas of mercury made to flow mechanically, beneath a ceiling set with pearls. The mound has never been excavated.

The evidence

Soil samples from around the mound have shown elevated mercury concentrations, which is consistent with the account but not proof of it. The tomb itself is sealed, and Chinese policy is not to excavate it — partly because the technology to preserve what is inside does not exist, and partly because of the reported mercury hazard.

The Terracotta Army pits nearby are excavated, and they are a fraction of the complex.

Where it stands

Documented: the account, the mound and the surrounding complex.

Documented: elevated mercury in the soil.

Not established: the rivers, the pearls or the traps.

Not excavated: the tomb chamber.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim from a text that the soil partly supports, and because the reason it is untested is a policy decision, not a lack of interest.

The Ninth Legion

Live debate

A Roman legion stationed in Britain disappears from the record, and has been sent to Scotland, annihilated, or transferred. The evidence points to the dull answer.

The unit

Legio IX Hispana was a Roman legion with a long history, stationed in Britain in the first century AD. Its last securely dated record in Britain is around 120 AD; after that it disappears from the epigraphic record.

The explanations

The romantic explanation is destruction in Scotland, and it has produced novels and films. The evidence points elsewhere: a building inscription from Nijmegen dated to about 121 AD refers to the legion, suggesting it was transferred to the continent. A tile stamp from the same region supports a posting there.

Its later fate is unknown, but the 'annihilated in Scotland' story is not supported by any find, and the transfer explanation fits the epigraphy.

Where it stands

Documented: the legion, its British service and its records.

Documented: the Nijmegen inscription of c. 121 AD.

Not supported: destruction in Scotland.

Unknown: the legion's final disposition.

The honest label: live debate, leaning to transfer.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-known 'lost legion', and because the answer is an administrative record in the Netherlands.

The Princes in the Tower

Live debate

Two boys disappeared in the Tower of London in 1483, and their uncle took the throne. Bones found in 1674 were never conclusively identified.

The events

Edward V, aged twelve, and his brother Richard were placed in the Tower of London in 1483. Their uncle, Richard III, had them declared illegitimate and took the crown. The boys were seen less frequently and then not at all; their fate was unknown even at the time.

The evidence

In 1674 workmen found a wooden chest containing two skeletons under a staircase in the Tower. Charles II had them placed in Westminster Abbey as the princes. The bones have been examined twice, in 1933 and in 1965, without DNA analysis; permission for modern testing has been refused.

Richard III is the traditional suspect, and Henry VII had motive too. The recent identification of Richard III's remains has not resolved it.

Where it stands

Documented: the boys, their confinement and their disappearance.

Documented: the skeletons and their placement.

Not established: the identity of the skeletons.

Contested: responsibility.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the physical evidence exists and cannot be tested, and where the political motive is shared by two dynasties.

Genghis Khan's Burial

Live debate

The khan asked to be buried without a mark, and the location has been secret for eight centuries. Searches have been conducted, and the Mongolian government has stopped them.

The account

Genghis Khan died in 1227, and the sources say he was buried in secret, without a marked grave, with the site concealed — in some versions by driving horses over it, in others by diverting a river. The burial place has never been identified.

The searches

Expeditions have searched the Khentii mountains and the Onon valley, using remote sensing and archaeology, without success. In 2015 the Mongolian government suspended further searches and protected the area, citing respect for the tradition and the risk to archaeology.

The secrecy is documented; the grave is not, and the search is now restricted by policy rather than by difficulty.

Where it stands

Documented: the death, the secrecy and the traditions.

Documented: the searches and the suspension.

Not found: the burial place.

Not permitted: further searches at present.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a lost tomb that is lost by design, and because the ethical question — whether to look — is now part of the record.

Roman Dodecahedrons

Live debate

Hollow bronze objects with twelve pentagonal faces and knobs at the corners, found across the northern provinces. Nobody knows what they were for.

The objects

Roman dodecahedrons are hollow bronze objects, roughly 4–11 cm across, with twelve pentagonal faces each containing a circular hole of a different size, and a knob at each corner. More than a hundred have been found, mostly in the northern provinces — Gaul, Britain, Germania — and they date from the second to fourth centuries AD.

The proposals

Proposed uses include a surveying instrument, a calendar device, a candle holder, a dice-like game, a knitting aid for gloves, and a decorative or religious object. None is supported by a written source: no Roman text mentions them, and they are not depicted in any Roman image.

The strongest arguments are functional — the varying hole sizes suggest something is passed through them — but no reconstruction has been demonstrated to work.

Where it stands

Documented: the objects, their distribution and their dates.

Not documented: any Roman mention of them.

Contested: the function.

Not demonstrated: any reconstruction.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the honest kind of mystery: a common object, a real gap in the record, and no need for anything exotic.

Voynich Alien Botany

Debunked

The Voynich manuscript's plants do not match any known species, which has been read as evidence of an alien or otherworldly origin. The plants are drawings in a medieval herbal tradition.

The manuscript

The Voynich manuscript is an illustrated codex, carbon-dated to the early fifteenth century, written in an unknown script. Its botanical section shows plants that do not match known species exactly, along with astronomical diagrams and bathing scenes.

The claim and the explanation

The claim that the plants are alien — or that the manuscript records another world — rests on the failure to identify them. Medieval herbals routinely contain stylised, composite and copied-from-copies illustrations, and identification is often impossible for genuine plants, let alone for drawings made at several removes from the original.

The manuscript is a real and unsolved problem — the script is undeciphered — but the plants are not evidence of extraterrestrial origin, and the 'alien' reading adds nothing that can be tested.

What is established

Documented: the manuscript, its date and its sections.

Documented: the herbal tradition it belongs to.

Not established: any alien origin.

Undeciphered: the script.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real mystery with a real explanation for the part that looks strangest, and because the unexplained part is the text.

Nero and the Fire

Debunked

Nero was said to have fiddled while Rome burned, and to have started the fire to clear space for his palace. The first is impossible and the second is unlikely.

The fire

In July 64 AD a fire broke out in the Circus Maximus area and burned for days, destroying much of Rome. Tacitus describes the destruction and the reconstruction, and reports that Nero was away at Antium when it began, returning to organise relief.

The accusations

The 'fiddling' story is a later invention: the violin did not exist, and Nero was not in the city. The arson accusation is reported by Tacitus as a rumour, and he notes that Nero blamed the Christians to deflect it — which is the part of the story that is best evidenced.

Modern historians regard accidental origin as most likely, in a city of timber tenements, and note that Nero's rebuilding — wider streets, brick instead of wood — was a sensible response.

What is established

Documented: the fire, its extent and the rebuilding.

Documented: Nero's absence at the start.

Documented: the scapegoating of Christians.

Not supported: the arson and the fiddle.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most durable character assassination in Western history, and because the source says it was a rumour.

Caligula's Horse

Live debate

The emperor was said to have made his horse a consul. The sources are hostile, and the story is probably a joke about a private plan.

The story

Suetonius reports that Caligula intended to make his horse Incitatus a consul, and that he gave the animal a marble stable, a jewelled collar and its own household. The story has become the standard example of imperial madness.

The problems

Suetonius wrote eighty years later and collected gossip; his biographies of the Caesars are notoriously hostile and anecdotal. The 'consulship for a horse' may be a satirical reading of a private remark — the emperor's habit of teasing the senate by proposing absurd candidates — and no official record supports an appointment.

The horse was real, and may have been a favoured racehorse; the consulship is the part that rests on a hostile anecdote.

Where it stands

Documented: the source, and its character.

Documented: Caligula's conflict with the senate.

Not documented: any actual appointment.

Plausible: a joke or a threat taken literally.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the classic case of an anecdote outliving its source, and because the source is a hostile gossip.

The Library of Alexandria

Documented

The greatest library of the ancient world, and the most over-explained destruction in history. It declined over centuries, and no single fire ended it.

The library

The Library of Alexandria was part of the Mouseion, founded in the early third century BC under the Ptolemies. It collected texts on an industrial scale — by purchase, by copying, and according to some sources by seizing scrolls from ships — and produced scholarship: Callimachus's catalogue, Eratosthenes's geography, and work on Homer.

The destruction

There is no single destruction. Caesar's fire in 48 BC damaged part of the complex; the library's decline continued through the loss of royal patronage, the expulsion of scholars, and the general decay of institutions. Later episodes — a war under Aurelian, the Serapeum's destruction in 391 AD — are sometimes cited, but the evidence for a deliberate burning of the library is thin.

The popular story, of one fire destroying all knowledge, is a moral fable about the fragility of civilisation; the historical record is slower and less dramatic.

What is established

Documented: the library, its scholarship and its decline.

Documented: Caesar's fire and later damage.

Not established: a single destruction.

The popular story: a fable.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most-cited example of lost knowledge, and because the real history is a better warning: institutions decay slowly.

Salting Carthage

Debunked

Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, and the story says the ground was sown with salt so nothing would grow. The salt is a modern invention.

The destruction

In 146 BC, at the end of the Third Punic War, Roman forces under Scipio Aemilianus destroyed Carthage: the city was taken, its population enslaved, and the site was formally cursed and abandoned. The destruction is well documented.

The salt

The salting story does not appear in the ancient sources. It emerges in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, in histories and textbooks, as a vivid way of expressing total destruction. The nearest ancient references are to ritual cursing and to the symbolic ploughing of the site, not to salt.

The practical objection is also decisive: salting a city's fields at scale would require enormous quantities of salt, and the site was later resettled and became a major Roman city.

What is established

Documented: the destruction and the cursing of the site.

Not documented: any salting.

Documented: the later Roman colony on the site.

The origin: modern historians' imagery.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a modern invention that everyone believes, and because the resettlement of the site is the plainest refutation.

The Bog Bodies

Documented

Hundreds of bodies have been recovered from northern European peat bogs, preserved by the chemistry of the peat. Many were killed deliberately.

The preservation

Peat bogs are cold, acidic and oxygen-poor, and contain sphagnan, a compound that preserves skin and hair while dissolving bone. Bodies placed in them can survive for thousands of years with skin, hair, fingerprints and stomach contents intact.

The deaths

Many of the best-known bodies — Tollund Man, Lindow Man, Grauballe Man, the Yde Girl — show signs of violent death: strangulation, throat cutting, blows to the head. Dating places them in the Iron Age and Roman period, and the pattern has been interpreted as human sacrifice, execution, or punishment.

The evidence is forensic and detailed: last meals, stomach contents, wounds and restraints. The interpretation of why they died is argued; that they died violently is not.

What is established

Documented: the bodies, their preservation and their dates.

Documented: the forensic evidence of violent death.

Contested: sacrifice, execution or punishment.

Documented: last meals and stomach contents.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is archaeology with the bodies still present, and because the forensics are as close to a witness statement as prehistory allows.

Ötzi's Murder

Documented

A man who died in the Alps 5,300 years ago was found in 1991 with an arrowhead in his shoulder. His last days have been reconstructed in detail.

The find

In 1991 hikers in the Ötztal Alps found a body melting out of the ice. It proved to be a man who died around 3300 BC, preserved with his clothing, equipment — a copper axe, a bow, arrows — and his tattoos. He is the best-studied prehistoric body in Europe.

The death

Imaging in 2005 found an arrowhead lodged in his left shoulder, with damage to a blood vessel; the wound would have been fatal. He also had a head injury, cuts to his hands, and his stomach contents showed a last meal eaten shortly before death. DNA from his equipment showed blood from other people on his knife and arrowheads.

The evidence supports a violent death, possibly after a fight or an ambush; the details are inference.

What is established

Documented: the body, the equipment and the tattoos.

Documented: the arrowhead and the fatal wound.

Documented: the last meal and the blood on his gear.

Contested: the circumstances of the fight.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the closest thing prehistory offers to a crime scene, and because the forensics are documented in the literature.

Neanderthal Cannibalism

Documented

Bones from several Neanderthal sites carry cut marks and fractures consistent with butchery. The evidence is direct, and the interpretation is not.

The evidence

Neanderthal remains from sites including Krapina in Croatia, El Sidrón in Spain, Moula-Guercy in France and Goyet in Belgium show cut marks, percussion fractures and burning consistent with the removal of flesh and marrow. At El Sidrón, the marks on a group of individuals are in the same places as those made in butchery.

The interpretation

Cannibalism is the straightforward reading, and it is accepted for several sites. What is argued is why: nutritional stress, ritual treatment of the dead, or something else. At some sites the pattern suggests the dead were processed like animals; at others, the marks are consistent with secondary burial practices.

The evidence is direct and unusual in archaeology — it is written on the bones — and the debate is about meaning rather than fact.

What is established

Documented: the cut marks, fractures and burning.

Documented: several sites across Europe.

Accepted: that the bodies were butchered.

Contested: the motive.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim about our closest relatives that the evidence supports, and because the uncomfortable part is the part that is documented.

Homo floresiensis

Documented

A metre-tall hominin found on Flores, dated to as recently as 50,000 years ago. The discovery was disputed for a decade and is now accepted.

The find

In 2003 excavations in Liang Bua cave on Flores, Indonesia, produced the remains of a hominin about a metre tall with a small brain, dated to between roughly 100,000 and 50,000 years ago. The species was named Homo floresiensis and nicknamed the hobbit.

The dispute

Some researchers argued the remains were modern humans with microcephaly or another pathology. The counter-evidence accumulated: multiple individuals, wrist bones with primitive morphology, and stone tools associated with the site. The species is now widely accepted, though its evolutionary relationships — possibly descended from an early Homo erectus population — are still argued.

The island setting explains the small body size: insular dwarfism is documented in other species.

What is established

Documented: the remains, their dates and their anatomy.

Documented: the stone tools and the cave context.

Accepted: that it is a distinct species.

Contested: its ancestry.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real discovery that was resisted and then accepted, which is how the process is supposed to work.

Troy Was Real

Documented

The city in the Iliad was treated as fiction until a German businessman dug up a mound in Turkey. The site is real; the war is another question.

The site

Hisarlik in northwestern Turkey is a mound containing the remains of nine cities, occupied from the early Bronze Age to the Roman period. Excavations by Heinrich Schliemann from 1871, and later by Wilhelm Dörpfeld, Carl Blegen and Manfred Korfmann, established the sequence.

The questions

Troy VI and VIIa — the latter destroyed around 1180 BC — are the candidates for the city of the Iliad. The archaeological evidence for a war includes destruction layers, but not a wooden horse, and the scale of any conflict is unknown. The Hittite texts mention a place called Wilusa, widely identified with Ilios.

The consensus is that a real city existed at a real place and was destroyed, and that the epic is a poetic composition built on distant memory.

What is established

Documented: the mound, its nine cities and their dates.

Documented: the destruction of Troy VIIa.

Documented: the Hittite references to Wilusa.

Contested: the scale and character of the war.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case that founded the discipline's public reputation: a poem led to a mound, and the mound had cities in it.

The Antikythera Mechanism

Documented

A bronze gear mechanism from a Roman-era shipwreck, built to model the heavens. Nothing of comparable complexity appears for a thousand years afterwards.

The object

The Antikythera mechanism was recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera, dated to around the second century BC. It is a bronze geared device with at least thirty surviving gears, enclosed in a wooden case with dials, and it was used to model the positions of the sun and moon, the phases of the moon, and — according to recent reconstructions — the planets.

The research

X-ray and CT imaging since the 1970s has revealed the gear trains and the inscriptions, which act as a manual. The mechanism also includes a pin-and-slot device reproducing the moon's variable motion, and a dial for predicting eclipses. It is the most complex known object of its kind from antiquity.

The absence of anything similar for a millennium is a genuine puzzle about transmission, not evidence of anything exotic.

What is established

Documented: the object, its gears and its inscriptions.

Documented: its function as an astronomical model.

Documented: the eclipse prediction dial.

Contested: some details of the planetary display.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest evidence that ancient technology could be extraordinary, and because it needs no myth to be astonishing.

Eratosthenes Measured the Earth

Documented

A librarian in Alexandria calculated the circumference of the Earth from a shadow and a distance, and got within a few per cent. The method is documented.

The measurement

Eratosthenes, chief librarian at Alexandria in the third century BC, knew that at Syene (modern Aswan) the sun was directly overhead at noon on the summer solstice — a well in the town was lit to the bottom. At Alexandria, on the same day, a gnomon cast a shadow, giving an angle of about 7.2 degrees, roughly a fiftieth of a circle. The distance between the two places was known from surveys.

The result

Multiplying the distance by fifty gave a circumference within a few per cent of the modern value, depending on which stade he used — the uncertainty is in the unit, not the method. The calculation assumes the sun's rays are parallel, which is a good approximation at that scale.

The work survives through reports by later writers, and the method is sound.

What is established

Documented: the method and the observations.

Documented: the result, within a few per cent.

Uncertain: the exact length of the stade used.

Documented: the transmission through later writers.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest demonstration that ancient people measured the world accurately, which is the fact that most of the previous shelves manage to avoid.

The Maya Tracked Venus

Documented

Maya astronomers recorded the movements of Venus with an accuracy that took European astronomy centuries to match. The tables survive in the Dresden Codex.

The record

The Dresden Codex, one of four surviving Maya books, contains a Venus table: a series of pages giving the positions of Venus over a cycle of 584 days, with corrections over longer periods. The Maya tracked Venus's appearances as morning and evening star and its periods of invisibility.

The accuracy

The table's average value for the Venus cycle is very close to the modern figure of 583.92 days, and the corrections built into it show that the astronomers were refining the value over centuries. The purpose is argued: divination, the timing of warfare and ritual, and the correlation of Venus with the maize cycle have all been proposed.

The astronomy is documented; the use is interpretation.

What is established

Documented: the table and its values.

Documented: the corrections over long periods.

Documented: the codex itself and its date.

Contested: the purpose.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest evidence that Mesoamerican astronomy was quantitative, and because it undercuts the 'ancient people as passive observers' framing on which the star-map claims depend.

Richard III Under a Car Park

Documented

The last Plantagenet king was buried in a friary that became a car park. His skeleton was found in 2012, under a marked parking bay.

The search

Richard III died at Bosworth in 1485 and was buried in the choir of the Grey Friars church in Leicester. The church was dissolved and demolished, and the site became a car park. In 2012 a project led by the University of Leicester and the Richard III Society excavated the site and found a skeleton in a hastily dug grave.

The identification

The skeleton showed a curved spine consistent with contemporary descriptions, battle injuries, and — critically — mitochondrial DNA matched to living maternal-line descendants. The identification was published in 2014, and the remains were reinterred in Leicester Cathedral in 2015.

The project is one of the few cases where a historical identification was made and confirmed by genetic evidence.

What is established

Documented: the burial place and the excavation.

Documented: the skeletal evidence of scoliosis and injuries.

Documented: the DNA match.

Documented: the reinterment.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best modern example of an identification being settled rather than argued, and because the answer was under a parking space.

The Coelacanth

Documented

A fish known only from fossils, and thought extinct for 65 million years, was caught off South Africa in 1938. A second population was found in Indonesia in 1997.

The discovery

In December 1938 a fisherman caught an unusual fish off the Chalumna River in South Africa. Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, a museum curator, recognised it as a coelacanth — a group known from fossils and believed to have died out at the end of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago.

The aftermath

A second specimen was caught in 1952 near the Comoros, and a distinct population was found in Indonesia in 1997, which was recognised as a separate species. Coelacanths are deep-water fish, which explains how they escaped notice.

The 'living fossil' label is misleading: coelacanths have evolved since the Cretaceous, and the group is not unchanged. But the discovery is a genuine case of a lineage surviving a mass extinction.

What is established

Documented: the 1938 specimen and its identification.

Documented: the Comoros population and the Indonesian species.

Documented: their deep-water habitat.

Overstated: the 'unchanged for 65 million years' framing.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the classic case of an absence of evidence being mistaken for evidence of absence, and because it happened to a professional rather than a crank.

Polynesian Navigation

Documented

Polynesians settled the Pacific without instruments, using stars, swells, birds and clouds. The claim that they did it deliberately was dismissed for centuries and then demonstrated.

The achievement

Polynesian voyagers settled islands across the Pacific, including Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand, over centuries, in double-hulled canoes carrying people, animals and plants. The navigation used the stars, the direction and pattern of ocean swells, bird behaviour, cloud formations and the colour of the sea.

The dismissal and the demonstration

European and American scholars argued for much of the twentieth century that the settlement was accidental — drift voyages. That view was challenged by scholars who studied the oral traditions, and it was refuted in practice: from 1976 the Polynesian Voyaging Society sailed Hōkūleʻa from Hawaii to Tahiti using only traditional navigation, guided by a Micronesian navigator, Mau Piailug.

Wayfinding is now taught and practised, and the crossings have been repeated many times.

What is established

Documented: the settlement of the Pacific.

Documented: the navigational methods.

Demonstrated: the crossings, from 1976 onward.

Rejected: the accidental-drift account.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where the 'primitive' explanation was the colonial one, and the demonstration settled it.

The Goldbach Conjecture

Open problem

Every even number greater than two is the sum of two primes. It has been checked to four quintillion and proved for nobody.

The statement

Goldbach wrote to Euler in 1742 proposing that every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes — 4 = 2+2, 6 = 3+3, 100 = 47+53. Euler could not prove it, and nobody has since. The conjecture has been verified computationally for all even numbers up to about 4×10¹⁸.

What is known

The weak Goldbach conjecture — that every odd number greater than 5 is the sum of three primes — was proved by Harald Helfgott in 2013. The strong version is still open. Related results establish that every sufficiently large even number is the sum of two primes plus a bounded number of powers of two, and that almost all even numbers satisfy the conjecture.

Computational verification is not proof: a counterexample could exist beyond any checked range, and the history of number theory includes exactly that.

Where it stands

Verified: to about 4×10¹⁸.

Proved: the weak version, in 2013.

Open: the strong version.

Not evidence: computation, in the sense that matters.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest example of a claim with overwhelming evidence and no proof, and because the difference is the whole of mathematics.

The Twin Prime Conjecture

Open problem

There are infinitely many pairs of primes two apart. Nobody can prove it, though we now know there are infinitely many pairs at some fixed distance.

The statement

The conjecture holds that there are infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by two: 3 and 5, 11 and 13, 41 and 43. It is one of the oldest open problems in number theory, and it remains unproved.

The progress

In 2013 Yitang Zhang proved that there are infinitely many pairs of primes separated by some bounded gap — initially 70 million, later reduced by the Polymath project to 246. That is a major result and it is not the conjecture: the bound has not been brought down to 2, and the method does not obviously reach it.

The conjecture is also supported by heuristic arguments and by computation, which is the same kind of support Goldbach has and the same kind that does not constitute proof.

Where it stands

Open: the conjecture itself.

Proved: infinitely many bounded gaps, 2013.

Best bound: 246, from the Polymath project.

Not reached: a gap of 2.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows what mathematical progress looks like when it is real: not a proof, but a bound that moves.

The Collatz Conjecture

Open problem

Halve even numbers, triple-and-add-one odd ones, and you always reach 1. Nobody knows why, and Paul Erdős said mathematics is not ready for it.

The rule

Take any positive integer. If it is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply by three and add one. Repeat. The conjecture is that every starting number eventually reaches 1, entering the 4-2-1 cycle. It has been verified for starting values up to about 2⁶⁸.

The problem

The sequences are wildly irregular — some numbers climb high before falling — and no proof of termination exists. The problem has been attacked with dynamical systems, number theory and computer search, and it has defeated all of them. Erdős's remark that 'mathematics is not yet ready for such problems' is the standard summary.

The conjecture's difficulty is a useful corrective to the idea that simple statements have simple proofs.

Where it stands

Verified: to about 2⁶⁸.

Proved: nothing general.

Open: the conjecture.

The obstacle: no known structure to exploit.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best example of a one-line problem that has resisted a century, and because it is often cited by people who think it must be easy.

P versus NP

Open problem

Is every problem whose answer can be checked quickly also solvable quickly? Almost everyone believes not, and nobody can prove it.

The question

P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time. NP is the class whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time. P is contained in NP; the question is whether they are equal. Stephen Cook formulated it in 1971, and it is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems.

Why it matters

If P = NP, then problems that underpin cryptography — factoring, discrete logarithms — become tractable, and much of modern security collapses. If P ≠ NP, as almost all researchers believe, then a large class of problems is genuinely hard.

Proof attempts have been numerous and have failed, and several barriers have been proved: relativisation, natural proofs, algebrisation. Those barriers show that the obvious techniques cannot work, which is why the problem has resisted for fifty years.

Where it stands

Believed: P ≠ NP, by most researchers.

Proved: several barriers to proof.

Open: the question.

Prize: Clay Millennium Prize.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most consequential open problem in computer science, and because the consensus about its answer is not a proof.

Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness

Open problem

The equations that describe fluid flow are used every day and have never been proved to have solutions that stay smooth. Turbulence is the reason it matters.

The problem

The Navier–Stokes equations describe the motion of viscous fluids. In three dimensions, nobody has proved that smooth solutions exist for all time from smooth initial data, or that they can blow up in finite time. It is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems.

Why it is hard

The difficulty is the nonlinearity: the equations contain a term that can concentrate energy at small scales, and whether it can concentrate enough to produce a singularity is unknown. Turbulence — the disorderly, multiscale motion seen in every real flow — is the physical face of the problem.

Engineers and physicists proceed regardless, using numerical methods that work well in practice. That gap between practical success and mathematical proof is the point.

Where it stands

Used: everywhere, in engineering and physics.

Solved: numerically, in practice.

Open: existence and smoothness in 3D.

Known: results in two dimensions.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a theory that works perfectly well without the proof, which is a useful thing for a reader of this archive to understand.

When Plate Tectonics Began

Live debate

The Earth's surface moves in plates, and nobody knows when that started. Estimates range from four billion years ago to seven hundred million.

The question

Plate tectonics is the framework of modern geology, and its onset is one of the largest open questions in Earth science. Estimates range from the Hadean, more than four billion years ago, to the Neoproterozoic, around 700 million years ago.

The evidence

The arguments use several lines of evidence: the chemistry of ancient zircons, which can record continental crust and its recycling; palaeomagnetic data, which show whether continents moved independently; the presence of blueschists and ophiolites, which form in subduction zones; and the isotopic signatures of mantle mixing.

The disagreement is partly about what counts as plate tectonics — modern-style subduction with rigid plates, or an earlier regime of sagduction and dripping — and partly about how to read ambiguous evidence from rocks that have been recycled.

Where it stands

Documented: modern plate tectonics in the Phanerozoic.

Contested: the onset date.

Evidence: zircons, palaeomagnetism, rock types.

Contested: what counts as plate tectonics.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a foundational question that most people assume is settled, and because the range of answers spans three billion years.

Mantle Plumes

Live debate

Hot rock rising from deep in the mantle is the standard explanation for Hawaii and Iceland. The seismic evidence for the plumes is weaker than the theory requires.

The theory

Mantle plumes were proposed in 1971 to explain hotspot volcanism: narrow columns of hot rock rising from the deep mantle, producing volcanic chains as plates move over them. Hawaii is the standard example, with its progressive age sequence along the chain.

The problem

Seismic imaging has not produced a clear, unambiguous plume beneath Hawaii or Iceland. Some tomographic studies find low-velocity anomalies extending deep; others find features confined to the upper mantle. The 'plume' debate has run for decades, with alternatives including edge-driven convection, lithospheric cracks and shallow decompression melting.

The hotspot phenomenon is not in dispute. The question is what is underneath it, and how deep the cause goes.

Where it stands

Documented: hotspot chains and their age progression.

Contested: whether deep plumes exist.

Mixed: the seismic evidence.

Alternatives: shallow and edge-driven mechanisms.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a textbook theory that a textbook reader would assume was settled, and because the imaging is genuinely ambiguous.

Peopling of the Americas

Live debate

People reached the Americas before the last glacial maximum or after it, by land or by coast. The dates have been moving earlier for thirty years.

The models

The Clovis-first model held that people entered the Americas around 13,000 years ago, after an ice-free corridor opened, and spread rapidly. It dominated for decades, supported by distinctive stone points found across North America.

The revisions

Pre-Clovis sites have accumulated: Monte Verde in Chile, dated to about 14,500 years ago; White Sands in New Mexico, with footprints dated to 23,000–21,000 years ago; and others. The coastal route — travel down the Pacific coast by boat — is now favoured by many, because the interior corridor may not have been viable until later.

The debate is about the reliability of the dates, the identity of the toolmakers, and whether some sites are genuinely cultural.

Where it stands

Documented: human presence before 13,000 years ago, at several sites.

Rejected: strict Clovis-first.

Contested: the earliest dates.

Favoured: a coastal route, by many researchers.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the textbook was replaced within a generation, and because the new dates keep arriving.

Dinosaur Metabolism

Live debate

Were the dinosaurs warm-blooded? Bone growth, isotopes and the nasal anatomy point in different directions, and the answer may be neither.

The evidence

Several lines of evidence bear on dinosaur metabolism: bone histology, which records fast, sustained growth in many dinosaurs; growth-rate estimates from size and age; oxygen isotopes in bones and teeth, which reflect body temperature; and anatomical features such as nasal turbinates, which in mammals help conserve heat and water.

The interpretations

The 'warm-blooded' reading fits the growth rates and the isotope data for many groups. The 'cold-blooded' reading fits the absence of unambiguous turbinates and the large body sizes, which reduce heat loss. The most influential modern position is that dinosaurs occupied a middle range — mesothermy — with metabolic rates between reptiles and mammals, and that the picture varies across groups.

The question has moved from a binary argument to a quantitative one about rates and thermoregulation strategies.

Where it stands

Documented: growth rates, isotopes and anatomy.

Favoured: intermediate metabolism for many dinosaurs.

Contested: the details, and the variation between groups.

Rejected: the simple binary.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the dinosaur question everyone asks, and because the answer turned out to be 'a bit of both', which is less satisfying and more accurate.

T. rex the Scavenger

Live debate

The claim that Tyrannosaurus was too slow and too small-eyed to hunt, and lived as a scavenger. The evidence points to an animal that did both.

The claim

Jack Horner argued in the 1990s that Tyrannosaurus was a scavenger: its arms were small, its legs were built for walking rather than running, and its sense of smell was better developed than its vision. The argument was deliberately provocative and it forced a re-examination of the evidence.

The evidence

Bite marks on healed bones of other dinosaurs show predation on live animals; a Tyrannosaurus tooth found embedded in a hadrosaur tail vertebra that had healed shows an attack that failed. Bite-force estimates are among the highest of any terrestrial animal, and trackways and growth data indicate active mobility.

The modern view is that Tyrannosaurus was an opportunistic predator and scavenger, like most large carnivores, and that the scavenger-only claim is not supported.

Where it stands

Documented: healed bite marks; an embedded tooth.

Documented: high bite force and active mobility.

Rejected: the scavenger-only hypothesis.

Supported: opportunistic predation and scavenging.

The honest label: live debate, largely resolved.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where a provocative claim did its job — it produced evidence — and then lost, which is the good version of a scientific argument.

Spinosaurus Lifestyle

Live debate

A dinosaur with a sail, a crocodile snout and dense bones, proposed as a swimmer. The 2020 tail find supported it; later work questioned whether it could dive.

The animal

Spinosaurus was a large theropod with a long, narrow snout, conical teeth, a sail on its back and — as described in 2014 from Moroccan material — relatively short hind limbs and dense limb bones. The combination suggested a semi-aquatic animal, unlike any other known dinosaur.

The evidence

In 2020 a paddle-like tail was described, and a study argued that it could propel the animal through water. Subsequent work has questioned the reconstruction: the 2014 specimen's proportions have been contested, and a 2022 analysis argued that Spinosaurus was too buoyant to dive and more likely waded in shallow water, hunting like a heron.

The semi-aquatic habit is widely accepted; the degree — wading versus swimming — is not.

Where it stands

Documented: the snout, teeth, sail and dense bones.

Documented: the paddle-like tail.

Contested: whether it swam or waded.

Contested: some of the 2014 reconstruction.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the fastest-moving argument in dinosaur palaeontology, and because the answer changes with each new specimen.

The Megafauna Extinctions

Live debate

Large animals disappeared from every continent except Africa at the end of the Pleistocene. Climate, humans, or both — and the answer differs by continent.

The pattern

Around the end of the Pleistocene, between about 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, most large-bodied mammals disappeared from the Americas, Australia, northern Eurasia and many islands — while surviving in Africa, where they had co-evolved with humans.

The explanations

The climate hypothesis points to rapid environmental change at the end of the last glaciation. The human hypothesis points to hunting and habitat modification, and to the timing: extinctions follow human arrival on each continent, most clearly in Australia and the Americas. The island cases — New Zealand's moa, Madagascar's elephant birds — are the strongest for human causation.

Most researchers now favour a combination, with the weight differing by region: humans as the decisive factor where animals were naive to them, climate as a contributor elsewhere.

Where it stands

Documented: the extinctions and their timing.

Documented: the correlation with human arrival.

Contested: the relative weight of climate and humans.

Strongest human cases: islands; Australia; the Americas.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the deepest historical case of human impact, and because the argument about it shapes how people read the present.

Heritability of Intelligence

Live debate

Twin and adoption studies put the heritability of adult IQ high. What that number means, and what it does not, is where the argument lives.

The finding

Twin and adoption studies consistently find that the heritability of IQ rises with age: in childhood it is around 0.4–0.5, and in adulthood estimates reach 0.7–0.8. Identical twins reared apart are more similar than fraternal twins reared together, and adopted children resemble their biological parents more as they age.

What it means

Heritability is the proportion of variance in a population attributable to genetic variation. It says nothing about the causes of a difference between groups, nothing about whether a trait can be changed, and nothing about an individual. A high heritability does not imply immutability — height is highly heritable and has risen sharply with nutrition.

The disputes are about the interpretation, about the environmental assumptions of twin models, and about the uses to which the numbers have been put historically.

Where it stands

Documented: the twin and adoption findings.

Documented: heritability increasing with age.

Contested: the interpretation and the models' assumptions.

Not implied: immutability, or group differences.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most abused statistic in the social sciences, and because the correct reading is narrower than either side usually admits.

Placebo Mechanisms

Live debate

The placebo effect is real, and it is not one thing: expectation, conditioning, regression and reporting bias all contribute, and the size depends on the outcome.

The effect

The placebo effect is the improvement observed after an inert treatment, attributable to expectation, ritual, conditioning and the clinical encounter. It is real and measurable, and it is largest for subjective outcomes such as pain and nausea, and smallest — often absent — for objective ones such as tumour size or blood counts.

The mechanisms

Expectation and conditioning are the main mechanisms: the ritual of treatment and prior experience of relief produce measurable physiological changes, including endogenous opioid release in some pain studies. Regression to the mean and reporting bias inflate the apparent effect in uncontrolled settings.

Open-label placebo studies, in which patients are told they are receiving a placebo, have found small benefits for some conditions — which is interesting and not yet a treatment.

Where it stands

Documented: the effect, its size and its variation by outcome.

Documented: expectation and conditioning as mechanisms.

Contested: the open-label results.

Not established: any effect on objective disease outcomes.

The honest label: live debate about mechanism and scope.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real effect that gets used to justify unreal treatments, and because the distinction between subjective and objective outcomes is the whole argument.

The Implicit Association Test

Live debate

A reaction-time test said to measure unconscious bias. It correlates weakly with behaviour and its test-retest reliability is poor, which is a problem for a measure used in training and policy.

The test

The Implicit Association Test, published in 1998, measures the speed with which participants pair concepts — for example, Black and White faces with positive and negative words. Faster pairings are interpreted as an implicit association, and the test has been used to claim that most people hold unconscious biases.

The problems

The test-retest reliability is low: an individual's score varies substantially between sessions. Its correlation with actual behaviour is weak, and meta-analyses find that it predicts behaviour only marginally better than explicit measures. The interpretation of the score — as bias, as cultural knowledge, or as task difficulty — is contested.

The test is still used, but the strong claims made for it in the 2000s have been substantially walked back by the researchers who developed it.

Where it stands

Documented: the test and its scores.

Documented: low test-retest reliability.

Documented: weak prediction of behaviour.

Contested: what the score means.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a measurement that outran its evidence and became policy, and because the correction came from inside the field.

Stereotype Threat

Live debate

The claim that reminding people of a negative stereotype about their group impairs their performance. It replicated in small studies and largely failed in large pre-registered ones.

The claim

Steele and Aronson (1995) reported that Black students performed worse on a test when told it measured ability, compared with a condition framed as a laboratory task. The explanation was stereotype threat: awareness of a negative stereotype about one's group creates anxiety that impairs performance. Similar results were reported for women and maths.

The replications

Small replications were mixed, and a large pre-registered multi-lab study in 2019 found effects close to zero for the standard manipulation. Meta-analyses find small average effects that vary widely by setting. The theory's defenders argue that the laboratory manipulation is a weak version of a real-world experience.

The practical implication — that subtle cues can affect performance — is plausible and much less well established than the original studies implied.

Where it stands

Documented: the original studies and their influence.

Failed: the large pre-registered replication.

Small: average effects in meta-analysis.

Contested: the real-world size.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is one of the most cited findings in social psychology and one of the clearest cases of a famous effect shrinking under replication.

The Uncanny Valley

Live debate

The claim that near-human figures provoke discomfort before realism is reached. The intuition is widespread; the experimental evidence is mixed.

The idea

Masahiro Mori proposed in 1970 that affinity for a figure rises with its human-likeness, then drops sharply as it approaches but does not reach realism, before rising again at full realism. The dip is the 'uncanny valley'.

The evidence

Empirical studies have found the dip for some stimuli — particularly faces and androids — and not for others. Replications vary with the images used, the measures, and the cultural background of participants. Proposed explanations include perceptual mismatch, the violation of expectations, and an avoidance response to cues of illness or death.

The effect is treated as real by designers, and its size and shape are not established. The graph in the original essay was a sketch, not a dataset.

Where it stands

Documented: the proposal and its influence.

Documented: some experimental demonstrations.

Mixed: the evidence across studies.

Contested: the mechanism.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a famous curve that was drawn before it was measured, and because the measurements have not matched the drawing.

Collective Intelligence

Live debate

The claim that groups have a measurable general intelligence, predicting performance across tasks. The original study was striking; the replications are mixed.

The claim

Woolley and colleagues (2010) reported a 'c factor' for groups: a single factor that predicted performance across a battery of collaborative tasks, and that correlated with the proportion of women in the group and with social sensitivity, rather than with the average intelligence of members.

The replications

Replications have been mixed. Some find a general factor; others find that it is weaker, task-dependent, or explained by group composition and communication style. The correlation with the proportion of women has not always held.

The concept is attractive and the evidence is thinner than the citations suggest — which is the standard pattern for a striking finding in group psychology.

Where it stands

Documented: the original study and its results.

Mixed: the replications.

Contested: the stability of the factor.

Contested: the correlates.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a finding about groups that groups like to cite, and because the replication record is the part that gets left out.

Illusionism

Live debate

The claim that consciousness as people describe it — the felt quality of experience — is an illusion produced by the brain. It is a serious position and it is hard to state without sounding absurd.

The position

Illusionism, associated with Keith Frankish, holds that phenomenal consciousness — the 'what it is like' quality of experience — does not exist as introspected. What exists is a set of cognitive processes that produce the powerful illusion that there is something it is like. The task of philosophy and neuroscience is then to explain the illusion.

The objections

The main objection is that the illusion is the thing that needed explaining: an illusion of experience seems to require experience. Illusionists reply that this intuition is exactly what has to be explained away, and that the position is the only one that makes the hard problem tractable.

The debate is entirely philosophical, and it is unresolved.

Where it stands

Documented: the position and its arguments.

Documented: the objections.

Not testable: by experiment, currently.

Respectable: argued by senior philosophers.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the position that sounds most absurd and is most carefully argued, which is a useful contrast with the pages where the reverse is true.

Type 3 Diabetes

Live debate

The claim that Alzheimer's is a form of diabetes in the brain, driven by insulin resistance. The mechanism is real; the label is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.

The claim

The term 'type 3 diabetes' was proposed in the mid-2000s for the hypothesis that Alzheimer's disease involves insulin resistance in the brain: reduced insulin signalling, impaired glucose metabolism, and a cascade of consequences for neurons. Brain insulin resistance has been documented in Alzheimer's patients.

The problems

The evidence is correlational and mechanistic rather than diagnostic. Insulin resistance is common in older adults, and Alzheimer's pathology — amyloid and tau — is not explained by it alone. Clinical trials of insulin-related treatments, including intranasal insulin, have produced mixed results.

The label is used in the research literature as a shorthand for a hypothesis, and in popular writing as though the disease had been reclassified.

Where it stands

Documented: brain insulin resistance in Alzheimer's.

Documented: impaired glucose metabolism.

Not established: a reclassification of the disease.

Mixed: trials of insulin-related treatment.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real mechanism attached to a name that implies more than the evidence supports.

The Viral Trigger for Schizophrenia

Live debate

Infections in pregnancy are associated with schizophrenia in the child, and the immune system is implicated. The effect is real and small.

The evidence

Epidemiological studies have found associations between prenatal exposure to influenza and other infections and later schizophrenia, along with season-of-birth effects and associations with autoimmune disease and maternal immune activation. The genetic evidence includes immune-related loci, notably the complement component C4.

The limits

The effects are small, the studies are heterogeneous, and confounding is difficult to exclude. The mechanisms proposed — maternal immune activation affecting fetal brain development — are supported by animal models, and the human evidence is indirect.

The consensus is that immune and infectious factors contribute to risk in some cases, alongside strong genetic and environmental contributions, and that no single trigger has been identified.

Where it stands

Documented: associations with prenatal infection and immune genes.

Documented: animal models of maternal immune activation.

Small: the effect sizes.

Contested: the causal pathway in humans.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real association that is often reported as a cause, and because the difference matters for how the illness is understood.

Chronic Lyme

Live debate

Some patients have persistent symptoms after treated Lyme disease. Whether that is an ongoing infection is the argument, and the trials have not supported prolonged antibiotics.

The claim

Chronic Lyme disease is the claim that persistent infection causes long-term symptoms — fatigue, pain, cognitive difficulty — after treatment. The medical literature recognises post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome: symptoms that persist in a minority of patients after standard treatment, with no evidence of ongoing infection.

The evidence

Randomised trials of prolonged antibiotic therapy have not shown sustained benefit and have shown harms, including serious infections. Laboratory testing after treatment is unreliable, and the diagnosis of 'chronic Lyme' in patients without evidence of prior infection is not supported.

The symptoms are real and often disabling; the disagreement is about the cause and the treatment.

Where it stands

Documented: persistent symptoms in a minority after treatment.

Documented: no benefit from prolonged antibiotics.

Contested: the cause of the persistent symptoms.

Not supported: the diagnosis in patients without prior infection.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where patients are right that something is wrong and the explanation offered to them is not supported, which is the hardest kind of page to write honestly.

The Carbohydrate–Insulin Model

Live debate

The claim that obesity is driven by insulin, and that carbohydrate restriction is therefore uniquely effective. The trials find that, matched for protein and calories, the diets perform similarly.

The model

The carbohydrate–insulin model holds that high carbohydrate intake raises insulin, which promotes fat storage and suppresses fat release, so that energy is partitioned into fat and the person becomes hungry and sedentary. On this account, calorie restriction fails because it does not address the hormonal cause.

The evidence

Low-carbohydrate diets do produce weight loss, and often more in the short term, largely because of water loss and reduced intake. In controlled feeding studies matched for protein and calories, low-carbohydrate and low-fat diets produce similar fat loss. Insulin resistance does not reliably predict who benefits most.

The model's defenders argue that the trials do not test the mechanism adequately, and the argument continues.

Where it stands

Documented: short-term weight loss on low-carbohydrate diets.

Documented: similar fat loss in matched feeding studies.

Contested: the hormonal mechanism.

Contested: individual variation in response.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a mechanism that sounds decisive and meets trials that are unimpressed, and because the practical advice is the same either way.

Seed Oils and Inflammation

Live debate

The claim that industrial seed oils cause inflammation through omega-6 fatty acids. The biochemistry is real; the clinical evidence does not support the harm.

The claim

The claim is that seed oils — sunflower, soybean, canola — are high in linoleic acid, an omega-6 fatty acid that is converted into inflammatory mediators, and that their introduction into the food supply has driven increases in chronic inflammatory disease.

The evidence

Linoleic acid is converted to arachidonic acid and to inflammatory eicosanoids in principle. In practice, controlled trials increasing dietary linoleic acid have not shown increased markers of inflammation, and some show reductions. Higher tissue linoleic acid has been associated with lower cardiovascular risk in cohort studies.

The epidemiological correlation with chronic disease is confounded by everything else that changed in the same period, and the trials are the stronger evidence.

Where it stands

Documented: the biochemical pathway.

Not supported: increased inflammation in trials.

Not supported: the disease claim.

Confounded: the ecological correlation.

The honest label: live debate, leaning against the claim.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim built from a real pathway to a false conclusion, and because the trials are the part that never gets quoted.

Legendre's Conjecture

Open problem

There is always a prime between n² and (n+1)². It has been checked far out and proved nowhere.

The statement

Adrien-Marie Legendre conjectured in 1808 that for every positive integer n there is at least one prime between n² and (n+1)². It has been verified computationally over very large ranges, and it remains unproved.

What is known

Related results give primes in short intervals but not short enough: the best general theorems guarantee a prime between consecutive cubes for large n, and between n² and (n+1)² only under stronger assumptions such as the Riemann hypothesis, and even then not unconditionally in the required form. The problem is a special case of a family about primes in short intervals.

The conjecture is weaker than the Riemann hypothesis and stronger than what can currently be proved.

Where it stands

Verified: computationally, over large ranges.

Proved: no.

Related: primes between consecutive cubes, for large n.

Not enough: short-interval results so far.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest statement of the gap between what computation shows and what proof establishes.

Odd Perfect Numbers

Open problem

A perfect number equals the sum of its divisors. Every one known is even, and nobody knows whether an odd one exists.

The question

A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors: 6 = 1+2+3, 28 = 1+2+4+7+14. Every perfect number known is even, and even perfect numbers correspond to Mersenne primes. Whether any odd perfect number exists is unknown.

What is known

The search has established strong constraints: an odd perfect number would have to exceed 10¹⁵⁰⁰, have at least nine distinct prime factors, and satisfy a long list of conditions on its structure. Those constraints make existence unlikely and do not rule it out.

The problem is ancient — it appears in Euclid's framework — and it has resisted every approach.

Where it stands

Known: all known perfect numbers are even.

Ruled out: odd perfect numbers below 10¹⁵⁰⁰.

Constrained: heavily, by structure theorems.

Open: whether one exists.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is an existence question that two thousand years of work has narrowed without settling.

The abc Conjecture

Open problem

A conjecture about the prime factors of a+b=c that would settle a family of Diophantine problems. A claimed proof has been disputed since 2012.

The statement

For coprime positive integers a, b, c with a+b=c, the abc conjecture bounds c in terms of the product of the distinct prime factors of abc, raised to a power slightly greater than one. It was proposed by Oesterlé and Masser in 1985.

Why it matters

The conjecture implies many results, including versions of Fermat's Last Theorem for large exponents, and it constrains Diophantine equations generally. It is one of the most consequential open problems in number theory.

In 2012 Shinichi Mochizuki published a proof running to hundreds of pages and introducing an entirely new framework, inter-universal Teichmüller theory. Years of scrutiny by specialists have not produced agreement: the proof has been published in a journal edited by Mochizuki, and most of the field does not accept it as verified.

Where it stands

Proposed: 1985.

Consequences: many, across number theory.

Claimed proof: Mochizuki, 2012.

Status of the proof: disputed; not accepted by most specialists.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the mathematics is real and the dispute is about whether a proof can be understood — which is unusual enough to be worth recording.

Beal's Conjecture

Open problem

If aˣ + bʸ = cᶻ with exponents above two, the three bases share a prime factor. There is a million-dollar prize and no proof.

The statement

Beal's conjecture holds that if aˣ + bʸ = cᶻ where a, b, c are positive integers and x, y, z are integers greater than 2, then a, b and c share a common prime factor. It was formulated by Andrew Beal in 1993 and generalises Fermat's Last Theorem, which is the case a, b, c coprime.

The evidence

Extensive computer search has found no counterexample, and the conjecture is supported by the same heuristics that support Fermat. It is closely related to the abc conjecture: a proof of abc would imply Beal's conjecture.

The American Mathematical Society offers a prize of one million dollars for a proof or a counterexample, funded by Beal since 1997.

Where it stands

Verified: by extensive search.

Implied by: the abc conjecture.

Prize: $1 million, since 1997.

Proved: no.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a clean example of a conjecture whose evidence is a search and whose proof would come from somewhere else entirely.

Yang–Mills and the Mass Gap

Open problem

Quantum field theory works, and nobody can prove that its simplest version is mathematically consistent — or that its particles have mass.

The problem

Yang–Mills theory is the framework of the strong and electroweak interactions. The Millennium Prize problem asks for a rigorous mathematical construction of a Yang–Mills theory in four dimensions that satisfies the axioms of quantum field theory and has a mass gap — a lowest energy above zero, which is why the particles have mass.

Why it is hard

Quantum field theories are notoriously difficult to define rigorously; even the simpler cases required decades of work. The mass gap is the physical content: in pure Yang–Mills theory the excitations are massive despite the theory having no mass parameter, which is the phenomenon of dimensional transmutation.

Lattice calculations confirm the mass gap numerically; a proof is another matter.

Where it stands

Used: as the basis of particle physics.

Confirmed numerically: on the lattice.

Open: a rigorous construction with a mass gap.

Prize: Millennium Prize.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of a theory that predicts correctly and has no mathematical foundation, which is a useful thing to know about physics.

The Hodge Conjecture

Open problem

A statement about which shapes can be described by equations. It is one of the hardest open problems in mathematics and one of the least explainable.

The statement

The Hodge conjecture concerns complex algebraic varieties — shapes defined by polynomial equations — and relates their topology to their algebraic structure. Informally, it says that certain topological features ('Hodge classes') are always the result of algebraic subvarieties: that geometry and algebra agree in a specific, technical sense.

Why it matters

The conjecture, formulated by W. V. D. Hodge in 1950, is a Millennium Prize problem. It is proved in some cases — for example for codimension one — and open in general. It sits at the centre of algebraic geometry, and a proof would reorganise the field.

It is also the hardest of the Millennium problems to state to a non-specialist, which is itself worth noting.

Where it stands

Formulated: 1950.

Proved: in special cases.

Open: in general.

Prize: Millennium Prize.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the open problem whose statement is least accessible, and because the archive should not pretend that everything can be explained in three hundred words.

Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer

Open problem

A conjecture connecting the number of rational points on an elliptic curve to a function attached to it. It is the Millennium problem with the most computational support.

The conjecture

For an elliptic curve — a curve of the form y² = x³ + ax + b — the set of rational points can be finite or infinite, and its structure is described by its rank. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture relates that rank to the behaviour of an associated L-function at a single point: the rank should equal the order of the zero of the L-function there.

The evidence

The conjecture is supported by enormous computation and by partial results: it is known in some cases, including for curves of rank 0 and 1 under certain conditions, and it is one of the Millennium Prize problems.

It connects two objects that look unrelated — a geometric count and an analytic function — which is why it is regarded as deep rather than merely hard.

Where it stands

Formulated: 1965.

Proved: in special cases.

Supported: by extensive computation.

Prize: Millennium Prize.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the open problem where the numerical evidence is strongest, and because that has not been enough for sixty years.

The Moving Sofa Problem

Open problem

The largest sofa that can be moved round a right-angled corridor. The best known answer has stood since 1992 and is not proved optimal.

The problem

Formulated by Leo Moser in 1966: what is the largest area of a sofa that can be manoeuvred around a right-angled corner in a corridor of unit width? The problem is a classic of recreational geometry and a genuine open problem in analysis.

The bounds

John Hammersley found a shape of area about 2.2074 in 1968; Joseph Gerver found a better one, about 2.2195, in 1992, and conjectured it optimal. A 2017 result proved that Gerver's sofa is locally optimal, and later work has narrowed the upper bound, but the exact answer is unknown.

The problem is unusual in that the answer is a specific number nobody can compute.

Where it stands

Best known: Gerver's sofa, about 2.2195.

Proved: locally optimal, 2017.

Open: global optimality.

Bounds: narrowed, not closed.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most accessible open problem in mathematics, and because accessibility is not the same as ease.

The Inscribed Square Problem

Open problem

Every closed curve contains four points forming a square. It is easy to state, proved for smooth curves, and open in general.

The problem

The inscribed square problem, also called the square peg problem, asks whether every simple closed plane curve contains four points that form a square. It was posed by Otto Toeplitz in 1911.

What is known

The answer is yes for smooth curves, for polygons, and for several other classes, and the proofs use topological and analytic methods. The general case — for an arbitrary Jordan curve — remains open, and the difficulty is the possibility of pathological curves.

Related results hold for triangles and rectangles under conditions, and the failure of some generalisations shows the problem is genuinely delicate.

Where it stands

Proved: for smooth curves and polygons.

Open: for arbitrary Jordan curves.

Obstacle: pathological curves.

Age: posed in 1911.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a statement a child can understand, a proof that has resisted a century, and a reminder that 'obvious' is not an argument.

The Lonely Runner Conjecture

Open problem

Runners on a circular track at different constant speeds: each will at some point be far from all the others. It is proved for small numbers of runners and open beyond.

The problem

The lonely runner conjecture, posed by Jörg Wills in 1967, concerns k runners moving around a circular track of unit length at distinct constant speeds. It states that for each runner there is a time at which they are at distance at least 1/(k+1) from every other runner — that is, each runner becomes 'lonely'.

The status

The conjecture is proved for up to seven runners and open in general. It has connections to number theory, view-obstruction problems and the study of Diophantine approximation, and several partial results give weaker bounds.

It is a good example of a problem whose difficulty grows with the parameter rather than with the statement.

Where it stands

Proved: up to seven runners.

Open: in general.

Connections: number theory; view-obstruction.

Posed: 1967.

The label: open problem.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a problem with a physical picture and a number-theoretic core, and because the picture makes it sound easier than it is.
