The Technosphere Layer

Documented

The claim that human technology has become a geological layer of the planet, with its own mass and dynamics. The concept is now used in Earth-systems science.

The concept

The technosphere is the global system of human-made materials, infrastructure and processes, considered as a layer of the Earth system comparable to the biosphere. The term was developed by Peter Haff and others, and it is now used in discussions of the Anthropocene.

The measurement

Estimates of the technosphere's mass — buildings, roads, machines, waste — put it in the order of trillions of tonnes, and studies have found that human-made mass now exceeds the total biomass. The figures are estimates with wide uncertainty, and the concept is a framework rather than a measurement.

The archive files it as documented because the concept and the estimates are in the literature.

Documented: the concept and its use.

Uncertain: the exact figures.

The label: documented.

Because it is a case where a new concept has changed how a whole field describes the planet, and the numbers are still being argued.

The Max Headroom Incident

Documented

Two Chicago television stations were hijacked by a masked figure in 1987. Nobody was ever charged.

The incident

In November 1987, a signal intruder interrupted two Chicago television broadcasts. The first, during a news programme, transmitted a few seconds of buzzing and a figure; the second, during a science-fiction drama, ran for over a minute with a man in a Max Headroom mask and a corset, speaking nonsense and being spanked with a flyswatter.

The investigation

The broadcasts were traced to a microwave signal intrusion, which requires equipment and line-of-sight to the receiver. The FBI investigated and no one was charged; the case remains open, and the culprits have never been identified.

The incident is documented on tape — the recordings survive — and it remains the best-known broadcast hijack.

What is established

Documented: the intrusion and the recordings.

Documented: the method, microwave injection.

Not established: the identity.

Investigated: by the FBI.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real hijack with a real recording and no culprit, which is the rare combination.

The Somerton Man

Live debate

A man found dead on an Adelaide beach in 1948, with a scrap of Persian poetry and an unbreakable code. He was identified by DNA in 2022.

In December 1948 a man was found dead on Somerton Beach in Adelaide, South Australia, in a suit with no identification. A scrap of paper in a fob pocket read Tamám Shud — 'it is ended' — from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, and a book found nearby contained a line of letters that has never been deciphered.

In 2022, researchers using DNA from the exhumed remains and genealogical databases identified him as Carl Webb, an electrical engineer from Melbourne. The identification was announced by the researchers and has been widely accepted, though some details of his life and death remain unexplained.

The Yuba County Five

Live debate

Five men drove into the mountains after a basketball game and were found dead months later. What happened in between has never been established.

The case

In February 1978, five men with mild intellectual disabilities left a basketball game in Chico, California, and drove into the Sierra Nevada. Theories have included exposure, an accident, and a third party. A key detail is that the car was drivable and the road led back to safety, which makes the decision to leave it unexplained. A 2020 documentary revived attention, and no explanation has been established.

The case is documented in police records and remains unresolved.

The Circleville Letters

Documented

A small Ohio town received anonymous letters accusing residents of affairs and worse. One man was convicted of a related crime; the letter-writer was never identified.

The case

From 1976, residents of Circleville, Ohio, received anonymous letters accusing them of affairs, corruption and worse. The letters stopped and started over years, and no one was charged with writing them. Gordon Gillispie was convicted of homicide in the booby-trap death and died in prison; the identity of the letter-writer remains unknown.

The archive files it as documented because the correspondence and the court record are preserved.

Live debate

The case

In November 1970 a woman's body was found in Isdalen, near Bergen, Norway. She had been burned, and her belongings had identifying labels removed. Investigation established that she had travelled under several identities, stayed in hotels across Europe, and used coded notes.

Isotope analysis of her teeth in 2016 suggested she had spent her childhood in central Europe or France and moved later. The Flannan Isles Lighthouse

Documented

Three lighthouse keepers vanished from a Hebridean island in 1900. The lamps were trimmed, the kitchen was abandoned mid-meal, and no bodies were found.

The event

In December 1900 the lighthouse at Eilean Mòr in the Flannan Isles was found abandoned. All three keepers had vanished. Inside, the lamps were cleaned and refilled, and there were signs that a meal had been interrupted. Damage to the landing stage suggested a storm.

The explanation

The Northern Lighthouse Board's investigation concluded that the men had gone to secure equipment at the west landing during heavy seas and been swept away by an exceptional wave. Later research has supported this, with debate about whether one man went first and the others followed.

The story has attracted supernatural explanations since; the documented account is a storm and a dangerous coast.

What is established

Debunked

Debunked

The story holds that in the 1950s a man arrived at Haneda airport in Tokyo with a passport from a country called Taured, which no one could locate, and that he vanished from a guarded room. Variants place it in different years and airports.

No contemporary record, newspaper report or immigration document supports it. The earliest versions appear in books of strange tales and on websites, with the details changing between retellings — the signature of an urban legend rather than an event.

Skinwalker Whistling Lore

Fiction

Internet posts claim that whistling at night attracts a skinwalker. The taboo is real in some traditions; the internet version is not.

The claim

Internet posts warn that whistling outdoors at night will attract a skinwalker — a shape-shifting figure from Navajo tradition. The claim is presented as a rule with consequences.

The tradition is real and specific, and it is not a set of internet rules; Navajo teaching about the figure is not intended as horror content, and the internet version strips it of context. Whistling at night is discouraged in some traditions for other reasons, including attracting animals.

The archive files it as fiction and notes that the borrowing is of a living tradition, which is a different kind of problem from a false claim.

The label: fiction.

Because it is a case where the fiction is harmless in itself and careless about its source.

The Fleshgait and the Wendigo

Fiction

Two creatures from different traditions, run together on the internet. One is an internet invention; the other belongs to Algonquian peoples.

The two

The wendigo belongs to the traditions of Algonquian-speaking peoples, associated with winter, hunger and cannibalism; it is a serious figure in those traditions, not a monster for stories. The fleshgait is an internet invention of the 2010s, described as a creature that mimics voices and replaces people.

The problem

Internet horror often treats the two as the same kind of thing, which flattens a living tradition into content. The fleshgait has no tradition behind it at all.

The archive files both as fiction, and separates them, because the difference matters to the people whose tradition one of them is.

Documented: the Algonquian tradition.

Not established: either creature as an animal.

The issue: a tradition used as content.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Capitalist Realism

Live debate

Mark Fisher's argument that capitalism has become the horizon of thought, so that alternatives are unimaginable. It is a diagnosis, not a measurement.

The argument

Mark Fisher's Capitalist Realism (2009) argues that capitalism has stopped appearing as one system among others and has become the background condition of thought — so that even its critics imagine change only within it. His line that it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism is the book's summary.

The problems

The thesis is a cultural diagnosis, and it is not testable in the way a social-science claim is. Critics note that alternatives are discussed constantly, that the claim risks being unfalsifiable, and that the book's examples are selected.

The archive files it as live debate because it is a serious argument with wide influence and no measurable test.

Where it stands

Documented: the book and its influence.

Contested: the thesis.

Not measurable: as stated.

The value: a description of a mood, precisely put.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is an argument about what people can imagine, and this archive is a record of what they did.

Bullshit Jobs

Live debate

David Graeber's claim that a large share of jobs are pointless and their holders know it. The essay struck a nerve; the survey evidence is thinner than the argument.

The claim

Graeber's 2013 essay, later a book, argued that a large proportion of modern employment is 'bullshit' — jobs the holder believes are pointless — and that this is a structural feature of contemporary capitalism rather than a personal failing. He offered a taxonomy: flunkies, goons, duct tapers, box tickers, taskmasters.

The evidence

Support comes from testimony and from surveys in which a substantial minority report their jobs as useless. The figures vary widely with the question asked, and critics note that self-report measures satisfaction and meaning rather than economic necessity. Graeber's estimate of the share was not derived from a representative sample.

The archive files it as live debate because the phenomenon is widely reported and the magnitude is not established.

Where it stands

Documented: the essay, the book and the testimony.

Documented: surveys reporting pointless work.

Contested: the proportion.

Contested: the structural explanation.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim that many people recognise and no one has measured well.

The Peter Principle

Live debate

The claim that people rise to their level of incompetence. It is a joke with a testable prediction, and the tests have been mixed.

The claim

Laurence Peter and Raymond Hull argued in 1969 that in a hierarchy, employees are promoted for performance in their current role until they reach a role they cannot do, and stay there. On the strong version, organisations end up with incompetents in most senior posts.

The evidence

The prediction has been tested with sales data and with models of promotion. Some studies find that top performers are promoted into roles where their skills do not transfer, reducing their output; others find that firms promote on expected performance and avoid the trap. The results depend on whether the new role requires different skills.

The archive files it as live debate because the effect is plausible, conditional and not settled.

Where it stands

Documented: the book and the prediction.

Documented: studies testing promotion outcomes.

Mixed: the evidence.

Conditional: on how different the new role is.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a joke that turned out to be a research question.

The theory that the show's plot is driven by a statistical curve of Mortys. It is a joke about narrative and it is treated as one.

In Rick and Morty, a character refers to a curve describing the distribution of Mortys across realities, used to explain why Rick is always paired with a Morty. The theory treats the curve as a real in-universe law governing the plot.

The problems

The curve is a narrative device introduced for a joke and a plot twist, and the show's creators treat its canon loosely. The theory's supporters build a cosmology on it, which the show neither confirms nor needs.

The archive files it as fiction and notes the mechanism: a joke's internal logic treated as worldbuilding.

What is established

Documented: the curve in dialogue.

Documented: the theory.

Not established: any in-universe law.

The mechanism: joke logic as canon.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows how a single line of dialogue can generate a cosmology.

Fiction

The theory

The theory holds that Cars takes place after humanity left or died out, with the vehicles as the inheritors of the planet, and that this places it in a shared continuity with other Pixar films. It circulated widely as a 'Pixar theory'.

The films present a world of living machines with its own history and no reference to human extinction. The theory is an exercise in connecting unrelated films, and Pixar has not endorsed it; the studio's films do contain in-jokes, which is a different thing.

Oppenheimer's Chain Reaction

Fiction

The film dramatises a fear that the first test might ignite the atmosphere. The fear was real, the calculation was done, and the answer was no.

The concern

Before the Trinity test in 1945, some physicists considered whether the explosion could ignite the atmosphere through nuclear fusion. The question was examined in a report by Teller and others, and the conclusion was that it could not — the calculated probability was effectively zero.

The film

Oppenheimer (2023) dramatises the anxiety for narrative purposes, and it is presented as a fear rather than a live possibility. The historical record shows the calculation was done and the concern dismissed before the test.

The archive files it as fiction because the page is about the film's treatment, and the underlying physics is documented elsewhere.

What is established

Documented: the pre-test calculation.

Documented: the conclusion.

Dramatised: in the film.

Not a live possibility: according to the physics.

The label: fiction (a dramatisation).

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the drama and the calculation are both real and only one is the story.

Tetris as a Soviet Weapon

Fiction

A joke that the Soviet Union built Tetris as a psychological weapon. It was written by a programmer in 1984, and it was not.

The claim

The joke, and sometimes the claim, is that Tetris was designed by Soviet psychologists as a weapon — a program that would occupy the minds of Westerners. It is a popular internet story.

The facts

Tetris was created in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov, a computer engineer at the Soviet Academy of Sciences, as a puzzle game based on pentominoes. It spread through the Eastern bloc on copied disks and then worldwide, and the rights history is documented and litigious. No psychological-weapon programme existed.

The archive files it as fiction because the story is a joke about a game that really is addictive.

Documented: the game and its author.

Documented: its spread and rights history.

Not established: any weapon programme.

The origin: a puzzle game, 1984.

The label: fiction.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a joke that a surprising number of people repeat as fact.

McDonald's Monopoly Rigging

Documented

The promotional game was rigged for years by the man who ran its security, who sold the winning pieces. The FBI investigation is documented.

The case

McDonald's Monopoly promotion gave customers game pieces with prizes. From 1989 to 2001, the man responsible for the promotion's security, Jerome Jacobson, took the rare winning pieces and sold them through a network, sharing the proceeds.

The investigation

The FBI investigated, ran a sting, and arrested dozens of people; Jacobson was sentenced in 2001 to prison. The case is documented in court records and in reporting, and the promotion was restructured.

The archive files it as documented because the fraud, the investigation and the conviction are all on the record.

Because it is a real rigged game, which is the best kind of story for this archive.

The joke holds that the Muppets are legal persons — citizens with rights and obligations — and that their status raises questions about labour, contracts and identity. It circulates as humour and occasionally as a sincere argument.

Newgrange and the Solstice

Documented

A passage tomb in Ireland aligned so that the rising sun at midwinter reaches the chamber floor. The alignment is measured every year.

The monument

Newgrange is a passage tomb in the Boyne Valley, built around 3200 BC, with a long passage and a chamber under a mound. Above the entrance is a roof box, an opening designed to admit light.

The alignment

For several days around the winter solstice, the rising sun passes through the roof box and along the passage, reaching the chamber floor. The alignment is precise enough that it cannot be accidental, and it is observed each year by visitors selected by lottery.

The monument is older than Stonehenge and the pyramids, and it is documented in excavation reports and in the annual observations.

Documented: the monument and its date.

Contested: the ritual meaning.

The label: documented.

Because it is a real astronomical alignment that anyone can watch, which is the answer to a shelf of claims about ancient astronomy.

The Barabar Caves

Documented

Caves cut into granite in Bihar with polished surfaces and an echo that lasts for seconds. They were made for an ascetic sect, and the finish is documented.

The caves

The Barabar caves in Bihar, India, were cut into granite in the third century BC under the Mauryan empire, and inscribed for the Ajivika sect. The interior surfaces are polished to a high finish, and the chambers produce a long echo.

The technique

The caves were cut with iron tools and finished by grinding and polishing — a process that takes time rather than lost technology. The precision is documented in surveys, and it is the result of sustained labour on a single rock mass.

The echo is a property of the geometry, and it is the reason the site is often described as mysterious.

Documented: the caves, their date and their patrons.

Documented: the polished finish.

Documented: the echo.

Documented: the tools available.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest case for ancient precision, and it needs no lost technology.

Kailasa Carved Downward

Documented

A temple cut from the top of a hill downward, removing everything that is not the building. The method is documented by the marks left behind.

The monument

The Kailasa temple at Ellora in Maharashtra was cut from a single rock in the eighth century, under the Rashtrakuta dynasty. Unlike a built temple, it was carved from the top down: the excavators removed rock to reveal a complete monument with courtyards, halls and towers.

The evidence

The method is documented by the unfinished sections and by tool marks, and by the sheer volume of rock removed — estimated at hundreds of thousands of tonnes. The work took decades and required planning on a scale that is itself the achievement.

The temple is often cited in claims about lost technology; the documented account is a large, sustained and well-organised project.

What is established

Documented: the monument and its date.

Documented: the top-down method.

Documented: the volume of rock removed.

Documented: the unfinished sections.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most impressive rock-cut monument in the world, and the explanation is organisation rather than mystery.

The city

Derinkuyu in Cappadocia, Turkey, is an underground city cut into soft volcanic tuff, extending to a depth of about 85 metres with levels for storage, stables, a church, schools and living quarters. It is one of several such sites in the region.

The engineering

The site's achievement is ventilation: vertical shafts carried air through the levels, and the tunnels and doors could be closed with large stone wheels. The city was used over centuries, with the deepest levels probably cut in the Byzantine period as refuge during raids.

The site is documented in surveys and is open to visitors.

The Longyou caves in Zhejiang, China, are a group of large chambers cut by hand into sandstone, discovered when a pond was drained in 1992. The walls and ceilings carry regular chisel marks, and the chambers are enormous, with some holding thousands of square metres.

No historical record mentions them, and their purpose is unknown; proposals include quarrying, storage and refuge. The chisel marks show the method clearly, and the scale shows organisation, but the absence of any documentation is what makes them strange.

The archive files them as documented because the caves exist and the method is visible.

The Yangshan Stele

Documented

A colossal stone monument left in its quarry, unfinished, still attached at one edge. It is the best evidence of how such monuments were made.

The monument

At Yangshan near Nanjing, a gigantic stone stele was cut in the early fifteenth century for the tomb of the Yongle Emperor. The main block is about 60 metres long and would have weighed tens of thousands of tonnes; it was abandoned, still attached to the bedrock at one edge.

What it shows

The unfinished state documents the method: the block was cut on three sides and underneath, leaving a spine of rock to support it, and was to be separated last. The scale defeated the project, which is why it remains.

The site is documented and open, and it is the clearest evidence of how monumental stonework was planned.

What is established

Documented: the block and its dimensions.

Documented: the cutting method.

Documented: its abandonment.

Documented: the intended purpose.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because a failure explains more about ancient engineering than a success does.

A city built on artificial islets from stacked basalt columns, in a lagoon in Micronesia. It is real, and it took centuries.

The site

Nan Madol lies off Pohnpei in the Federated States of Micronesia: around 90 artificial islets built in a lagoon, with walls and platforms of stacked basalt columns, constructed between roughly the twelfth and seventeenth centuries by the Saudeleur dynasty.

The achievement

The columns were quarried elsewhere on Pohnpei and moved by raft and canoe, then stacked without mortar into walls up to several metres high. The labour and logistics are the extraordinary part, and they are documented in archaeology and in Pohnpei's oral tradition.

The site is often cited in claims about lost civilisations; the documented account is a Pacific society with organisation and boats.

What is established

Documented: the islets and the walls.

Documented: the quarrying and transport.

Documented: the dynasty and the dates.

Documented: the oral tradition.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real Pacific achievement that gets borrowed by Atlantic-focused legends.

Mercury Under Teotihuacan

Documented

Liquid mercury was found in a tunnel under the Feathered Serpent pyramid. It is documented, and it is not evidence of anything exotic.

The find

In 2003 a tunnel was found beneath the Feathered Serpent pyramid at Teotihuacan, sealed around 1,800 years ago. Excavation from 2009 revealed offerings, pyrite mirrors and, in 2015, liquid mercury in a chamber.

The interpretation

Mercury occurs naturally and was used in Mesoamerican ritual; its presence is interpreted as a representation of an underworld river or as a reflective surface. The find is documented in the excavation reports, and the interpretation is archaeology rather than anomaly.

The archive files it as documented because the material and its context are published.

What is established

Documented: the tunnel and the offerings.

Documented: the liquid mercury.

Documented: Mesoamerican use of mercury.

Interpreted: as a ritual representation.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the kind of find that generates headlines and has a plain archaeological reading.

Zhang Heng's Seismoscope

Documented

A bronze vessel that detected earthquakes and indicated direction. The instrument is described in a text and its principle is understood.

The instrument

Zhang Heng, an astronomer at the Han court, presented a seismoscope in 132 AD: a bronze vessel with eight dragons holding balls, which dropped into the mouths of toads when an earthquake occurred, indicating direction. The device is described in the Book of the Later Han.

The reconstruction

The original is lost and its internal mechanism is not described in detail, so modern reconstructions are hypotheses. What is documented is that the instrument was used and that it reportedly detected a distant earthquake that no one at court had felt.

The archive files it as documented because the text and the record are real, and it flags the mechanism as reconstructed.

What is established

Documented: the instrument's description.

Documented: its reported success.

Not preserved: the original.

Reconstructed: the mechanism.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real early instrument, and because the gap between the record and the reconstruction is instructive.

Al-Jazari's Automata

Documented

A book of machines — clocks, water-raising devices and automata — with drawings clear enough to rebuild. The book survives.

The book

Ismail al-Jazari completed The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices in 1206. It describes about fifty machines — water clocks, automata, pumps and a hand-washing device — with drawings and instructions detailed enough for modern reconstructions.

The significance

The book is the fullest surviving record of medieval Islamic engineering, and several of its mechanisms are the earliest known descriptions of their kind. Working replicas have been built from the drawings, which is the test of the documentation.

The archive files it as documented because the manuscript survives and the designs have been reconstructed.

What is established

Documented: the manuscript and its date.

Documented: the machines and their drawings.

Documented: modern reconstructions.

Documented: the engineering principles.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the instructions survive and the machines can be built, which settles the question.

Hero's Steam Engine

Documented

A sphere turned by steam, described by Hero of Alexandria. It is a real device and it was not used for work.

The device

Hero of Alexandria described the aeolipile in the first century AD: a sphere mounted on a pivot, with bent nozzles, heated from below so that steam escapes and spins it. It is the earliest documented steam turbine.

The limits

The device was a demonstration, not a power source: it produced little torque, and the ancient world lacked the metallurgy and the economic pressure that made steam power useful. Claims that Hero 'invented the steam engine' overstate a described toy.

The archive files it as documented because the text survives and the device has been rebuilt.

What is established

Documented: the description and its date.

Documented: the working principle.

Documented: modern replicas.

Not established: any industrial use.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the classic case of a principle discovered without a use, which is a different thing from a technology lost.

Neolithic Trepanation

Documented

Skulls with holes cut into them, and bone regrowth showing that some people survived. The surgery is documented; the motive is not.

The evidence

Skulls with deliberately cut holes are found at Neolithic and later sites across Europe and elsewhere, some dating to around 6500 BC. Many show regrowth of bone at the edges, which means the patient survived the operation, sometimes for years.

The interpretation

The operation was performed with stone tools, and the survival rate implied by the healed cases is high. The motive is argued: treatment of head injury, relief of pressure, or ritual. There is evidence for all three at different sites and periods.

The archive files it as documented because the bones are the evidence and the healing is measurable.

What is established

Documented: the skulls and the technique.

Documented: bone regrowth and survival.

Documented: the dates and the spread.

Contested: the motive.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is prehistoric surgery with a measurable outcome, which is rare and valuable.

Ley Lines

Debunked

Straight lines drawn between ancient sites, said to be channels of earth energy. They are drawn after the fact.

The claim

Alfred Watkins proposed in 1921 that ancient sites in Britain lie on straight lines, which he called leys, and later writers described them as channels of earth energy or as prehistoric trackways.

The problems

The lines were drawn by selecting sites from a dense landscape of churches, mounds and crossroads; with enough points, straight alignments occur by chance. Statistical tests have found no more alignment than random points produce, and the 'energy' has never been detected.

The archive files it as debunked, and notes that the landscape is so full of marked places that any line will pass through several.

What is established

Documented: the proposal and its history.

Documented: the density of sites.

Tested: no excess alignment.

Not detected: any energy.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the classic case of a pattern produced by the drawing method rather than found in the world.

Vimanas

Debunked

Flying machines described in Sanskrit epics, read as aircraft. The texts describe palaces and chariots, and the reading is modern.

The texts

The Sanskrit epics and puranas describe vimanas — flying palaces or chariots used by gods and kings. The Vaimanika Shastra, a twentieth-century text presented as ancient, describes aircraft in technical detail.

The problems

The epic vimanas are divine vehicles described in poetic terms, not machines with specifications. The Vaimanika Shastra was composed in the early twentieth century and its drawings are not aeronautical; its provenance was established decades ago.

The archive files it as debunked because the aircraft reading depends on a text that is not what it claims.

What is established

Documented: the epic descriptions.

Documented: the later text's date.

Not ancient: the technical descriptions.

Not aeronautical: the drawings.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where a genuine tradition was amplified by a modern document pretending to be old.

The Mohenjo-daro Blast

Debunked

A claim that an ancient city was destroyed by an atomic blast. The 'evidence' is a scattered set of bones and a misread verse.

The claim

The claim holds that Mohenjo-daro was destroyed by a nuclear explosion, citing scattered skeletons, 'vitrified' surfaces and a verse from the Mahabharata describing a weapon of terrible brightness.

The problems

The skeletons are from different periods and contexts, and there is no crater, no shocked quartz, no glass of the kind an atomic blast produces, and no radiation anomaly. The Mahabharata verse describes a divine weapon in poetic terms. The city's decline is attributed to the Indus system's changes, including the shifting of rivers.

The archive files it as debunked because the physical evidence that would settle it is absent.

What is established

Documented: the ruins and the skeletons.

Not found: a crater, shocked quartz or blast glass.

Not measured: any radiation anomaly.

Explained: by the city's decline.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most cinematic ancient-war claim, and the evidence for it is a mood.

The Bat Creek Stone

Debunked

A stone with an inscription said to be Hebrew, found in a Tennessee mound. It is a nineteenth-century inscription, and it is upside down.

The object

A small stone with an inscription was found in a mound in Tennessee in 1889 and published as evidence of ancient Hebrew contact with North America. For decades it was cited in books about pre-Columbian voyages.

The problems

The inscription is a nineteenth-century script, and it reads as a known phrase only when the stone is turned upside down; the 'Hebrew' is a modern reading of a design that appears on other objects of the period. The archaeological context was poorly recorded.

The archive files it as debunked because the object's date and the misreading are both established.

What is established

Documented: the object and its discovery.

Documented: the inscription's script.

Documented: the upside-down reading.

Not established: any Hebrew contact.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the object is genuine and the interpretation collapses when it is turned over.

The Los Lunas Stone

Debunked

A boulder in New Mexico inscribed with the Ten Commandments in Hebrew, said to be ancient. The inscription is modern.

The object

The Los Lunas Decalogue Stone is a large boulder near Los Lunas, New Mexico, inscribed with a version of the Ten Commandments in a Hebrew script. It has been cited as evidence of ancient transatlantic contact.

The problems

The script is a form used in modern printed Hebrew, and the inscription includes a carving of a figure that is not part of the Decalogue. The earliest references to it are from the 1930s, and the site has no archaeological context. It is widely treated as a modern inscription.

The archive files it as debunked because the script dates the object.

What is established

Documented: the stone and the inscription.

Documented: the script's modern form.

Documented: the first references in the 1930s.

Not established: any ancient origin.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a clean case where palaeography settles a claim that archaeology could not.

The Newport Tower

Debunked

A stone tower in Rhode Island said to be a medieval Norse church. The mortar dates it to the colonial period.

The claim

The Newport Tower in Rhode Island has been attributed to Norse explorers, to the Knights Templar and to Portuguese navigators, as evidence of pre-Columbian European presence in New England.

The evidence

Mortar analysis dates the structure to the seventeenth century, and the tower's architecture matches colonial building of the period, including a mill. Documents place it in the colonial record, and no medieval artefact has been found at the site.

The archive files it as debunked because the dating is physical and the documentary record agrees.

What is established

Documented: the structure.

Dated: seventeenth century, by mortar.

Documented: colonial records.

Not found: any medieval artefact.

The label: debunked.

Because it is a case where two independent methods agree against a popular story.

The Michigan Relics

Debunked

Thousands of inscribed objects 'found' in Michigan, said to record ancient migrations. They were made and planted.

The corpus

From the 1890s, thousands of objects — clay tablets, copper ornaments and inscribed slates — were reported from mounds in Michigan, bearing inscriptions in scripts that were said to record ancient peoples in America.

The problems

The objects were traced to a network of people who manufactured and planted them, including a former state archaeologist's associate; the scripts are inconsistent and the contexts were fabricated. Modern examination has confirmed the objects are modern.

The archive files it as debunked because the forgery is documented.

What is established

Documented: the corpus and its scale.

Documented: the manufacture and planting.

Documented: the inconsistent scripts.

Not established: any ancient origin.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the largest archaeological forgery in North America, and it was believed for decades.

The Ica Stones

Debunked

Stones carved with dinosaurs and surgery, said to be ancient. The carver admitted making them.

The stones

The Ica stones are a collection of andesite stones from Peru carved with images of dinosaurs, advanced surgery and maps. They were promoted from the 1960s as evidence of ancient knowledge and of human coexistence with dinosaurs.

The problems

The farmer who supplied most of them said he had carved them himself, and the carvings include imagery from modern sources; the surface treatment shows recent work. Museums have rejected the collection, and no excavation has produced a stone in a secure context.

The archive files it as debunked because the maker's account and the physical evidence agree.

What is established

Documented: the stones and the collection.

Documented: the maker's admission.

Documented: the modern imagery.

Not found: in any excavation.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the cleanest forgery case in the collection: the forger explained himself.

The Acámbaro Figurines

Debunked

Thousands of ceramic figures showing humans with dinosaurs, said to be ancient. The dating and the context failed.

The collection

From 1944 a German shopkeeper in Acámbaro, Mexico, assembled thousands of ceramic figurines said to depict humans with dinosaurs and other animals. They were promoted as evidence of ancient coexistence.

The problems

Excavations at the site by professional archaeologists found no figurines in secure contexts; thermoluminescence testing of a sample gave modern dates; and the figurines' manufacture and surface treatment are consistent with contemporary work. The collection's origin is a single supplier.

The archive files it as debunked because the dating and the context both failed.

What is established

Documented: the collection and its scale.

Documented: the professional excavations.

Dated: modern, by thermoluminescence.

Not found: in secure contexts.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows what happens when a collection is tested by a method its promoters did not choose.

The Grand Canyon Citadel

Debunked

A newspaper story about an ancient citadel in the Grand Canyon, with Egyptian and Tibetan artefacts. It was a hoax.

The story

In 1909 a newspaper reported that an explorer had found a cave in the Grand Canyon containing an ancient citadel, mummies and artefacts from Egypt and Tibet. The story was repeated in books about lost civilisations.

The problems

The report appeared in a single newspaper and was not corroborated; the explorer's identity and credentials do not hold up, and the Smithsonian has stated that it has no record of the find. No such cave has been located, and the geology of the canyon does not support the described structure.

The archive files it as debunked because the story's source is one newspaper article.

What is established

Documented: the newspaper report.

Documented: the absence of corroboration.

Documented: the Smithsonian's statement.

Not found: any such site.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the classic newspaper-origin legend, and the paper is the only evidence.

The Pyramid as a Pump

Fringe claim

A claim that the Great Pyramid was a hydraulic machine. The chambers and shafts are real; the machinery is not.

The claim

The claim holds that the Great Pyramid was a water pump or a hydraulic lift, using the chambers, the shafts and the Grand Gallery to move water, and that this explains features that the tomb theory does not.

The problems

The features cited are documented, and their interpretation is argued among archaeologists. The pump hypothesis requires machinery for which there is no evidence, and it does not explain the burial equipment, the sarcophagus or the site's context. It is presented as an engineering demonstration rather than as an excavated finding.

The archive files it as fringe because it is a serious engineering proposal without archaeological support.

Where it stands

Documented: the chambers, shafts and gallery.

Contested: their function.

Not found: any machinery.

Not explained: the burial context.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most technically literate alternative claim, and it still fails on evidence.

Mica in the Pyramids

Fringe claim

A claim that mica sheets in Egyptian monuments served an electrical purpose. Mica is present; the electrical use is not.

The claim

The claim holds that sheets of mica found in some Egyptian monuments were insulators in an electrical system, and that this supports a technological reading of the pyramids.

The problems

Mica occurs in Egypt and was used in cosmetic and decorative contexts; its presence in a monument is documented in some cases and its function is not established. No wiring, no conductors and no power source have been found, and the electrical hypothesis rests on the material's modern uses.

The archive files it as fringe: the material is real, the function is invented.

Where it stands

Documented: mica in some monuments.

Documented: mica's other uses in Egypt.

Not found: conductors or a power source.

Not established: any electrical function.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim built from a material's modern use rather than its ancient one.

Stone Softening in the Andes

Fringe claim

A claim that Inca masons softened stone with plant acids to fit it perfectly. The fit is real; the method is not established.

The claim

The claim holds that Inca builders softened andesite and granite with plant acids or by heating, so that blocks could be moulded to fit, which would explain the tight joints and irregular shapes of Inca walls.

The problems

The joints are documented and extraordinary, and the fitting was achieved by patient shaping, trial and error — a process visible in unfinished blocks. The softening hypothesis has been tested experimentally and does not produce the observed surfaces; the acids available would not dissolve andesite at the rates required.

The archive files it as fringe: a real observation with an untested mechanism.

Where it stands

Documented: the masonry and its precision.

Documented: unfinished blocks showing shaping.

Tested: softening, without success.

Not established: any chemical method.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-known 'lost technique' claim, and the unfinished stones answer it.

The Etruscans

Documented

The civilisation that taught Rome its rituals, and whose language is still only partly read. Their origin was argued for centuries and settled by DNA.

The civilisation

The Etruscans dominated central Italy before Rome, with a league of cities, elaborate tombs, and a religion whose rites Rome absorbed. Their language is written in an alphabet derived from Greek and is only partly understood.

The origin question

Herodotus said they came from Lydia; Dionysius said they were indigenous. A 2021 study of ancient DNA from Etruscan individuals found them genetically similar to their Italian neighbours, supporting a local origin with a distinctive culture rather than a migration.

The archive files it as documented because the DNA result and the archaeology agree.

What is established

Documented: the cities, tombs and inscriptions.

Documented: Roman borrowing of Etruscan rites.

Documented: a local origin, by DNA.

Partly understood: the language.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where genetics closed a question the ancient sources could not.

The Picts

Documented

The painted people of northern Scotland, known from carved stones and a king-list, whose language left almost nothing.

The people

The Picts were the peoples of northern and eastern Scotland in the late Roman and early medieval periods, forming a kingdom that fought and allied with Rome and later with the Scots. Their name comes from the Latin for 'painted'.

The evidence

The evidence is carved symbol stones, a king-list, place names and archaeology. The Pictish language survives only in fragments — place names and a few words — and its classification is disputed. The symbols on the stones remain undeciphered.

The archive files it as documented because the kingdom and its material culture are well attested.

What is established

Documented: the kingdom and its history.

Documented: the symbol stones.

Documented: the king-list.

Lost: the language, except fragments.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real people who became a blank in the record, and the blank is what the stories fill.

Denisovan Inheritance

Documented

A hominin known from a finger bone, whose genes are in living people from Tibet to Melanesia.

The find

In 2010 a finger bone from Denisova Cave in Siberia yielded DNA from a previously unknown hominin, named the Denisovans. Later finds included teeth and a jaw, and the genome showed interbreeding with modern humans.

The legacy

Denisovan DNA is found in living populations across Asia and Oceania, at the highest levels in Melanesia. A variant of the EPAS1 gene, inherited from Denisovans, helps Tibetans cope with low oxygen — the clearest case of an extinct hominin's gene doing something measurable in living people.

The archive files it as documented because the genome and the inheritance are published and replicated.

What is established

Documented: the genome from a finger bone.

Documented: interbreeding with modern humans.

Documented: EPAS1 and high-altitude adaptation.

Documented: the Melanesian signal.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest case of an extinct relative still present in living bodies.

Chaco's Straight Roads

Documented

Hundreds of kilometres of roads radiating from Chaco Canyon, built straight and often ending nowhere.

The roads

From Chaco Canyon in New Mexico, a system of roads radiates outwards — several hundred kilometres in total, some up to nine metres wide, engineered with cut and fill and running remarkably straight across rough country.

The purpose

The roads often end at nothing in particular, and some lead to outliers and great houses. Proposals include pilgrimage routes, processional paths, trade and communication. The engineering is documented by survey; the function is inferred.

The archive files it as documented because the roads are surveyed and mapped.

Documented: the road system and its scale.

Documented: the engineering.

Contested: the purpose.

Documented: the connection to great houses.

Because it is monumental infrastructure that no one built for vehicles, which is the interesting part.

Aristarchus Put the Sun at the Centre

Documented

A Greek astronomer proposed a heliocentric system eighteen centuries before Copernicus. The report survives, and the idea was rejected.

The proposal

Aristarchus of Samos, in the third century BC, proposed that the Sun is at the centre and the Earth orbits it, and estimated the Sun's distance and size. The proposal is reported by Archimedes and by later writers, and his surviving treatise on sizes and distances uses geometric methods.

The reception

The idea was rejected by contemporaries and successors, largely because it required the Earth to move and because no stellar parallax was observed. It survived as a reported curiosity rather than a tradition, and Copernicus does not appear to have known it directly.

The archive files it as documented because the report is in Archimedes and the geometry is in the treatise.

What is established

Documented: the proposal, via Archimedes.

Documented: the surviving treatise.

Documented: its rejection.

Not a tradition: it did not carry forward.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it shows that having the right idea is not the same as having it accepted.

Democritus and Atoms

Documented

A Greek philosopher argued that matter consists of indivisible particles. He had no evidence, and he was right.

The argument

Democritus and his teacher Leucippus argued that matter consists of indivisible particles moving in void, and that their arrangements produce the properties we perceive. The argument was philosophical: change requires something unchanging, and divisibility cannot continue forever.

The status

The idea survived through Epicurus and Lucretius and was rejected by Aristotle, whose authority dominated. It was revived in the seventeenth century and confirmed experimentally in the twentieth. Democritus had no evidence and the right answer.

The archive files it as documented because the texts and the later confirmation are both real.

What is established

Documented: the atomist texts.

Documented: Aristotle's rejection.

Documented: the revival and the evidence.

Not evidence: in Democritus's time.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the counter-example that keeps the archive honest: sometimes the guess is right.

Rome Traded with India

Documented

Roman coins are found in India, and a Roman-era text describes the monsoon route. The trade was large enough to worry Roman writers.

The evidence

Roman coins, especially of Augustus and Tiberius, are found in large numbers in southern India, and excavations at Muziris and Arikamedu have produced Roman pottery and glass. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a first-century navigational text, describes the route and the ports.

The scale

Roman writers complained about the outflow of silver to the East, and the monsoon crossing — discovered to be predictable — made the voyage routine. The trade was substantial and is documented by finds on both ends of the route.

The archive files it as documented because the coins, the ports and the text agree.

What is established

Documented: the coin hoards in India.

Documented: the ports and the goods.

Documented: the Periplus.

Documented: Roman complaints about the outflow.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a globalised trade route that people are surprised to find in the first century.

The Terracotta Army

Documented

Thousands of life-size soldiers buried with the First Emperor, individually modelled and painted, found by farmers digging a well.

The find

In 1974 farmers digging a well near Xi'an found fragments of terracotta figures. Excavation revealed pits containing thousands of life-size soldiers, horses and chariots, buried around 210 BC for the tomb of Qin Shi Huang.

The figures

The figures are individually modelled, with different faces, hair and equipment by rank, and were originally painted. They were armed with real weapons, many of which were looted. The main tomb itself has not been excavated.

The archive files it as documented because the excavation and the analysis are published.

What is established

Documented: the pits and the figures.

Documented: the individual modelling.

Documented: the original paint.

Documented: the looting of weapons.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most famous excavation in the world, and the detail is better than the legend.

The Dead Sea Scrolls

Documented

Manuscripts hidden in caves near Qumran, including the oldest surviving copies of biblical texts. They were found by Bedouin shepherds.

The find

From 1947, manuscripts were found in caves near Qumran by the Dead Sea. Around 900 scrolls and fragments were recovered, dated between roughly the third century BC and the first century AD, and including the oldest known copies of books of the Hebrew Bible.

The significance

The scrolls document the diversity of Judaism in the period, including sectarian texts, and they pushed the textual history of the biblical books back by a millennium. Their publication was slow and contentious, and the last fragments were published decades later.

The archive files it as documented because the manuscripts, the caves and the scholarship are all on the record.

What is established

Documented: the manuscripts and their dates.

Documented: the biblical copies.

Documented: the sectarian texts.

Contested: the connection to the Qumran community.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the discovery that changed what we knew about the texts, not just about the place.

Pompeii and Herculaneum

Documented

Two towns buried by Vesuvius, preserving streets, food, graffiti and a library of carbonised scrolls.

The eruption

In 79 AD Vesuvius buried Pompeii in ash and Herculaneum in pyroclastic flows. The towns were preserved with their streets, houses, shops, food and inscriptions, and the casts of the dead made from voids in the ash are among the most recognisable objects in archaeology.

The finds

Excavation since the eighteenth century has produced frescoes, mosaics, household objects and a library of carbonised papyrus scrolls at Herculaneum, which modern imaging is beginning to read. The site is documented in excavation reports and in the modern conservation work.

The archive files it as documented because the towns and their contents are the evidence.

What is established

Documented: the eruption and the burial.

Documented: the streets and houses.

Documented: the casts of the dead.

Documented: the scroll library.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-preserved ordinary life in the ancient world, which is rarer than any treasure.

Knossos

Documented

The Minoan palace excavated by Arthur Evans, reconstructed in concrete, and argued about ever since.

The site

Knossos on Crete was excavated from 1900 by Arthur Evans, revealing a large complex of courts, storerooms and frescoes which he called a palace and attributed to a 'Minoan' civilisation. The site is the largest Bronze Age complex in the Aegean.

The controversy

Evans reconstructed parts of the palace in reinforced concrete, painted frescoes in interpretations that are now questioned, and named the civilisation after a myth. The reconstruction is documented and is itself part of the site's history; later work has revised his chronology and his readings.

The archive files it as documented because the excavation and the reconstruction are on the record.

Documented: the complex and its contents.

Contested: the reconstructions' accuracy.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the excavation itself became an artefact that has to be interpreted.

The Hittites

Documented

An empire mentioned in the Bible, recovered from a Turkish mound with an archive of cuneiform tablets.

The recovery

The Hittite capital Hattusa, near modern Boğazkale in Turkey, was excavated from 1906, revealing a royal archive of thousands of cuneiform tablets in Hittite and other languages. The empire had been known from Egyptian and biblical references and was recovered as a documented state.

What the archive shows

The tablets include treaties, laws, letters and ritual texts, including a peace treaty with Egypt after Kadesh. The language was deciphered in the early twentieth century, and it proved to be Indo-European — an unexpected result that reshaped the map of the family.

The archive files it as documented because the tablets and the decipherment are published.

Documented: the capital and the archive.

Documented: the treaties and laws.

Documented: the language and its family.

Documented: the treaty with Egypt.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case where an empire was found by digging up its filing system.

Egyptian Surgery

Documented

A papyrus describes forty-eight surgical cases with examinations, diagnoses and treatments, including the brain.

The text

The Edwin Smith Papyrus, dated around 1600 BC, is a surgical treatise describing forty-eight cases from head to spine, each with an examination, a diagnosis and a treatment or a verdict of 'not to be treated'. It describes the brain, the meninges and the pulse.

The practice

The text shows a rational, observational approach, and its descriptions are consistent with injuries seen in skeletal remains. Whether its procedures were performed as described is inferred; the text is a manual, and manuals record intention.

The archive files it as documented because the papyrus survives and has been translated.

What is established

Documented: the papyrus and its cases.

Documented: the observational method.

Documented: the anatomy described.

Inferred: the actual practice.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the oldest surgical manual, and it is more careful than most modern summaries admit.

Chinese Gunpowder Weapons

Documented

Gunpowder was formulated in China for medicine and fireworks, and by the Song dynasty it was a weapon.

The development

Gunpowder appears in Chinese texts from the ninth century, first in alchemical and medical contexts, then in weapons: fire arrows, bombs and eventually cannon. Song dynasty sources describe defences against siege using explosive weapons.

The transmission

The technology spread west along trade routes, reaching the Islamic world and Europe by the thirteenth century, where its metallurgy and chemistry developed further. The Chinese origin is documented in texts and in the archaeological remains of bombs.

The archive files it as documented because the sources and the finds agree.

Documented: Song weapons and defences.

Silk Road Glass

Documented

Roman and later glass found along Asian trade routes, showing how far goods travelled and how technology spread.

The evidence

Roman and Mediterranean glass has been found at sites across Asia, from Central Asia to China and Japan, and glass-making techniques spread in the other direction. The finds are documented in excavation reports and in chemical analyses that can identify the source of the raw materials.

What it shows

The glass trade shows that goods moved along routes that carried silk, spices and ideas, and that the traffic was not one-way. Chemical analysis is the key: it can match an object to a production region.

The archive files it as documented because the finds and the analyses are published.

Sweet Potatoes Crossed the Pacific

Documented

A South American crop was being grown in Polynesia before Europeans arrived. Someone crossed the ocean with it.

The evidence

The sweet potato is native to the Americas, and it was cultivated in Polynesia before European contact. The word for it in several Polynesian languages resembles a Quechua term, and a 2020 genetic study found that the Polynesian varieties came from a single introduction from South America.

The route

Polynesian voyagers reaching South America and returning is the leading explanation, and it fits the evidence for Polynesian seafaring. A 2024 study of Polynesian genomes also found an ancient signal consistent with contact with South American peoples.

The archive files it as documented because the crop and the genetics are both evidence.

Because it is pre-Columbian contact proven by a vegetable.

The Giant Squid

Documented

A deep-sea animal known from carcasses and beaks for centuries, filmed alive only in 2004.

The animal

The giant squid, Architeuthis dux, is known from specimens that wash ashore or are caught by trawlers, and from beaks found in sperm whale stomachs. It can reach over ten metres. Its existence has been recorded since the sixteenth century.

The living animal

The species was photographed alive in 2004 and filmed in its habitat in 2012. The difficulty is depth and behaviour: it lives in the deep ocean, avoids light and is rarely encountered. Genetic work has found that the species is remarkably uniform worldwide.

The archive files it as documented because the species is described, sequenced and filmed.

Gorillas

Documented

A great ape described by Western science in 1847, and known to the peoples who lived beside it for far longer.

The description

Western science named the gorilla in 1847 from specimens collected in Gabon, after earlier reports going back to the Carthaginian navigator Hanno. The animal had been known to local peoples throughout, and the name comes from a Greek term for a hairy people.

The problem with 'discovery'

The species was not discovered in 1847; it was described and named for European readers. The archive files it as documented and notes the distinction, because 'discovered' claims are usually about who wrote it down.

Gorillas are now documented in detail, and are endangered.

Documented: the species and its range.

Documented: the 1847 description.

Documented: earlier reports.

Documented: local knowledge throughout.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is where the archive's language has to be careful: described is not discovered.

Pytheas in the Arctic

Documented

A Greek navigator sailed to Britain, described sea ice and a frozen sea, and was disbelieved for centuries.

The voyage

Pytheas of Massalia, around 325 BC, sailed to Britain and beyond, describing the tin trade, the length of the days in the north, and a 'congealed sea' — sea ice. His account survives only in quotations by later writers, some of whom doubted him.

The reception

Strabo called him a liar, and the description of sea ice was one reason. Modern assessment treats the voyage as substantially credible, with the ice description matching Arctic conditions and the latitude reports consistent with northern waters.

The archive files it as documented because the quotations and the plausibility of the account are on the record.

Because it is the case where the traveller was right and the scholars were wrong.

Babylonian Trigonometry

Documented

A clay tablet of Pythagorean triples, interpreted in 2017 as the world's oldest trigonometric table.

The tablet

Plimpton 322, a Babylonian tablet from around 1800 BC, lists sets of numbers that satisfy the Pythagorean relation. It has been studied for decades as a table of triples, possibly for teaching or for solving problems.

The interpretation

A 2017 paper argued that the tablet is a trigonometric table, using ratios rather than angles, which would make it the oldest known. Other historians agree it is a table of triples but are less convinced by the trigonometric reading, noting that the tablet does not use angles.

The archive files it as documented because the tablet is real and the debate is about what it is.

Documented: the tablet and its numbers.

Contested: the trigonometric reading.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real mathematical object whose meaning is still argued by specialists.

Ragnarök and 536 AD

Live debate

A volcanic winter darkened the sun for eighteen months, and Norse legend describes a winter with no summer. The parallel is suggestive.

The event

In 536 the sun dimmed across the northern hemisphere for months, and tree-ring and ice-core records show a series of volcanic eruptions producing a decade of cold. Crops failed, and the period is documented in written sources from Constantinople to China.

The parallel

Norse tradition describes Fimbulwinter, three winters with no summer before Ragnarök, and the imagery is close to what the climate records describe. Whether the myth encodes a memory of 536 is a proposal, not a finding: the texts were written centuries later, and the motif is common.

The archive files it as live debate because both halves are real and the connection is inference.

Where it stands

Documented: the 536 climate event.

Documented: the written sources.

Documented: the Fimbulwinter motif.

Not established: a causal link.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where myth and ice cores describe the same weather, and that is not the same as proof.

The Toba Catastrophe

Live debate

A supereruption in Sumatra and a theory that it nearly ended humanity. The eruption is documented; the bottleneck is contested.

The eruption

Around 74,000 years ago the Toba caldera in Sumatra produced a supereruption, one of the largest known, with ash deposits found across Asia and a global cooling signal in some records.

The bottleneck

The theory holds that the eruption caused a volcanic winter that reduced human populations to a few thousand, producing the genetic bottleneck seen in modern humans. The genetic evidence for a bottleneck is real but its timing and cause are disputed, and archaeological evidence from India and South Africa suggests human populations continued through the period.

The archive files it as live debate: the eruption is documented, the catastrophe for humans is not.

Where it stands

Documented: the eruption and its ash.

Documented: the genetic bottleneck signal.

Contested: the timing and cause.

Contested: the human impact.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real catastrophe attached to an overstated consequence.

Live debate

The achievement

The Hohokam of the Salt and Gila river valleys in Arizona built an extensive canal system, some of it kilometres long, to irrigate fields in the desert. The canals are documented by survey and some are still visible.

By around 1450 the system was abandoned and the settlements dispersed. Proposed causes include drought, flooding that destroyed canals, salinisation of soils, and social disruption. The evidence supports several factors rather than one.

Why We Stood Up

Live debate

Bipedalism is the oldest human trait and the least explained. Several hypotheses compete and none is settled.

The fact

Bipedalism is the earliest distinctive human trait, appearing in the fossil record more than four million years ago, before large brains and stone tools. The anatomy of the pelvis, spine and foot records it clearly.

The hypotheses

Proposals include freeing the hands for carrying and tools, thermoregulation in open savanna, energy efficiency in travel, and provisioning of offspring. Each has support and problems: the earliest bipeds lived in woodland, not open grassland, which weakens the savanna argument.

The archive files it as live debate because the transition is documented and its cause is not.

Documented: the woodland setting.

Contested: the driver.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most familiar fact about us and one of the least explained.

How Animals Sense Magnetism

Live debate

Birds, turtles and bacteria navigate by the Earth's field. The mechanism is still argued.

The behaviour

Many animals respond to magnetic fields: migratory birds orient by them, sea turtles use them to navigate, and magnetotactic bacteria align with them. The behaviour is documented in experiments that manipulate the field.

The mechanism

Two mechanisms are candidates: magnetite crystals that act as tiny compasses, and a light-dependent chemical process involving the cryptochrome protein, which would make the sense depend on the visual system. Evidence supports both in different species, and neither is fully established in birds.

The archive files it as live debate because the phenomenon is documented and the sensor is not.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a sense that exists and cannot yet be fully explained.

Tachyons

Fringe claim

Particles that always travel faster than light. They are mathematically possible and physically absent.

The idea

Tachyons are hypothetical particles with imaginary mass that always travel faster than light. They appear in some solutions of relativity and in string theory, and the term is used for unstable fields in cosmology.

The problems

A tachyon that carries energy and signals would violate causality, allowing effects before causes in some frames. No tachyon has been detected, and the 'tachyon' of string theory is an instability of the vacuum rather than a particle that travels. Searches at colliders have found nothing.

The archive files it as fringe because the mathematical object is real and the particle is not.

Where it stands

Documented: the mathematical solutions.

Not observed: any tachyon.

Problematic: causality.

Different: the string-theory usage.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the particle everyone has heard of and nobody has seen.

Zero-Point Extraction

Fringe claim

The claim that usable energy can be drawn from the quantum vacuum. The vacuum energy is real; the extraction is not.

The physics

Quantum field theory assigns energy to the vacuum, and the Casimir effect — a measurable force between close plates — demonstrates that vacuum fluctuations have physical consequences. The energy density is enormous in theory and inaccessible in practice.

The claim

The claim that machines can extract usable energy from the vacuum has been made repeatedly and has never been demonstrated under test. Thermodynamics constrains it: a device in equilibrium cannot extract net work from the vacuum, and the Casimir force does work only as plates move together.

The archive files it as fringe because the physics is real and the engineering claim is not.

Where it stands

Documented: vacuum energy; the Casimir effect.

Not demonstrated: any extraction device.

Constrained: by thermodynamics.

Tested: and failed, repeatedly.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real phenomenon that has been used to sell machines that do not work.

Superdeterminism

Fringe claim

The proposal that quantum experiments violate Bell's inequalities because the settings were fixed in advance. It saves locality and gives up free choice.

The proposal

Bell's theorem rules out local hidden variables unless one assumes that the experimenter's choice of measurement settings is independent of the hidden variables. Superdeterminism denies that independence: everything, including the settings, is determined from the beginning.

The problems

The position is logically available and defended by serious physicists, notably Gerard 't Hooft. Its problem is that it gives up the statistical independence that makes experiments meaningful, and it has not produced a testable prediction that distinguishes it from standard quantum mechanics. Critics call it unfalsifiable.

The archive files it as fringe because it is a minority position that is hard to test.

Where it stands

Documented: the proposal and its motivation.

Documented: Bell's theorem.

Not testable: as currently formulated.

Costly: it gives up statistical independence.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the most respectable way to keep locality, and the price is the point.

Maya Blue

Documented

A pigment that survived a thousand years of tropical rain, and whose chemistry was only explained in the twentieth century.

The pigment

Maya blue is a vivid pigment used in murals and ceramics from around the eighth century. It resists weathering, acids and biodegradation — unusual for an organic pigment in a tropical climate.

The chemistry

Research in the twentieth century established that the colour comes from indigo molecules trapped inside the channels of palygorskite, a clay mineral. The encapsulation protects the dye, which explains the durability, and modern reproductions have confirmed it.

The archive files it as documented because the pigment and its structure are both established.

What is established

Documented: the pigment and its use.

Documented: its durability.

Documented: the indigo-clay structure.

Documented: modern reproduction.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where ancient craft anticipated a nanomaterial, and the explanation is chemistry.

The Ark in Ethiopia

Fringe claim

A church in Aksum claims to hold the Ark of the Covenant. The claim is a matter of faith, and no examination has been permitted.

The claim

The Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that the Ark of the Covenant is kept in the Chapel of the Tablet at Aksum, and that it was brought there in antiquity. The claim is part of the church's tradition and is defended on theological grounds.

The problems

Only one guardian is permitted to see the object, and no independent examination has been allowed. There is no archaeological or documentary evidence for the transfer, and the biblical Ark's own history ends with the destruction of the First Temple. The claim is not testable as things stand.

The archive files it as fringe, and notes that it is a religious claim rather than a hoax.

Documented: the tradition and its antiquity.

Not examined: the object.

No evidence: for the transfer.

Not testable: under current rules.

The honest label: fringe.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim that could be settled in an afternoon and is protected from being settled.

Debunked

The claim

The claim holds that Jesus survived the crucifixion, travelled east, and lived and died in Kashmir, where a tomb is identified as his. It was popularised by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad in 1894 and repeated in later books.

There is no documentary, archaeological or genetic evidence. The tomb's identification is modern, the route is unsupported by any ancient source, and the historical evidence for the crucifixion and death is early and independent. The claim is not accepted by historians of any tradition.

The Black Sea Deluge

Live debate

A hypothesis that the Black Sea flooded catastrophically when the Mediterranean broke through. The flood is argued; its scale and date are not settled.

The hypothesis

In 1997 two marine geologists proposed that around 7,600 years ago the Mediterranean broke through the Bosphorus and flooded the Black Sea basin, raising its level rapidly and displacing populations. The proposal was linked to flood myths and to the spread of farming.

The evidence

Sediment cores, shell chemistry and shoreline data have been used both for and against. Critics argue the Black Sea was already brackish and the rise was gradual; supporters point to drowned shorelines and abrupt faunal changes. A 2000s review found the evidence inconclusive.

The archive files it as live debate: the water rose, and how fast is the question.

Documented: the rise of the Black Sea.

Contested: its speed and scale.

Because it is a real geological event that has been recruited for a very old story.

In the eighth century BC the Assyrian empire deported populations of the northern kingdom of Israel, and the biblical account describes ten tribes removed and resettled. Their subsequent history is not recorded in any contemporary source.

Groups around the world have been identified as descendants — in Central Asia, Africa, Japan, Britain and the Americas — on the basis of customs, names or scripture. The Gospel of Judas

Documented

A Gnostic gospel in which Judas is asked to betray Jesus. The manuscript is real, and it was published and then conserved.

The text

The Gospel of Judas is a Coptic text from a codex found in Egypt in the 1970s and published in 2006. It presents Judas as acting on Jesus's instruction, which reverses the canonical account, and it belongs to the Gnostic tradition.

The manuscript

The codex was radiocarbon dated to around 280 AD, and its contents were reconstructed from fragments that had deteriorated badly. Its publication was accompanied by conservation work, and its text is now in the scholarly record.

Live debate

The theory

A 2001 study reported that a fault passes beneath the temple of Apollo at Delphi and that hydrocarbon gases including ethylene could rise through it, which would explain the Pythia's trance and the ancient reports of a sweet smell.

Later work has questioned the gas concentrations, the geology of the temple's exact position, and whether ethylene at the levels found would produce the described state. Ancient sources describe vapours, which supports the idea in general; the specific mechanism is not established.

The Amazons

Documented

Greek writers described warrior women. Archaeology has found women buried with weapons on the steppe.

The evidence

Excavations of Scythian and Sarmatian burials on the Eurasian steppe have found women buried with weapons, armour and horse gear, in numbers that imply real female warriors. The finds are documented in burial reports across Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan.

The myth

Greek writers described the Amazons as a nation of warrior women; the archaeological record shows that the reality behind the stories was probably mounted warriors of the steppe, of both sexes. The myth's details — a separate society, the removal of a breast — are literary.

The archive files it as documented because the burials are the evidence.

The fossils are abundant in the region and the resemblance is real. The difficulty is transmission: there is no source describing the interpretation, the griffin's iconography predates the relevant contact in some accounts, and the gold-guarding motif has its own literary history.

WIMPs versus Axions

Live debate

Two candidates for dark matter, decades of experiments, and no detection of either.

The problem

Galaxy rotation, gravitational lensing and cosmic structure all require mass that does not emit light. The candidates include weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) and axions, a light particle proposed to solve a problem in the strong force.

The searches

WIMP detectors have grown from kilograms to tonnes and have produced no confirmed signal; the parameter space has been closed over decades. Axion experiments have also found nothing so far, and the allowed range is being narrowed. Both remain viable.

The archive files it as live debate: the evidence for the mass is documented, the particle is not.

Because it is the largest unexplained mass in the universe and it is being looked for properly.

Live debate

Several distinct ideas go by 'multiverse': eternal inflation producing bubble universes, the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics, and the landscape of string theory. They are not the same claim and have different evidential status.

None is directly testable at present. The strongest criticism is that an untestable multiplication of universes is not science; the strongest defence is that these are consequences of theories that are themselves tested, and that some versions make statistical predictions.
