Model Collapse

Live debate

Training on model output is said to degrade models. The phenomenon is documented in some settings; the generality is argued.

The claim

A 2023 paper argued that training generative models on their own output leads to 'model collapse' — a progressive loss of diversity and fidelity. The effect was demonstrated in text and image models.

The qualifications

Later work found that collapse depends on the ratio of synthetic to real data, and that accumulating real data or retaining original samples prevents it. The phenomenon is documented; the claim that it is inevitable is not.

Where it stands

Documented: the effect in some settings.

Documented: the conditions.

Contested: inevitability.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim about evidence degradation, which is the archive's oldest subject in a new form.

Deepfake Detection

Live debate

Tools to spot synthetic media, and the arms race against them. Detection works sometimes.

The state of detection

Detectors use artefacts, physiological signals and learned features, and benchmark results are documented. Performance drops on new generators, compressed video and adversarial manipulation, which is documented in evaluation studies.

The argument

Some researchers argue detection will always lag; others argue that provenance standards — signed capture — are the more durable answer. Both are documented, and no method is reliable enough to settle a disputed video.

Where it stands

Documented: detector performance.

Documented: degradation on new generators.

Contested: the durable solution.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because the archive's answer to 'is this real' has always been provenance, and that is now a technical standard.

Bite Mark Evidence

Debunked

Dentists testified that a wound matched a suspect's teeth. The science was never validated, and people were convicted.

The practice

Forensic odontologists compared bite marks on skin with dental casts of suspects, and testified to matches in criminal trials from the 1970s. Convictions followed, some in capital cases.

The evidence

The 2009 National Academy of Sciences report found no scientific basis for bite-mark comparison, and subsequent reviews documented wrongful convictions. Skin is elastic, wounds distort, and different dentists disagree. The practice has been abandoned in several jurisdictions.

What is established

Documented: the practice and the convictions.

Documented: the NAS finding.

Not validated: the comparison.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is testimony presented as science, and the archive can show the difference.

The Polygraph

Live debate

A machine that measures stress and is said to detect lies. It measures stress.

The instrument

The polygraph records blood pressure, pulse, respiration and skin conductance while a subject answers questions. It was developed in the 1920s and is used by police and employers in some countries.

The evidence

The 2003 National Academy of Sciences review found that polygraph accuracy is above chance but insufficient for security screening, and that countermeasures are effective. It measures arousal, and arousal has many causes. Most jurisdictions do not admit it as evidence.

Where it stands

Documented: the instrument.

Documented: the NAS review.

Above chance: but not reliable.

Contested: in screening use.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because 'the machine says he lied' is a claim about evidence, and the machine measures sweat.

Hair Comparison

Debunked

FBI examiners testified that hairs 'matched' a suspect. The testimony overstated what the method could do.

The practice

Forensic examiners compared hairs found at crime scenes with samples from suspects, using microscopy, and testified in hundreds of trials that the hairs were consistent with a particular person or excluded others.

The review

A 2015 FBI review of cases with hair testimony found that examiners had overstated the significance of matches in the large majority of cases reviewed, and that errors contributed to convictions. Microscopic hair comparison is now treated as a screening tool at most, with DNA as the identification method.

What is established

Documented: the practice.

Documented: the FBI review.

Overstated: the testimony.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because the finding was that the words used in court were the problem.

Fibre Analysis

Live debate

Fibres transfer between people and places. The transfer is real; the identification is weaker than it sounds.

The method

Fibres recovered from a scene are compared with textiles associated with a suspect, by colour, type and sometimes dye composition. The method is documented and has contributed to convictions.

The limits

Fibre comparison generally identifies a class, not an individual, and common fibres are found everywhere. The strength of the evidence depends on rarity and on the transfer circumstances, which are documented as the crux of the argument.

Where it stands

Documented: transfer and comparison.

Documented: class-level identification.

Contested: the strength in individual cases.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because 'consistent with' and 'came from' are different claims, and the difference is the whole case.

Arson Myths

Debunked

Investigators read patterns in fire damage as proof of arson. Many of the signs were normal fire behaviour.

The myths

For decades, investigators testified that crazed glass, deep charring, 'alligatoring' and multiple origins indicated accelerants and arson. Those indicators were based on experience rather than experiment.

The correction

Full-scale fire experiments in the 1980s and 1990s showed that these patterns occur in ordinary fires. Reviews documented wrongful arson convictions, and several have been overturned. The episode is documented in fire-science literature.

What is established

Documented: the indicators used.

Documented: the experiments.

Not valid: the indicators.

Documented: the wrongful convictions.

The label: debunked.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where experience was mistaken for evidence, and people were convicted on it.

Fingerprint Individuality

Live debate

Fingerprints are unique in practice, and examiners' claims of certainty are a separate matter.

The method

Fingerprint identification compares ridge patterns, and the method has been used for over a century with a strong practical record. Examiners have traditionally testified to identification 'to the exclusion of all others'.

The problems

The uniqueness of fingerprints has never been proven statistically, and error rates in examiner studies are not zero, with documented misidentifications including the 2004 Madrid bombing case. The method is documented as reliable in practice and not as certain as it was once presented.

Where it stands

Documented: the method and its record.

Not proven: statistical uniqueness.

Documented: examiner error.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the strongest forensic method and its weakest claim is about certainty.

Ballistics Matching

Live debate

Marks on bullets and casings are matched to a gun. The marks are real; the certainty is argued.

The method

Firearms examiners compare striations and breech marks on recovered bullets and casings with test firings from a suspect weapon, and testify that they came from the same gun.

The problems

Studies of examiner accuracy have found error rates that are low but not zero, and the 2009 National Academy report criticised the lack of statistical foundations and the practice of testifying to a 'match' without an error rate. The method remains widely used.

Where it stands

Documented: the method.

Documented: examiner studies.

Not established: a statistical foundation.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because 'the gun that fired the bullet' is a strong claim resting on visual comparison.

Bloodstain Pattern Analysis

Live debate

The shapes of bloodstains are used to reconstruct events. The physics is real; the inferences are argued.

The method

Bloodstain pattern analysis uses the size, shape and distribution of stains to infer the events that produced them — impact, cast-off, arterial spatter, transfer. The underlying fluid dynamics is documented.

The problems

The inference from pattern to event involves judgement, and studies have found wide disagreement between analysts and errors in complex cases. The 2009 National Academy report criticised the field's foundations, and research continues on the physics.

Where it stands

Documented: the fluid dynamics.

Contested: the reconstruction.

Documented: analyst disagreement.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because the physics is sound and the story told from it is a separate step.

Voice Identification

Live debate

Recognising a voice is something people do well and can do badly under stress.

The methods

Voice comparison is done by earwitnesses, by phonetic experts and by software. Earwitness identification is documented as unreliable, with studies showing high error rates, particularly across languages and under stress.

The state of the field

Forensic speaker comparison by experts has better performance than earwitnesses, and it is documented as variable and dependent on recording quality. Courts have treated it cautiously, and the field is working on validated methods.

Where it stands

Documented: earwitness error rates.

Documented: expert comparison.

Contested: reliability in court.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because recognising a voice feels reliable and tests badly, which is the archive's recurring theme.

Eyewitness Identification

Documented

The most persuasive evidence in a courtroom and one of the least reliable, as DNA exonerations showed.

The evidence

DNA exonerations of people convicted on eyewitness testimony documented the error rate, and laboratory studies show that stress, cross-race identification and suggestive procedures increase it. Confidence after an identification is a poor guide to accuracy.

The reforms

Double-blind lineups, sequential presentation and recorded confidence statements are documented reforms adopted in some jurisdictions. The research is extensive and the reforms are unevenly applied.

What is established

Documented: the error rate.

Documented: the causes.

Documented: the reforms.

Uneven: the adoption.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the best-evidenced failure of human testimony, and the fix is procedural.

False Confessions

Documented

People confess to crimes they did not commit, and the reasons are documented.

The phenomenon

DNA exonerations have documented cases of people who confessed to serious crimes they did not commit, sometimes with details, and sometimes after hours of interrogation.

The causes

Documented mechanisms include compliance under pressure, internalisation of guilt during long interrogations, minimisation of consequences, and the use of false evidence ploys. Recording of interrogations and limits on techniques are documented reforms.

What is established

Documented: the cases.

Documented: the mechanisms.

Documented: the reforms.

Because a confession feels like the strongest evidence and is sometimes the weakest.

Graphology

Debunked

The claim

Graphology holds that handwriting reveals personality traits, and it has been used in hiring and in some legal contexts. Practitioners describe features such as slant, pressure and spacing as indicators.

Meta-analyses have found validity near zero, no better than chance, and the method is documented as a failed validity claim. Handwriting analysis for document authentication is a different, legitimate practice.

Companies and researchers have proposed using fMRI to detect deception or to determine whether a defendant recognises a stimulus, and the technique has been offered commercially in some countries.

Studies show above-chance but unreliable performance, vulnerability to countermeasures, and a gap between laboratory conditions and real cases. Courts have largely excluded it, and the scientific consensus is documented as negative for forensic use.

The bacteria on a body or a phone may identify a person or a place. The research is early.

Microbial communities on skin, in the gut and on surfaces vary between individuals and change after death, which suggests uses in identifying contacts, estimating time since death, and linking objects to people.

The Gold Standard

Live debate

Money redeemable in gold, praised for discipline and blamed for depression. The history is documented; the lesson is argued.

The system

Under the classical gold standard, currencies were convertible into gold at fixed rates, which limited money creation and linked national price levels. Britain adopted it in 1821 and much of the world followed before 1914.

The record

The documented record includes long-run price stability before 1914 and severe deflation and unemployment in the interwar period, when countries returned to gold at pre-war parities. Whether the discipline was worth the cost is an argument about policy, not a fact.

Where it stands

Documented: the mechanism.

Documented: the interwar experience.

Contested: the net merits.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a monetary claim where the mechanism is certain and the verdict is politics.

Trickle-Down Economics

Live debate

A nickname for supply-side tax cuts, and a claim about who benefits. The evidence is contested and the term is a slogan.

The claim

'Trickle-down' describes the argument that tax cuts for high earners and businesses raise investment and growth, benefiting everyone. It is used more as a label by critics than by advocates, who prefer 'supply-side'.

The evidence

Studies of tax cuts find effects on growth that are small and disputed, and documented increases in inequality after major cuts. The mechanism by which gains would spread is argued rather than demonstrated, and the term itself is a rhetorical device.

Where it stands

Documented: the policies.

Documented: inequality outcomes.

Contested: growth effects.

The Laffer Curve

Live debate

Tax revenue is zero at 0% and at 100%, so somewhere in between it peaks. The shape is argued.

The argument

The Laffer curve holds that tax revenue is zero at a zero rate and at a 100% rate, and rises to a maximum somewhere between. It is used to argue that cutting rates can raise revenue.

The evidence

The endpoints are arithmetic; the position of the peak is empirical and disputed, and most estimates place it well above current rates in developed countries. Claims that specific cuts paid for themselves are documented and mostly not supported.

Where it stands

Documented: the endpoints.

Contested: the peak's position.

Mostly not supported: self-financing cuts.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a curve with two certain points and one contested one, and it is quoted as if all three were known.

The Phillips Curve

Live debate

Inflation and unemployment trade off — until they stopped doing so in the 1970s.

The relationship

A. W. Phillips documented an inverse relationship between wage inflation and unemployment in British data, and the curve became a policy menu: accept more inflation for less unemployment.

The breakdown

In the 1970s, high inflation and high unemployment occurred together, contradicting the simple curve. Expectations-augmented versions survive as a short-run relationship, and the long-run trade-off is documented as absent.

Where it stands

Documented: the historical correlation.

Documented: the 1970s breakdown.

Short-run: still used.

Long-run: no trade-off.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the clearest case of an economic law that stopped working in public.

Quantitative Easing

Documented

Central banks created money to buy assets. The policy is documented; its effects are argued.

The policy

From 2008, central banks bought government and corporate bonds with newly created reserves, expanding their balance sheets by trillions. The operations are documented in central-bank accounts.

The effects

Studies find that QE lowered borrowing costs and supported asset prices; effects on growth and inflation are smaller and disputed, and distributional effects are documented. Claims that it caused hyperinflation are not supported by the record.

Not supported: hyperinflation claims.

Documented

The index

The Economist's Big Mac index compares the local price of a McDonald's burger across countries to illustrate purchasing power parity. It has been published since 1986.

The index is documented and deliberately light-hearted; it ignores transport costs, local taxes, brand positioning and non-traded inputs. Adjustments for local income improve it, and it is a teaching device rather than a trading signal.

Live debate

Paying above the market rate can raise productivity. The theory is documented; the size is argued.

The theory

Efficiency-wage theory holds that paying above market rates can raise productivity by reducing turnover, attracting better applicants, improving morale and making dismissal costly. It explains why firms sometimes do not cut wages in a slump.

The evidence

Field experiments, including a well-known study of fruit pickers, have found productivity gains from wage increases; the size varies and some studies find no effect. The theory is documented and its magnitude is contested.

Documented: the theory.

Contested: the magnitude.

Because it is an economic claim that has been tested in the field, which is rarer than it should be.

Dutch Disease

Documented

A resource boom that hollows out the rest of the economy by raising the currency.

The mechanism

A natural-resource boom brings foreign currency, raises the exchange rate and pulls labour into the booming sector, making other tradable industries less competitive. The pattern was named after Dutch manufacturing after the Netherlands' gas discoveries.

The cases

Cases are documented in the Netherlands, Nigeria, Venezuela and elsewhere, with varying severity depending on institutions and policy. Whether a boom causes the effect depends on how the revenue is managed, which is documented in the literature.

What is established

Documented: the mechanism.

Documented: several cases.

Documented: the policy dependence.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a curse with a mechanism, which is more useful than a curse with a moral.

Sources for this part

  • Wikipedia, “Dutch disease” — the effecten.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Resource curse” — the broader claimen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Exchange rate” — the mechanismen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Natural resource” — the sourceen.wikipedia.org

Comparative Advantage

Documented

The clearest idea in economics, and the one most often misstated.

The theorem

Ricardo showed that two parties gain from trade if each specialises where its opportunity cost is lower, even if one is better at everything. The proof is documented and standard.

The conditions

The gains depend on assumptions — mobility, adjustment costs, distribution — that real economies violate in part. The theorem is documented as true under its assumptions; arguments about trade policy are about the assumptions, not the arithmetic.

What is established

Documented: the theorem.

Documented: its assumptions.

Contested: the policy conclusions.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a proof that is quoted to settle arguments it does not address.

Sources for this part

  • Wikipedia, “Comparative advantage” — the theoremen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “David Ricardo” — the authoren.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “International trade” — the fielden.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Opportunity cost” — the concepten.wikipedia.org

The Kuznets Curve

Live debate

Inequality rises with development and then falls. The data behind it were thin and the pattern is not general.

The claim

Simon Kuznets proposed that inequality rises during early industrialisation and falls later, based on limited data from a few countries. The 'environmental Kuznets curve' applies the same shape to pollution.

The evidence

Later data show no consistent inverted-U across countries; some grow with rising inequality, others with falling. The environmental version holds for some pollutants and not others, and the shapes are documented as case-specific.

Where it stands

Documented: the proposal.

Documented: the thin original data.

Not general: the pattern.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a curve drawn through six points and quoted for seventy years.

  • Wikipedia, “Simon Kuznets” — the economisten.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Environmental Kuznets curve” — the varianten.wikipedia.org

The Easterlin Paradox

Live debate

Richer countries are happier; richer people within them are happier; but growth over time does not raise happiness much.

The paradox

Richard Easterlin found that although richer people report higher wellbeing within a country, average happiness does not rise much as countries get richer over time. The pattern has been replicated and disputed.

The debate

Some studies find a continuing rise in wellbeing with income across countries; others find a plateau after a threshold. The measurement of wellbeing, the time frame and the country sample all matter, and the disagreement is documented.

Where it stands

Documented: the original finding.

Documented: replications and disputes.

Contested: the plateau.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a claim about what money does, and the answer depends on how you ask.

  • Wikipedia, “Happiness economics” — the fielden.wikipedia.org

The Trillion-Dollar Coin

Documented

A legal loophole proposed in 2011 to bypass a debt-ceiling standoff. The proposal is documented; it was never used.

The proposal

During debt-ceiling standoffs, commentators proposed that the Treasury mint a platinum coin of very high face value and deposit it at the Federal Reserve, creating room to spend without new borrowing. The idea rests on a statute allowing platinum commemorative coins with discretionary face value.

The status

The proposal is documented in legal and economic commentary; the Treasury and the Fed indicated they would not use it, and it has never been attempted. Its legality is argued rather than settled.

What is established

Documented: the statute and the proposal.

Documented: the refusal to use it.

Argued: its legality.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a real loophole that a serious argument was had about, and it never happened.

  • Wikipedia, “Trillion dollar coin” — the proposalen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Debt ceiling” — the contexten.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “United States Department of the Treasury” — the actoren.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Seigniorage” — the mechanismen.wikipedia.org

The 2008 Bailouts

Documented

Governments bought stakes in banks and insurers. The scale and the recovery are documented; the verdict is argued.

The interventions

In 2008 the US Treasury's Troubled Asset Relief Program and central-bank facilities injected capital into banks, insurers and carmakers; European governments took stakes in their banks. The amounts, recipients and repayments are documented in official accounts.

The verdict

Most TARP funds were repaid with interest, and the programme is documented as having cost less than initially feared; the wider economic costs of the recession and the fairness of rescuing shareholders and executives are argued. Criminal referrals produced few convictions.

What is established

Documented: the amounts and repayments.

Documented: the recipients.

Contested: the fairness and the necessity.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a case where the numbers are public and the story told about them often is not.

  • Wikipedia, “2008 financial crisis” — the contexten.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Bailout” — the concepten.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Too big to fail” — the argumenten.wikipedia.org

Zimbabwe's Hyperinflation

Documented

A currency destroyed by printing, with documented causes and documented consequences.

The episode

Zimbabwe experienced hyperinflation in the late 2000s, with official inflation reaching astronomical rates and the currency abandoned in favour of foreign exchange in 2009. Banknotes of a hundred trillion dollars were issued.

The causes

The documented causes include monetisation of fiscal deficits, land reform's effect on agricultural output, price controls and loss of confidence. The episode is a standard case in economics textbooks, and the statistics are published.

What is established

Documented: the inflation.

Documented: the causes.

Documented: the currency's abandonment.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the case people cite when they claim inflation is coming, and the details matter.

Sources for this part

  • Wikipedia, “Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe” — the episodeen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Hyperinflation” — the phenomenonen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Seigniorage” — the mechanismen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Currency substitution” — the responseen.wikipedia.org

The Velocity of Money

Live debate

How fast money circulates, and why its apparent collapse puzzled economists.

The concept

Velocity is the ratio of nominal output to the money stock — how many times a unit of money is spent in a period. It is documented in monetary statistics and features in the equation of exchange.

The puzzle

Velocity fell sharply after 2008 in several economies, which simple monetarist predictions did not anticipate. Explanations include excess reserves, changed payment behaviour and measurement problems with broad money, and the interpretation is documented as unsettled.

Where it stands

Documented: the measure.

Documented: the post-2008 fall.

Contested: the explanation.

The honest label: live debate.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is a number that behaved unexpectedly, and the explanations are still being argued.

Sources for this part

  • Wikipedia, “Velocity of money” — the concepten.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Equation of exchange” — the frameworken.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Money supply” — the measureen.wikipedia.org
  • Wikipedia, “Monetarism” — the theoryen.wikipedia.org

Seigniorage

Documented

The profit from issuing money, and the reason governments can fund themselves by printing.

The concept

Seigniorage is the revenue a government obtains from issuing currency — the difference between the face value of money and the cost of producing it, plus the purchasing power gained by creating reserves.

The limits

The mechanism is documented and is how hyperinflations happen: as the public reduces holdings of a depreciating currency, the revenue from printing falls and the temptation to print more rises. The relationship is documented in the hyperinflation literature.

What is established

Documented: the mechanism.

Documented: the inflation dynamic.

Documented: the historical cases.

The label: documented.

Why it is in the archive

Because it is the mechanism behind the inflation claims the archive keeps meeting.

How to use this bibliography

If you want to check a specific sentence, find the dossier it came from and follow the matching link. If a claim in the archive is not backed by one of these sources, it does not belong here — tell me and it will be removed or fixed.

For the creationist and flat-Earth material, the fringe sources are listed on purpose. The right way to assess an argument is to read it as its author wrote it, then read the response, then decide.

Keep the archive open

No ads, no accounts, no tracking, nothing for sale. Hosting, image licensing and the reading behind every dossier are paid out of pocket. If the archive earned its keep, you can put something back.

Nothing is gated behind it — every dossier stays free, unpaywalled and readable offline.
